Tuesday, 24th November, 1936.
The Fourth Session of the Fourth
Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed
to meet 24th November, 1936, in the First
year of the Reign of King Edward VIII,
was opened by the Governor (His Grace
the Duke of Abercorn, K.G., K.P.) in
person.
The House met at Five Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland, M.P.)
in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

Sessional Orders.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one
ne week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on
behalf of his Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The coming year will be rendered
memorable by the Celebrations solemnising the Coronation of King Edward
the Eighth. I am satisfied that in no
part of his Majesty's far flung Empire
will greater loyalty and devotion be
exhibited than here in Northern
Ireland.
I am pleased to learn that the
improvement which has been evident
in our industrial position for some time
past has been well maintained throughout 1936. While last year I observed
that the increase in exports of linen
goods was largley attributable to the
development of Dominion markets, I
am glad this year to note that a further
expansion has been experienced in
foreign markets.
The aggregate tonnage of vessels
launched from our shipyards during
the past twelve months did not reach
the high level attained in 1935, but I
rejoice to learn that, taking that period
as a whole, the volume of employment
has been substantially maintained.
I am gratified that prospects of
further activity in the shipyards are
promising, and that agriculture and the
linen industry are exhibiting signs of
considerable improvement in their
respective spheres. Favourable conditions in our three primary industries
will be reflected in all other undertakings and tend to increase the
purchasing power of the community.
It is also a source of great satisfaction
to me to know that in the near future
the manufacture of aircraft is to be
established in our midst, and I have
every reason to believe that the products
of this new important enterprise will
gain a reputation equally as high as
that enjoyed by other manufactures
of Northern Ireland.
The number of persons registering
at the Employment Exchanges has
fallen by almost five thousand since
the beginning of the year, and it is
encouraging to find that our principal
industries continue to provide employment for increased numbers. On the
average over ten thousand more persons
are being employed in the insured
industries than twelve months ago, and
over twenty-five thousand more than
five years ago. As a result, there are
substantial increases in the contribution income of Unemployment, Health
Insurance, and Pensions Funds respectively.
Two extensions of the Social Services
call for my special mention. The scheme
for including agricultural workers in
Unemployment Insurance, which was
sanctioned last Session, has been inaugurated smoothly with a general measure
of acceptance. The Unemployment
Assistance Scheme contemplated by the
Act of 1934 will be completed during
the currency of this Session by the
enlargement of its scope from the 1st
April next to include all persons
employed in occupations insurable
under the Contributory Pensions
Act.
In order to make further financial
provision to relieve Local Authorities
of the burden left with them until
that date, a Measure will be introduced
continuing for the present financial
year the temporary assistance which
has been afforded to them since 1934
by way of Government grants, and you
will also be invited to consider proposals providing from 1st April next
for the amount of contribution to be
paid by the Local Authorities to the
Unemployment Assistance Fund.
The statutory date fixed for holding
Local Government Elections falls within
the period next year when preparations
will be far advanced in connection with
the Coronation Celebrations. I am
advised that difficulties would inevit-

ably result from the holding of Elections
at such a time, and it is considered
by my Ministers that it would be
fitting that existing members of the

should not have to vacate office on the
eve of bringing them to successful
fruition. A Measure will, therefore, be
laid before you enabling Local Government Elections to be postponed to a
more convenient date subsequent to the
period of the Coronation Celebrations.
You will be invited to consider proposals empowering Local Authorities to
regulate and control the exhibition of
advertisements.
Legislation will be introduced to
amend and consolidate the law regulating conditions of employment in
factories and workshops; to enable blind
persons to receive pensions at a lower
age than at present; to make medical
treatment available for young persons
below the age of sixteen who have
entered employment; and to establish
a voluntary scheme, on a contributory
basis, to provide pensions for persons
of limited means.
Legislation will be submitted for
your consideration amending the Horse
Breeding Act, 1926, and the Measure
which was introduced last Session for
improving the quality of ice-cream sold
in Northern Ireland and for ensuring
that it is manufactured and sold only
under hygienic conditions will be laid
before you during the forthcoming
Session.
It
was found impracticable last
Session to proceed with the Bills
dealing with Miscellaneous Law Reform
and the principles of Arbitration, consequently these matters will be brought
forward for your consideration.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I rejoice to learn that conditions in
regard to law and order are satisfactory,
and I am confident that it will be the
desire of all sections of the community
that this happy state of affairs should
continue.
I commend the steps taken by my
Government in tendering every assistance to the Departments concerned
with National Defence.
I am pleased to observe that the
been
which have
several Measures
passed during the last few years for
the purpose of improving generally the
marketing of agricultural produce and
regulating the prices paid to farmers
are meeting with continued success.
It is to be hoped that Local Authorities will take full opportunity of the
facilities afforded by the Act passed
last year in regard to labourers' cottages.
It is a matter of gratification to me
to know that substantial progress continues to be made in the development
of the tourist traffic industry, which is
year by year increasing in importance,
and that satisfactory results continue to
be achieved by the campaign to stimulate within Northern Ireland
demand for goods produced at home
and in the Empire overseas. The two
voluntary organisations carrying out
these important services are to be congratulated on the success which has
attended their efforts.

Debate on the Address.
Major HALL-THOMPSON (in military uniform): I beg to move:
"That a humble Address be presented to his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth :
Your Grace,
"We His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern
in
Ireland,
Parliament
assembled, beg leave
to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
The enthusiasm, with which we express
our loyal devotion to His Majesty King
Edward VIII and look forward to his
Coronation, is mellowed by the respect
which we feel for the memory of that
faithful King and great English gentleman,
King George V. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We are proud of the fact that
he in person opened our first Parliament,
and that King Edward, as Prince of
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
24 NOVEMBER 1936
Wales, opened these Houses on behalf
of his late Majesty.
I hope that in due course, after visiting
our Overseas Dominions, it may be
possible for His Majesty to open a future
Session of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. He has taken up the reins of
office at a very critical period in the
history of our Empire and the world.
May it be possible for him to follow in
the footsteps of his grandfather, and
become known as Edward the Peacemaker. He has our fervent prayers that
his reign may be happy and glorious, and
that he may long remain the guardian
of liberty, freedom and justice.
It is satisfactory to note that increased
prosperity is reported in linen, shipbuilding, and other local industries. I cannot
help feeling that present-day fashions
will have to change very considerably if
linen is ever to return to anything
On
approaching its former prosperity.
the other hand, the present prospects for
shipbuilding are distinctly bright. I
hope the day is not far distant when we
will see aircraft being launched from The
Island, thus directly and indirectly helping to reduce a still too heavy roll of
unemployed. It only remains for other
manufacturers to realise the advantages
of establishing industries in Northern
Ireland. Skilled labour is more plentiful,
industrial disputes rare, and the geographical position is much safer than in the
South of England.
It is refreshing to know that 25,000
more insured persons are employed in
Northern Ireland to-day than five years
ago, which is reflected in the healthier
condition of the funds of unemployment
and health insurance. Much has been
done, much is being done for the unemployed; more than in any country in the
world, but there yet remains the necessity to take energetic steps to maintain
in physical and mental health those who
are unable to obtain employment. The
trend of international relations at the
present time suggests the necessity of
Britain having an A.1. race, as an
insurace against extremists, be they Red
or Black.
I am proud of the fact that Northern
Ireland is one of the best recruiting areas
in the United Kingdom. It is to me
surprising that any able-bodied man
should hesitate about joining the Army,
where he is well paid, clothed, housed,
fed, educated and made into an A.1.
citizen, proud to claim "Civis Britannicus
sum,
"well able to defend that liberty
and freedom for which our fathers made
such sacrifices.
I hope that when local authorities receive permission to control the exhibition
of advertisements they will show more
energy and expedition in handling this
subject than they have done in townplanning and ribbon development.
I note with much pleasure that the
Speech contains a proposal to introduce a
voluntary contributory pension scheme.
for the lower paid black-coated profession,
who find it harder to live than any other
type of citizen. Up to the present they
have been eligible for very few of the
benefits of our very generous social
services.
I hope the time is not far distant when
it may be possible to extend unemployment insurance to this particular class.
I am sure Members are gratified to
note that success attends the efforts of the
Ulster Tourist Development Association
and the Ulster Industries Development
Association. The Tourist Trophy Race
gives much impetus to tourist development, as also do good roads and good
hotels. As Chairman of the Belfast
Local Employment Committee, I appeal
to my fellow citizens to support home
industries by every means in their power,
and to employ both directly and indirectly Northern Ireland citizens. This
would be a very practical method
to
of helping solve unemployment.
Especially do I make this appeal to the
housewife, be she farmer's wife or
daughter, or city wife or daughter, who
can in this way serve wisely and justly
her day and generation.
Other important subjects referred to in
the Gracious Speech deal with Agriculture and Local Government Administration. My hon. Friend, the Member
for Coleraine, is better qualified to deal
with these subjects, and I therefore leave
them to him.
Mr. CHRISTIE (in morning dress):
I have the honour to second the vote of
thanks so ably proposed by the hon. and
gallant Member for Clifton. We share
with his Grace the Governor the confidence that in no part of His Majesty's
far-flung Empire are greater loyalty and
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Christie]
devotion exhibited than here in Northern
Ireland. The loyalty and devotion
which were unstinted towards our late
Sovereign King George V will be given
in equal measure to his Gracious Majesty
King Edward VIII, and in the coming
year, when the celebrations solemnising
the Coronation take place, Northern Ireland will again demonstrate the great
loyalty and devotion which have long
characterised the Province. (Hon.
Members, Hear hear.)
It is very gratifying that the improvement in our industrial position has been
SO
well maintained throughout 1936,
the increase in the exports of linen to
foreign markets being on the upgrade,
and it is our sincere wish that this expansion may continue, and that at no
distant date the linen industry may
attain to that level of prosperity which
it enjoyed before the slump.
While the aggregate tonnage of vessels
launched from our shipyards during the
last few months did not reach the high
level of 1935, it is very gratifying to
know that, on the whole, the volume of
employment has been substantially maintained. The Government deserve credit
for the outstanding part they took in
securing work for our shipyards by
guaranteeing loans - (hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and, while they have been
criticised in some quarters for their
action in taking the risk, one must remember that the position in the shipyards was very serious, and that the
Government has been justified by the
volume of employment their action
brought to Belfast.
We have in our Province some outstanding shipowners, and I trust that as
they require new tonnage they will do
all they can to keep the work in Northern Ireland. The prospects are promising, not only for the shipyards but
for industry, as a whole, in Northern
Ireland, and it should be the effort of
every resident in the Province to do all
possible to attract other industries. We
have the labour-second to none-and
the sites not only in Belfast, but throughout the Province. Manufacturers can
rest assured that the Government will
give them all the support they can, and
that local authorities will do their part.

It is gratifying that the number of

The extensions of the social services

We welcome the proposed Measure

I do not think that any of us regret

It has been expressed in this House that

The Gracious Speech refers to the conditions with regard to law and order,
and states that they are satisfactory.
With that we agree. Our Province in
regard to law and order is in a very
satisfactory condition, and we share the
confidence expressed that it will be the
desire of all sections of the community
that this happy state of affairs should
continue. We have a police force second
to none-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—–
but the police require the assistance of
the citizens in carrying out their duty in
an efficient manner.
Reference is also made to the steps
taken by the Government in offering
assistance in matters of national defence.
I feel sure that they will continue to do
so, and, if possible, get the departments
concerned to establish bases in Northern
Ireland.
The several Measures which have been

able to devise similar schemes for the

only help the present generation but

Mr. BEATTIE: Before proceeding to
criticise the programme of the Government for the new Session which we are
entering upon, I would like to extend
my congratulations to the Mover and
Seconder of the Address on the able and
clear manner in which they set out their
views. A speech of this kind really purports to present the programme of the
Government to the people. And what
does the future hold out for the people
and their livelihood? There are promises
once again-promises, perhaps, that will
be broken as they have been broken in
the past. I give all the credit I can to
the Minister of Labour regarding the all
important problem of unemployment, but
I must say that owing to the position
we are in to-day no improvement can be
looked forward to. We have had a year
of prosperity in the shipbuilding industry,
but at least one-third of our workers
have failed to find employment although
the tonnage output in the shipbuilding
industry has been the highest for many
years. What is to be the future of that
one-third of industrial workers who have
failed to find employment?
What is the position of the Government? No effort whatever has been made
to endeavour to bring new industries into
the area. That is left to private enterprise, which, as we all know, has failed
in the past. (Hon. Members: No, no.)
Private enterprise has had in Northern
Ireland over 100,000 unemployed, and
private enterprise to-day is continuing
with 70,000 unemployed. Therefore,
the Government, as the representatives
of the people, should take drastic steps
to secure work for those who are out of
employment-work which they are competent to carry out. How can that be
arranged? I am not so stupid as not to
see the progress that science is making in
the world, resulting in the elimination of
the human element in industry. Every
process to speed up industry has been
exploited by the employers, but the
acceptance by the employers of a machine
or machinery means unemployment for a
very large number of workers, to whom
unemployment means a reduced standard
of life for their wives and families.
The Government should come in with
a programme and say that we are fast
approaching the day when we require a
reduction of working hours. There should
be a reasonable number of hours per day,
so that we could absorb into employment
a certain percentage of those who are
outside employment at the moment. We
made a start in 1919 by reducing hours
from 54 to 47. I am satisfied from the
knowledge I have at my command that
if we had held out on that occasion it
would have been less than 47 hours. Some
say if we had held out it would have been
40. In any case, that is what we got-47
hours. The position, so far as the production per head in industry to-day is
concerned, has certainly improved since
1920. I remember previous to the
shorter working week that the output per
man in the Queen's Island was three
tons. Four years ago the return of
tonnage per head was five. I am satisfied
in my own mind that there is a bigger
production each year. In order to stop this
lowering of the standard of workers, and
give an equal share of the labour available
in the community, a reduction of working
hours must take place. That would be
a useful subject for discussion. It would
be an interesting subject for those outside who are depending on the Government to bring relief of some kind to
their doors.
The next thing I find is that the linen
industry has shown a little improvement,
and we are asked by the seconder of the
Address to buy Ulster goods. I would
say to him that he can do a great service
to the workers in the linen industry if
he can spare an hour or two per week

I will be met again by the argument
that the step by step policy cannot be
violated. We have in addition to over
60,000 unemployed men and women
army of 5,000 to 7,000 widows and
orphans who have been denied the right
to participate in the insurance pension
scheme. That was not through any fault
of their own, but because of the position
that the husbands occupied during their
life's work. Some of the 5,000 are
victims of circumstances which prevailed
when their husbands, owing to international causes being reflected in Northern
Ireland, were put out of employment.
They were so long out of employment
that before they could qualify as insured
contributors again death had overtaken
them, and left their widows and orphans
without any assistance from the fund.
Now, I want to say to the Minister of
Labour that if it is possible to get away
from the step-by-step policy with Great
Britain in regard to the insurance qualification, and I think it is, there is nothing
to prevent him from extending the scope
of insurability to other classes outside the
250,000 and bringing in an Ulster assurance scheme to include the 5,000 deserving widows and orphans whom the first
Measure does not cover. The Minister is
not making any efforts to meet the
requirements of these people. That extension of unemployment insurance is a
very necessary Measure in Northern Ireland. I am prepared to make another
suggestion, if he is willing to accept it,
to the effect that there are funds at his
disposal which would enable him to establish another fund for these deserving
widows and orphans. Each year there is
a surplus in the Budget, and portion of
that surplus could be allocated to this
social service.
The Minister of Finance need not stand
aloof any longer.
He has in his control
the regulation of the finances of Northern
Ireland, and if he has £100,000 more this
year than last year as long as he can
justify the expenditure the Imperial Government will not censure him for it. Those
widows and orphans are a responsibility
of the Government, and that responsibility is not due to conditions brought about
by this Government, but by the Great
War; and in so far as the dislocation of
industry in Northern Ireland was due to
the British Government I feel the British
Government are now entitled to meet the
requirements of those widows and orphans
now denied the right to the pension. That
being so, I hope the Mover and Seconder
will spend a few hours with the Government in that connection. It is really a
most deserving matter, and one that
requires to be dealt with very quickly.
I want to ask the Government next if

of one-room dwellers has been reduced to

The Admiralty and the First Lord
may have thought they gave the Prime
Minister a great handshake when they
gave him H.M.S. Penelope. They may
have said they would give him another,
but I want to say to the Prime Minister
that according to the number of ships
that are turned out we are entitled to at
least three ships a year from the Admiralty. We are not receiving that number,
and we never received anything like it.
The Prime Minister may say that our
yards are not adapted to that kind of
shipbuilding, but I challenge any Member of the British House of Commons, no
matter on what side of the House he sits,
to say that a better or more serviceable
ship ever sailed the seas than H.M.S.
Glorious, built during the war by
Harland and Wolff with merchant ship
equipment. There is Penelope, but it is
too short a time after her departure to
say anything of her workmanship, but
in my opinion it equals anything done in
the Government works in England. I
want for the workers of Belfast at least
three Admiralty orders per year, not for
ships of the small cruiser type, but in
view of the nature of our workmanship,
of the heavy cruiser type.
The next thing I want to say is that
the Ice-Cream Bill seems to be a contentious matter with many people outside
this House. The only ice-cream I ever
got was a "slider." (Laughter.) I am
given to understand that if this Measure
is brought forward it is going to dislocate the whole trade in Northern Ireland which is carrying on a very
extensive business in ice-cream. I do not
want it conveyed to the Government that
I am objecting to cleanliness or the
preservation of the public from any
germs or disease in the manufacture of
ice-cream. No, but I would be inclined
to say that if greater supervision was
exercised in connection with the manufacture of ice-cream and the ingredients
used in its composition the selling conditions could remain as they are. I do
not know that it is a good thing to sell
it by weight because ice-cream will certainly lose weight. If you keep a slider
in your hand I think you will soon find
it will decrease until there are only the
two wafers left.
The King's Speech contains nothing
about juveniles. I read that the
problem of juveniles between the ages of
14 and 18 is being tackled in England.
We heard nothing in the Speech about

the raising of the school-leaving age, but
there are plenty of rumours. We will
be told that a Committee is going to be
set up. Many committees have been
established by this House, and after they
have sat for months, perhaps years, we
find still existing the evils they were
established to remove. We have got to

not tackle it in the way it should be
tackled there is absolutely no use in
establishing a Committee to
appease
public opinion in regard to the great evil
confronting Northern Ireland owing to
the number of unemployed juveniles.
We have never in this House heard
the number of juveniles between 14 and
18 who are unemployed. Perhaps the
excuse can be made that juveniles did
not heretofore go to the Labour Exchange until they were 16, but now that
they go at 14 we should know the number
taken into employment each year, and
also the class of employment into which
they are taken. I know juveniles are
being used by the employing classes of
Northern Ireland as a sort of cheap labour
instrument, and then when they become
of an insurable age they are cast out and
become unemployable, because they have
had no experience between the ages of
14 and 18. They are cast on the labour
market to compete with those who have
got the experience enabling them to
carry on the work in a better way.
If the Minister of Labour is sincere in
tackling the question of juvenile employment he will have to drop his Conservative views. He must live up to the
reputation he has got among the working
class. I do not deny him that reputation. He has got the reputation of being
a humanitarian, not a politician. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I hope that
greater things will come out of this
question here than in Great Britain.
Although we have a limited outlet for
our juveniles, I hope that perhaps
through the efforts of the Government in
securing new industries we may be able
to guide those juveniles into channels
which are not likely to be blind alleys.
I believe a great part of the course
should be of an educational character,
and that the remainder should be of a
practical nature to suit the needs of the
individuals. I hope the Minister will
get his Committee together in the spirit
of doing the best they can to solve the
juvenile unemployment problem in Northern Ireland.
I have left this point to the last,
although it is by no means the least
important. In fact it is the most important. We have heard about the
old regulations and the new regulations.
Everyone seems to sit back in his chair,
snug, comfortable and happy, and to say
that everything in the garden is lovely.
We have passed new regulations, we have
eased the situation of the unemployed, and
they should not grouse any longer. It is
an unfortunate fact that everything in
the garden is not lovely. Owing to the
means test the purchasing power of
working class homes is not sufficient to
provide the common decencies of life. I
do not begrudge to the farmers the setting
up of the marketing boards. I believe
that the farmers and producers are
entitled to a fair reward for their labour,
but I do not want the benefits that they
have received to react on the weakest
section of the community.
The prices imposed to-day by the Milk
Board are too high for working class
homes. The result is seen in the increased sales of condensed milk, which
have gone up by 20 per cent. Those
increased sales of condensed milk are to
be attributed entirely to the high prices
asked for liquid milk. Therefore, if the
Government want to give the people of
Ulster pure milk they must reduce the
prices in accordance with the purchasing
power of the people. I am sorry to say
that the workers have had to revert to
condensed milk, because their position
would not warrant their paying the
prices demanded for liquid milk.
Potatoes are the staple food of the
home, but the increase in the price of
potatoes has also reacted on the working
class homes, and particularly on the
homes of the unemployed. There is also
an Egg Board. Every Board that you
have set up for the marketing of commodities has increased the prices. The
Government may have set up those
boards with the best intentions, with the
object of seeing that the goods sent from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain are
equal to the goods imported from any
other part of the world. But the Government have also to consider the consuming
power of the people at home. The local

If the workers of Great Britain are

In England, Scotland and Wales there is

the unemployed in Great Britain.
I want to make this my last comment.
I am pleased to know that the register
of unemployed is down by 5,000.
I am
happy to know that, because of my personal and family connection with shipbuilding and engineering. Is this really
a genuine reduction of 5,000, without
great hardships being inflicted? Great
Britain has reduced her number of unemployed considerably. She has reduced
the number by means of a certain amount
of expenditure, and has graded the areas.
Great Britain has distressed areas where
Government grants are given, and any
worker who is transferred from a distressed
area to another area receives a Government grant for subsistence during the
period he is away from his home. That
enables a worker in England to accept a
transfer without seriously damaging the
standard of life maintained in his home.
In Northern Ireland what are we doing?
We are driving our unemployed workers
across the Channel to accept a lower
district rate of wages than that prevailing
in this area. The lowest amount that a
Belfastman can get lodgings for in any of
the principal centres of England is 25s.
Three men who arrived home last week
told me that for four weeks they had to
sleep on two planks placed across a bath,
and for their board and lodging they had
to pay 25s a week. Those men were paid
£2 15 9d a week. Taking off the deductions and the 25s for board and lodging,
they were in a worse position across the
water than they would have been at home
under the Unemployment Insurance Acts.
or the Unemployment Assistance Scheme.
Mr. ANDREWS: The fact that they
took the work shows the morale of those
men.
Mr. BEATTIE: No, it does not. I
want to compare their position with that
of an Englishman who was transferred
from South Wales to the South of
England. He was paid the district rate
or £2 15s 9d, plus a subsistence allowance
of 12s 6d. Why are we not able to get
our proportion of that allowance? Why
can we not get that subsistence allowance
of 12s 6d for Belfast workers who go
across the Channel to obtain employment
in various districts? Why is this treatment given to England and denied to
Northern Ireland? Because the representatives of the Government here have
failed in their duty to demand that certain portions of this area should be
graded as distressed areas.
Will any
hon.
Member of this House deny that Shrigley
is a distressed area?
Mr. ANDREWS: It is not a distressed
area in the sense in which the term is used
across the Channel.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will any hon. Gentleman deny that Whitehouse is a distressed
area? I am sorry that the hon. and
gallant Member for East Down (Lieut.-
Colonel Gordon) is absent. If the Minister
of Labour looks around him, outside the
city of Belfast, he will find many places
in the same position as the distressed areas
across the water. We are paying our
proportion of that amount, and we are
entitled to receive our share in return.
Before I sit down I wish to express the
hope that the Mover and Seconder of the
Address will use their influence with the
Government to see that we are treated
in accordance with the step-by-step policy.
We are rated equally with Great Britain,
and we are entitled to equal consideration. We do not ask for anything more
or for anything less, but we do demand
even-handed justice.
Debate on the Address
24 NOVEMBER 1936
Debate on the Address
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): In the first instance, I must
add to what has already been said in the
way of tendering hearty congratulations
to the hon. and gallant Member for Clifton
(Major Hall-Thompson) and the hon.
Member for North Derry (Mr. Christie)
for the admirable way in which they have
moved and seconded the Humble Address.
It is, I am sure, a great satisfaction—at
any rate I am glad to know that after
the passing of 16 years so many of the
original Members of this House, including you, Sir, are still with us. I find that
out of the 52 Members who constituted
our Assembly in 1921 there are still 20
in this House. With my Colleagues and
myself they have emerged from a very
trying period of financial difficulties, and
other troubles to which I have no intention of referring to-day, into a period.
which I think is regarded as more rosy
for the future.
It is some satisfaction to think that we
can take credit to ourselves that during
those 16 years the whole of this House
has conducted itself certainly as well as
any other Assembly that I know of, including the Mother of Parliaments and
the Legislatures of the Dominions that I
have had the honour of attending from
time to time. We were a new House,
and we were established under conditions in which a very large number had
no previous Parliamentary experience;
and yet for decorum, for the serious way
in which our problems have been tackled,
and generally for the moderation of
language and the conduct of the affairs
of this country, I am fully justified in
saying that this particular Assembly
stands second to none in the British
Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I may reflect that democracy is still
on its trial in a great many parts of the
world. We see very serious matters in
the Press from day to day, and all of us
who are Members of a democratic
Assembly like this realise that any
attempt to interfere with its freedom,
or with its absolute right to treat
every subject as it comes up in the manner
which both the Government supporters
and the Opposition desire, should be confronted in the clearest and most open
way, in order that our old British system
of democracy may be fully justified. I
think we can also take credit to ourselves
that in those 16 years Members on all sides
of the House have endeavoured to frame

to any substantial extent. That is to the

The Loans Guarantee Acts have such
an important bearing upon the prosperity
of our shipbuilding industry that I
should like to give hon. Members a short

right hon. Friend the Minister of

out that there is no feature of our

effects of the operation of our Loans
Guarantee policy generally, and especially
in relation to our shipbuilding interests.
The House will recall the universal and
acute depression of some three or four

opposite rang the changes on impending.
disaster in Ulster which was sure to

decision to protect at any cost our important shipbuilding interests on which
the welfare of some 50,000 of our Belfast

I am very happy to be able to say to-day
that our optimism has been fully
vindicated.
Of all the guarantees entered into by
the Government in connection with shipbuilding it can be said with assurance
that there is hardly one case which admits
of
any doubt as to the ultimate
ability of the firm concerned to
redeem its obligation to the full 100

followed the policy of the Government. By our action we have ensured

it possible to create and develop

The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.

the Admiralty orders, not only the order

The hon. Member says with regard to

of employment, and therefore it is impossible for anyone to make a comparison
between 1911 and November, 1936. It

we will be able to struggle through, no

Anything that can be done for national
defence or home defence I am here to
support, because I am sure that the
position is not appreciated here or across
the water. When I came from Australia

powers to-day in
Europe, and but for fear of the consequences, and if they thought they would

as they are. My complaint is that such

I know that happened, but it did not

Reference is made in the Gracious

any further housing schemes inaugurated

With regard to ice-cream it, too, is

Debate on Question (24th November),
"That an Humble Address be presented to His Grace, the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as follows:-
"Your Grace,
-
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg
leave to offer our humble thanks to Your
Grace for the speech which Your Grace
has addressed to both Houses of Parliament." (Major Hall-Thompson).
Question again proposed.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I would like,
if I may, to be permitted to join with.
the Prime Minister and the other
speakers in the tribute they paid
to the Mover and Seconder of the
Address in Reply to the King's
Speech It is a difficult job they
had to perform, because they are
so tied up by tradition that they find
it more difficult than ordinary Members
to discuss public questions. If I may
say so, I think the Mover and Seconder
of the Address did their work in a very
fine way.
The King's Speech contains no
sensation. To me it is a very agreeable
Speech, because it is cutting down legislation to the minimum. I might use a
military phrase and say that the Prime
Minister and his Cabinet have reached a
position now that they are able to settle
down and consolidate the ground that
they have won. The Prime Minister gave
an interesting review of the last sixteen
years.
The difficulties with which the
Government and this House have been
confronted during these sixteen years
have been very serious, indeed. I am glad
to think that at last we have got into
quieter times, and that the difficulties
which undoubtedly helped to accentuate
the evils of unemployment are one by one
disappearing.
In the sixteen years that this Parliament has been in operation I think we
have justified our existence. In the first
place, we have established on a firm basis
law and order, without which progress in
all civilised countries is absolutely impossible. We have reorganised the educational services which, next to law and
order, are probably the most important
functions that a State can look after. We
have helped in a very considerable degree
to bring agriculture out of the Slough of
Despond into which it has been allowed
to fall. The agricultural policy of the
Government has been one under which as
much help as the means of the Government will allow has been given to farmers
and those engaged in agriculture; and I
think we can say, taking a broad view
of the whole situation, that there has been
steady progress all round.
In the Gracious Speech we are reminded
that since the beginning of this year the
number of persons registering at the unemployment exchanges has fallen by
almost 5,000; also that, on the average,
over 10,000 more persons are employed in
insured industries than twelve months ago
and over 25,000 more than five years ago.
If that does not point to a steady though
slow improvement I do not know what
does. Unemployment has been one of our
most serious difficulties during the last
sixteen years, and I think we can claim
for this Government and this Parliament
that they have done all that is humanly
possible to help those who were or are unemployed, first, by trying to find work,
and, secondly, by giving help to those who
could not get it. I know there are some
people who talk as if the waving of a wand
would dispose of unemployment.
hon. Friend the Member for Pottinger
dealt with that aspect of the question yesterday. I remember in his first Parliament he assured the House that he had
got a cure for unemployment, and in every
Parliament since then I have been asking
him to produce that cure. I have never
yet heard it. I do not think my hon.
Friend seriously thinks that he has got
a
My
cure for unemployment, because the
party to which he belongs had the opportunity of grappling with this difficult
problem, and to say the very least they
did not make a success of the job.
On
the contrary, during the time they were
in office the number of unemployed increased to one a minute, and towards the
end of their career the number had increased to two a minute, night and day.
The right hon. Gentleman, the Minister
of Labour, has not found himself in that
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
25 NOVEMBER 1936
difficult position yet.
The Member for
Pottinger seems to think that the cure
for all these things is Socialism.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The hon. Member for Dock with a courage that is really
remarkable at this stage of the history
of the world says, "Hear, hear" to that.
I have come to the conclusion that intelligent men all over the world are
dropping Socialism as quickly as they
can. The hon. Member for Pottinger
said that private enterprise had failed.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May I remind
him that at the present time there are
three great nations on the Continent of
Europe all supporting one form of
Socialism or another-Russia, Germany,
and Italy-
Mr. MIDGLEY: Shame!
Sir ROBERT LYNN- -and I ask my
hon. Friend does he think the condition
of affairs in this country is worse than in
any of those three nations? No. Private
enterprise has not failed. Private enterprise has succeeded pretty well, and has
lifted the condition of civilisation and
social service in this country higher
than in any other country in the world.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Let my
hon. Friend look back over the history of
the country during, say, the last hundred
years. Can he seriously get up in this
House and say after that that private
enterprise has failed and that Socialism
would succeed? Where Socialism has
been tried it has been a huge failure.
Mr. MIDGLEY: What about Russia?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: If the hon.
Member for Dock wants any information
on that subject the best thing he can do
is to turn round and ask the hon. Member for Foyle (Mr. McCarroll) who, I
know, can give him some very useful
advice on the subject.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about the Road
Transport Board?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Mr. Speaker
has ruled that I am not allowed to deal
with that subject as it is not in the
King's Speech-
Mr. BEATTIE: That was private
enterprise.
Sir ROBERT LYNN- -and, therefore, I cannot be tempted by the hon.
Member to break Mr. Speaker's ruling.
Mr. BEATTIE: You are a wise man.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I know I am,
and it is because I am a wise man I am
trying to give the hon. Member for
Pottinger wise advice which he sadly
needs. I hope that when he knows more
of what is going on he will discard all
these things. Reference has been made
to the extension of social services.
Representing, as I do, an agricultural
constituency, and having been interested
all my lifetime in agricultural labourers,
I am grateful for the Agricultural Bill
that was passed to give agricultural
labourers the benefit of unemployment
insurance.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is that not Socialism?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: No, far from
it. It shows how little the hon. Gentleman opposite understands his own faith
and the creed he is supposed to represent.
I know the agricultural labourers in my
Division are grateful for what has been
done. Then again there is the Act for
the building of labourers' cottages. An
appeal has been made in the Gracious
Speech to the local authorities to make
the greatest possible use of that Act.
I can say, so far as my constituency is
concerned, that they are already doing
In fact, since the Act received the
Royal Assent the principal rural council
in North Antrim passed a large scheme,
and Members may have noticed in the
Press to-day that a local government
inquiry has been held, and they are proceeding to build about 400 or 500 houses
in Ballymoney rural district. I know the
people there are very anxious to remove
the hovels which are a disgrace to this
Province, and I hope the example the
Ballymoney Council is setting is one
that will be followed by other councils.
So.
In this connection, might I be allowed
to appeal to the Government on behalf
of the smaller towns? I know the
Labourers Act will cover the villages, but
there are small towns like Ballymoney
that are most anxious to improve the
housing conditions of the poorer class of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Lynn]
people. As things stand at present the
amount of the subsidy is not sufficiently
large to enable these councils to undertake big schemes for rebuilding houses.
The Prime Minister said the Minister
of Labour would reply to the debate, and
as the right hon. Gentleman has a close
knowledge of the conditions that exist in
the smaller towns throughout Ulster and
knows their need, I think if he would

I commend this subject to the hearty
and sympathetic consideration of the
Government.
I need not deal with marketing schemes,
as they have already been dealt with by
my hon. Friends who have spoken, but
there is one subject which the Prime
Minister mentioned in his speech in which
I was greatly interested. He announced
that no fewer than 20,000,000 trees have
been planted in Northern Ireland during
the last sixteen years. This happens to
be a subject in which I am deeply interested, and in one of the very first
speeches I made in this House I urged
the reafforestation of all waste land in

I know some people seem to think

greatly impressed the other day by some

In the year

Mr. NIXON: Hard lines.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: He said:

state unless he has a reasonable prospect of being able to support a wife
and family in frugal comfort. I can
see no possibility of the small farmer,
much less the agricultural labourer,

The wages of the agricultural labourers,
he pointed out, were very small, but
small as they were it was impossible for
the farmers to pay them. Our wisest
course is to go on steadily as we have
been doing for the past sixteen years.
We have made considerable progress, and
if we divert either to the left of Socialism
or to the right of Nationalism I am
afraid we would land ourselves in the
bog at the end of the road. The road
that we are on is the road of safety; it
is the road to prosperity; it is the road
that the people of Ulster want to tread,

tread behind the Government.

That is not so. If he looks into the

remained practically stationary.
Mr. GRANT: I did not suggest that
there was an increase in the number of
clubs. My point was that they are a
danger to the community.
Sir DAWSON BATES: That may be
so, but I would remind the hon. Member
that whereas in England it is only
necessary for twenty people to sign a

club, in Northern Ireland they have to
appear before a Resident Magistrate and
show some reason for having a club,
other than the supplying of drink. They
must show that it is necessary, and that
the club can be run without profit from
the sale of drink. Those licences can
be revoked at any time.

I think it is right to say that the
Northern Ireland Government regard the
offence of being drunk in charge of a
motor-car far more seriously than any
other Government does. I do not want
to criticise other places, but in other
countries very often a penalty in the way
of a fine is inflicted. Here, notwithstanding the opposition of certain people
in this House, we succeeded in passing
a Measure which imposed a minimum
penalty for the offence of being drunk
in charge of a motor-car. That penalty
is the suspension of the man's licence
for twelve months. It may under certain
conditions be far more than that.
I want to say publicly that I have
been rather surprised and pained at the
petitions I have received from time to
time on behalf of people who have lost
their licences, asking that I should recommend that the licences should be
restored. As long as I stand here I hope
to enforce that law. I feel very strongly
that I should have the backing of every
Member in this House, and of every
right-thinking man, in stamping out the
terrible offence of being drunk in charge
of a motor-car.
There is another offence in connection
minimum
with which we imposed a
penalty. If anybody drives a car after
he has been deprived by the Court of his
licence he can be sent to jail for one
month. There again I have received
petitions. I would like to ask the House
to back me and back the Government
in trying to stamp out what is one of
the most serious crimes. I believe if that
course is taken we will ultimately have
fewer accidents in Northern Ireland.
The hon. Member has referred to certain
sentences that were imposed. I am sure
that on reflection he will agree that it
would be most improper to criticise any

Majesty's judges.

for war.

country.

we have certain high traditions which I

The capitalist representatives in this

seek Parliamentary assistance, directly

that the fundamental

I will go further. They want to use

using it in order to say this: When the

When the greatest statesmen in a big

Time has vindicated the judgment of

problem could not be solved along those
lines. I mention that because I am
beginning to understand a little bit the
psychology of the hon. Member for North

statement, or when there is any big ceremonial associated with our Parliamentary
life, he has developed the habit of resurrecting a few old thoughts and sentiments, dressing them in new clothes, and
putting them forward in such a way that
he always assumes the offensive.
He is evidently of the military mind
that believes that the best form of defence
is offence. He always takes the offensive,
and in order to cover up the deficiencies
of the Parliament to which he belongs,
in order to cover up his own deficiencies,
in order to cover up the deficiencies of
the social system of which he is the

that the one Assembly in Europe that
has had undiminished sway and dominion
and unchallenged authority. right from
its inception is this Parliament in which
we sit at the present time.
During all that time of undiminished
and unchallenged authority this Parliament has utterly, completely, effectively
and conclusively failed to deal adequately
with the problem of unemployment, and
in order to cloak that fact over the hon.
Member for North Antrim accuses others
of being guilty of deficiencies which are
more apparent here than in any other
part of the world. I merely mention
that in order that the hon. Member for

it a little reflection. Let him come forth

solve the unemployment problem, then it

use instead of private profit.

there are still wages conditions. Wages

less cumbersome.

Mr. MINFORD: I did not intend to
take any part in the debate on the
Amendment proposed by the hon. and
gallant Member, but I know that there
is a number of people in Northern Ireland
who are dissatisfied at their lorries having
been taken away. This House passed a
Measure to acquire the transport services,
and they put in the chair of the Board
created a gentleman who is very competent, but as I say, there are a number
of people who are dissatisfied.
I feel,
however, that this matter could be
settled in far better atmosphere
than in the House of Commons.
It has been the custom to notify these
operators one month beforehand, and they
have got to hand over their lorries or buses
to the Board. The complaint is that they
are not being paid sufficient money to
enable them to begin life again in another
sphere. I fail to see why the Board
could not alter its policy of giving one
month's notice. I suggest to the Minister
of Home Affairs that it would be far
better to give them three months' notice
before taking over. That would enable
the Board to arrive at the compensation
payable to the operators. A month's
notice is quite inadequate in which to
arrive at the amount of compensation,
because no time is afforded for the
operators' accountant and the Board's
accountant to get the figures together and
calculate what the compensation should
be. Then if the Board saw that three
months was too short to get the accounts
gone into they should make the time four
months.
I also suggest that the vehicles ought
not to be taken from the operators and
the operators kept waiting three, or four,
or five months without getting fair
remuneration or a sum of money to enable
them to start in another business. I
quite appreciate that the Board have a
number of difficulties to overcome. It is
certainly true they will certify a sum of
money for physical assets, but the question of compensation for ownership or
profits takes a considerable time. I know
it is a very big undertaking, and I am
quite satisfied the Board are prepared to
do what is fair and just to every operator
in Northern Ireland. I believe that if
the Prime Minister and the Minister of
Home Affairs could get into touch with
the operators these difficulties could be
resolved.
These men have carried on this business
as a means of livelihood for probably ten
or fifteen years, and the owner-drivers are
bound to feel very sore upon this question
of compensation. When the Measure was
before this House in Clause 36 we gave
an undertaking that the servants of the
companies would either get a job or be
compensated to the extent of one year's
salary. What applies to the servants of
the operator I say should apply in a far
greater degree to the owner, because the
owner is a man who is self-employed. He
is unable to take advantage of our social
services, such as unemployment insurance.
Consider the case of a man of middle age,
say 55, who has his living taken from him.
We must not forget that it is difficult
for a man of 55 or 60 years of age to adapt
himself to another position, and from the
time the operators lose their vehicles until
the time compensation is paid, these men
are in the position of having no money
with which to start any other business.
I am not finding fault with the Board.
The difficulty is one of finance. Supposing my vehicles or your vehicles were taken
from us and we had to wait five or six
months, only getting part of our physical
assets in cash, and we went to the bankers
and told them we expected £10,000 or
£15,000, the bankers would not take our
word for it. And so I appeal to the

Minister of Home Affairs to get the Board
to arrive at the compensation to be paid
before taking over the lorries. Then if
the figure is not satisfactory to the

amount of ready cash to enable him to
carry on while the case went before the

In regard to the question of law costs,
while the Board may pay the lawyers'
fees, we have had three cases before the
Arbitration Board, in one of which the
operator, in addition to being involved
in a loss of £500 between the award and
the offer made, had a very heavy bill for
law costs. I appeal to the House from
the human point of view. In Northern
Ireland there are hundreds of these men
with their wives and families, and they
have to wait for months. The crucial
point is that of the owner-driver who has
not got compensation. How is he going
to keep his wife and family if he has his
money all locked in the concern?
Something should be done.
up
The Board is not to blame for all these
difficulties, because many of the operators
are not pressing the Board for settlement,
as they are afraid of where they are
going to stand. I think it should be well
known at the present time that the
operators have established a fund and
are going to carry a case to the High
Court. That should not be allowed
in Northern Ireland, because I believe
that with common-sense and businesslike methods these difficulties could be
overcome. The Board consists of sound
businessmen, who have at heart the
prosperity and welfare of Ulster, and
these gentlemen, with the Chairman, and
having the advice of some Members of
the Cabinet, could obviate, I have no
doubt, such proceedings as an action in
the High Court. All these High Court
actions cost much money.
There is another question. In County
Tyrone, where labour is not so well paid
as in Belfast, an operator may pay his
man 30s a week and the boy helper 15s
a week. The Board brought those wages
up to 40s and 30s, and when these
figures are multiplied by ten the results
are very detrimental to the operator. If
these operators employed men at lower
wages they gave the farming community
cheaper freights. However, I do not
want to occupy the time of the House,
as this is a question which I feel should
not be brought up here when the Bill has
been passed. The differences should be
settled between responsible persons. Some
of these men were the pioneers of transport, and I hope that Members of the
Cabinet will get in touch with the Board
and bring about a peaceful settlement
once for all. I am prepared to help in
every possible way. This Board has
taken upon itself a tremendous responsibility, and it is up to the general public
to give it a fair trial. I believe that the
Board, with the Chairman and members
at the head of it, and with the manager,
will render good service to the people of
Northern Ireland.

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the

teachers who qualified in 1929, 1930,
1931, 1932, 1933, 1934, 1935, 1936, respectively, who have not up to the present obtained permanent teaching
appointments, and whether he will take

obtain permanent appointments within.
a reasonable time.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

although qualified, have not yet obtained
permanent appointments in a a public
elementary school is as follows:-


Nil.

15878


Of these 105 teachers, 65 are at present
in temporary posts.
It will be appreciated that the work
of the schools cannot be efficiently
carried on unless there is a certain
number of persons available to fill the
places of teachers laid aside by illness.
With regard to 1936, 146 students
qualified for employment in the schools.
The Ministry understands that, up to the
end of last month, 19 of these had
obtained permanent posts, whilst 21 were
serving as substitutes.
Under regulations which the Ministry
proposes to lay before Parliament as soon
as possible it is expected that there will
be a substantial increase in the temporary
employment of teachers as substitute for
teachers absent owing to illness.
With regard to the second part of the
Question, I may say that the Ministry
has already reduced the number of
students admitted to the training colleges.
and that this should accelerate the
eventual employment of teachers at present awaiting posts.
The question of the appointment of
teachers is provided for in the Education
Acts of 1923 and 1930. The selection
rests with the education committee and
other local managers, and the Ministry
cannot compel these parties to appoint
any particular person from amongst the
teachers qualified. It is not the intention.
of the Ministry to introduce legislation
which would in this respect alter the
powers of those local managers.

Mr. ROBB: Plans for the erection by
the Down County Regional Education
Committee of the proposed new school at
Dromore, at an estimated cost of £17,120,

were approved by the Ministry in July,
1934, but the work of building was postponed pending the settlement of difficulties which had arisen with the committee's former architect.
In April, 1936, fresh proposals were

considerable increase over the former
estimate. As this cost was considered
high, suggestions were made by the
Ministry to the Regional Education
Committee for the amendment of the
plans with a view to a reduction of the
cost. As a result of the negotiations
which took place with the Regional
Education Committee the estimated cost

November, 1936, gave its approval to the
revised plan and the further action for
the erection of the new school rests with
the Regional Education Committee.
a
The building by the committee of a new
school at Rathfriland (instead of
previous proposal for enlarging an existing school) was projected in 1933. This
scheme also was postponed when the
building activities of the committee were
suspended in 1934.
On the 19th March, 1936, the project
was formally reopened by the committee,
when a plan of the proposed site was
forwarded to the Ministry for approval

March this approval was given.
The matter of accommodation in the

necessary to consider the desirability of

two neighbouring small schools, with a

educational services in this area.
An investigation was carried out by

was sent to the committee on 6th October
inviting their views on the question of
transferring the pupils of Drumdreenagh
school into the new school.
The observations of the committee on

by the Ministry.

asked
the
3. Major McCORMICK
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry

but it would neither be practicable nor

The number of children in a class

age-group; in some classes there may be

In normal circumstances the staff
allotted to a school under the Ministry's
regulations ought not to require classes

should be made for the exceptional cases
in which these numbers have to be exceeded, but the hon. and gallant Member
will appreciate that additions to the
present staffing would involve an increase
in the existing substantial expenditure on
teachers' salaries. It must also be kept
in mind that a reduction in the number
of pupils permissible in a class would
diminish the amount of accommodation
available in our new school buildings and
might involve the local education authorities in increased expenditure under this
head.
The Ministry, however, has the matter
under consideration, and is anxious to do
anything that is possible to keep the size
of the classes within reasonable limits.

THE USE OF RING NETS.
the
5. Major McCORMICK asked
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state the regulation governing the use of
ring nets, and whether he has received
representations from the Portavogie
fishermen and districts of County Down
regarding disabilities from which they
suffer in this respect.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE :
The use of ring nets in herring fishing is
not subject to special regulations in any
On the
part of the United Kingdom.
recommendation of the Northern Ireland
Area Committee of the Herring Industry
Board, on which County Down fishermen
are represented, the Board in May last
issued directions restricting the number
of boats permitted to fish from Northern
Ireland ports from 29th May, 1936, to
11th July, 1936, to a maximum of 45
and prohibiting during the same period
all first sales in Northern Ireland
of fresh herring caught by means
of ring nets. The effect of these directions was to limit the number of boats
landing at Northern Ireland ports to that
representing the locally owned fleet, and
although not restricting the use of ring
nets on the herring grounds to prohibit
the landing of fish caught by such nets in
Northern Ireland ports during the part of
the season when our local fishermen have
no outlet for the disposal of their catches
except the local market for fresh herring.
As regards the second part of the question, I would add that my Ministry was
fully apprised of the views of the County
Down fishermen in reference to this
matter of ring netting, and that the
Ministry gave its support to the recommendation of the Northern Ireland Area
Committee on which the directions, to
which I have referred, were framed. I
would remind the hon. and gallant
Member, however, that, as herring fishing
in Northern Ireland equally with other
parts of the United Kingdom, is now
under the control of the Herring Industry
Board, any proposal for action of a like
nature in any future season would be
primarily a matter for the Northern Ireland Area Committee of that Board.
DEATHS FROM VACCINATION
AND SMALLPOX.
6. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of deaths resulting from vaccination in Northern Ireland since 1922, and
the number of deaths in the same period
from smallpox.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In accordance with
international practice, deaths from
vaccinal causes are included in the
Registrar-General's returns under the
heading "other infections and parasitic
diseases" and are not shown separately.
To ascertain the number of deaths consequent on vaccination would, therefore,
entail an examination of a very large
number of medical certificates of death
over the period referred to, which would
hardly be a practicable undertaking.
There have been no deaths from smallpox.

steps to ensure that this action on the
part of the police will not be repeated,
and that the members will be free from
all intimidation in the exercise of their
elementary rights of citizenship.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to
the first part of the Question is in the
affirmative. The police did, however,
avail themselves of the offer to examine
certain documents relating to the association. The names and addresses of the
persons present were taken.
I regret that I am not in a position to
give the hon. Member the assurance
asked for in the last part of the Question,
but I can assure the hon. Member that
no intimidation of persons exercising
their legitimate rights of citizenship will
take place.
BELFAST WATER COMMISSIONERS'
SPECIAL ACTS.
9. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he informed
the Belfast Water Commissioners that the
Commissioners Special Acts supersede the
Local Officers Superannuation (Ireland)
Act, 1869; whether he will state upon
what authority and in what circumstances
he gave such an opinion; whether he
can state the difference in treatment, if
any, which would follow if retiring allowances, or retirement, were governed by
the Commissioners Special Acts instead
of by the Local Officers Superannuation
(Ireland) Act, 1869; and whether, in
the event of any adverse effect operating
in either case, he will take steps to ensure
that the minute of the Belfast Water
Commissioners guaranteeing that none of
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
its officials would be placed in any worse
position than Corporation Officials covered
by the Local Officers Superannuation
(Ireland) Act, 1869, will be honoured
and carried out.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer
to the first part of the question is in the
negative. I would, however, inform the
hon. Member that the point has recently
been raised as to whether the local Act
of the Water Commissioners overrides the
general Act, and should a case come
before the Ministry in the future which
would not be covered by the local Act the
Ministry will have to give careful consideration to the question as to whether
or not the Superannuation Act of 1869
can be applied to the Water Commissioners. It is impossible to say in general
terms what difference in treatment would
result from the application of the general
Act as compared with the special Act, as
this would entirely depend upon the
individual circumstances of particular
cases.
While the relevant sections of these
two Statutes can, of course, be compared,
it is not possible to say in general terms
whether the one is more favourable than
the other to officers of the Commissioners,
as the awarding and the amount of any
superannuation is entirely within the
discretion of the Commissioners.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I am sure he
will appreciate that this is a matter for
the Water Commissioners themselves in
the first instance, and that he will agree
that the honouring of any minute passed
by them can safely be left in their hands.

A 40-HOUR WEEK.
13. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Labour whether in view of the fact
that other countries have adopted or are
considering the adoption of the fortyhour week in the textile industry, he has
considered the adoption of the fortyhour week in the industry here.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The adoption of a 40-hour
week in the textile and other industries
in Northern Ireland could only be considered if it were adopted generally, not
only throughout the United Kingdom
but also by other competing countries.
The matter is one which cannot be
dealt with satisfactorily except
except by
means of an international convention. It
is at present being considered by the
International Labour Organisation, of
which body the Government of the
United Kingdom is a member.
REDUCTIONS IN OUTDOOR RELIEF
ASSISTANCE.
14. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
authority for the reduction made in the
amount of outdoor relief assistance in the
case of tenants of Corporation houses
when the Belfast Corporation reduced its
house rents.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not the
case that the allowance of outdoor relief
to any person occupying a Corporation
house was reduced because the rent of
the house was reduced.
Some of these persons may have had
their relief reduced for other reasons,
but I am informed that the reduction of
the rent was not taken into account by
the Board of Guardians or other officers
when deciding the amount of relief to
be allowed.
ACTIONS AGAINST TENANTS FOR
RENT ARREARS.
15. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
increased number of actions against
tenants for rent arrears and ejectment
which have been taken under, and since
the coming into operation of, the Summary Jurisdiction Act as compared with
the number of such actions taken within
the same period before the operation of
said Act, and the total amount of the
collective costs imposed as a result of the
former actions compared with that of the
actions last mentioned.
Sir DAWSON BATES: So far as I
have been able to ascertain in the time
available, 1,709 additional summonses
have been issued so far during the
current year, as compared with the same
period in 1935, but only 858 additional
cases actually came before the courts for
hearing.
The increase in the number of
warrants issued in respect of these cases
was only 10.
I regret that the compilation of the
figures asked for as to costs would take
some considerable time, and I am therefore, not in a position to supply them.

application was made at the Inspector-
General's Office on the 19th November,
1936, to broadcast an inquiry as to the
whereabouts of Robert McFetrich, 57
Donaldson Crescent, who was missing
from his home since 17th November;
whether the request was made by his
doctor and other friends; and what
steps, if any, the police have taken, or
are taking, to trace this man; and
whether he can state the objection, if
any, to comply with the request for a

Sir DAWSON BATES: An application was made by the Reverend Mr.
Maxwell on the 19th instant to the
Inspector-General that he should request
the British Broadcasting Corporation to
broadcast inquiries as to the whereabouts
of Mr. Robert McFetrich, who was reported to have been missing from his
home since the 17th instant. Unfortunately the regulations of the British
Broadcasting Corporation relating to the
broadcasting of messages in respect of
missing persons did not permit of the case
being dealt with in this manner, and
Mr. Maxwell was so informed by the
police.
The police, however, circulated immediately to every constable on street
duty, and to the detective department,
a special description of the missing man,
and special inquiries were also instituted
in the Counties of Antrim and Down.
I am satisfied that the police did everything in their power to assist in tracing
the missing person.

endeavour, if he considers that right, to
SO that

they would broadcast when the police.
thought it necessary?

hon. Member will appreciate that I have

Corporation. The regulations I referred
to do not apply to a case where the police
are looking for a criminal or where foul

WHOLESALE AND RETAIL
TAILORING TRADE.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number of
inspections carried out by his Department
of the wholesale and retail tailoring trades
for the past five years, and the number of
prosecutions for non-payment of rates as
fixed by the Trade Board during this
period; whether he has received a resolution from the Retail Tailoring Trade
Board requesting the Government to place
this trade under the Merchandise Marks
Act, or other statute, and, if so, what
action, if any, he has taken to conform to
the unanimous decision of the Trade
Board; and whether he is aware of any
dismissals from employment due to
workers claiming the Trade Board rate
during the five years.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The numbers of inspections.
carried out in the trades in question since
the beginning of 1932 have been 82 and
346 respectively. One firm was prosecuted for paying wages at less than the
minimum rate.
The resolution mentioned by the hon.
Member was received in February, 1929.
Although the administration of the
Merchandise Marks Acts is a reserved
service, the Department invited the promoters of the resolution to submit supporting evidence, but no such evidence
was receievd.
I am not aware of any dismissals of
workers solely for claiming the Trade
Board rate of wages during the period
under review.
