ACCESSION OF KING GEORGE VI.
Address to His Majesty.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move:
-
That an Humble Address be presented to his Majesty as follows:-
Most Gracious Sovereign,
We, your Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
respectfully tender assurance of our
steadfast devotion to the Crown and
Person of your Majesty and to her
Majesty the Queen. The people of
Northern Ireland look forward with
complete confidence to the future, in
the knowledge that your Majesty's constant concern will be the happiness and
prosperity of the United Kingdom and
of the whole Empire, to which Ulster is
proud to belong.
There is no necessity for any of us to
make reference to the circumstances leading up to to-day's proceedings; they are,
in his present Majesty's own words, "unprecedented," but perhaps I may be permitted to interpret the feelings of the
House by saying that the late King, whom
we here knew better and for longer as
Prince of Wales, carries with him into
retirement, our full appreciation of his
services to the Empire and our best wishes
for his happiness in the years that lie
ahead. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I am very proud that our place in the
Empire confers through this Parliament
the privilege of participating in to-day's
happy event. We join the Mother of
Parliaments at Westminster and the legislative assemblies throughout His Majesty's
world-wide Dominions, in complete
unanimity in acclaiming King George
VI on his accession to the Throne. The
dignity with which his Grace the Governor
accompanied by the Duchess of Abercorn,
performed the Proclamation ceremony this
morning causes in us all a feeling of
pride and high appreciation.
It is interesting to reflect that during
the lifetime of those of us who are
between the sixties and seventies, no
fewer than sixteen Monarchs abroad
have lost their Thrones, possibly never
to be recovered, and that we here have
`served under five Sovereigns, our Throne
being unassailable.
Mr. Baldwin, to whom the nation
owes so much-(Hon. Members, Hear,
hear) has carried the country and the
Dominions through a terrible crisis, most
ably supported by Mr. Attlee, the
leader of the Labour Party. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). Both rose to the
occasion with commendable statesmanship
and thus convinced the world of the
solidarity of the British peoples. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. Baldwin, in the British House of
Commons this day last week, said:—
"The Crown in this country through
the centuries has been deprived of
many of its prerogatives, but to-day,
while that is true, it stands for far
more than it ever has done in its
history."
The burden has become a very heavy one,
and it is our duty by increased loyaltyif that be possible-to lighten it in every
way in our power. He will prove a
great King, and an Elizabeth is bound
to be a great Queen-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)—and we must neither overtax them nor "kill them with kindness"
when they visit our shores.
His Gracious Majesty has already
honoured us with his presence as Duke
of York. He has moved among us and
is known to the people; he is a Freeman
of Belfast and of Londonderry, and one
of his last gracious acts as Duke of York
was to join with three other Freemen of
the Maiden City in erecting a memorial
tablet to the memory of the late Sir
Henry Miller, who, as Town Clerk,
administered the Oath in the Guildhall
to him. On that occasion he swore to
be "obedient, profitable, and true to his
Sovereign Lord the King." To-day we
have sworn allegiance to him, who is now
our Sovereign Lord the King. Let us be
profitable to him, each in our own way.
We all know how deeply moved
citizens throughout the Empire must be
165 The King's Accession-
Address to His Majesty 166
17 DECEMBER 1936
at the Accession of our new Monarch.
We here feel the same. We cannot but
be thrilled when there is called to the
highest position in the Empire a man
whom we all trust, and one who has
vindicated the highest opinions of him
held prior to his Accession. I have
already said how delightful it is to the
Ulster people to know that we are in
the privileged position of being able to
support and back up in every way in
our power the actions taken by the other
members of the Great Commonwealth of
Nations. It is a proud position, and
although we may differ, and will continue
to differ, from time to time on matters
of local concern, there are four words in
the Ulster language that
language that everyone
understands and appreciates, and with
them I shall close my few remarks: God
save the King. Long may he reign over
us. I beg to move the resolution standing in my name.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to join
with the Mover of the Motion in the
sentiments that he has expressed. I feel
that as part of the British Empire it is
our privilege to give some sort of comfort
to those who have been called upon to
take up such a high position in the land.
I also feel that we should pay a tribute
of respect to the former King. We have
known him for a period of at least
twenty-five years. We have known him
to be a man of many parts, one who
devoted himself to the interests of the
working classes and one who always gave
time and attention to the requirements
of that class of the community who have
to seek comfort from the governing
power. We regret the passing of the
former King-known to
us
more
popularly as the Prince of Wales-from
the high position he held in the land, but
I think we can find consolation in the
fact that his brother has come into the
position as King George VI. We can
assure King George VI, the Queen, and
members of their family of the same
loyalty, the same affection and the same
support as we have given to the ex-King
in the management of State affairs.
we
We have not, perhaps, just got to know
the present King as intimately as
knew his predecessor, but we find from
his actions throughout life that his
interest in the youth of the country has
been very sincere. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We also find, in the words
of Hollywood people, that he is a good
mixer. He has mixed well with the
people. He has indulged in their recreations, and while Duke of York tried to
improve the lot of the people. I want in
this House to associate myself with the
remarks offered by the Prime Minister
and to say along with him long life and
prosperity to the King and Queen.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. NIXON: I should like to support
the Motion moved by the Prime Minister
and to endorse all that he and the hon.
Member for Pottinger have said. I think
we are all in agreement. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) There is no better
Constitution than the British Constitution,
and the Crown is the head of that Constitution. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think those responsible got over
the difficulty very well, but they were.
greatly assisted by the ex-King. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I am sorry it is
not possible to send a message from this
House to the ex-King in accordance with
what the Prime Minister has said about
him. It would have passed unanimously.
There are people-I do not know if I
should say it, but there are ill-mannered
people-reflecting on the ex-King. I
hope the day is coming when representatives of all loyal churches the great
Presbyterian
Methodist
Church, the
Church and our other churches-will have
a part in the Coronation ceremony as well
as the Archbishop of Canterbury. Such
an alteration could be made and should be
made and is due. We in this part of the
Empire and England-I know something
about the people of England-put the
Crown above everything else, including
the Archbishop of Canterbury, who will
never be allowed to put himself up as
a Pope in this part of His Majesty's
Dominions. God save the King. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Question, "That an Humble Address
be presented to his Majesty as follows:-
"Most Gracious Sovereign,
"We, your Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, respectfully tender assurance of our steadfast devotion to the Crown and Person
of your Majesty and to her Majesty the
Queen. The people of Northern Ireland
look forward with complete confidence to
167 The King's Accession-
Address to His Majesty
HOUSE OF COMMONS

the future, in the knowledge that your
Majesty's constant concern will be the
happiness and prosperity of the United
Kingdom and of the whole Empire, to
which Ulster is proud to belong," put
and agreed to.
Resolved, "That this House do approach
his Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland with the request that he be pleased
to cause the said Address to be presented
to his Majesty."-(The Prime Minister.)
Ordered, That the said Humble
Address and Resolution be presented to
his Grace the Governor by such Members
of this House as are Members of his
Majesty's Privy Council of Northern Ireland.
Adjournment.
Resolved: "That this House do now
adjourn." (Captain Dixon.)
the
Adjourned accordingly at

Three o'clock until

Tuesday, 24th November, 1936) of the
Fourth Parliament of Northern Ireland
in the first year of the Reign of His
Majesty King George the Sixth.

A PROCLAMATION
BY THE GOVERNOR OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
WHEREAS it is provided by section eleven of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as modified by and in
pursuance of certain other enactments, that the Governor
of Northern Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name, summon
the Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS both Houses of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland stand adjourned at this present time:
AND WHEREAS, it having pleased Almighty God to
take to His mercy Our late most Gracious Sovereign Lord
King George of blessed memory, His late Majesty's Most
Honourable Privy Council and others, did meet on Tuesday,
the 21st January, 1936, and did direct that His Royal
Highness Prince Edward Albert Christian George Andrew
Patrick David be proclaimed King by the Style and Title
of Edward the Eighth:
NOW, THEREFORE, I, James Albert Edward,
Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the Most Noble Order of the
Garter, Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of Saint
Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland, in His Majesty's
name, do hereby summon the Parliament of Northern
Ireland to meet on Friday, the 24th January, 1936, to the
intent that such proclamation of His Majesty's accession as
may be signed in the Privy Council of Northern Ireland
may be read to the Members of both Houses of the said
Parliament:
And the Senators and Members of the House of
Commons are hereby required to give their attendance
accordingly.
Given this twenty-second day of January, nineteen
hundred and thirty-six.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN,
Governor.

IN THE

FIRST YEAR OF THE REIGN OF
HIS MAJESTY KING
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Friday, 24th January, 1936.
DEATH OF KING GEORGE V.
It having pleased Almighty God to
take to His Mercy our late Most
Gracious Sovereign Lord King George
of blessed memory, who departed this
life on Monday, the 20th of this instant
January, between the hours of eleven
and twelve of the clock in the evening,
at Sandringham House; and the Most
Honourable Privy Council of Northern
Ireland, and others, having met this
day at Parliament Buildings, Stormont,
and having signed a Proclamation proclaiming His Majesty King Edward the
Eighth as King, it was directed by His
Grace the Governor that the said Proclamation should be read to both Houses
of Parliament.
At Twenty-five minutes after Twelve of
the Clock the House met, pursuant to
Proclamation by His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland, Mr. SPEAKER in
the Chair.
Mr. SPEAKER: His Grace the
Governor commands this Honourable
House to attend him immediately in the
Central Hall.
Mr. SPEAKER, with the House, proceeded to the Central Hall, where
His GRACE THE GOVERNOR said:
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons, My Lords, ladies, and
gentlemen, we are met to-day under the
shadow of a grievous loss, and as a token
EDWARD VIII.
of respect to our late well-beloved King,
His Gracious Majesty George V, I would
ask you now to pause for one brief moment
with me.
The House stood for a short time in
silence.
His GRACE THE GOVERNOR: It
is now my duty to proclaim the Accession
of His Majesty the King.
His Grace then read the Proclamation
as followeth :
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
AND PRIVY COUNCIL OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION.
WHEREAS it hath pleased Almighty
God to call to His Mercy our late
Sovereign Lord King George the Fifth,
of Blessed and Glorious Memory, by whose
Decease the Imperial Crown of Great
Britain, Ireland and all other His late
Majesty's dominions is solely and rightfully come to the High and Mighty Prince
Edward Albert Christian George Andrew
Patrick David;
WE, therefore, the Governor of
Northern Ireland, being here assisted with
these of His late Majesty's Privy Council
with Numbers of other Principal Gentlemen of Quality, with the Lord Mayor
and Citizens of Belfast, do now hereby,
with one Voice and Consent of Tongue
and Heart, publish and proclaim, That
the High and Mighty Prince Edward
Albert Christian George Andrew Patrick
David, is now, by the Death of our late
Sovereign of Happy Memory, become our

Mr. POLLOCK: I am sure that all

"That a Message of Condolence be

25 JANUARY 1936
Death of

King George V.
of his subjects, who never saw His Majesty
in the flesh, will recall and cherish these
beautiful and intimate talks as long as
memory endures, and the future will,
undoubtedly, declare the value of this
family relationship when questions of
Imperial unity arise.
There are moments in the lives of all
men when feelings are so deeply stirred
that it is difficult, if not impossible, to express them in adequate words. Such a
moment has come to us to-day, when,
although removed from the central scene
at Westminster Hall, in spirit and in
thought we bow
bow in reverential awe
before the bier which bears all that is
mortal of a greatly beloved King, who,
during a glorious reign of 25 years,
devoted his whole life to the welfare of
a people whom he loved so dearly.
It is difficult for us to estimate the
character or gravity of the loss which
we have sustained. A few days ago Mr.
Baldwin, who was in a position to know,
delivered a moving address in the British
House. He said that the passing of our
late King was "a staggering blow" to
the Kingdom and Empire. This
thought expresses a deep and fundamental truth, although we have not yet
fully realised how great that blow may
be. We are too near to the stupendous
events of the King's reign to enable us
to appreciate them in their proper
perspective.
But the future historian, when he
comes to relate the story of this exciting
period, will have no difficulty in assessing
it as the most momentous epoch in
British history, whilst the name of our
King will stand out in shining letters on
the page as one of the greatest and,
above all, certainly the best and most
beloved of British monarchs.
During the great tragedy of the war,
when thrones were tumbling and ancient
dynasties overthrown, our good King
stood calm and resolute with a fortitude
that never wavered, secure in the
sacredness of our cause, in the impregnability of our institutions, and the
love and affection of his people.
Many fitting tributes have been paid
to the noble qualities of our dead King,
but there is one feature of His Majesty's
reign which I think should be stressed
more particularly, that is, his close
intimacy with all his subjects at home
and abroad-an intimacy which none of
his predecessors enjoyed. The ether
waves, which carried his voice from time
to time with sympathy and sincerity over
continent and farthest ocean, drew all
the units of the Empire as it were into
one common family relationship. Millions
I am sure that all hon. Members will
agree that nowhere in the Empire is the
loss of the King more deeply felt and
mourned than in this ardently Imperial
Province of Ulster. Throughout the
length and breadth of this Province of
ours the people are mourning not only
the death of a revered King, but also the
death of a dearly-loved friend. Even
now, with hearts both proud and sad,
they are hearing in the deep, musical and
familiar tones the "My dear friends,"
with which the King opened his Christmas
message to his people.
The King's interest in his subjects in
Ulster was always deep and continuous.
It was never more clearly shown than
when in June, 1921, accompanied by our
beloved Queen, he opened the first Parliament of Northern Ireland. Those of us
who were privileged to be present on that
historic occasion will not readily forget
his wise and statesmanlike speech. Then
again we will never forget that he commissioned the Heir to the Throne to open
the stately building in which this House
now meets, and during our whole career
encouraged the members of his family
to pay us their greatly appreciated visits.
And what shall I say about the beloved
Lady, our Queen ? All our hearts go out
to her in the supreme bereavement of her
life. We can only hope and pray that
she will be sustained in her hours of
sorrow by the love and sympathy of all
her people who are devoted to her.
And now, with regard to His Majesty
King Edward VIII, His Majesty is no
stranger to us here in Ulster. As Prince.
of Wales he was a familiar and popular
figure in the imagination of the people of
the Province. When he visited us just
over three years ago he left a deep and
abiding impression in the hearts of the
people by his unassuming manner and his
thoughtful concern for all classes of the
people. Loyalty to the Throne and all
it stands for is in Ulster akin to religious
devotion, and I can assert with assurance,
on behalf of the people of the Province,
that their attachment to the Throne and
King George V.

the future with the same unswerving
devotion as in the past. We earnestly
pray that his reign will be long, peaceful
and happy, and that Almighty God will
sustain him in the grave responsibility
which he has been called upon to bear.
I beg to move.

sympathy. No reign has ever been
That an humble Address be presented fuller of national suffering, triumph,
to his Majesty as follows:-
Most gracious Sovereign,
We, your Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg
leave to convey to your Majesty the
heartfelt sympathy of this House in the
grievous affliction and loss which your
Majesty has sustained by the death of
the late King, your Majesty's father, of
blessed and glorious memory, whose
reign this House will ever remember
with grateful affection;
To offer to your Majesty our loyal
congratulations upon your Majesty's
accession;
To assure your Majesty of our devotion to your Majesty's person, and of
our sure conviction that your Majesty's
reign will, under the favour of Divine
Providence, be distinguished by unswerving efforts to promote the virtue,
prosperity, and contentment of the
realm, and to guard the rights and
liberties of your Majesty's faithful
people.
Mr. BEATTIE: I rise to support the
two Motions which have been moved by
the Acting Prime Minister, but before
doing so I should like to supplement his
remarks in regard to the absence of our
own Prime Minister. I feel that this
period of grief at home will be felt by him
to an even greater extent owing to his
being away.
As we all know, his absence
is due to ill-health, which we cannot
guard against.
The whole world has been profoundly
moved by the death of King George V.
Everywhere the highest tributes are paid
to his character as a man and a ruler. In
every part of the Empire the passing of
the King is mourned with deep grief, and
in all foreign countries there have been
remarkable expressions of sympathy and
sorrow.
and disappointment. No monarch could
have led his people with greater insight
into their varying needs or with steadier
devotion to the largest interests of the
whole Empire. None strove more manfully beneath the burden of war, nor
carried the cause of peace nearer to his
heart. The condition of his people was
his everyday thought.
In his last broadcast message he spoke
again of all the peoples of this realm
and Empire as bound to him and to one
another by the spirit of one great
family, and in that spirit we should overcome our anxieties, remembering the
other members of the family who were
suffering from sickness or from the lack
of work and hope. He continued:-
"May I add very
very simply and
sincerely, that if I may be regarded
as in some true sense the head of this
great and widespread family, sharing
its life and sustained by its affection,
this will be a full reward for the long
and sometimes anxious labours of my
reign of five and twenty years."
To his people of all races, creeds, and
nations the King spoke in person as a
father to his family. It is as a father,
wise, loving, and dutiful, working for
the welfare of his family, that we mourn
him now, and that he will live in our
memories hereafter.
To the Queen Mother the hearts of all
her people go out in this her hour of
sorrow, and we pray that the Great
Protector, who has promised He will not
leave us in our hour of trouble, will
sustain and comfort her.
King Edward VIII is dear to the
hearts of all Ulster people. As a King
the nation and the Empire will be able
to look up to him as one who has a
statesmanlike knowledge and sympathetic
understanding of the wants and interests
of the people of all creeds and races over
Death of
King George V.
25 JANUARY 1936
whom he has been called to reign, and
a worthy successor of the beloved
Sovereign whose loss we now deeply
deplore. May I say in conclusion that,
if the choice of the nation was to be
asked for as to who should occupy that
proud position over the British Empire,
I am quite satisfied our new King would
be the unanimous selection. I beg to
second the Motion proposed by the
Acting Prime Minister.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Among the multitude of messages of condolence which have
been sent this week from the world over
to her Majesty Queen Mary and the
members of the Royal Family have been
messages from President de Valera and
ex-President Cosgrave conveying the deep
sympathy of the people of the Irish Free
State. The Motions just proposed to the
House by the Acting Prime Minister give
expression to the deep sympathy of the
people of this part of Ireland and to their
high hopes and good wishes for King
Edward VIII. One touch of nature
springing from and honourable to our
common humanity makes all men kin.
The Acting Prime Minister has referred
to-day to the visit of late Majesty to
Northern Ireland in 1921. To-day, perhaps, we may be permitted to give a passing thought to some of the words used by
his Majesty on that occasion in opening
this Parliament of Northern Ireland. His
message was, in his own words:
"for all who love Ireland, as I do with
all my heart."
He voiced the hope that that occasion
would be the prelude to the day when the
people of Ireland, in one Parliament or
in two Parliaments as those Parliaments
themselves might decide, would meet together in common love for Ireland upon
the sure foundations of mutual justice and
respect. Then his late Majesty continued:
"I am speaking from a full heart
when I pray that my coming to Ireland
may prove to be the first step towards
the end of strife among her people,
whatever their race or creed. In that
hope I appeal to all Irishmen to pause
to stretch out the hand of forbearance
and reconciliation, and to join in making for the land which they love a new
era of peace, contentment and goodwill."
And his late Majesty then exhorted all his
hearers to do their utmost to make of this
Parliament an instrument for happiness
and good government for all parts of the
community.
Such was the late King's message on
that occasion-a message breathing high
hopes, hopes of peace, and concord, and
tolerance.
He would have you remember
that you were Irishmen. He would have
you be of good-will towards other Irishmen. He would have you treat with
equality every class and creed in your
area. To-day I would not strike a jarring
note. No-not to-day. How you have
reacted to that appeal by his late Majesty,
a clarion call to worthy aims and worthy
endeavours-how you here have reacted
to the spirit and the true intent of that
message it boots not to inquire to-day.
History will pass the verdict. What his
late Majesty did on that occasion he did
from an impelling and compelling sense
of duty. It was well done.
In his wireless broadcast last Christmas,
to which the Acting Prime Minister has
referred, the late King struck what seemed
to some who heard him a wistful and a
poignant note. He was referring to his
anxieties and responsibilities, and he said
with a kind of aside, "God help the
man who fills my Throne." He spoke
like a man who was heavily laden and
very tired. He spoke on that occasion
from his country home in Norfolk,
surrounded by his children and his grandchildren. Men and women of every
nation and every class may recall with
thankfulness that the late King held
very high the ideal of the home, of the
sanctity of the home as the symbol and
power of the home as the symbol and
shield of our civilisation.
This King,
unlike many Kings, was a very human,
a very humble, and a very home-loving
King. Claims to respect closed in him
as a son, as a husband, as a father, as
a constitutional King, never deviating by
one hairbreadth from the constitutional
path, even when urged during the Home
Rule struggle by influences high in society
and mighty in politics to step beyond it.
To the English people as the years went
on he became more and more the pater
patria-the father of his country. For
the Irish people men say, and believe the
truth to be, that he never had anything
but generous thoughts and never wished

SALARIES OF MEMBERS OF
GOVERNMENT, CIVIL SERVANTS,
ETC.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state
how many persons hold offices in Northern Ireland (a) with salaries and emoluments of £800 a year to £1,500 a year
charged on the Consolidated Fund of
Great Britain or Northern Ireland, or
met by Parliamentary grants; and (b)
with salaries and emoluments of £1,500
a year and upwards so charged or met,
and the aggregate salaries and emoluments of each class in the financial year
1935-1936.
Mr. POLLOCK: The number of persons holding offices in Northern Ireland
with salaries and emoluments of £800
a year to £1,500 a year charged on the
Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland
or met by grants made by the Parliament of Northern Ireland is 117; and
the estimated aggregate salaries and
emoluments of these persons for the
financial year 1935-36 is £115,109.
The number of persons with salaries
and emoluments of £1,500 a year and
upwards similarly charged or met is 22;
and the aggregate salaries and emoluments is £39,883.
The hon. and learned Member will of
course appreciate that included in the
foregoing statement are Members of the
Government, officials of Parliament,
civil servants, officers of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary, and legal and other
professional advisers of the Government.
I have not included in the figures
those judges or clerks of the Crown and
Peace
in
Northern Ireland whose
salaries are paid from the Consolidated
Fund of the United Kingdom or civil
servants in reserved departments operating in Northern Ireland, whose salaries
are borne upon Imperial Votes, as any
question in regard to those should
obviously be put in the Parliament at
Westminster.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government (Finance) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In 1929 I had the
honour of introducing to this House the
Derating Bill, which I described at that
time as an epoch-making event. The
effect of that Measure during the past
six years has not made me change my
opinion. It has been a costly one to the
Government, the sum paid out by way
of derating grants to local authorities
during the past six years being no less
than £7,201,015, but I am sure that
hon. Members will agree with me that
this expenditure has been well justified,
and that we have no reason whatever to
regret the introduction of the derating
system. It has proved a great help to
businesses in Northern Ireland when they
were passing through a difficult and
critical period and gave many of them
a new lease of life. Its benefits have,
of course, been particularly felt by our
staple industry, agriculture, and I think
I can say without fear of contradiction
that, without derating, our farmers
would be in a very much worse position
than they are in to-day.
In this connection I wish to make one
point perfectly clear with regard to this
second Derating Bill, which I have now
the honour of introducing, and that is
that it is not the object of the Bill to
save money on the derating grants. In
view of the unfair and inaccurate statements that have been made by certain
individuals, I feel it necessary to emphasise that no sinister intentions whatever of this or any other kind are
concealed behind the Clauses of the Bill,
and that it is not intended in any way
to prejudice local authorities financially
or to place them in any difficulties in
financing the services they administer. On
the contrary, I may say that the general
effect of the Bill is towards the simplification of the derating system.
As hon. Members are aware, the
system of derating that is now in force
in Northern Ireland is somewhat
different from that operating in Great
Britain. It is, incidentally, a considerably more generous one to the local
authorities, but the point I wish to bring
under hon. Members' attention is that it
is entirely our own system; that it is
necessarily a somewhat complicated one,
and that, accordingly, the operations of
the past six years were somewhat in the
nature of an experiment, in so far as
administrative machinery is concerned. I
am pleased to be able to say that the
administrative procedure that was
adopted has proved, on the whole, suitable and adequate, but, as was only to be
expected, time has proved that in certain
details it gave rise to avoidable difficulty
and complication. This Bill now deals
with these details and substitutes alternative arrangements which I am confident
will be appreciated by all those concerned
in the administration of the Bill when
they come into operation. Apart from
these, perhaps I may say technical,
details the Bill contains two main provisions.
The first of these main provisions meets
a situation that has arisen as a consequence of revaluation. Hon. Members
are aware that as a result of revaluation
the net annual value of buildings has
very substantially increased throughout
the Province. Buildings, of course, are,
roughly speaking, the underated hereditaments, so that the effect of revaluation
would have been that the hereditaments
in respect of which the Government do
not pay rates would be liable for a
greater proportion of local expenditure
than formerly, while, conversely, those in
respect of which the Government do pay
rates would be liable for a smaller proportion than they were in the past. It
would, of course, appear prima facie that
this would only mean that in the past
the Government have been paying a
greater share of local rates than they
were properly entitled to pay, so that
with the adjustment that has been made.
149 Local Government Bill-

18 FEBRUARY 1936
Second Reading
in the valuation they are only being
placed now in the position in which they
should always have been. But this is
not, perhaps, quite a fair view of the
situation, and after hearing the representations of local authorities the Government reached the conclusion that it would
be fair and equitable that part of this
saving in grants which revaluation would
give it should be handed back to local
authorities. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
It has been a matter of very great difficult to determine exactly what proportion should be handed back in this way,
but I am glad to be able to say that the
attitude of local authorities in this, as
in the other matters arising out of the
preparation of the Bill, has been most
helpful. The local authorities appreciated the Goverment's difficulties just as
the Government appreciated theirs, and it
has been possible to reach agreement on
the matter. With this agreement I
think I may say local authorities are
entirely satisfied, and Clause 5 and the
Schedule to the Bill give effect to this
agreement. I do not think I need take
up the time of the House on this point
further than to say that the main effect
of the agreement is that 80 per cent. of
the saving I have referred to is to be
handed back to the rural authorities who,
in turn, will hand on an agreed proportion of this to the urban authorities.
The second main principle of the Bill
concerns the payment of the derating
deficiency contributions which, as hon.
Members are aware, are, in the words of
the 1929 Act, grants paid to local
authorities
"Towards making good the losses
occurring by reason of the provision of
the Act."
These grants are paid in two separate
and distinct ways. One of them applies
to rural authorities, who receive about
nine-tenths of the total derating grants,
and the other to the urban authorities.
In the case of the rural authorities I
would remind the House that the grants
consist of standard grants and supplemental grants, the standard grant being
based on what I might call normal expenditure, and the supplemental grant
being intended to cover expenditure
above normal expenditure. The standard
grant under the existing arrangement is subject to revision every
five years, but the supplemental grant
is an annual one, being fixed every year
on the basis of estimates submitted by
local authorities and is limited to the
amount of a 6d rate on the full net
annual value of the county. In the case
of both standard and supplemental
grants the 1929 Act provides that the
grants are, in effect, in the first instance
only made provisionally, and that final
adjustments will be made after the
accounts of the local authorities are
audited. It can then be determined
that the estimates, on the basis of which
grants were calculated, have, in fact,
proved accurate.
It will be obvious to hon. Members who
take an interest in local affairs that this
arrangement has, as regards standard
grant, given rise to very considerable
difficulties both from the point of view of
the Government and of the local authorities. The standard grant being fixed
with the intention of covering normal
expenditure, taking one year with
another over a period of five years, it
has been agreed that it would obviously
be unfair to make reductions in the
amount of standard grant in any case
where the estimates were not realised in
any one particular year, and accordingly
it has been necessary to adopt the
practice of deferring comparisons of
actual and estimated expenditure for the
purpose of standard grants until after
It will
the expiration of five years.
easily be appreciated that this has led to
considerable difficulties, both from the
point of view of local authorities and of
the Government, and that if the arrangement were continued as time went on
these difficulties would become greater,
and we would find ourselves in a very
difficult position in trying to straighten
things out.
The Bill, therefore, in order to meet
this provides that in future standard
grants shall be fixed at a permanent
figure, and shall not be subject to any
reduction on account of under-spending
on the part of local authorities. It will
be seen, therefore, that in any year in
which there is a saving on the local
authorities' estimates they will be in a
position to build up a credit balance to
meet any possible over-spendings in
other years.
Both the local authorities
and the Government will, therefore,

With regard to the supplemental grant,
the Bill continues this on the same lines
as heretofore. The increased valuations
of course, necessitated a revision of the
original limit of the amount of a sixpenny rate.
Hon. Members will see that the limit
now proposed in the Bill is 5d., which
represents a very generous adjustment
to meet the new valuations, but since
the printing of the Bill-and after all
no Bill is perfect, as hon. Members have
occasionally reminded me a question
has been raised by the Rural District
Councils' Association regarding the effect
that the Bill might have on any new
services which may be commenced in the
future and which were not in existence
at the fixing of the standards. They
have referred in particular to operations
under the Labourers Acts, which, as hon.
Members are aware, have been suspended
for some years past but are now about to
be resumed. Reference has also been
made to district hospitals, new schemes
for which it is possible may be undertaken by Unions which have not
present a district hospital.
at
The Government have given the most
careful and sympathetic consideration to
these representations and have reached
the conclusion that the most suitable way
of dealing with the matter is to increase
the limit for supplemental grant.
Accordingly, an Amendment will be
introduced at a later stage raising the
5d. limit now in the Bill to 6d. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I feel confident that it will be agreed
that this is an ample margin to provide
for all new services of any kind that can
be visualised as being undertaken in the
future. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Before I leave the question of these
grants to the rural authorities I would
just like to say a word with regard to
the grants to education authorities. It
will be remembered that when the 1929
Derating Act was introduced the educational services were in their infancy, and,
accordingly, no limit was made for the
payment of supplemental grants. That
Act, in fact, left the position as regards
the education authorities more or less in
the air, no provision being made for any
revision of the standard grant either upwards or downwards at the conclusion of
the first five-year period. Since that
time the expenditure by education.
Committees has become very much more
settled, and accordingly the time seems
appropriate for placing education
authorities on the same footing as other
local authorities of a similar kind. As
hon. Members will see sub-Clause 5 of
Clause 4 of the Bill proposes to do this,
the limit for supplemental grants in their
case being 3d. in the £ on the full net
annual valuation of the area. I am sure
that hon. Members on both sides of the
House will agree that this is a very
generous limit.
With regard to urban local authorities,
the system adopted by the 1929 Act was
that in each case the local authority
should be recouped the actual loss of
revenue sustained by them. Hon. Members may remember that the first Committee appointed to consider the
machinery necessary for derating recommended an identical system, that is to
say, standard and supplemental grants,
for both urban and rural authorities.
The second Committee, however,
suggested that a system of paying off the
actual loss would be more suitable and
convenient for the urban authorities, and
this recommendation was adopted in the
1929 Act. Experience has justified its
adoption, and this Bill accordingly continues the procedure at present in force
for paying the deficiency contribution in
the urban areas, the only change being
the institution of a maximum limit for
such payments. The limit that is proposed is a very generous one, being in
the case of each local authority the
highest sum which has been paid to that
local authority in respect of any year
since derating came into operation.
It may not, perhaps, be immediately
obvious that this arrangement affords the
urban authorities a very generous margin
for increased expenditure, but that this is
so will be realised at once from a glance
at the valuation figures. These figures
show very clearly that in the urban districts the valuations of derated premises
153 Local Government Bill

Housing Grants
have not increased to anything like the
same extent as the valuations of other
hereditaments, for example, shops and
dwelling houses, so that the proportions
of the valuations derated in the towns
are, under the new valuations, very much
lower than they used to be. This means
that a given sum paid as the deficiency
contribution to an urban authority will,
in the future, cover very much higher
expenditure than it did in the past, so
that it will be possible for urban
authorities, without approaching the
maximum limit which the Bill provides,
to increase their expenditure by a very
substantial percentage. For example,
the limit allows the Corporation of
Belfast a margin of £400,000 for
increased expenditure, and I think
hon. Members will agree, when they
appreciate the rise in the rate that
increased expenditure of this amount
would involve, that the margin is an
ample one to meet all reasonable requirements for the future. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
In the preparation of this Bill my
Ministry has kept very closely in touch
with the local authorities throughout the
Province, and it gives me very great
pleasure to take this opportunity of
acknowledging the great assistance and
co-operation we have had from the local
bodies in dealing with this somewhat
complicated matter. Differences of
opinion, as is inevitable, have arisen from
time to time, but I am glad to say that
with goodwill on both sides these have
been met, and it may be taken now that
the Bill in its present form is acceptable
to the rural local authorities and to all
the urban local authorities, except,
possibly, the Belfast Corporation.
regret that we have not been able to
reach complete agreement with the Corporation. The point on which we have
differed is, in my opinion, of very little
practical importance from the point of
view of the Corporation, and I am not
without hope that they may, perhaps,
yet come round to look at the matter
as we do.

As I have said, the other sections of
the Bill deal with technical points which
have arisen in the administration of the
Derating Act. They are, in general,
matters of detail, and I do not think I
need weary the House attempting to
explain them.
I might, however, mention just one
other Clause, that is, No. 13, which deals
with lighting charges. Hon. Members
will recollect that the 1929 Act abolished
small areas of charge for works dealing
with the construction or maintenance of
sewers or the providing of a water
supply. It has been found that apart
from these matters practically the only
separate charge that is at all general
throughout the Province is the separate
charge to cover lighting schemes. The
retention of this separate charge involves
a very considerable amount of work in
the offices of local authorities and of my
Ministry, and the Government feel that,
while the extension of the area for these
charges to the entire rural district would
involve a larger charge on Government
funds, the advantages to be derived from
such an arrangement would amply
justify it, and the Bill accordingly makes
that provision. It is one that I feel sure
will be very greatly appreciated by those
concerned in the administration
derating.

Mr. BARBOUR: My right hon.
Friend in his Second Reading speech
made known the Government's policy in
relation to the continuation of the
housing subsidy when he expressed the
view that we were within sight of the
housing shortage being met, and that it
was, therefore, only necessary to extend
the scheme for another six months. Since
that statement was made the Government
have decided upon an Amendment, which
appears upon the Order Paper, and this
has necessitated an extension of the wording of the Financial Resolution from that
which first appeared upon the Order
Paper.
I should, therefore, explain that the
original intention was simply to extend
the subsidy for a further period of six
months, until the 30th September, 1936.
It was found, however, that in the case
of one urban authority, which intended to
erect a number of subsidy houses as part
of its slum clearance scheme, sites for the
new houses would not be ready in time
for the houses to be completed by the
30th September, 1936, as the sites had
to be cleared by the demolition of old
houses. Additional delay was anticipated by reason of the fact that some of
the houses to be demolished were
occupied and arrangements had to be
made for new accommodation for their
occupants. In order not to deprive this
and other urban authorities which might
be similarly circumstanced of the benefit
of the application of the subsidy for a
further limited period to slum clearance
of this kind, it has been decided to extend until the 31st March, 1937, that is,
for a period of one year, the period for
the completion of houses falling within
this category, and the subsidy will be
payable only on condition that the sites
have to be cleared after January 1st,
1936, by the demolition of old houses,
and that the contract for the erection of
new houses is completed between the 1st
January, 1936, and the 1st October, 1936.
The actual financial effect of the proposal in the Bill to extend the scheme for
six months in the case of ordinary subsidy
houses and twelve months in the special
case to which I have alluded, is estimated
to involve total grants amounting to
approximately £65,000, being in respect
of 2,600 houses.
In conclusion, I shall, perhaps, be permitted to give the House some figures to
show the financial burden which has been
placed upon our Exchequer in achieving
what has been achieved for the housing
of the working classes. No less a sum
than £2,232,580 has been paid in the
form of subsidies under the Housing Acts,
1923-1933, during the period up to the
31st ultimo. The total number of houses
built with the assistance of subsidies
between 1919 and the present date is
no less than 31,989. As hon. Members
are aware, the method of financing this
activity has been for issues to be made
from the Government's Loan Fund, this
Fund being recouped over a number of
years by means of terminable annuities
included annually in the Vote for grants
to local authorities. The estimated
amount required to be paid in respect of
these annuities in the current year is
£176,308 and hon. Members will
appreciate that provision will have to be
made over a number of years on this scale
before the State is clear of this liability.
The Finance Minister must, therefore,
welcome the cessation in the growth of

this heavy expenditure, involving the
stabilisation of the annuity at a figure
not appreciably in excess of £180,000.
I beg to move.

Mr. HENDERSON: Since the Government introduced this Bill for the construction of houses for the working classes
there have been complaints all over the
country as to the manner in which the
Government are allowing this money to be
given away without regard to how the
houses are being built. Representing the
working-class community of Northern
Ireland, I want to complain very bitterly
of the use of foreign material of every
description in the construction of these
houses. The Minister who introduced
this Bill apparently does not realise the
gravity of the situation at all. The fact
is that grants are being given by the
Government themselves, and by the local
authorities with the consent of the
Government, to persons who are building
houses throughout the length and breadth
of this country, and that those houses
have nothing but stud walls. I call it a
conglomeration of pasteboard.

[Mr. Henderson]
The houses of even a hundred years
ago were built of laths and plaster, but
the houses built under this subsidy
scheme are practically of this class of
wood and plaster. Throughout Belfast
there have been fires and unless the
Government take drastic action I am
afraid that the right hon. Gentleman may
be held responsible for any lives that may
be lost. When fire gets a grip on some
of these houses no fire brigade on earth
could put it out. I think the Government are guilty of neglect in this matter.
The Government should see, as far
as is humanly possible, that these
houses are constructed of laths and
plaster. It is
is absolutely impossible
to repair this pasteboard. I believe
that these houses will be nothing
more or less than the slums of the future.
This is a matter of interest to the Prime
Minister, who, I hope and trust, is in
good health again. The unfortunate
thing about this is that the specification
for these houses is all wrong. There are
many things put into these houses that
should not be put into them. In a great
many cases the jerrybuilders who are constructing these houses, instead of trying
to make them habitable and comfortable,
are doing away with the use of tiles or
flags. They are abolishing tiles and
cementing the kitchen. Anyone who
knows anything about the construction
of houses will realise that it is absolutely
impossible for any person to put down a
little bit of linoleum or oilcloth or carpet
on that floor. And yet, when the representatives of the municipalities raise this
matter they are told that under Government regulation they have no power to
compel them to put in tiles.
Another vital matter I want to
draw attention to is the burden being
placed on the people who are supposed to
benefit by this Government grant. It is

the brickmakers to put up the price about
25 per cent. That should not have been.
Immediately the Government contemplated extending this housing subsidy till
September they should have seen that a
Clause was inserted whereby the cost of
pipes and bricks and timber for this class
of house should have been fixed. It
means that the £50 that was supposed to

introduce an amending Clause whereby
the
persons constructing these houses
should be compelled to use nothing only
Ulster material and that would comply

"Buy Ulster Goods."

want to say this, now that certain slighting references have been made inside the

Then I noticed the type of brick now

thing I found was the very high percentage of unseasoned timber, which is
disastrous from the house point of view.
The moment the timber begins to dry
you will find the ceiling moving, the

landings moving, and everything becomes

I would like to see Magheramorne

That is a résumé of what I found in my

better to move a step further than the
£25 to provide proper material and proper workmanship than to skimp it by

evils to enter in.
I was told by a builder that the reason

would go to prove that the house we are
getting is not a proper house, and it is

Another matter referred to on a number of occasions when this subject has

Oral Answers to Questions.
GOVERNMENT LOAN TO ULSTER
FARMERS' PRODUCE SOCIETY.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Prime
Minister whether he has personally considered the views expressed by the Public
Accounts Committee, in their Interim
Report on the accounts for 1933-34, with
reference to the Government loan to the
Ulster Farmers' Produce Society; whether
the present arrangement under which
the Society recoup the guarantors for
payments made by them to the Governmeets with his approval; and
whether he will insist that if the Society
can make such recoupments they will
take steps to reduce their own debt to
the Exchequer.
ment
The PRIME MINISTER: I should
like to preface my reply by stating that
I invariably study the Reports of the
Committee of Public Accounts with particular care because I recognise that it
is carrying out on behalf of this House
a duty of great public importance; and
during the past 14 years has performed
it with a zeal for which all Members on
both sides of this House must feel grateful.
I have considered their views on the
special transaction now mentioned and,
with regard to the arrangement under
which the Society recoups the guarantors
for payments made by them to the Government, I would like to explain that, as
matters developed after the passing of
the Government Loans Act, 1931, it was
realised that action by the Government
to prevent the guarantors from exercising their undoubted legal right of
recourse to the Society's funds would
have seriously impaired the usefulness
of the Society and in all probability
threatened its existence. Any priority
which the Government might possess
over the guarantors arose from the
mortgage and bill of sale on the Society's
assets, and these were not considered of
sufficient value to the Ministry on a possible liquidation to be worth holding in
perpetuity. For this reason and also in
order to assist the Society in raising
money from time to time on overdraft
they were released in June, 1932, thus
leaving the guarantors and the Ministry
on equal terms. The policy of the Government has always been one of enabling
Oral Answers
Supplementary Estimates
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
the Society to continue in operation,
and, accordingly, the Government determined that it would not challenge the
arrangements in question under which
the Society makes good any loss incurred
by the guarantors.
If, however, the Society, after meeting
its more urgent obligations, is at any
time in a position to make payment in
respect of that part of the debt which
was written off the Government Loans
Fund but is still due to the Exchequer,
the hon. Member may rest assured that
the Society will be required to honour its
obligation.
I should state, in conclusion, that since
the Act of 1931 was passed no opportunity has arisen of acquainting the
House of the later developments except
through the medium of the Committee
of Public Accounts.

Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Labour whether

the representatives of the Belfast and
North of Ireland Hotel Association, and
the National Union of Distributive
Workers to be called at an early date,
to consider the possible settlement of
the present hotel strike in the City of
Belfast in view of the likely serious
developments that may occur through
the continuance of this strike.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I need scarcely say that I
regret the prolonged strike referred to
and some weeks ago I suggested that a
conference between the parties concerned
should take place, but apparently the
employers' association are unwilling to
agree.
I would point out that I have no power
to insist on either party meeting the
other. If I am asked by both parties
to endeavour to bring about a settlement I shall gladly accede to such a
request.
Mr. BEATTIE: I will take the opportunity on the Motion for Adjournment
to make a further appeal to the Prime
Minister and Minister of Labour on
grounds which I will then state.
Death of King George V.
HER MAJESTY QUEEN MARY'S
MESSAGE.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to acquaint
the House that I have received the
following message from His Grace the
Governor :
-
Her Majesty Queen Mary having
received from the Commons of Northern Ireland the message of sympathy
on the occasion of the lamented death
of His Most Gracious Majesty King
George the Fifth desires me to convey
her grateful appreciation of this manifestation of their sympathy, and to
state that Her Majesty is deeply
touched by the kind thought which is
conveyed by the Message.
Abercorn,
Governor.
HIS MAJESTY KING EDWARD'S
THANKS.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock) (at the Bar) reported the following Message from His Grace the
Governor :
I have received the King's Command to convey to the Commons of
Northern Ireland His Majesty's thanks
for their sympathy, expressed in their
loyal and dutiful Address, in the
grievous loss which His Majesty has
sustained by the death of his father,
the late King.
His Majesty appreciates the congratulations of the Commons and the
assurance of their loyal devotion to his
person.
Abercorn,
Governor.

staff in the Works Division of the Ministry on account of an intensified building

the greatest difficulty, and to commend
the forbearance and restraint which they
exercised in the face of the most severe
provocation, without which it would have
been difficult to avoid a greatly increased
loss of life.
The item in the Estimate in respect of
pension is simply due to the fact that
this sub-head is obviously one which is
incapable of exact estimation and the
number of men who retired on pension or
gratuity has, in fact, proved greater than
was anticipated. As a set-off against the
increased expenditure to which I have
referred above, there are savings under
other sub-heads, viz:-A saving in the
cost of cloth purchased for the force which
was obtained at a cheaper rate than had
been estimated, and a saving also on provision for the purchase of rented barracks,
which it is now found will not be required
during the current year. I beg to move.

BELFAST HOTEL STRIKE.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I would have liked
if the Prime Minister had been present,
so that I could have made my appeal to
him arising out of the question which I
had the privilege of asking at the commencement of business to-day. Hon.
Members are aware that the hotel industry in Belfast at the present moment is
in the throes of a strike. That strike
may confine itself for the time being to
the hotels, but, on the other hand, one
never knows how far it may extend. I
was at a meeting last night of representatives of all the trade unionists of
Northern Ireland, when decisions were
arrived at and preparations made which,
if they were brought to fulfilment, might
disorganise the whole industries of our
city and of the Six Counties. I say that
is too big a sacrifice for the industries of
Northern Ireland to be asked to make
because of a dispute which I might
define as being between two units of an
industry which they, themselves, did not
do very much to build up.
This House by its efforts during the
past ten years has established for these
people a trade which we should endeavour to safeguard. My reason for
asking the indulgence of the Prime
Minister was that, as he has been the
guest of the Hotel Owners' Association
each year at their annual dinner, I
thought, perhaps, he might be in
position to give to the obstinate mema
Adjournment-
Belfast Hotel Strike
19 FEBRUARY 1936
bers of that association a word of advice,
and that that word of advice might go towards bringing together the two parties,
who up to the present have failed to meet
one another face to face. The origin of the
dispute is fresh in the memories of all
within the city of Belfast, but it is not
too well-known outside the city of Belfast. Whether the hotel proprietors
were wrong in refusing to recognise the
right of the workers to organise, or
whether the workers had a right to stop
work without due notice being given,
I am not going to say at the moment.
I am interested in the matter from
another angle.
Year after year we in this House,
because of the lack of industries and the
financial stringency in our area, have
had to cater for something that would
bring money into the Province. We
have actually spent the taxpayers' money
on the development of the tourist
traffic, and we are not now going to see
the tourist industry destroyed and
driven away from this area because of
any obstinacy that may prevail either
in the Hotel Owners' Association or in
the National Union of Distributive
Workers. We have to bring the two
bodies together and make them realise
that our help in the past must be appreciated, and that the position we have
created for them whereby one hotel in
our city has been able to return a dividend of 15 per cent. last year is one they
should be very careful not to destroy.

BELFAST HARBOUR BOARD
CONTRACT.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware that the
Belfast Harbour Board have placed their
contract for iron castings to the Portadown Foundry Company for the current
year; whether he is aware that this firm
does not conform to the Fair Wages
Clause and is, therefore, in a position to
cut prices at the expense of the workers;
whether he will make representation to
have this contract cancelled, in view of
the low rate of wages paid, ranging from
30s per week to 40s per week, against the
district rate of 68s 9d per week, as paid
by the foundry employers.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
I am
informed that a contract for iron castings has been placed by the Belfast
Harbour Commissioners with the Portadown Foundry Company.
I agree with the hon. Member that all
contracts placed by public bodies should
contain a Fair Wage Clause, and I shall
be happy to make representations to this
effect to the Commissioners.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he is
aware that these castings which come to
the Belfast Harbour Board may be
classified as tainted goods, and that the
trade union employees of the Harbour
Board may refuse to handle them when
they arrive at their destination?
ADVERTISING OF ULSTER GOODS.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state if the Government of Northern
Ireland are taking any special steps to
advertise goods manufactured in Northern
Ireland in all parts of the British
Empire.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Milne Barbour): The Government
has at all times, within the means at its
disposal, endeavoured to secure useful
publicity for goods manufactured in
Northern Ireland throughout the markets
of the world. To this end it has contributed considerable sums towards a
campaign for advertising the linen made
in Northern Ireland both in the United
States of America and in the Dominions.
Moreover, my Ministry has consistently
encouraged firms in Northern Ireland to
be represented at the British Industries
Fair, which constitutes, without question,
one of the greatest publicity media for
overseas' trade in the world to-day.
Úral Answers
Oral Answers
20 FEBRUARY 1936
As the hon. Member is doubtless
aware, a Northern Ireland exhibit at the
Fair, comprising both the agricultural
products and the manufactured foodstuffs of the Province, is organised
regularly by my Ministry, and this
exhibit has now been a feature of the
Fair for many years past. The British
Industries Fair, as the hon. Member will
realise, is visited by trade buyers not
only from the Empire overseas, but also
from all parts of the world.

the
5. Major McCORMICK asked
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): There is no
general regulation in the Ministry's
statutory rules and orders in the terms as
stated in the hon. and gallant Member's

TRANSFER OF TRANSPORT
CONCERNS.
6. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the slow progress in admitting
and settling of claims in the taking over
of transport concerns and the consequent
hardship on many small owners during
this waiting period, he will make representation to the Transport Board to
hasten settlement of such cases.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. Member
will realise that considerable investigation
is necessary before an offer as to the compensation payable can be made by the
Transport Board to the owner of an
undertaking which it has acquired, and
I am informed that these investigations
have been greatly hampered by the very
unbusinesslike methods adopted by many
owners in keeping accounts relating to
their undertakings, and in fact, in only
half the cases have accounts as yet been
received.
The Board informs me that they fully
realise the possibility of inconvenience such
as the hon. Member suggests arising, and

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): With regard to these resolutions, I have had copies of the British
Government White Paper on the subject
circulated amongst our Members. This
document is so fully descriptive of the
new Agreement made between the
Treasury and my Ministry I will be
saved the necessity of entering into the
minutiae of the arrangement itself, with
all its algebraical calculations.
I should like to say, that in my view
-and I think this view is shared by my
right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour-the Agreement to which they
refer is the adjustment of a question,
which since the beginning of our
Government's career has given us great
concern. Our financial sheet-anchor is
the report of the Colwyn Arbitration
Committee, the main principle of which
is that we in Northern Ireland, so long
as we maintain taxation approximately
on the British scale, are entitled to
enjoy equal social services with our
fellow-countrymen on the other side of
the water.
This principle, however, was
endangered in practice because of the
liabilities incurred on one particular
service not altogether because of the
amount of money involved in financing
the service-but because it was impossible to foresee the violent fluctuations
which took place in unemployment in
our area over varying periods.
The Agreement which was made in
1926, was the first recognition of the
necessity for special arrangements to
meet the situation thus created. Without the benefit of that Agreement our
borrowings would have risen to an
intolerable level; but the 1926 Agreement has been thrown out of gear by
reason of the revolutionary change in
the whole scheme of unemployment
relief, and has failed to provide the protection that our financial budgetary
framework required against the fluctuations in cost that I have mentioned.
The main reason for the failure of the
1926 Agreement was that Northern Ireland had to bear her total population
proportion, namely, 2.8 per
per cent. of
British expenditure on unemployment,
before qualifying for a contribution from
Great Britain. This arrangement nullified the intention of the Agreement
when, by reason of financial and other
changes in the administration of unemployment, principally the payment of
transitional benefit, the British cost rose
from £19 millions in 1930 to £70
millions in the present year. Hence the
necessity for the new Agreement, which
takes the insured in place of the total
population as is proper and accordingly
provides for Northern Ireland bearing
only 2 per cent. in place of 23 per cent.
of the British expenditure before
qualifying for a contribution.
I shall now give the Committee, in a
nutshell, the purport of the Agreement.
First of all, we maintain our Insurance
Fund in parity with the British Fund
on the ratio of insured populations
instead of total populations. This ratio
is roughly 1 to 50. The cost of maintaining our Fund in parity with the
British is borne by the Exchequer.
Each year the Exchequer cost of unemployment insurance and unemployment
assistance is ascertained in Great
Britain and in Northern Ireland. If these
services have cost us more than our proper ratio according to the number of
persons within these schemes, then our
excess is the basis of a contribution from
the British Exchequer. In the White
Paper the contribution to our excess cost
is put this year at £722,000, although
it will not be possible to give a final
figure until the end of the financial year.
I have now dealt with the changes in
the original Agreement introduced by
the new Agreement. I should, however,
like to remove certain misunderstandings
regarding the propriety of such an agreement being made at all, and the equitable claim which Northern Ireland has
for its existence. It must be remembered
that our Province is not a self-governing
dominion, responsible for its entire
finances. No less than 89 per cent. of
our tax revenue is imposed and collected
by the Imperial authorities on a scale
in accordance with the needs of the
Kingdom as a whole, and, moreover,
even the remaining 11 per cent., which
Unemployment-
Committee
20 FEBRUARY 1936
of course comes within our own control,
hardly admits of any expansion or other
variation.
But on the expenditure side of our
Budget we have the service of unemployment which costs in the present year no
less than 27 per cent. of our tax revenue,
liable to severe fluctuation owing to the
fact that in the main it depends upon
the state of employment in the larger
industries. Linen and shipbuilding, the
two largest industries, are themselves
liable to fluctuate considerably under
present world conditions, whereas in
Great Britain the fluctuations are
averaged out over a large number of
occupations.
It was obvious that no Budget could
achieve any
reasonable degree of
stability under such conditions, and
accordingly it was agreed that it was
equitable that the brunt of the fluctuations in our unemployment expenditure
should be borne by the two Exchequers
and not by one Exchequer alone, and
allowing no one year of depression to
throw our Budget into chaos.
For that
reason I wish to refute the charge that
this Agreement is in effect a subsidy.
The real outcome of the new arrangement, looking at our finances as a whole,
is that in years of depression we will
pay less Imperial contribution and
receive a considerable sum for unemployment expenditure, in normal years we
will receive less for Unemployment and
pay more Imperial contribution, while
in prosperity we would receive nothing
for unemployment and pay a still larger
Imperial contribution. In fact, if we
are more prosperous than Britain we are
liable to contribute towards her unemployment as well as to pay Imperial
contribution.
I might easily give further reasons for
the existence of an agreement which
ensures that this necessary social service
should be carried on at the same level
here as in Great Britain. For instance,
it would create an impossible situation
if we had a migration of unemployed
people to Great Britain in order
obtain higher rates of benefit. Further,
I might say that the causes and remedies
for unemployment are matters of worldwide concern, and in this we are inseparably bound to the policy and fortune;
of the United Kingdom as a whole.

There is just one point on which I
would like to put a question to the Minister. That is, with regard to the debt on
the old Fund. At the time of the
Agreement of 1926 the Fund was in debt
to the extent of £3,424,000 odd. That

writing off of £100,000 annually. From

this write-off is to be a direct charge of
£40,000, together with the accrued
interest outstanding, against the Unemployment Insurance Fund. It would
appear to me that by altering this
arrangement from writing off £100,000
to writing off £40,000 each year, we are
going to take sixty years instead of
twenty-four, to pay off the debt of
£2,400,000, but it will be a direct charge
upon the Unemployment Insurance Fund.
That appears to me to have a further
effect, and I would like to be corrected if

which now stands at £1,171,000, has been
the security for the writing off of that
£100,000 a year from the old debt. It
would appear to me that when the new
Bill comes into force this Capital Fund
will be released from the obligation which

become available for any purpose to which
the Minister of Finance may wish to put
it. I would like to know if I am right
or wrong in my reading of this important paragraph 5 in the White Paper,

believe I am right in the belief that the
new arrangement will write off the debt
by a direct charge upon the Unemployment Insurance Fund, and that this
Capital Fund will be released from this
liability and will be at the disposal of the
Minister of Finance as a reserve fund
that I hope he will hang on to.

20 FEBRUARY 1936

Committee
Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions) (Extension) [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made and question proposed:
"That it is expedient-
(1) to amend the Unemployment
Assistance (Temporary Provisions)
(No. 2) Act (Northern Ireland),
1935, by extending to a date not
later than the thirty-first day of
March, nineteen hundred and
thirty-six the period in respect of
which grants are to be payable out
of moneys provided by Parliament
to the county borough councils,
urban district council, and county
councils mentioned therein, and to
make certain amendments in regard to the amount of such grants;
and
(2) to authorise the payment out of
moneys provided by Parliament of
such sums as may fall to be
defrayed by reason of the aforesaid amendment to the said Act."
(Governor's Recommendation
signified. Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: This Resolution is
a necessary preliminary to the introduction of a Bill. As hon. Members are
aware, the effect of the postponement
from March 1st, 1935, of the Second
Appointed Day under the Unemployment Act, 1934, was that local authorities had to continue to bear the cost of
assisting the able-bodied unemployed
which, but for that postponement, would
have been taken over by the Unemployment Assistance Board as from March
1st, 1935. The purpose of this Resolution is to authorise the payment out of
voted moneys for a further period of six
months, until the 31st March, 1936, or
until the Second Appointed Day, whichever is the earlier, of grants to local
authorities at the same rates as are set
out in the Unemployment Assistance
(Temporary Provisions) Act (N.I.),
1935.
As I explained in the course of discussion on the earlier Bill, the grants
are calculated so as to put the local
authorities concerned as nearly as possible
in the same financial position as they
would be in if the Second Appointed
Day had not been postponed.
As regards County Down, it is proposed to make special provision in the
Bill for the urban and rural districts of
Killyleagh and Castlewellan, where, since
the previous Act was passed, Orders made
by the Ministry of Home Affairs have
been in operation authorising the payment of out-door relief on account of
special distress in those areas, and there
will be corresponding provision in the
Bill for an increased grant to the County
Council. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I feel that the claim
I made when a Motion similar to this
was before the House, that the percentage allowances allocated to Belfast
were not sufficient has now been confirmed by the right hon. Gentleman so
far as County Down is concerned.
County Down has applied under Section
15 of the 1898 Act to grant outdoor
relief. Belfast applied for that in 1924.
They paid strict attention to the needs
and requirements of the people at that
period, but no special benefit under this
money arrangement has been made on
their behalf.
The CHAIRMAN: I think that would
properly relate to the Bill of which this
is merely the preliminary. The Minister
did mention that the Bill would make
special provision.
Mr. BEATTIE: I quite agree that in
the Bill an Amendment could be brought
in whereby Belfast could get special
consideration, also in regard to the
apportioning of the amounts in the
Money Resolution. Belfast Borough was
apportioned a certain figure which I complained of.
also
County Down was
apportioned a certain figure and the
other areas also. I feel we are going to
have, for a further six months, a continuation to the Belfast Borough of a
similar amount to that laid down in the
first Money Resolution introduced by the
right hon. Gentleman. I want, once
more, to make my strong protest against
the apportionment, in so far as Belfast
was the only city in Northern Ireland
that applied themselves to the starving
population so early, and they have only
been treated in the same fashion as those
areas that did not come in in all these
years and neglected their responsibilities.

They are now coming in and getting the

£350,000 that Belfast got?
The CHAIRMAN: I hope the hon.

Mr. HENDERSON: I want to say

Mr. HENDERSON: It is not my

the only thing you can provide?

1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether he will, in
accordance with the step-by-step policy
of this Government, undertake to place
the horse-power tax on a more equitable
basis in comparison with the reduced tax
imposed in Great Britain.
aware
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The hon. and gallant Member
must be
that the step-by-step
policy of the Government relates solely
to essential social services. In any event
I feel sure that he would not expect me
to anticipate my forthcoming Budget
statement.
Major MCCORMICK: May I ask the
Minister is he aware that motor licences
cost 5s more in Ulster than in England?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, I am aware of
that.
QUOILE DRAINAGE SCHEME.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he is aware
that owing to his refusal to complete the
Quoile Drainage Scheme last summer by
removing the obstruction under the
Quoile Bridge, Downpatrick was flooded
on the 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 28th,
29th and 30th January, 1936; whether
he is aware that this obstruction banks
the water on the up-stream side of the
bridge, 15 inches above the water level
on the down-stream or lock side, and
that 40 per cent. of the efficiency of
this drainage scheme is thereby lost; and
whether he will now complete this work.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am aware of the
flooding to which the hon. and gallant
Member refers and I can assure him that,
although the works completed have not
succeeded in keeping the flood levels
below 11ft. 6ins. on the
the
gauge,
duration of the flooding has been considerably shortened and the depth of the
flooding considerably reduced, despite
the fact that the rainfall in the catchment area was of an exceptionally abnormal character. I can, however, inform
the hon. and gallant Member that the
data compiled by my Ministry's engineers during the course of the floods are
at present being carefully sifted with a
view to a decision being arrived at by
the Government in regard to future
action in relation to the drainage scheme.
I will inform both the Downpatrick
Urban District Council and the County
Council of Down of the Government's
decision in the matter as early as possible.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it not a
fact that an agreement was made between the County Council, the Ministry
of Finance and the Urban District
Council of Downpatrick, and that this
agreement was implemented by Act of
Parliament? May I ask, therefore, why
the Minister does not implement this
Act, and do the drainage as requested.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Government is
in the process of implementing the Act
to which the hon. and gallant Member
refers. The Government through their
technical people must be permitted to
