FINANCES OF PUBLIC
VOLUNTARY HOSPITALS.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether the public
voluntary hospitals in this area face a
heavy annual debt on their working;
whether their waiting lists of patients
are congested; whether such hospitals are
rate-aided in various centres in England
and Scotland; whether in the Irish Free
State such hospitals receive public assistance; whether in several Australian
States for every £1 such hospitals raise
the State contributes another £1; and
whether he can hold out any prospect of
public aid for such hospitals here.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Ministry has
no function regarding voluntary hospitals and receives no information regarding their financial position; but so far
as the Belfast institutions are concerned,
I understand that in most
cases the
position is fairly satisfactory.
I am not aware that voluntary hospitals in England or Scotland are rateaided. In the Irish Free State assistance
is given from a fund raised by sweepstakes and not from the rates or the
State. I have no information as to what
is done in Australia.
I am afraid I cannot hold out any
hope of assistance to voluntary hospitals
from the rates or the State. I have
reason to believe that none of the voluntary institutions which carry on such
good work in Northern Ireland is prepared in any way to relinquish the independence which they at present enjoy
and which has had such beneficial results
in the development of medical and surgical science.
GOVERNORSHIP OF ARMAGH
PRISON.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
what precedent he followed in the recent
appointment of a Governor for Armagh
Prison; whether it is a fact that the
gentleman appointed is an officer of the
"B" Special Constabulary; whether he
will be allowed to carry on the two
positions; whether he can state what is
the salary of the Governorship; whether
he is prepared to explain why he overlooked fully trained prison officials in
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
this appointment; whether the gentleman appointed has any previous experience of the duties attached to this
office; whether he is prepared to close
this prison and transfer the thirty
prisoners to Belfast where accommodation is available for at least 400
prisoners with all the necessary requirements for female prisoners.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not the
practice in the prison service in Northern Ireland or in Great Britain to limit
the field of selection for appointment to
the post of governor of a prison to officers
in the prison service, and no departure
from precedent is, therefore, involved in
the appointment referred to by the hon.
Member.
It is a fact that the gentleman in
question was an officer of the "B"
Special Constabulary, for which he received the nominal fee of £5 5s per
annum, but on taking up duty as
governor of the prison he will, however,
relinquish his Special Constabulary
appointment.
The salary of the post is £396, rising
by annual increments of £12, to £515.
It is not a fact that in making this
appointment members of the prison service were overlooked. The most careful
consideration was given to the claims of
all candidates, and the candidate finally
selected was the one who appeared to be
the best fitted for the post.
The gentleman in question has mot
had previous experience of the duties
attached to the office. The post of
prison governor is one, however, which
demands qualifications of administrative
ability and personality rather than mere
acquaintance with the routine conduct of
a prison, and previous experience of
prison work is not, therefore, regarded
as an essential condition of appointment.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
100 per cent. of these governorships in
Northern Ireland are now in the possession of outsiders, and that 60 per cent.
of these appointments in England are
taken from the ranks of the officials in
the prison service, only 40 per cent.
being taken from outside sources. In
view of the anomaly which the Minister
has now created will he endeavour to
have a reconsideration of the appointment to the Armagh governorship?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. I
believe in making this appointment the
Government are very fortunate in having
such a suitable gentleman to take up the
position.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that the question of personality is not in
dispute at the moment? It is the question
of precedent that you have established
in Northern Ireland against the precedent in Great Britain.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not
regard precedent in any way.
I believe
the proper thing is to get the best man
suitable for the position.
6.
NUMBER OF UNEMPLOYED
SINGLE PERSONS.
Mr.
HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state
the number of single persons unemployed
in Northern Ireland; whether many of
them have been signing on at the Labour
Exchange for the past five years, and,
if so, what steps the Government are
taking to provide work for single men
and women.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): As I informed the hon. Member in reply to a similar question which
he asked on 19th March last, no separate
statistics are kept showing the division
of the unemployed register as between
single and married persons.
As regards the last part of his question,
the hon. Member has no doubt kept himself fully informed of the many steps
which are being actively pursued, both
by the Government of the United Kingdom and by the Government of Northern
Ireland to promote trade and employment generally for the benefit of all.
Mr. HENDERSON: The Government
is taking no action to provide work for
single men and women. Will the right
hon. Gentleman tell the House what
steps the Government is taking to provide work for those starving men who
are parading the streets of Belfast and
other towns throughout the length and
breadth of Northern Ireland?
You are
not in starvation, but they are.

SUBSIDIES TO FARMERS.
8. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the total amount paid to Northern
Ireland for the benefit of the producer
under each of the following:-Milk
Marketing Act, Cattle Subsidy Act,
Wheat Subsidy Act, since they came into
force.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The total amount of
equalisation payments made to Northern
Ireland producers under the Milk Act,
1934, in respect of milk supplied to
creameries up to and including 8th
February, 1936-a period of 22 months
--was £285,168.
The whole of this sum is paid to the
Northern Ireland Exchequer by the
Imperial Government.
As the hon. and gallant Member is
aware, this assistance is being continued
by the Imperial Government to Northern
Ireland producers until September, 1937,
on the same basis as to producers in
Great Britain.
The sum paid under the Cattle Industry (Emergency Provisions) Act for the
period extending from the 1st September, 1934, to the 15th February, 1936,
in respect of cattle certified in Northern
Ireland, was £352,808.
The total deficiency payments made to
Northern Ireland growers of wheat under
the Wheat Act, 1932, from the 1st
August, 1932, until the end of the cereal
year 1934-35, amounted to £56,989.
Advances made to date to Northern
Ireland wheat growers during the cereal
year 1935-36 amount to £16,984.
The total payments made to date to
Northern Ireland wheat growers, therefore, amount to £73,973.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Thank you.

(Rating and Finance) Act (Northern

under the said Act in respect of industrial hereditaments; to amend the law
relating to the chargeability of certain
expenses of rural district councils; and
for other purposes connected therewith," it is expedient to authorise the
payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament of such grants as are under
the provisions of such Act to be payable:-
(a) For the purpose of an annual
deficiency contribution in respect
of each local financial year, subject to and in accordance with the
Local Government (Rating and
Finance) Act, 1929, as amended
by any such Act of the present
Session as aforesaid, to be paid to
or on behalf of local authorities
towards making good the losses
occurring by reason of the provisions of section one, two and three
of the Act of 1929;
(b) For the purpose of a revaluation
contribution, to be paid to or on
behalf of a local authority together
with the deficiency contribution,
in respect of any local financial
year beginning on and after the
first day of April, nineteen hundred and thirty-six, subject to and
in accordance with the provisions
contained in any such Act of the
present Session as aforesaid, in

and the amount of the unreduced

in a case where the amount of the

(Governor's Recommendation
signified. Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will,
doubtless, expect that in moving the
Resolution, which is on the Order Paper,
I should give them some figures showing
what is the cost of this new derating
legislation to the Government.
Let me explain briefly what this Bill
in common with the 1929 Act does. In
the counties a standard expenditure for
each local authority is calculated, and
towards this the Exchequer gives a standard grant-in-aid, representing the loss
brought out by reason of the derating of
agricultural land, and so forth. The
standard grant for the first period, up to
March 31st, 1936, was approximately
£834,000. The standard grant for the
new period, from 1st April, 1936, will be
£727,000. Hon. Members will appreciate that I am using round figures. This
diminution is not due to any falling off
in expenditure of county councils in the
last three years as compared with that
in the years prior to 1929. For, in fact,
the standard expenditure on which the
grant is calculated has gone up from
£1,342,000 in that year to £1,425,000.
Hon. Members may ask, why then has
not the standard grant-in-aid of this expenditure risen instead of fallen? The
simple answer is, revaluation. From 1st
April next the total valuation of agricultural land in Northern Ireland will
bear a smaller proportion to the valuation
figure of all hereditaments than on the
31st March next; consequently, as the
Government pays the rates on agricultural
land, its contribution will fall in the same
proportion.
When the revaluation figures were published county councils at once realised
what was going to happen and appealed
Local Government-
Committee
25 FEBRUARY 1936
to my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, to relieve the
to relieve the resulting
burden. They found in him a sympathetic listener, and he agreed that he
would make good 80 per cent. of their
loss. This remedial grant, if I may use
the phrase-others may prefer the phrase
revaluation grant-is the subject of the
second part of the Resolution before the
Committee, and what is its financial
effect? It will amount to a
£114,000.
sum of
The total then of this figure and the
new standard grant amounts to £841,000,
that is to say, £7,000 more than the
original standard. County councils will,
therefore, realise that they have been
very fairly met, even when account is
taken of the fact that they have agreed
to hand over about £6,000 of the revaluation grant to urban councils for reasons
which I will now explain.
Urban and county borough councils
were treated differently from counties
under the 1929 Act. There was no standard expenditure fixed and no standard
grant-in-aid. Instead they were repaid
the actual loss arising on derating, and
this derating was mainly, if not wholly,
in respect of industrial concerns who only
now pay one-fourth of the normal rate.
Now these concerns on revaluation
have not had their values increased in the
same proportion as ordinary dwellinghouses, and consequently the Exchequer,
as payer of the rates on this part of the
valuation of the industrial concerns,
makes a small saving. The total amount
of this saving spread over all the urban
districts and the two county boroughs,
is in the region of £26,000, so that from
the point of view of individual local
authorities the matter is inconsiderable.
In one respect, however, the urban
districts which form part of the county
areas for certain charges stood to suffer
somewhat. Hon. Members will understand that the increase in the total valuation of urban areas was very much greater
than that in the rural areas, and as a
consequence of this the urban districts
would have become liable to pay a considerably larger share than formerly of
those charges which are shared by the
urban and rural areas in proportion to
their valuations. The rural areas have
agreed to make good to the urban areas
this loss to the extent of about £6,000
by credit being given by the counties in
the manner set out in the Schedule of the
Bill. The immediate effect of this Bill,
therefore, will be a saving of some
£19,000 to the Government, a trifling
sum compared with the saving of
£140,000 which it might have expected
as the result of revaluation.
And now how will the Exchequer and
the local authorities stand for the future?
It will be recollected that over and above
the standard grant there was a supplemental grant paid to county authorities
as an aid towards expenditure beyond
the original standard. It was in two
parts, one in respect of educational
services without any money limit, the
other for all other services with a limit
related to a rate of 6d in the £. At the
end of the first five years of derating the
counties were drawing annually about
£70,000 by way of supplemental grant,
and this is now provided for in the combined new standard grant and revaluation grant.
In the new scheme there is also provision for similar development of services
by way of supplemental grant; it will
still also be in two parts, one in respect
of education with a limit related to a
rate of 3d in the £, the other in respect
of other services with a limit related to a
rate in the £ of 5d in the Bill, but which
hon. Members will see is to be increased
to a figure of 6d by an Amendment which
will be moved in Committee.
And what is the possible increasing
burden on the Government from these
supplemental grants to counties? It may
reach, but can never exceed, a total of
£119,000, for the supplemental grant is
now fixed at a maximum for all time, but
it is unlikely that it will reach such a
figure as it would imply that rates.
would touch a point in the counties which
no prudent county council would ever
allow, and also that every subsidiary body
in the county was spending up to the last
pound on which it was entitled to draw.
Turning now to future expenditure in
the urban districts and boroughs, it has
already been stated firstly, that in the
past they received the actual loss arising
out of derating, and secondly, that the
Government will save a sum of £26,000
by reason of revaluation. Under the
provisions of the Act this saving may not
be permanent. The deficiency which the
Local Government-
Committee

[Mr. Barbour]
Government would be liable to pay the
urban districts will increase if their
internal expenditure grows. Whether
or not it will do SO depends on
themselves. I hope that it will not,
not from the Exchequer point of
view, but from the point of view of the
ratepayers in each urban area, because
for every additional £1 that is added to
the deficiency contribution the ratepayers
in most places will have themselves to
find a sum of £9. I hope that in these
remarks I have made a complicated subject a little clearer to hon. Members. I
beg to move.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in Clause 4, page 6, line 23, to leave out
"five pence" ("the produce of a rate of
five pence in the pound") and to insert
"six pence".
This Amendment gives effect to the
promise I made in my speech on the
Second Reading of the Bill, namely that
the limit for supplemental grant for
services other than education would be
increased from 5d to 6d, so as to mak
provision for services which were not in
existence at the fixing of the standard.
Mrs. PARKER: I want to take this
opportunity not only of supporting the
Amendment moved by the right hon.
Gentleman, but also of saying something
which for some reason was not said on the
Second Reading, possibly because hon.
Members on this side of the House were
expecting that some Members of the
Opposition would speak on and criticise
the Bill; but evidently they found it
impossible to criticise after the Minister
had forecast this concession. I want to
take this opportunity, as it was impossible
on the former occasion, of thanking the
Government for what they are doing for
the local authorities. I wish to state that
my local authority was the first to raise
this particular matter by question and
resolution, and to point out to the
Ministry of Home Affairs the difficulty
in which all councils would be placed if
the standard were to be based on a period
of years during which the Labourers Acts
were not in operation. We, in common
with other district councils, were most
anxious to discharge our obligations
towards the labourers in this respect, and
we requested the Government to put the
Act into operation again. We would
have been placed in a very considerable
difficulty, because, as I have said, the
standard would have been based upon a
period during which we had been doing
no building of this kind. So, in that
way, the Government really would have
been taking away with one hand what
they had already so generously given
with the other.
The Minister of Home Affairs, by this
Amendment increasing the supplemental
grant, has met not only the Association
of District Councils but the wishes of all
the local authorities throughout the Province, and has met them in the most
generous manner.
I do feel that it was
a great pity that none of us rose to
express our gratitude during the Second
Reading of this Bill. We were taken by
surprise. We were waiting for the Opposition. That, of course, was our fault. It
was my fault, because I was quite prepared
to thank the Government, and I do so now.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that in
what they are doing they are really conferring a tremendous benefit on the
labourers who are anxious to have these
cottages, and on the district councils who
are anxious to get on with the necessary
work.

Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions) (Extension) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: The purpose of this
Bill is to extend to a date not later than
the 31st March next the powers conferred
upon the Government by the Unemployment Assistance (Temporary Provisions)
(No. 2) Act.
Hon. Members will doubtless recollect
that that Act gave the Government
powers to compensate local authorities by
way of grants from the Exchequer so that
the local authorities would be placed in as
nearly as possible the same financial
position that would have obtained if
postponement of the second appointed
day under the Unemployment Assistance
Act, 1934, had not taken place. The
grants being made under the present Bill
will be on exactly the same basis as those
made under the Unemployment Assistance (Temporary Provisions) (No. 2)
Act-that is to say, in monthly payments
to each local authority the amounts of
which approximate in general to an
annual rate equivalent to the yield of
2d in the pound on the rates in urban
areas and 1d in the pound in rural areas.
The amounts paid to Belfast, Newry and
Londonderry are calculated on a somewhat different basis from that for the
other areas owing to the fact that special
factors operate in these areas.
Since the Unemployment Assistance
(Temporary Provisions) (No. 2) Act was
passed the Ministry of Home Affairs have
made special Orders authorising the payment of outdoor relief on account of
special distress in the urban and rural
districts of Killyleagh and Castlewellan.
Clause 1 of the Bill accordingly makes
provision for an increased grant to the
Down County Council to be applied in
respect of outdoor relief in these areas.
I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.
Amendment of Old Age Pensions Acts.
Mr. HENDERSON: I beg to move,
That in the opinion of this House the
time has arrived when, owing to the
surplus population unable to find
employment it will be in the interest of
the State to amend the Old Age Pensions Act to enable the pension to be
raised from 10s to £1 5s Od per week,
with compulsory retirement at 65.
This is one of the most vital matters
that concern the Province of Northern
Ireland, and it is a matter to which I
have given the deepest and most earnest
consideration. What I am surprised at
is that the Prime Minister of this country
and the Minister of Labour are doing
practically nothing to cure the evil of
unemployment. Rightly or wrongly, I
have come to the conclusion that this
Government stand for looking after the
interests of the rich, and forgetting about
the poor. I want to prove my case that
a pension of 25s a week should be paid.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Do you
mean that 25s a week should be paid to
all pensioners?
Old Age Pensions Acts 272
Old Age Pensions Acts
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. HENDERSON: Yes. The Government of this country make it their business to provide pensions for those servants
who earn from £150 to £2,500 a year.
Is that not rather strange? Is that not
a law for the rich? If the Government
of this country think that it is a
Christian-like act to provide pensions for
men who have been receiving in some
instances £2,500 a year, do they not
think it would be just as Christian-like to
provide for the people who work in the
shipyards and in the streets of Belfast?
The Government of the country, the
municipalities, the banks, and the insurance companies all provide for their employees when they are compulsorily retired.
at the age of 65. They give those people
a pension so that they may end their days
in comfort and in happiness. But this
Government go one better. What do
they do? They allow civil servants to
retire with pensions of from £750 to
£1,000, and they recommend them for
positions worth almost £2,000 to the
detriment of young men coming from the
University and others. I cannot understand the mentality of this Government.
There are 60,000 people unemployed in
Northern Ireland. The Minister of
Labour will correct me if I am wrong in
this statement. Is that not so?

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Government Loans Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Bill seeks the authority
of Parliament to write off the principal
from the Government Loans Fund and
extinguish both principal and interest ast
a debt due to the Exchequer in respect
of a loan of £1,000 made by my Ministry on the 11th September, 1922, to the
Londonderry Port Sanitary Authority.
The loan was part of a loan originally
sanctioned by the Local Government
Board for Ireland prior to transfer of
the local government services to our Government, for the purpose of building an
Intercepting Hospital near Moville, in
County Donegal, which is now in the
Free State. The hospital in the events
that have happened has proved to be
something in the nature of a white
elephant, having never been used for its
original purpose, and is now lying derelict. Infectious disease cases are, I understand, treated in the Derry Infirmary
instead. In these circumstances the
Government decided that the meeting of
the instalments on the loan constituted
an unnecessary and unfair burden on the
ratepayers of the Borough of Derry, and
certain areas in the county, brought
about by circumstances over which they
have had no control.
This Bill accordingly provides for the
writing off of £567 which is the amount
of the principal still outstanding of that
part of the loan made by my Ministry
from the Government Loans Fund and
the final extinction as a debt to the Exchequer of both principal and interest
still outstanding. As explained in the
financial memorandum attached to the
Bill, the amount so written off will be
made good to the Government Loans
Fund by Vote.
The Government also propose, as an
ancillary Measure, to redeem that part
of the loan made from the Imperial
Government Loans Fund before the
transfer of local government services to
our Government which is still outstanding, and a Vote for the purpose will be
introduced contemporaneously with the
Vote to which I have just referred. I
beg to move.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.

Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This is a short but
important Bill. Its object is to extend
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
26 FEBRUARY 1936
until the 1st May, 1940, the protection
afforded in regard to the control of rents
by the Rent and Mortgage Interests
(Restrictions) Acts (N.I.), 1920 to 1932,
which will expire on the 1st May, 1936.
The position at present is that all
houses not exceeding £8 valuation are
subject to control, and that all houses.
between £8 and £26 valuation are also
subject to control unless they came into
the landlord's possession before the 12th
April, 1932.
the
As hon. Members are aware,
necessity for rent restriction arose from
the abnormal shortage of houses following on the war period, which, if the law
of supply and demand had been allowed
to operate without limitation, would
have led to prohibitive increases in
rentals and consequent hardship on
tenants.
When introducing the 1932 Act, which
prolonged the operation of rent control.
until May of the present year, it was
hoped that with this extension the housing situation would have been sufficiently
eased to admit of the restriction being
removed. While the position in regard
to housing has, I am glad to say,
materially improved-mainly as a result
of the efforts of the Government and
the local authorities to encourage building by grants of subsidies-it has by no
means yet arrived at normality. The
demand for small working-class houses is
still in some cases acute and it is to be
feared that if rent restriction were now
taken off, an opportunity would be given
to a few unscrupulous owners to exploit
their unfortunate tenants and a general
rise in rents would be inevitable, with
consequent hardship on those least able
to support it.
For these reasons the Government has
decided to continue the existing rent control until 1940, by which time it is hoped
that the necessity for such restriction will
no longer exist.
I may remark that no reference is
made in this Bill to the effect of revaluation on controlled houses, which, if no
adjustment were made in the existing
limits of valuation would in some instances, on account of the general
increase in valuation, be taken outside
the scope of the Rent Restriction Acts.
This point, however will be met in the
forthcoming Revaluation (Consequential
Provisions) Bill, which will contain a
provision designed to maintain control
of all houses which are at present subject to the Rent Restriction Acts. I
beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.”
Mr. BEATTIE: I thought perhaps
after the long experience the Minister
has had in regard to the inability of the
present law to safeguard the rights of
tenants that when he was bringing forward a Bill for the continuation of the
old Measure he would have asked the
House for new Clauses to be inserted. I
regret his neglect in that direction because to-day we have in our midst what
I might call a chronic disease-chronic
in the form that some tenants who are
living side by side are charged at least
50 to 100 per cent. more than their
next-door neighbour, whose house is of a
similar kind with the same amount of
accommodation. The anomaly I have
referred to was due to the Government's
haste in endeavouring to bring about the
decontrol of all house property. They
decontrolled houses between £8 and £26
valuation
when they became vacant.
Those houses were never considered
worthy of being brought in again under
the Rent Restrictions Act. The Government did recognise and admit its folly
in the creation of chaos and disorder as
far as house rents were concerned, and
in the year 1932 they had to re-establish
control. I want them to go a step
further and to remove the great menace
they let loose under the Measure they
introduced giving the landlord the right
of possession and the right to charge
whatever rent he liked when the old
tenant had given notice to leave.
This is not what one would call a small
question which can be lightly looked upon
as a grumble from the few; it is a
grumble from the many who reside in
artisans' dwellings, that is those dwellings
which were permitted to become decontrolled from the time they were allowed
to go into the possession of the landlord.
If it is good in the year 1936 for houses
from £8 to £26 valuation to be still under
control, surely the same houses that
became decontrolled before 1932 should
be brought into the same grade and have
the same protection given to them.

before some date in 1923 he is entitled
to come in on six months' notice, and get
possession of the house, but the man who
has bought since 1923 has bought with
his eyes open to the position, and it would
be a great hardship if such a man, who
bought with his eyes open, would be entitled to claim that the tenant should be
ejected. It would not only be a hardship to a particular person, but it is open
to another objection-the great objection
of individual houses being exempted from
the purview of the Acts.
In 1925 the Act referred to was passed,
enabling landlords who got possession of
houses between £8 and £26 valuation, to
take those houses out of control. That
created a number of exceptions, and this
House, in its wisdom, saw that that was a
mistaken step, for a few years later they
went back on that step to this extent,
that hereafter, if a house under £26
valuation becomes vacant, it will not be
taken out of control. Accordingly, one
sees in 1932, that the House recognises
that what was done in 1925 was a mistake.
I think nobody is much to blame for
making a mistake. The man who never
makes a mistake never accomplishes anything. The criticism offered, particularly
by the hon. Member for Pottinger is this,
that in streets you will find houses side
by side, some of which came into the
landlord's possession between 1925 and
1932, and became decontrolled, and for
these he can charge any rent, and other
houses did not come into possession and
did not become decontrolled. I
assure the House that whether the House
wants to go back on that and adopt the
suggestion of the hon. Member for
Pottinger or not, it is a thing that is felt
by many people living in these streets
to be a great hardship. I do not mention
that for a moment to suggest that that
should be done now. I do mention it
because I think it is a great mistake to
create particular exceptions under these
Acts. Let the Acts remain as general
Acts applicable to the houses to which
they are applicable. Do not make
individual exceptions. That makes for
individual hardships.
There is one matter which I would like
to refer to, and I regret it has not been
put into an Act and that the Government
has not proposed to legislate about it, that
is, the rates payable in respect of these
houses. The House is aware that by a
decision given in the House of Lords some
years ago, with regard to an English
estate, it has been held that in estimating
the valuation of one of these houses you
are not allowed to take into account the
fact that the house is a controlled house.
I may not be stating the law quite
correctly, but the valuation to be put on
the house is not a valuation referrable to
the rent which the house, in fact, produces, but a valuation referrable to a rent
which certainly cannot be got out of that
house before 1940. That is a hardship,
and that hardship is partly on the tenant
and partly on the landlord, because the
landlord has to pay income tax in respect
of what is entirely an artificial valuation,
a valuation not fixed by reference to the
actual rent he gets out of the house,
which is the general basis of valuation,
but with reference to an artificial rent
which, as the law stands, he does not get
and cannot get out of the house for many
years. That is another anomaly and an
anomaly that creates a hardship.
Whether it is appropriate that that
should be introduced into a Bill brought
in by the Ministry of Home Affairs, or in
one brought in by the Ministry of
Finance, it is still a difficulty which has
not been coped with. The Recorder of
Belfast has got to recognise the law laid
down by the House of Lords and follow
that law. The time is come, I think,
when the Government should take the
matter up and attempt to rectify that
anomaly and provide that so long as a
controlled rent is imposed on
can

Mr. CAMPBELL: I had not intended
to intervene in this debate, but some
remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary
disappointed, or rather disturbed me. I
take it that there is no going back on
the decision of the Government. They
can afford no relief by this Act to those
tenants of houses of a valuation between
£8 and £26. At the present time they
have only fragmentary protection, and
the Government cannot give them the
full protection accorded to tenants of
houses of a valuation of £8 or under.
There is one feature of the case which is
very regrettable. The Parliamentary
Secretary attempts to justify the exclusion of subsidy houses from this Act of
Parliament. Subsidy houses have
absorbed a tremenduous amount of State
and rate money, and I for one could
never understand why that exceedingly
large volume of houses should be entirely
excluded from the ambit of this Rent
Restrictions Act. The whole Act bristles
with anomalies.
You will find examples of them in any
typical working class street in Belfast.
The tenants on one side of the street are
protected by these Acts and are probably
paying a fair rent, while the tenants on
the other side of the street are outside
the Acts, and they are paying excessive
rents. The strange anomaly is that
although tenant A is paying 15s a week
in rent because he has no protection, and
tenant B on the other side of the street
is paying 7s or 8s a week for the same
size of house, for the same accommodation, the income of both families is
exactly the same. The one is getting the
same wages as the other, one is getting the
same house accommodation as the other,
and yet one tenant in the same street in
the city of Belfast is paying twice the
rent of the other tenant. The whole
thing bristles with anomalies.
With regard to subsidy houses, one
would have thought that that was the
very class of house over which pubiic
control would have been exercised first of
all.
Take the case of a house in Belfast,
and I want to take the figures as fairly
as I can. Take the case of a subsidy
house built for the sum of £400, and I
think you will get a very good subsidy
house if you spend £400 on it.
Mr. BEATTIE: The best on
market.

Mr. CAMPBELL: There is contributed by the public authorities a sum

YIELD OF PROPERTY TAX.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the yield
of property tax accruing to the Imperial
Exchequer from Northern Ireland for
the year 1935-36, and the estimated yield
of the same tax on the new valuations
for the year 1936-37.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As I have already informed the
hon. and learned Member in a letter sent
to him on the 4th June last, I regret
that it is not possible for me to give him
the information which he desires, as the
Imperial authorities concerned inform
me that for various reasons it is not
possible to give estimates of the yield
of Income Tax under the various
schedules.
CUTS IN TEACHERS' SALARIES.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the cost of restoring in full the cuts made
in teachers' salaries in the year 1931.
Mr. POLLOCK: The cost of restoring
in full the cuts made in teachers' salaries
in 1931 would be approximately
£122,000 in the first complete financial
year of restoration. This figure does not
of course include the increase in pension
costs which the restoration of the cuts
would involve.
UNION JACK ON R.U.C.
BARRACKS.
3. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
why Royal Ulster Constabulary Barracks
are not provided with proper fixtures or
brackets to hold the poles from which
the Union Jack is flown on public
occasions, and whether he considers the
present method of having the flag flown
out of a bedroom window of the Barracks
seemly and proper.
Mr. POLLOCK : I agree with the
hon. and gallant Gentleman that the
present method of flying the Union Jack
out of a bedroom window in the case of
the smaller Royal Ulster Constabulary
Barracks outside Belfast is hardly in
keeping with the dignity associated with
the flag, and I am taking steps, as, and
when the opportunity presents itself, to
have the matter rectified.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Hear, hear.

VIEW ESTATE.

can appeal before April, 1936; whether
the present valuation must stand for

HOMEWORK IN P.E. SCHOOLS.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether the Minister has considered the abolition of homework in
schools, in accordance with principle
affirmed at Westminster that children
should have their evenings for rest and
recreation, and that preparation in
schools should take the place of homework.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): As regards
the public elementary schools, I would
refer the hon. and learned Member to
a reply which I gave on 24th April,
1934, to the hon. and gallant Member
for the St. Anne's Division.
While the Ministry deprecates an
excessive amount of time being devoted
to homework by any class of pupil, the
complete abolition of homework in the
case of secondary school pupils would be
highly inadvisable on educational
grounds and, owing to the distances which
many pupils have to travel to secondary
and technical schools, it would not be
generally possible to detain them longer
in school or to bring them back during
the evening for the purpose of doing
their daily preparation there.

Secretary aware that many people are of
the opinion that this enormous amount
of homework is the cause of many school
children now having to wear glasses, a
practice which was practically unknown.
before this craze for excessive education?
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

accept it.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask has the
Minister made up his mind in the case of
elementary schools for or against the
abolition of homework?
Mr. ROBB: I have referred the hon.
and learned Member to the answer I
gave last year to the hon. and gallant
Member for St. Anne's.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Two years ago.

RETURN OF ELECTION DEPOSITS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
deposits lodged by Members of this
House who have not subscribed to the
Oath and taken their seats are returnable before the dissolution of the Parliament to which they have been elected.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to reply.
In the opinion of the legal advisers to
the Government the deposits referred to
by the hon. Members are returnable.
Mr. BEATTIE: Am I to take it from
the answer-and altering my previous
question that after the dissolution of
Parliament these deposits are returned
if applied for?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, if applied for.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it not a
fact that these deposits are only returnable if the candidate takes the Oath?
Mr. POLLOCK: As far as I understand it the legal position as laid down by
the law officers of the United Kingdom
is that the £150 deposit is returnable
in every case if the candidate has been
elected.

APPEALS TRIBUNAL.
2. Major MCCORMICK asked the

state when he proposes to set up the
Appeals Tribunal under the Road and
Railway Transport Act; and whether he
is now in a position to give the names of
the gentlemen who will be members of

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is hoped to set
up this tribunal at an early date, but
I am not yet in a position to give the
names of the gentlemen who will be
members of the tribunal.

3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he

can state the reasons for the delay in

STOLEN MOTOR CARS.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been drawn to recent cases
of stolen motor cars in Northern Ireland; whether he can state the number
of cars stolen and give a return of cases
that have been made amenable since 1st
January, 1935; and whether he will take
more drastic action to deal with this
form of crime.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Since the 1st
January, 1935, 274 motor cars were reported to the police as having been stolen.
In 67 cases the offenders were made
amenable in respect of these offences.
The motor cars were recovered and returned to their owners by the police in
every case, usually within 24 hours.
The hon. and gallant Member can rest
assured that the resources of the police
are being and will continue to be used
to the fullest possible extent to deal with
this type of crime.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The purpose of the first
part of the Financial Resolution which is
on the Order Paper to-day is to authorise
the transfer of a sum of £50,000 to the
Civil Contingencies Fund from the
Reserve Fund. As hon. Members are
aware, the purpose of the Civil Contingencies Fund is to provide the Government with the means to meet
unexpected emergency expenditure, and
it has been found in practice during the
last few years that the limit of £50,000
at which the Civil Contingencies Fund
has stood since 1922 is not entirely
adequate. It is accordingly proposed to
increase the Fund to £100,000.
As regards the second part of the
Resolution, hon. Members will recollect
that the Government were empowered by
the Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Act, 1927, to make grants not exceeding
£80 per house in respect of houses
erected by the Irish Sailors' and Soldiers'
Land Trust. The maximum limit fixed
for the total of these grants is £37,000.
This limit has recently been attained and
unless further statutory powers are conceded by hon. Members the grants for
this most excellent object, the housing of
our ex-Service men will cease.
Authority is accordingly sought to make
further grants not exceeding a total of
£3,000. The grants will be at the rate
of £50 for each house.

Mr. BEATTIE: On this Resolution I
would like to ask a question with regard
to the Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust.
The number of complaints I have received
from disabled and other ex-Service men
who thought they had a right to the houses
built by the Trust have been a source of
annoyance to me. I am given to understand from a reliable source that a very
large percentage of Englishmen and
Scotsmen are tenants of the houses erected
by the Trust. The terms of the Trust,
as drawn up by the British Exchequer,
were that Northern Ireland was to have
its proportion, and that Southern Ireland,
England, Scotland and Wales were also
to have their proportions. The proportion for Northern Ireland was intended
to be used in providing Northern Ireland
ex-Service men with houses. I am not
going to criticise unduly, but I would like
to know from the Minister responsible
how it is possible for an ex-Service man
to get possession of one of these houses.
I thought there was a qualification of
nationality and that the applicant was
only qualified for a house in the country
to which he belonged. I raise this point
because I have had continual annoyance
from the grumblings and grievances of
ex-Service men in regard to the occupation of these houses, in order that I might
get some explanation as what really are
the qualifications necessary.
Mr. BARBOUR: The administration
of this Trust is in the hands of trustees
appointed by the Imperial Government.
I may say I can quite understand the disappointment entertained by a considerable
number of ex-Service men when they find
they are unable to secure a house. I do
know, from having interested myself on
behalf of many such men that the
qualifications of the different applicants
are gone into most carefully, and
really every condition of which the
Members of the House would approve
is taken into consideration, such
as the nature of the service given,
the number of children the man may
have, and his claims generally. The
claim of any one applicant is a relative
and not an absolute claim, and is in
relation to the other applicants seeking
houses. I believe the administration is
as careful as it can be.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is there any qualification as to nationality?
Mr. BARBOUR: I understand that so
long as a person is living in Northern
Ireland he is qualified to be considered.
Mr. BYRNE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman let us know the number of

Mr. POLLOCK: If hon. Members will
refer to the first page of the Measure of
which I now move the Second Reading,
they will see a description of the Bill and
also the different parts into which it is
divided. Its main purpose is to apply
one single general principle to a number
of detailed cases. The Bill moreover is,
I am glad to inform hon. Members, almost
entirely a non-controversial Measure, as
the changes which it seeks to make have,
with possibly one exception, all been
agreed with the interests affected.
general principle embodied in the Bill is
clearly enunciated in the Preamble of the
Bill itself and is as follows:-
The
It is intended that the first general
revaluation of rateable property in
Northern Ireland shall not disturb the
effect of such existing enactments and
instruments as operate by reference to
specified amounts of rateable value or
specified rates in the pound.
Except in the few cases with which I
shall deal separately later on, the application of this general principle is purely a
matter of a simple arithmetical adjustment, based in general on the average
percentage increase in valuations in the
Province consequent on revaluation. For
example, sub-clause (1) of Clause 1 seeks
to amend the rating qualification of jurors
in the cities, based on the revaluation
figures, so as to render eligible for jury
service largely the same classes of persons
as were rendered eligible by existing enactments based on the old valuation.
other words, where before revaluation a
person in the city occupying property
which had a rateable valuation of £20 or
over was eligible for jury service, now,
under sub-clause (1) of Clause 1 of the
Bill, only those persons occupying
property of rateable valuation of £29 or
over on the new valuation will be eligible
In
for jury service. The percentage increase
represented by the increase of £9 in the
minimum rating qualification thus laid
down in the Bill approximates to the
average percentage increase in the valuation of rateable property in the cities
consequent on revaluation. An exactly
similar arithmetical method of giving
effect to the general principle of the Bill
has been applied in Clauses 2, 4, 5, 6, 7,
10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
Clause 2 applies exactly the same
principle to those entitled to vote for the
election of Harbour Commissioners;
Clauses 4 and 5 deal with matters in connection with liquor licences; in Clause 6
it will be found that the contribution from
local authorities and the cost of public
libraries will be settled; under Clause 7
the contribution for the purpose of public
parks will be dealt with; Clause 10 deals
with the rates to be paid by the owners of
small house property, and Clause 11
deals similarly with the water rates
to be paid by the owners of small
house property; Clause 12 provides
for the poundage to be paid into the
General Cattle Diseases Fund; Clause 13
is in connection with the contributions
from the rates of Bangor and Carrickfergus towards the harbours in those
towns, and Clause .14 deals with the net
annual value of certain industrial hereditaments. All these Clauses are adjusted
upon the general arithmetical principle I
have outlined.
The Clauses to which this arithmetical
method has not been applied and in
respect of which it will be necessary for
me to give hon. Members some expłanation, are Clauses 3, 8, 9, 15, 16 and 17.
Clause 3 is merely declaratory and is
designed to remove any doubts as to the
effect of revaluation on the Rent Restriction Acts. It declares that these Acts
shall continue to apply to the same
dwelling-houses and mortgages to which
they applied before revaluation.
The effect of Clause 8 is to leave unchanged the existing minimum rate which
may be levied over a rural district for
the purpose of agricultural education.
At present a rate of at least 1d in the
pound has to be levied over rural districts
for the purpose of agricultural schemes.
which are administered through County
Committees of Agriculture. The State
contribution is in the proportion of about

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
3 to 1 to the local contribution. County
Committees of Agriculture, speaking
generally, are at the moment in need of
additional funds. It is not an uncommon
failing. The position arising out of the
new valuations has been discussed with
County Councils, and the Association of
these Councils has passed a resolution
unanimously agreeing to the suggestion
that the existing rate should be levied
on the new valuations; consequently, so
far as this point is concerned, no modification of existing legislation is necessary.
The effect of Clause 9 is to continue on
the new valuation the existing maximum
domestic water rate of 4s 6d in the
pound, which may be paid to the Belfast
City and District Water Commissioners
under the Belfast Water Acts. As this
represents in effect an appreciable increase in the Water Commissioners'
rating power it will be necessary for me
to explain to hon. Members the reasons
why the Government have decided to
leave the existing limit of 4s 6d in the
pound untouched. When during the
course of the preparation of the Bill the
Government submitted to the Water Commissioners the proposal that the existing
rating limit of 4s 6d should be reduced
in accordance with the percentage increase in the new valuations so as to leave
the Commissioners' rating power approximately the same, the Commissioners submitted arguments which convinced the
Government that any reduction in the
existing rating limit would be prejudical
to the financial interests of the ratepayers
whom the Commissioners represented.
The Commissioners pointed out that a
reduction of the present rating limit
would not only adversely affect their
future borrowings, but that it also would
be a breach of faith with their existing
stock-holders, in both of which views I
entirely agreed. Hon. Members will
readily appreciate how the market value
of the Commissioners' stock depends on
the margin of the available rating power
behind the stock. If the Government,
therefore, were to give effect in this particular case to the general principle of
the Bill, investors in both existing and
future stock of the Commissioners would
simply note a reduction in the maximum
limit of rating, but would not readily
appreciate that the increased valuation
to which the limit applied rendered the
actual rating power unaltered. As the
interest on borrowings, which have been
obtained at very low rates, forms nearly
50 per cent. of the Commissioners' annual
expenditure hon. Members will appreciate
the Government's anxiety that it should
do nothing which would adversely affect
the Commissioners' borrowings and thus
ultimately the water ratepayers. The
water ratepayers, moreover, are afforded
a measure of protection against any tendency of the Water Commissioners to
take advantage of the increased rating
power given by this Clause, by the fact
that the Commissioners are precluded by
statute from levying a rate that would
produce a greater sum than is required
for any one year's expenditure. That in
itself is almost sufficient guarantee that
the maximum rate of 4s 6d in the pound
may be perfectly safely admitted.
Clause 15 lays down an amended basis
for the valuation of the contribution
towards the rates to be made during the
next five years by the Belfast Harbour
Commissioners. The Clause gives effect
to what, in the opinion of the Government, is a reasonable compromise on a
matter which has been the subject of a
difference of opinion between the Belfast
Corporation and the Harbour Commissioners. I do not propose to weary
hon. Members with a long statement of
the arguments, pro and con, in this
matter, but in order to make the Clause
intelligible to hon. Members it will be
necessary for me to give a short explanation of the existing method of fixing the
Harbour Commissioners' contribution to
city rates, and then, perhaps, briefly
indicate the opposing points of view of
the effect of revaluation on it. Partly
owing to the special difficulties inherent
in an attempt to value the Harbour Commissioners' property-hon. Members will
understand that that would be impossible
in the case of such a vast area as the
Harbour property-and partly owing to
the fact that the property is to a large
extent a self-contained estate providing
most of its own services-that is to say
the services which are ordinarily provided
by a municipality for its ratepayers-a
special statutory arrangement for the
assessment of the Commissioners' contribution to city rates was entered into
with the Corporation in 1896. This
arrangement was re-affirmed as recently
as 1925 by section 13 of the Belfast Cor-

of the growth of the tonnage in the port

increasing contribution from the Board.
That is the Harbour Commissioners' case.
an
The Belfast Corporation, on the other
hand, submitted that the tonnage rates of
2d and 4d on which the existing assessment was based should be increased in
proportion to the general increase of
valuations in the city consequent on revaluation.
While the Government were strongly
impressed by the weight of the arguments on both sides, they felt that a
reasonable compromise should be effected.
As, however, the parties were unable to agree amongst themselves,
the Clause as it now stands represents
what in the view of the Government is a
reasonable compromise in the matter. It
ensures that the Harbour Board will not
get substantial relief from the burden of
rates at the expense of other ratepayers,
and yet at the same time gives some
expression to the fact that the Harbour
Board's property has, unlike other property, been subject to what was in effect
an annual revaluation.
Before turning from this Clause I
desire to inform hon. Members that, in
I come now to Clause 16. In many
leases a Clause is inserted restricting the
lessee from building houses of less than
a certain valuation. Provision is made
in Clause 16 for altering this valuation
either by agreement or by reference to a
tribunal.
Turning to Clause 17, which deals with
the rates payable by tenants under housing schemes, in some housing schemes
under the Housing Acts (N.I.), 1890-
1933, there are agreements between the
local authority, who is the landlord, and
the tenants that all or part of any
increase in the poundage of local rates
after a date specified in the agreement
will be borne by the tenant.
In Belfast, for example, the effect of
revaluation will be that although the
actual amount of rates payable on a Corporation house may be the same or even
greater, the poundage will be less. The
intention of the agreement would thereby
be frustrated, and the present Clause has
been inserted at the request of the Corporation. Its effect is to substitute the
actual sum payable as rates for the
poundage. I repeat that this Clause has
been inserted in response to the desire
expressed by the Belfast Corporation.
Provision is also made in the Clause
for the settlement by the Ministry of
Home Affairs of disputes between a local
authority and its tenant about the correctness of any addition of the kind to rent.
In case some hon. Members may, perhaps, be wondering why the Bill does not
include a reference to the education and

the unemployment levies, I would remind

arrangement is, therefore, that local
authorities will make a net contribution

towards the cost of educational services.
With regard to the unemployment levy
imposed upon local auhorities by the
Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934,
hon. Members are no doubt aware that
this levy does not come into operation
until after the second appointed day has
been fixed, and moreover that the amount
of the levy to be paid after the financial
year ending on 31st March, 1937, is to
be determined by Parliament. The
Government, therefore, think it unnecessary to include any reference to the
unemployment levy in this Bill. I beg
to move.

Mr. HENDERSON: The right hon.
Gentleman has explained very fully the
provisions of this Bill, but I think this is
an opportune time for the Prime Minister
and the right hon. Gentleman to be a
little more democratic so far as Clause 2
of this Bill is concerned. I want to know
why this Government think themselves fit
to make a law whereby no one in Northern
Ireland will have an opportunity of standing for the Harbour Board unless he lives
in a house of £100 valuation. This is
the greatest crime that has ever been perpetrated. The object of this Clause is to
keep the brains of the country out of the
Harbour Board. I am not going to say
that the Member for Pottinger, the Member for Falls, or I, myself, have great
qualifications, but I will say this, that if
we were members of this Board the
citizens of Belfast would know more about
its workings.
I do not think there is in existence
to-day any organisation which keeps its
business more secret than the Harbour
Board, and if there is any body in real
need of live wires it is that Board. I can
compare the Board to nothing but a beehive without bees. The Harbour Commissioners have greater power than the
Government of the country. But I
protest in the strongest manner possible
against the provisions of this Bill so far as
the Harbour Commissioners are concerned.
I protest on behalf of the intelligent
people of Northern Ireland, whom I have
the privilege of representing in this
House. I want to know why the Prime
Minister of this country, in the year 1936,
should introduce an undemocratic Clause
like this. Is it fair? How many citizens
of Northern Ireland are in the fortunate
position of living in a house of £100
valuation? Owing to the manner in
which they are being taxed the people are
going into smaller houses. I think this
is a great penalty the Government are
inflicting upon the middle class and
working-class people as a whole.
I want to ask the Prime Minister to
tell the House why this Clause has been
introduced. Is it with the object of
keeping the Harbour Board a select body,
and of refusing to allow working men the
privilege of sitting on that Board? Under
this Clause no working man will have the
privilege or the honour of becoming a
member of the Harbour Board. That
state of things should not exist in a
democratic country. One would expect
that kind of thing in Germany or in Italy,
but I could not bring myself to think that
the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland,
for whom the citizens, as a whole, have
such high respect, would identify himself
with such an undemocratic Clause.
The Minister of Finance has pointed
out that we require a man with a
thorough knowledge of grain. If it were
a case of brains, all I ask is that Members should look at a list of the Harbour
Commissioners and say to yourselves,

stood as an Independent. For the first

upon being one of the finest Boards,

third it certainly used to stand about

of the Board in years gone by, and I am

Secondly, I think that Belfast itself is

with the Government, and, secondly,
that they should work harmoniously
among themselves. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) You cannot divorce the
importance of our harbour and the

they are bound together in every sense
for trade and commerce, and for the

That was done rather than have it said

The other point made by the hon. Member was that this Board should be treated
in exactly the same way as Parliament, that is to say, there should be the
same franchise. It may interest him to

Vagrancy Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. CAMPBELL: In asking the
House to give a Second Reading of this
Bill, I am asking it to purge from the
Statute Book as a means test of crime.
It is 112 years since the passing of the
Vagrancy Act of 1824. This injustice is
a survival of barbaric conditions of a time
when there was no organised police force.
The blot was removed from the Statute
Book in June 1935 so far as it related to
England. The repeal of the obnoxious
section in the Vagrancy Act was accomplished with the assent of the Unionist,
Labour, and Liberal parties in the
British Parliament. The Bill at Westminster was presented by Brigadier-
General Spears, and supported by Lord
Eustace Percy, Mr. Churchill, Admiral
of the Fleet Sir Roger Keyes, Mr. Lansbury, and Major-General Sir Alfred Knox,
From no quarter was it criticised or
opposed.
The principle they all agreed on
that no man should be sent to jail because
he cannot buy a night's lodging. That
was the principle that won universal commendation at Westminster. If you have
money and delight to meander about the
country lanes or sleep under the hedges
the police are powerless to stop you. You
commit no offence. Some people make
a hobby of sleeping out in the summer
time. If you are well-to-do you are all
right. You break no law. If, however,
you are poor, or to put it as the Section
puts it,
"not having visible means of
subsistence, and not giving a good
account" of yourself, this enactment
makes you a rogue and a vagabond. It
makes you a criminal. You are liable to
three months' imprisonment.
Vagrancy Bill-
Second Reading
3 MARCH 1936
It is a strange law which in the year
1936 sends a man to jail because he cannot buy a night's lodging. Surely this
enactment goes some way to give colour
to the old outcry of one law for the rich
and another for the poor. Its continuance among the enactments affecting
Northern Ireland is an outrage on the
public conscience. Why does it cumber
the Statute Book? A man on this charge
can be brought before one ordinary
justice of the peace. This is not one of
the offences withdrawn from their jurisdiction and entrusted to two trained
magistrates. This offence is still within
the purview of any ordinary inexperienced magistrate.
The Vagrancy Act is not a dead letter.
It is very much a live Act. It has not to
be raked from the dust of forgotten laws.
From the last statistics of the Ministry
of Home Affairs there were 345 convictions under the Vagrancy Acts in 1930,
307 in 1931, 331 in 1932, 376 in 1933,
and in 1934 the number shot up to 452.
What stirred the public mind in
England was the tragic case of Thomas
Parker, who died in Winson Green Jail
in June, 1933. That led to the repeal
of this obnoxious section in 1935. Parker
was an ex-Guardsman. He enlisted
during the war while under age and
served in France. In the piping times of
peace he had long spells of want of work.
In the summer of 1933 he started walking
to Tamworth in search of employment.
He was arrested for sleeping out. A
policeman woke him and he confessed he
had no money. The policeman did his
duty. His duty was plain because the
law was plain. He arrested Parker.
The magistrates at Coleshill did their
duty. They sentenced this man, who
had never been in jail before, to fourteen
days' imprisonment.
a
According to the prison doctor Parker
probably suffered from claustrophobia, a
nervous disease which gives a man
horror of being shut up. He cannot
stand confined places and longs for the
broad and wide open spaces. Parker
probably became frenzied by resentment
against what he must have felt to be an
injustice. He was sent to three days'
solitary confinement by
by the prison
governor for creating a disturbance in
prison and on the way to the punishment
cell met with injuries from which death
ensued in fifteen minutes.
That was a tragic chapter of accidents
in the case of a man of his antecedents,
his war service, and his unimpeachable
character. So intense was the indignation of the public that the Home Secretary made inquiries among the Chief
Constables of England, and as a consequence was convinced that the law
needed amendment. Thus was tragedy
worked under this enactment. Can anyone possessed of common humanity stand
for a
law which makes this possible?
Parker's fate is not only possible but also
probable in this area in the case of some
poor honest wayfarer for whom the
world has been too much.
This Bill in no way touches the case
of the dishonest wanderer. The police
have ample powers for dealing with him,
but I would like this House to say, as
the British House said unanimously,
there should be a shield of protection
thrown round the honest man, say the
honest ex-service man, wandering in
search of work, with his last penny gone.
He has no work and no funds, and may
be, perhaps, within ten or twenty miles
of a workhouse. Workhouses are getting
less common in this country than they
used to be. A man of that kind, with
an unimpeachable record, if he falls
asleep and is wakened by a policeman and
cannot give a good account of himself
is sent to jail because he has not the
money to pay for a night's lodgings. I
do not propose to touch upon those words

a
give a good account of himself." In
the case of the honest wayfarer I have
visualised the police have no alternative
but to arrest. In fact, as the law stands
now, anyone may arrest the man,
civilian may arrest him under those circumstances, and when he is brought
before the magistrate the magistrate must
discharge his duty and sentence him to
imprisonment.
A County Tyrone instance of the working of this enactment may be given. A
wayfarer who had no shelter for the night
was directed by a compassionate constable to a place where he might rest
overnight. He went there obedient to
the directions. Whilst resting in this
place another constable, who knew
nothing of what had happened earlier in
the night, came along, questioned him,
brought him to the police barrack and
detained him there. In the morning he
was charged before a justice of the peace
Vagrancy Bill---
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
under the enactment, and as a rogue and
vagabond was convicted and sentenced to
the maximum term of imprisonment.
Somehow, probably through the police,
the facts came under the notice of the
Home Office which, to their credit,
ordered the man's immediate release. Is
it not strange that a law of that kind
should be still on our Statute Book, when
they have got rid of it in England? Why
should the law affecting poor, honest
people be different in the two areas?
I have already said that the Bill proposes in no way to touch the case of the
dishonest wayfarer. Section 57 of the
Summary Jurisdiction Act of 1935 still
leaves the dishonest wayfarer within the
meshes of the law, because if a man is
found in any open area, or dwelling
house, or any place, for an unlawful purpose, or is suspected of anything of a
felonious kind, he is still exposed to the
perils of the Act of 1924. There the
police have ample powers to deal with the
dishonest wayfarer. I would not stand
up to defend a man of that type and
class.
I do not know what the attitude of the
Government will be with regard to this
Bill. To successive reforms of the
criminal law during the past hundred and
fifty years there has been one recurring
and retrograde ground of opposition,
that is, that no change was necessary.
"Do nothing" was the advice given, and
it was very often taken. If that plea
had been accepted in days gone by a great
many of the 200 offences which at the
close of the eighteenth century were
capital offences under our criminal law
would still be capital offences to-day. The
necessity for cleansing and I use the
word "cleansing" advisedly-our Statute
Book of this odious enactment, by which
an honest, poor man can have three
months' imprisonment inflicted upon him.
by an ordinary magistrate is, I submit,
obvious. How many honest poor men will
have to go to jail as rogues and vagabonds, because they are penniless, before
opponents of this Bill will see that a
change is necessary? How
have
many
gone there already, branded as rogues and
vagabonds, smarting under a burning
sense of injustice, and probably under
that sense of injustice transformed into
enemies of society?
Of course it may be said that if a man
can give a good account of himself he is
perfectly safe, but I do submit to the
House that, in the case of a destitute
man, out of work, hungry and ragged,
run in without a penny in his pocket,
those words, "not giving a good account
of himself," are a mere form of speech
under such circumstances. I do ask the
House to remember that one factor in this
matter is the increasing dearth of workhouse or other accommodation. I do not
know whether, coming from the Opposition, a Bill of this kind will get very much
favour, but I do hope that some hon.
Members will be found to give it a hearing
on its merits. If you think it is a fair,
progressive Measure, I ask you to give
it a hearing on its merits. I bring it
forward, and I ask the House to accept
it in the same spirit-for the protection of
the poor, however down and out, if of
good character-and as a matter of
elementary justice. Give this Bill a
Second Reading and purge the Statute
Book, as it was purged in England in
1935, of the one surviving enactment
which, so far
far as my knowledge and
memory go-and I do ask the House to
bear this in mind-makes honest poverty
a crime.
Very, very briefly shall I advert to the
Clauses of the Bill. Clause 1, sub-clause
(1) provides that the part of Section 4 of
the Act of 1824 as amended by Section 57
of the Summary Jurisdiction and Criminal
Justice Act of 1935 which enacts that a
person found under the circumstances I
have described to the House, shall be
deemed to be a rogue and a vagabond,
shall have effect, subject to the provisions
of this Clause.
Sub-clause (2) repeals the words "not
having any visible means of subsistence."
These are the only words repealed by this
Bill. It is not proposed to repeal any
other part of the Act. The words, "not
giving a good account of himself," remain
untouched. A person wandering and
lodging under the circumstances I have
attempted to describe to the House will
still, under the law, have to give a good
of himself. Surely that is
sufficient safeguard against any possible
mischief on
the part of undesirable
wanderers.
account
Sub-clause (3) provides that a person
wandering abroad and lodging in these
circumstances shall not be deemed a rogue
Vagrancy Bill—

and a vagabond, unless certain facts are
proved, for instance:
"That, in relation to the occasion on
which he lodged as aforesaid, he had
been directed to a reasonably accessible
place of shelter and either did not apply
for, or refused to accept, accommodation there; or
"That he is a person who persistently
wanders abroad and, notwithstanding
that a place of shelter is reasonably
accessible, lodges or attempts to lodge

"That by, or in the course of, lodging
as aforesaid he caused damage to

to do."
Then there is a definition of the words,
"a place of shelter," and in sub-clause (4)
there is an enactment that a person
lodging under a tent or in a cart or
waggon shall not be deemed to include a
person lodging under a tent or in a cart
or waggon with or in which he travels.
For the reasons I have mentioned, I commend this Bill and ask the House to adopt
the principle of it as a right, humane,
and progressive principle.
Mr. BYRNE: I have great pleasure
in seconding this Bill. It has been so

Mr. HANNA: I have been greatly
impressed by the manner in which the
hon. and learned Gentleman has introduced this Bill, and I at once acquit him
of any intent other than to try to reduce
the possibility of undue interference with
people simply because they are poor and
in humble circumstances and have no
visible means of subsistence. But I would
point out that the law in regard to this
matter, as established by the Summary
Jurisdiction Act of last year, makes the
position very clear. Two conditions
must exist before the wayfarer can be
interfered with. The first condition is
that he must not have any visible means
of subsistence. But he cannot be
arrested simply because he has no means
of subsistence. The other condition is
additional, and it is that he fails to give
a good account of himself. I do not care
how poor or how humble any person is,
I think it is only reasonable and right, if
he is trespassing on other people's
property, lodging in other people's barns,
sleeping in other people's hay, that the
man who owns the barn, or the man who
owns the hay, should have the right to
ask that gentleman what occasions his
being there, and if he cannot give a satisfactory answer then he can either arrest
him himself or cause him to be arrested.
I would like to feel that I share the common humanity about which my hon.
and learned Friend talked, but I cannot
see that there is any lack of humanity
in adopting a course of that kind.
I freely admit that this Bill, as introduced by my hon. and learned Friend, is
exactly in the same terms as the Bill that
passed all its stages in the Imperial House
and that now stands upon the Imperial
Statute Book. But my respectful submission to the House is that there was a
great deal of misunderstanding in regard
to the matter there. The hon. and
gallant Gentleman who introduced the
Measure in the British House of Com-
Vagrancy Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
mons used language pretty much the same
as my hon. and learned Friend has used
here to-day. He began by saying:
"The purpose of the Bill is simple.
It is to ensure that in future no person
shall be sent to jail for sleeping out just
because he has not the money to find
himself a night's lodging. The law as
it stands is flagrantly unjust."
That is not the fact. No man can be put
in jail simply because he has not got
money to pay for a night's lodging. It is
true, as the hon. and learned Member
pointed out, that there was a case in
Tyrone, and the facts of that case were
as he represented them. But that was no
fault of the law. That was the fault of
a wrong interpretation of the presiding
magistrate's duty in the matter. Our
attention was immediately drawn to it by
the police, who were not satisfied that the
man was a rogue and a vagabond. Indeed
it was the only way, after having shown
him some clemency, that they could have
him dealt with when, to their very great
surprise, they learned that this had
happened. But because the law was
administered in that way once is no
reason why there should be this change in
the law. The case of Parker, which has
been referred to, I respectfully submit,
could not take place here, because, when
a person is arrested, either by the police
or by any other person, he must be
brought forthwith before a magistrate,
and there the case has to be proved, that
the man had no visible means of subsistence and that he did not and could not
give a proper account of himself.
If to that law, as I have stated it,
the Amendment suggested by the hon. and
learned Gentlemen in this Bill were introduced let us see what the position would
be. He proposes to delete or to repeal the
words "not having any visible means of
subsistence." But that would not prevent this innocent man, who had no
money in his pocket, from being arrested.
It would only increase the right of the
police and all other people to arrest anybody they found wandering, whether they
had money in their pockets or not or
whether they had visible means of subsistence or not so long as they could not
give a proper account of themselves. I
cannot see that in the repeal of those
words there is any protection for the
innocent man. Of course, every hon.
Member of this House knows that the
hon. and learned Gentleman opposite is
not desirous that the dishonest wayfarer
should get out of the difficulty that he
makes for himself. If the hon. and
learned Gentleman's Amendment were
taken, the proofs that would have to be
offered to the magistrate next morning, or
when any wayfarer was brought before
him, would be almost impossible.
Secondly, there are no places of shelter
in Northern Ireland, such as are described
in this Act. As the hon. and learned
Member has pointed out, the number of
workhouses has been very considerably reduced. Take the first thing that would
require to be proved, that the wayfarer
had been directed to a reasonably
accessible place of shelter, and that he had
not applied for or had refused to accept
accommodation there. It occurs to me, as
a result of my experience, that it would be
almost impossible to prove that.
Let us visualise a case. A man is
found lying in a haystack, and under our
law the farmer who discovers him can
arrest him if he cannot give a proper
explanation of why he is there and if he
has no money.
But assume that this Bill
becomes law. What has the farmer got
to do? He has first to ascertain if on
this particular occasion the gentleman
whom he finds lying in his haystack has
been directed to a reasonably accessible
place of shelter, and that he either
has not applied for shelter or has refused
to accept it. In other words he would
have to waken him up, direct him to the
nearest workhouse, and follow him to see
that he went there and made application
for admission. I cannot see how that
could ever be proved. If he failed in that
proof, he would have to prove that the
man was a person who persistently
wandered abroad. How many proofs
would be required for that? He cannot
keep him in jail until he goes for his
witnesses. The direction of the law is that
he be taken forthwith before a magistrate, and how can the farmer get the
evidence that this gentleman, whom he
does not know, who may have money or
who may not, but who has given an
explanation that is not satisfactory, persistently wanders abroad? A reasonably
accessible place of shelter means a place
where provision is regularly made for
giving, free of charge, accommodation for
the night to such persons as apply there.

I know of no places, outside the workhouses of Northern Ireland, where there
is shelter within the meaning of that provision. Another thing that he could not
prove would be that the man was persistently wandering about, or that he had
been directed to a reasonably accessible
place of shelter. He would have to prove
that he had caused damage to property,
or was infected with vermin. To ascertain the facts in relation to some of these
matters I suppose something in the
nature of a cursory search would require
to be made, and again it would be left
