Mr. HANNA: I am asking this House
to give protection to our farmers. Hon.
Members who live in towns do not know
the effect of this in the country. Let us
give the people the protection that they
are entitled to. Why should our farmers
be left at the mercy of such people?
I had hoped that I would not be
asked to express my views forcibly,
but the hon. and learned Member has
suggested that I was taking this Bill too
lightly. To me, as a lawyer, that portion
of it is a joke. I do not care where this
law is in operation. It is incapable of
being administered. I ask this House to
hesitate before it takes away any
right of our farmers to examine these
gentlemen that they find hiding in their
haystacks or barns, and to ask them to
give an explanation of what they are
doing there. I ask the House to hesitate
before they take away the right of the
farmers to protect their own property.
Those of us who are acquainted with the
condition of things in the country know
how many times great losses have been
incurred by farmers by reason of the
burning of their produce, and how difficult it is for the farmers to get damages
for the harm that is done for the very
reason that it is possible the harm is done
by a tramp. Then they cannot get compensation. I hope the House will hesitate
before they make it easier for people,
with or without money, to be out in the
middle of the night in our area if they
cannot give a good account of themselves.

Belfast Hotel Strike.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move, "That
in the opinion of this House the Government should spare no effort to secure a
settlement of the hotel strike.”
This Motion has been so long delayed
that I feel it will not get the attention
its importance deserves. If the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs would remain I would tell
him why these people take to the country
roads, but he is going away. I think
there is a quorum present, but not more.
There are 700 people in Belfast affected
by this strike, and every Member for
Belfast should be here. There is not a
division of the city which has not a
number of waiters or waitresses affected
by this strike. Whether the strike is
right or wrong at the moment is not my
concern. I want to place before the
House the actual facts, and the reason
why these people are walking the streets
of Belfast. The hotel workers are paid
wages, running in the case of men from
10s to 25s a week, and in the case of
girls from 5s to 15s a week, with food
while on duty valued at from 5s to 7s
a week. Their hours run from 60 to 100
for those wages. If the Parliamentary
Secretary for the Ministry of Home
Affairs had been here I would have told
him why those people are out of work,
and why they have to take to the country
to sleep in barns. He has never had to
do that; hence his abuse of the Bill that
was before the House a short time ago.

worker, but
you are not opposed to
taking all the Government can give you

Whether Belfast likes it or not, trade

the right to organise. They will go on

Mr. CAMPBELL: I rise to second the

Motion being adopted by the House today. It exhorts the Government to use
every effort to bring this strike to a
peaceful end. It is a matter for congratulation that so far the strike has
been conducted with perfect propriety
and peace.
There has been no disturbance, no breach of public order.
There has been a long and, apparently,
increasingly bitter struggle. The Member for Pottinger has spoken of the conditions affecting organised labour in the
Free State and Northern Ireland, and
has shown that conditions in the South
imply a better recognition of the rights
and status of organised labour.
The fear of many citizens is that this
strike, if prolonged, will adversely affect
the tourist traffic. It is not a mere local

this dispute to a peaceful end.

There is a large field for persuasion,
for wise action and for efforts of that kind.
Whatever efforts of the kind have been

when asked by both parties to act as conciliators, and that, if I may presume to
say so, we have done now for fifteen years
with, to put it modestly, some success.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The hon. Member for Pottinger also
suggested that a trade board should be
set up in connection with this industry.
That question was thoroughly inquired
into in Great Britain. It was decided
there after very careful inquiry, that this
was not an industry for which a trade
board was suitable.
Then, again, the question of tipping
was discussed by, I think, every Member
who has spoken in this debate. Tipping
may be good, or it may be bad. It is not
my duty to express any opinion in connection with it, but this I say, you might
as well try to stop the tide with a pitchfork as try to stop tipping. The fact is
that certain people like to give a consideration for service rendered. Tipping,
I may say, is almost universal throughout
the world. It is very general in
America; it is general on the Continent;
it is general in the United Kingdom;
and where attempts have been made to
stop it those attempts have not been successful. For instance, some hotel proprietors have adopted the course of adding
ten per cent. to the bill and telling their
employees that they were not to accept
tips, but still the tipping system is found
to exist.
I would just like to say in conclusion
that no one regrets this strike more than
I do. No one is more desirous to see it
ended-and when I speak in that strain I
speak for all my colleagues as well as for
myself-but the difficulties associated
with it are exceptional and outstanding,
and hon. Members opposite cannot expect me to act in a way in which I have
no power to act.

BELFAST CORPORATION AND
MALICIOUS INJURY CLAIMS.
Sir ROBERT LYNN (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Finance
whether the Government have come to
any decision with regard to the Belfast
Corporation's appeal that the Government should meet a portion of their
malicious injury claims.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Yes, sir, I have to inform my
hon. Friend that at a meeting of the
Cabinet, held to-day, it was decided that
the Government could not comply with
the Corporation's request, but were
willing to meet their desire for spreading
the payments over a period not exceeding five years. The Corporation have
been so informed.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the Government being partly responsible for the
protection of property in the city of Belfast, do they not think the Corporation's
claim a justifiable one, and will they,
therefore, make a contribution to the
rates of the city?

follow the Prime Minister's attempt to
is

a very restricted

What is the franchise? A Belfast
citizen in order to become a member of
the Belfast Harbour Board must reside
in one of these Olympian mansions which
are worth at least £100 a year in value.
To be an elector of that Commissioner
the elector must have a comfortable home
of a value of at least £30 a year. That
means that the vast majority of the
citizens of Belfast can have no say in
the constitution of the Belfast Harbour
Board so long as the Prime Minister can
prevent it. They may be good citizens,
they may be highly educated, they may
be competent to elect Cabinet Ministers.
I see the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Labour looking at me. They
may even become Parliamentary Secretaries. They may have all those
qualifications, but they must not aspire in
the city of Belfast to penetrate the
recesses of the Belfast Harbour Office.
That is forbidden ground.
One may admire the frankness of the
challenge, but one rarely nowadays does
hear such almost contemptuous defiance
of democracy. Why does the Prime
Minister think that four out of five of
the citizens of Belfast are unworthy to
be electors of the Belfast Harbour Board?
If this franchise is to be stereotyped,
why are only rich men fit to become Harbour Commissioners? What is their
qualification? It is not necessarily
brains; it is not necessarily good name;
it is not necessarily civic service. The
only qualification is property-always
property. That is a very strong attitude
to take; it is a very defiant attitude to

take. It makes one feel that English

It is unique in these days to hear a

The franchise of the Harbour Board is

the controversy that has arisen seems to
range round the question of who should

members to this Board, and it has been
suggested that a person who is qualified
to vote for a city councillor should
equally be qualified to vote for a harbour
commissioner. In my opinion, those who
make this argument forget one thing,
and that is that when you vote in connection with a local government election
for members of a county council, a city
council, or an urban council, you are
voting for a body that administers matters affecting the lives of the people in
the area, such as the supply of light,
water, and so on.
On the other hand, in voting for members of a harbour board you are electing
a body which administers something outside the business of the ordinary individual, and that is the trade of the city
and port. The distinction is this: that
business interests on which a city exists
and for which the port exists should have
paramount consideration. In an ordinary
local government election it is more a
question of individual interests, but in
the case of a harbour board it is the
trade of the city which is the paramount
interest. To say that Clause 2 of this
Bill restricts the franchise to individuals

that to the notice of the Land Trust.

1. Mr. BYRNE (for Mr. Henderson)

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) The responsibility for putting

CHEAPER MILK FOR
UNEMPLOYED.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he has considered the plan of the English Milk
Marketing Board to distribute milk to
the families of the unemployed in the distressed areas of England and Wales at
2d a pint; whether a sum of £50,000 has
been set aside to meet the cost; and
whether, seeing that milk is the most
necessary element in the dietary of
children, he will give the families of the
unemployed here the benefit of a like
scheme.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I have noticed with
interest that the Milk Marketing Board
and the Commissioner for the Special
Areas in England and Wales propose to
co-operate in a scheme for the provision
of milk at 2d a pint to unemployed
families in distressed areas, and to make
this possible by a subsidy of £50,000. The
main reason for this proposal is that the
minimum retail price of milk in England
and Wales is 3d per pint, and this price
makes it difficult for the poorest consumers to get sufficient milk for their
nutritional needs.
The prices for milk which have been
fixed by the Joint Milk Council for
Northern Ireland, however, enable milk
to be purchased in Belfast at present at
a price of 2d per pint. Outside of
Belfast milk can be purchased at 1d per
pint at the farm. Without any assistance from the Milk Fund or the Treasury,
therefore, poor persons in Northern
Ireland can obtain milk on equally
favourable, if not more favourable terms
than those offered by means of this
subsidy to poor consumers in the distressed areas of England and Wales.
Since all persons, including unemployed,
Northern Ireland, can, therefore,
obtain milk upon the same terms as under
the special scheme for the distressed areas

Ireland; whether it is a fact that this

whether it is a fact that this lady taught
the junior demonstrators who are at
present employed by the Board throughout the Six Counties; whether he is
aware that this lady received from the
late manager on the 24th February, 1936,
a letter stating that he was profoundly
shocked to hear that the Board had
decided to dispense with her services, that
she gave absolute satisfaction to him and
his superiors, that as a mark of appreciation of her services she had been
appointed to take charge of the largest
area in Northern Ireland, and that he

an
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. J. Milne Barbour): I have made
inquiries on the various points raised in
the hon. Member's question, and am
informed that the Electricity Board has
now reached a stage of development
which, in their view, warrants a reduction in administrative charges involving
a retrenchment of staff. Accordingly,
the services of three employees in the
Bangor area have been terminated, and it
is presumed that the hon. Member has in
mind the case of Miss Fox, who was
employed in the Board's show-room at
Bangor.
I am further informed that not until
the notice terminating Miss Fox's
appointment had been issued had the
Board any information as to the offer to
her of an appointment in England. It is
not, I gather, the practice of the Board
at this stage to give any undertaking as
to the permanency of employment, and
there is nothing in the Board's records to
indicate that any departure from the
normal practice has been made in this
case.
The Board has never failed to appreciate
the services which Miss Fox has rendered,
but I am informed that her transfer from
Armagh to the larger area at Bangor was
made to suit her personal convenience.
The Board assure me that the necessity
for a reduction of staff is viewed by them
with the utmost regret, and that it is
their policy, as far as practicable, to
utilise the services of redundant employees in other sections of the undertaking. On this point they have given
an assurance that in the event of any
vacancy for a demonstrator falling to be
filled, the claims of Miss Fox will receive
full consideration.
As regards the final part of the hon.
Member's question, the answer is in the
negative.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment (Agreement) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In moving the Second Reading
of this very important Measure I would
like to remind the House that when I
moved the Money Resolution, which was
its precursor, I entered with very considerable detail into all the minutiae of
the scheme, giving the reasons for the
introduction of the Bill, and also what it
was hoped would be accomplished. I feel,
in view of what I have said, and in view
of the fact that a large number of our
Members have engaged in a detailed discussion of it, that it would be mere
reiteration on my part if I were to enter
to any great extent into the Measure
itself. I may therefore be permitted to
summarise it in a few sentences.
In the year 1926 a Reinsurance Agreement was made between the British
Government and ourselves by which it
was hoped to ensure that our unemployed
people should enjoy similar advantages to
those who were unemployed in other
parts of the Kingdom. But as time went
on it was found that the radical changes
in the whole scheme of unemployment
relief, especially the introduction of the
transitional benefit system, rendered the
Act of 1926 practically abortive and
unfitted to accomplish the end in view.
The Treasury, therefore, generously
Supplementary Estimates
Adjournment

[Mr. Pollock]
agreed to review the whole position
afresh, with the result that a new Reinsurance Agreement has been reached
whereby the Exchequer burden in the
two areas per head of insured population
is equalised.
This Agreement is now printed as a
Schedule to the present Bill, which is
expected to be introduced at Westminster to-day. A White Paper giving
exhaustive details of the scheme was
issued when I moved the Money Resolution and circulated amongst Members.
These documents have
have provided the
fullest details of the conditions of the
Agreement as well as the reasons which
rendered it necessary. I beg to move.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 10th March, 1936.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
ACCIDENTS AT ALBERTBRIDGE-
MADRID STREET JUNCTION.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
the total number of accidents reported
at the junction of Albertbridge and
Madrid Street since the change of traffic
control to the roundabout system;
whether he is aware that this change is
very dangerous to pedestrians and residents in this area; whether he will state
the total number of accidents for a
similar period at this point under the
old system of control; whether he is
aware that children have to cross to and
from school at this point; and, in view
of the grave danger due to this change,
whether he will revert to the old system
of control in the best interests of the
citizens.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): During the four
months ended 29th February, 1936, a
total of 22 accidents, mostly of a
trivial nature, occurred at the junction
mentioned in the hon. Member's
question. During the same period in
the previous year 10 accidents occurred.
The increase in the number of
accidents which has occurred since the
roundabout system of control was introduced was due entirely to want of
familiarity on the part of motorists with
the route to be covered.
The system was introduced in order
to lessen congestion of traffic on the
adjoining section of the Albertbridge
Road, and notwithstanding the increase
in the number of accidents which has
occurred it is too early to decide that it
should be discontinued.
There are no grounds for assuming
that this system of controlling traffic is

of the control of traffic at this point

to life and limb at this point by the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not to

system shall be continued or not. Personally, I believe it should be continued.

does he not think it would be wise to

Sir DAWSON BATES: I would suggest to my hon. Friend that he should
exercise a little patience until we have

TRANSPORT BOARD AND BUS
OWNER.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that an offer of part payment was
recommended by the Transport Board
authorities to one private bus owner,
and that this offer has not been implemented by the Board, and whether he
can give any reasons why this payment
was withheld.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I find some
difficulty in following the drift of the
hon. and gallant Member's question.
The Road and Railway Transport
Act does not require the Board to make
payments on account in advance of the
compensation being settled in accordance
with the terms of the Act, but I am
informed by the Board that, in order to
convenience the former owners, they have
made substantial payments on account,
without prejudice to either side, pending
the settlement of claims for compensation.
I understand that each case is
separately considered, but the Board are
not prepared to disclose the considerations applying to individual cases.
BUS COMPANIES AND
COMPENSATION.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
make a statement as to the basis on
which bus companies are taken over by the
Transport Board, and whether there is
a differentiation in compensation between
what is known as the "big five" and
similar concerns of proportionate value
and importance.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In default of
agreement between the Board and the
vendor, it is provided by the Act that
the amount of compensation is to be
determined by the Arbitration Tribunal
to be set up under the Act, and it is,
therefore, obvious that I can make no
statement on the subject.
I am, however, informed by the Transport Board that in the offers which have
been made by the Board they have
followed principles which were not less
favourable to the owners than those
applied in the case of the five companies.
Major MCCORMICK: In view of the
unsatisfactory nature of the reply, I will
raise this matter on the Adjournment.

CHEAPER MILK FOR CHILDREN
OF UNEMPLOYED.
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he will hold
an inquiry as to the necessity, in the
interests of the nutrition of the children
of the unemployed for a grant of a
reasonable sum to meet the cost of distributing milk to such children at a price
less than the lowest officially fixed price
of milk, having regard to the grant by
the British authorities to the distressed
areas of England and Wales for that
purpose.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The answer
is in the negative. I would refer the
hon. and learned Member to the reply
which I gave to a question raised by him
on Thursday last, and repeat that prices
for milk have been so fixed by the Joint
Milk Council for Northern Ireland that
poor persons in Northern Ireland can
obtain milk on equally favourable if
not more favourable terms, than those
offered by means of a subsidy to poor
consumers in the distressed areas of England and Wales.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Minister does he realise that numbers of
unemployed fathers and mothers in this
area have not the means to provide for
sufficient supply of milk for their
children?
a
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I quite realise
that the hon. and learned Gentleman is
prompted by a very kindly nature. I
think he will also realise that owing to
the very fine work of the Milk Council
composed of all interests, milk has been
put on the market for these poorer people
at a cheaper rate than the subsidised
milk in the distressed areas in England.
He will understand further that if we
went out of step with England in this
matter we should be placed in a very
difficult position financially.
We are a
poorer country and the subsidy that
would be required to carry out what the
hon. and learned Member suggests would
be disadvantageous to us.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Minister
rule out any hope of a reasonable grantin-aid for this purpose?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I cannot say
that I would rule out any hope, but
there is no possibility of doing it at the
present moment. Something may happen
in the future, but at present there is no
reason for it.

£7,196,000. The valuations in the lists
about to become obsolete are £5,367,000.

assume that the hon. and learned Member desires to know what the total of the
rates struck next year will be: this information will not, however, be available
for some months.

Mr. HENDERSON: It is not a matter

The PRIME MINISTER: If there
had been any mismanagement of the
Harbour Trust, if, instead of its being
one of the best conducted of our public
bodies, we had to complain of actions
which they had taken to the detriment of
the general good of the city of Belfast
and the Province, then I should have
listened with some sympathy to the remarks that have been made. But so far
as I have been able to judge during the
past, say, sixty years, the tradition of the
Board has been one of which we may all
be proud. I know what is at the bottom
of the suggestions of the hon. Members
opposite, but I can assure them, as they
seem to doubt it, that our Harbour Board
is the most democratically elected Board
in the United Kingdom, as far as I can
ascertain, dealing with harbour matters.
In order to be able to satisfy hon.
Members if the question was raised again
to-day, I got particulars of the qualifications of the Trustees of the Clyde
Navigation, and also of the Mersey Docks
and Harbour Board. I shall give these
particulars to the hon. Members, because
I do not wish to weary the Committee.
These show that most of these harbour
authorities are composed of people who
are connected in some way with the shipping industry. In Liverpool they will
observe that those who have the right
to be elected as Commissioners must have
paid not less than £25 in dock and
harbour dues in the year prior to election,
and in the case of electors, they must
have paid not less than £10 in dock and
Revaluation Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
harbour dues in the year prior to the
election. Those qualifications concentrate the management of the Trust in
those who are accustomed to shipping
affairs.
It must be remembered, as I said the
other day, that the same thing applies to
nearly all of the harbour authorities. I
have not got the particulars of the Port
of London Authority, but I am sure the
same satisfactory arrangement prevails
there. The Trustees of the Clyde Navigation Company must have paid not less
than £25 in harbour dues during the
year, and the electors must have paid not
less than £10 in harbour dues during the
year. Therefore, hon. Members have
been carried away. I do not know
whether it is genuine or not, or whether
it is a case of putting forward arguments
simply in order to raise the question.
But we must look to the future of our
area. There is no doubt whatever in the
minds of
anyone that the Belfast
Harbour Commissioners are the proper
management for the best interests of the
people.
I am taking this matter on my own
shoulders at the request of the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Commerce,
because he, too, like the Minister of
Finance, is a Harbour Commissioner. At
the beginning of this matter they asked
me to take this off their hands, as they
did not wish, directly or indirectly, to
be associated with the arguments that
might take place. Therefore, I am
apologising for the Minister of Commerce,
who is in charge of the Bill, on this
ground. I do hope that the Committee
will pause before acceding to a suggestion which would gravely alter the situation as it is to-day, because, as you, sir,
have very lucidly explained to the Committee, this Bill is not intended to make
alterations of that kind. The time to
make alterations with regard to the
qualifications of those who may sit upon
the Board or of those who may elect the
Commissioners is when a proposal to
change the constitution of the Board
comes up, if it ever does. This is not
the place by a side wind to get in something which would gravely alter the situation as it is to-day, because the Bill has
been framed most cautiously to preserve
the ratio in the qualifications as it was
before the introduction of the Bill.
At any rate, under no circumstances
will I go back on my statement of the
other day, that no change will take place
as long as I have the honour to be in the
position I am in to-day, because I feel
I am doing the right thing in the interests
of the public, in the interests of Belfast,
and in the interests of Ulster.

declaratory Clause,
is not

two, could clarify the air a good deal.
Mr. BLACK: This Clause is quite a
proper Clause to have in the Bill, which
would be defective without such a Clause.
It is essential that this revaluation should
not take out of protection houses already
within the protection of the Acts.
Mr. BEATTIE: We agree.
Mr. BLACK: My objection to the
Clause is that it does not go to the root
of the matter. What I think ought to
have been done is that the Clause ought
to have provided that houses subject to
the Rent Restrictions Acts, when being
valued, should be valued in the light of
the rents obtainable under the Rent
Restrictions' Acts. A few days ago we
extended the duration of the Rent
Restrictions Acts to 1940, and I venture
to say there is no man in this Committee
but is well aware they will eventually be
extended to 1950 and 1960. The result
of that is that the amount of rent any
landlord gets out of houses now is limited
by Act of Parliament. My suggestion
is that the valuation ought to take place
upon the basis of the actual rent obtainable out of the houses and not upon the
basis of some fanciful rent which is not
obtainable out of the houses, which will
not, under present legislation, be obtainable before 1940, and which, I venture
to say, will not be obtainable until 1950
or 1960 at the earliest.
The CHAIRMAN: I have to call the
attention of my hon. and learned Friend
to the fact that we are not now debating
the principle of valuation. That is not
the purpose of this particular Clause. It
proposes to keep within the protection of
the Rent Restrictions Acts exactly such
houses as are now under it.
Mr. BLACK: What this Clause purports to do is to deal with a problem raised
by the Rent Restrictions Acts, and what
I am venturing to suggest to the Committee is that this Clause in its present
form does not deal adequately with it,
and that it should have been presented in
another form dealing in a proper manner
with this question. As the Committee
is aware, by the decision of the House
of Lords in the Poplar case, it was held
that under the law then existing in the
metropolis-in London-that in making
valuations the provisions of the Rent
Restrictions Acts were not to be taken
into account, and accordingly, valuations
in England are made on the basis that
the Rent Restrictions Acts never existed.
That has been followed by the Recorder
of Belfast.
My suggestion is that this Clause ought
to be put in such a form that you should
get back to the actual rent arising out of
a house. The result of the Clause in this
form is that it presses hard upon both
Revaluation Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
the tenant and the landlord, because the
tenant will be paying the rates on a rateable valuation which has no reference to
the rent of the house but to a fanciful
rent, while the landlord will be paying
Schedule A income tax on a basis which
is quite inequitable when compared with
other owners of property. The result in
regard to the landlord is this, that if two
men have two streets of property, one
protected and one not protected, by the
Act, if they are similar houses they are
valued on the same basis. In respect of
the houses which are decontrolled, the
landlord pays Schedule A income tax on
a valuation which is quite right, but in
regard to the houses which are controlled,
though the landlord of those houses may
not be getting from them more, perhaps,
than half the rent his neighbour gets,
nevertheless he has to pay Schedule
A income tax on exactly the same basis
as the other man.
That is a great injustice, because what
you have is two men paying income tax
at the same rate on what are two quite
different amounts of income. That seems
to me to be quite wrong. I have raised
this matter in this House before, but
nobody seems to pay any attention to it.
Instead of this Clause I should have
welcomed a Clause going to the root of the
matter.
The CHAIRMAN: That would require
a separate and distinct Clause.
Mr. MURPHY: While I quite agree
with what has fallen from the hon. and
learned Member before me, it may be
that that would require a new Clause. I
do not know if it does require a new
Clause introduced into this Bill or some
other Bill. May I say a word or two in
regard to what the hon. Member for
Pottinger has said? He is apprehensive
that under this Clause, as it stands, if the

to £30 the occupier of that dwelling-house
will not have a vote for the Harbour
Board because the dwelling-house continues subject to the conditions of the
Rent and Mortgage Interest (Restrictions) Acts, 1920 to 1932. So far as I
am acquainted with the Belfast Harbour
Acts there is nothing in them that I am
aware of that would in any way prevent
a person who is in occupation of a
dwelling-house with the necessary ratable
qualification from voting in a harbour
election; nor can I conceive any wording
in any Harbour Act that would include
any reference to the Rent and Mortgage
Interest (Restrictions) Acts.
I apprehend that the hon. Member for
Pottinger, who has raised this point, is
definitely under a misconception as to the
results of this increase in valuation. It
seems to me, subject to what we hear
from the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Commerce, that once a house
is increased in rateable value, say to £30,
the person who occupies that house,
whether that house is subject to the Rent
and Mortgage Interest (Restrictions)
Acts or not, will become entitled to
exercise the franchise at harbour
elections, because he is in rateable occupation of premises with the necessary rateable value.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Minister
who is putting this Clause before the
Committee give me that assurance ?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes, certainly.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is, you confirm
what the hon. and learned Member for
the City of Derry has said, and you

Clause, accordingly, ordered to stand

Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to move that
this Clause be rejected, or deleted from
the Bill. I do so because I have a great
deal of knowledge of the operation of
this Clause. For many years I served on
the local authority under the old provision which laid down that the limit of
expenditure from the public authorities
should be 3d in the pound. That limit
of 3d in the pound was in operation at
a time when conditions in the city of
Belfast bore absolutely no relationship to
the conditions under which the 3d was
brought into existence. There was a time
gap or difference of about sixty to
seventy years as between the bringing in
of the 3d limit and the conditions which
prevailed at the time I first came into
Revaluation Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
contact with the operation of this Clause.
Subsequently to that a lot of the more
public-spirited representatives in the
Belfast Corporation started a campaign
for the abolition of the limit altogether.
Why should there be a limit imposed
by the Government upon the expenditure
on parks? A local authority like the
Belfast Corporation is deemed to be a
gathering of public-spirited people,
possessed of a certain amount of common
sense, and having some regard to public
expenditure. That is what they are
generally deemed to be. If those people,
who are entrusted with the destinies of
the city of Belfast, cannot be held to be
capable of deciding what shall be the
legitimate expenditure I do not see who
is better entitled or qualified to do it.
The most public-spirited citizens in the
Belfast Corporation espoused the point
of view that the 3d limit ought to be
removed, and that 3d limit was changed
to 6d by the Ministry of Home Affairs, I
believe.
Now, in accordance with the general
provisions of this Bill, it is deemed expedient to reduce that 6d to 44d, leaving
the actual financial position in much the
same condition as it was under the 6d.
I concede that fact immediately. In so
far as the Government seek to maintain
the status quo ante they are going as
near to it as mathematical calculation
will permit them. But I was in disagreement with the limitation of 6d. I
would point out to the Government that
when the Ministry of Home Affairs
granted this limit of 6d we in Belfast
had not all the parks and public places
under our control. Since we got this
6d limit from the Government we have
taken under our control the Grove playing fields in the city of Belfast, and
any of the public representatives either
in Parliament or the City Council, who
are cognisant of the trend of events
throughout the city of Belfast, will
appreciate the enormity of the task which
confronted the Corporation when they
began the work of developing that site,
and making modern provision in the
realm of equipment to cater for the
requirements of the sporting populace
and child life in that end of the city.
Consequently, before the ink was right
dry upon the paper the 6d limit imposed
by the Ministry of Home Affairs had
ceased to be as practicable as the 3d rate
was before, or very near it. Therefore,
those of us in the Corporation who were
brought into direct contact with this
question from week to week realised that
the Corporation was being saddled with
responsibilities owing to the increasing
civic demand for improved amenities for
which there was no adequate allowance
as permitted by the Government.
Therefore, I am to-day in favour of
rejecting this Clause, which seeks to limit
the amount of expenditure on the part of
a municipality like the city of Belfast to
44d in the pound, and allowing the 6d
limit to remain. I am going to suggest
to the House of Commons, the Prime
Minister, the Minister of Commerce, and
all concerned, that an overwhelming case
can be made out in Belfast at the present
time for a limit of 6d in the pound being
placed in the hands of the municipality
for the development of parks and public
places. In view of our municipal commitments in the city of Belfast to do
otherwise would undoubtedly be tying
the hands of the public representatives
who have been sent by the citizens to
discharge a trust and who are endeavouring to do it to the best of their ability.
For those reasons, therefore, I move the
deletion of this Clause.
Mr. HENDERSON: I rise to second
the rejection of this Clause. The hon.
Member for Dock has very ably pointed
out the restrictions that are going to be
placed upon the Belfast Corporation by
this provision. In fact, it applies to
every municipality throughout Northern
Ireland. I do not see any reason why
there should be any restriction. At the
present time there are too few parks.
We do not want the hands of the Belfast
Corporation to be tied, and I am sure
many hon. Members on the other side of
the Committee will support us in this
matter. If they do not, then I say they
are not doing their duty in the interests
of the people who returned them here,
because outside Belfast the situation is
absolutely hopeless. Nothing is being
done in the matter of providing parks
for the people unless some well-to-do
person leaves a bit of ground that would
not make a decent cabbage plot.
We are anxious to see greater facilities
provided for the people in Northern Ireland to become Al citizens. I am sure

and the abolition of

Schedule, page 14, line 7, to leave out

It is hardly necessary for me to give

has been hit. Two years ago the Minister

reduction of a million pounds from the

the business has been reduced by more
than one-half by increased taxation,

should be taken as the basis. This is
infinitesimal so far as the finances of the
Government are concerned, and it will
be an indication from the Government
that they do not want to starve the trade.
Take, for instance, the Government
legislation with regard to clubs.

representatives of the police with a view
to the better control of our city's traffic.
If it was the Belfast Corporation I could

given in reply to my question to-day. I
can prove beyond the shadow of a doubt
that for the four months 22 accidents have
taken place owing to the adoption of the
round-about system, and none of them
was of a minor description. They were
all of a very serious kind. That system
will never work at that place owing to the
four roads lying convenient to one
another.
I want to draw the right hon. Gentleman's attention to the Holywood Arches
in his own division. When the change
was made there I was greatly concerned
about the traffic going up Grampian
Avenue, but with all the concern I had
about the crossing at the junction of
Grampian Avenue it was not as dangerous
as at the Albert Bridge, Madrid Street,
the entrance to Woodstock Road, and the
crossing to Ravenhill Road. There are
five or six outlets, and at every point you
are subject to traffic going and coming.
To cross the road at that point has become very dangerous. I do not wish to
make any political capital out of this. It
is in my division the right hon. Gentleman
is experimenting. When representations
were made to him in regard to his own
division he acceded to the request and
changed the traffic from the Holywood
Road via Grampian Avenue to the Upper
Newtownards Road to the old straightthrough system. The old straight-through
system there is slower than the straightthrough system at the Albert Bridge.
Therefore, he cannot justify the retaining
of it at the Albert Bridge and the abolition

as a result of the round-about-if there

-but at the Albert Bridge twenty-two
of a very serious kind have taken place.
I have given personal attention to three
of them.

last week a child was knocked down cross-

What we feel is that if provision is made
for new cottages these other houses will
eventually disappear. But that does not
take away from the responsibility of the
various rural authorities, and if a house
is unsanitary their duty is to have it
examined by their own medical officer and
then go to court and get a closing order.
There is nothing to prevent that house
being opened afterwards if it is properly
repaired. But what the Government feel
is that the first duty of the local authorities is to see how many unsanitary houses.
they have, and then promptly serve notice
on the owners with a view to having them
put right. If they are not prepared to
put those houses right they must be
closed.

Personal Explanation.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I desire to make
a personal explanation regarding a
statement which I made yesterday in
replying to the hon. Member for Antrim
on the Adjournment of the House.
While it is perfectly correct that
nothing has come before my Department
officially from the Antrim Rural Council
in the nature of a proposal for the
erection of labourers' cottages, I now find
that the Council have in fact been
engaged upon the preparation of a
scheme, and that such scheme will shortly
be submitted to my Department.
From further inquiries I am satisfied
that far from refusing to put into
operation the Labourers Acts as
suggested in the hon. Member for
Antrim's question, this District Council
are anxious and willing to co-operate
with my Department in carrying out
their functions in the matter.
I would very much regret if, as a
consequence of this misunderstanding,
any of my remarks may have been unjust
to, or hurt the feelings of, this excellent
local body or its officers. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Motion made, and Question proposed:

be granted to His Majesty on account

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Resolution to grant
a Vote on Account is called for, as hon.
Members are aware, by the fact that
the Estimates for next year cannot be
considered in detail and dealt with in
an Appropriation Bill until some time
later in the Session. In the past it has
been customary to ask the House to vote
a three months' provision, but it will be
observed that the amount required on
account for 1936-37 has been based upon
a four months' provision instead of three,
it having been found in practice that the
smaller amount based on three months
is scarcely adequate having regard to the
date of the passing of the Appropriation
Bill into law.
It would be premature to enter
into the details of any of the Estimates before they are in hon. Members'
hands, and, accordingly, any observations
from me in moving the Resolution will
be of a general character and will merely
deal with the totals as they are shown
in the tabular statement now before the
Committee.
The total for 1936-37 shows a decrease
of £325,467 over the total for the current
year. This result is not, however, a true
indication of the probable saving to the
Exchequer on the Services which are
financed out of Votes. In the first place
the Supplementary Estimate for Unemployment Insurance in respect of the
current year is not included. In the
second place, an examination of the two
columns will show that following the procedure adopted this year suitable provision for grants to local authorities on
account of the postponement of the
Second Appointed Day is omitted in the
meantime, and will be the subject of a
Supplementary Estimate later. In consequence of these two omissions from the
comparative columns, adjustments must
be made before any true comparison can
be effected.
Finally, to get at a true indication of
the net cost to the Exchequer of the Services in question, account must be taken
in each year of the Treasury contribution
towards Equalisation Payments under
the new Unemployment Reinsurance
Vote on Account-

we have had officials carrying on the

if the Minister would consider the
establishment of those officials it really
would be a saving, and would be giving
to them what they are entitled to receive
from the Government. It is pretty unfair to make a man occupy for ten or
fifteen years a post as temporary assistant when his job is a permanent one.
This House is a permanent fixture, in
the meantime anyway, and the staff
attached to it are permanent officials.
Why they should all be rated as temporary
is more than I can understand. Some
have been attached to this House for
fifteen years and they are still graded
as temporary. Such a thing is unknown
outside this Province, and so I would ask
the Minister to consider the advisability
of doing justice to those men and making
their work more efficient by having them
established. One of these officials passed
away recently, and the position in which
his relatives were placed was tragic, due
to his being classified as a temporary
man, although he was in the employment
of the House since the establishment of
this Parliament. On this Vote on
Account I ask that this question which
I have raised should be considered by the
Ministry for the future welfare of the
officials associated with the Houses of
Parliament.

I will refer next to the Minister of

I wish to refer in the first place to the

is an important body in the Six Counties,
had qualified electricians who had served.
their apprenticeships in the Council's

but after the transfer took place,

Then there is the matter of unemployment insurance. We are still longing
and waiting for the second appointed
day. I would be very happy and pleased
to know that the second appointed day
was near at hand, but I am inclined to
think that the object of the British
Government in deliberately holding back
the second appointed day is to shift the
burden of unemployment on to the
shoulders of the local authorities. I
have always claimed that unemployment
was a national responsibility, and I claim
so still. If Britain does not name the
second appointed day I would appeal to
our own Minister to come out and make
the declaration. We are going to have
very heavy burdens on the rates. Belfast
has a difficult period ahead, according to
the speech of the Lord Mayor. Of course
I do not know very much about the
financial affairs of the city of Belfast,
but the Lord Mayor's speech is not in my
opinion, a very heartening one, for the
people of the city. I ask the Minister
now to shoulder his responsibilities and
to make the declaration of the second
appointed day, so that the responsibility
of the State in regard to unemployment
may be fully borne.
Coming back to the Ministry of Home
Affairs, I also wish to refer to the question of prisons, which is a very contentious matter in Northern Ireland. In my
opinion the cost of our prisons is far, far
too high. We have too many prisons
and no prisoners to put into them. I
am glad to know that we have no
prisoners to put into them, because it
shows the peaceful state of the Province.
But why should we keep up buildings
our
that could be rightly done without? I
ask the right hon. Gentleman to close
the Armagh Prison. I believe that that
prison could be closed without any injury
to our prison service. I think the Committee will agree with me that we have
accommodation that would house not
only Armagh prisoners but all
prisoners in any emergency. We have in
Armagh Prison 30 to 40 female prisoners.
For those 30 to 40 female prisoners we
have one governor, one matron, two
principal wardresses, thirteen wardresses,
one male clerk, one warder artificer, one
part-time doctor, three part-time clergymen; a police van runs from Armagh to
Belfast Prison with discharges and from
Belfast Police Courts to Armagh Prison
daily; one constable R.U.C. is employed.
When you total up the cost of that
Armagh prison in itself you find that it
is a pretty heavy responsibility. I claim
that that could be done away with without any injury. In Belfast Prison we
have the old female prison with 150 cells,
six rooms, hospital accommodation,
laundry, two workshops, one kitchen, one
mess room, one reception room, and one
bath room for wardresses, with clothing
stores. That is in the female part of the
Crumlin Road, in which there are only
thirty convicts at the present time. I
am wrong. The convicts do not occupy
that. Those 150 cells and all the accommodation are lying idle at the moment,
because there are no female prisoners up
there.
Then there is the question of the convicts. I have claimed all along that a
short-term prison never should be allowed
to house life prisoners. Convicts may be
reaping the reward of the offences they
have committed, but there is no use in
pursuing a policy of torture, and torture
is the only word I can apply to the conditions of convict prisoners in a shortterm prison such as we have on the
Crumlin Road. It has been put forward
on authority that those who relegate
convicts to prisons such as we have at
the moment on the Crumlin Road are
not travelling on Christian lines. No
man should be housed in that prison for
more than three years. For sentences
longer than three years the prisoners
should either be sent to England or Scotland or you should provide a convict
settlement for them in Northern Ireland,
a thing which I have advocated time

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
after time. It is cruelty and torture to
confine those convicts in that short-term
prison.
For those thirty convicts we have also
to employ nine warders, and we have to
ask those warders to work 454 hours per
week on convict duty. Those men have
to be engaged for that number of hours
on convict duty, which is not a light duty
by any means. As we all know when
a convict gets domiciled for life inside
those four walls there are periods when
he would be likely to make a burst and
would not respect either life or person
or anything else, and the warders have
to be very attentive to their work and
very watchful during their periods on
duty.
I also want to make my protest to the
Minister about convicts' working hours.
In this matter reform must take place.
It is inhuman, cruel, and unkind
that a man who is in for from three to
twenty years should have the daily
routine as set out by the authorities. He
gets up at 6-30 in the morning, cleans
his cell, and breakfasts. At eight o'clock
he goes into the workshops. And what
are the workshops?. If any hon. Members have been in the Belfast Prison I
am sure they will agree that the workshops for convicts on the Crumlin Road
are not the healthiest places in the world.
At 11-30 a.m. he exercises in the open
air. At 12-30 he goes back to his cell
for dinner. At 2 o'clock he returns to
the workshop, and at 6 o'clock he is put
back in his cell again. For all the work
he does in the workshops he gets 2s 6d
a month to buy jam, and he can associate
with others out of the cells from 6 to 8.
His daily toil is useful to the Post Office
in the supply of mail bags, and he makes
uniforms for attendants in Northern
Ireland. He is prohibited from having
a smoke.
The conditions in Scotland and England are altogether different, as I have
explained to the Minister on a previous
occasion. There the prisoners who work
are allowed to smoke, and enjoy healthy
recreation in the open air. They are not
compelled to exist in the confined space
which is the lot of prisoners in the
Crumlin Road Jail. Let us go step-bystep with Great Britain, and treat the
prisoners as human beings. Perhaps an
investigation would show that they are
not responsible for being there. They
are probably there because of the environment in which they were brought
up. I ask the Minister of Home Affairs
to give this matter his attention.

interests of the ratepayers. It is true
that two firms entirely ignored the fact
that they had due notice, in the latter
part of 1934, that in 1936 these machines
would not be permitted to use the roads
in future unless they used pneumatic
tyres. After all, one cannot legislate for
individual firms. Apparently these two
firms think they must be a law unto
themselves, and while other ratepayers
and other motor owners have complied
with the law, these two firms decline to
do so. I think the Committee will agree
that it would be perfectly ridiculous if
individuals were allowed to take the law
into their own hands against the wishes
of this House.
With regard to what the hon. Member
for Pottinger said about prisons in
Northern Ireland, I have a great deal of
sympathy, but he will appreciate this,
that in England they have separate
prisons for convicts and a separate prison
for first offenders and for juvenile
offenders and so on. We, on the other
hand, have only one modern prison, that
is, the Crumlin Road. There we do our
best to divide up these different prisoners
and convicts and give them, as far as we
can, the amenities they are accustomed
to get in England. I think he will
appreciate the great difficulty of having
separate convict prison for thirty
convicts, and similarly he will agree with
me that it would be a practically uneconomic proposition to provide separate
prisons for all the classes to which I have
referred. We have done our best to
ameliorate the lot of these unfortunate
people in prison. The hon. Member
mentioned one matter in regard to
smoking. I have already taken steps to
see how we can ameliorate the lot of
convicts, because convicts in England are
permitted to smoke after a certain period
but others are not. I am trying to see
to what extent we can meet the point.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The hon. and gallant Member has raised a very important matter,
and I am very glad to have the opportunity of explaining the position.
think it is most unfortunate that statements such as he has referred to appear
in the Press, because they have a most
unsettling effect upon the people and
make some of them often feel that public
money is foolishly spent, and make other
people dissatisfied because they have not
got what they are led to believe others
are obtaining. As a matter of fact, if
old persons transfer property or investments for the purpose of obtaining a
pension it is no advantage to them whatever, because the pension authorities take
into consideration the value of the
property or the investment, as the case
may be, as if it belonged to them,
if it has been transferred with the
object of obtaining the pension. It
is taken into account just the same as if
it were actually in their possession.
Further, the greatest possible care in
order to do justice both to the claimants
and to the taxpayers is taken in connection with this matter. Take the pension
courts. A legal man is chairman, and he is
appointed by myself. There is a representative of those who would be likely
to claim, and there is also a representative of the general taxpayers. Again,
there is an appeal to the umpire in case
the claimant thinks any injustice has been
done to him or her. I am thankful to
say that every claim is most carefully
considered with a view to doing justice
to the claimant on the one hand and protecting the public purse on the other
hand.

tion payment under the Unemployment

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I am asking
the Committee to grant the sum of
£275,000 as a contribution towards the
Unemployment Fund. The payment of
unemployment benefit and other payments has exceeded our Estimate.
When we drew up our original Estimate
we based our figures of employment and
unemployment on the position then existing, and presumed that would be our
probable experience over the financial
year.
The Committee is aware that a new
Unemployment Agreement has been concluded between the Government of the
United Kingdom on the one hand, and
the Northern Government on the other,
and at the moment, legislation is before
the Parliament of the United Kingdom
and this Parliament for confirmation of
that Agreement. The new Agreement
differs in some respects from the old
Agreement of 1926. I shall not trouble
the Committee with an exhaustive
explanation of these differences but,
perhaps, I should mention one or two
of them in order that the Committee may
understand the reason for this Vote.
There are two debts standing against
the Unemployment Fund-the suspense
debt and the current debt. There is an
obligation placed upon the Unemployment Fund to repay the suspense debt by
annual instalments of £40,000. This
amount was not budgeted for in our
original Estimate. There is a further
non-recurring amount of £97,000 which
has grown up over the past number of
years, and which we now propose to wipe
out. This excess deficit cannot arise
again, due to the new Agreement we
have entered into with Great Britain.
Hon. Members know that both the old
Agreement and the new one provide for
our Unemployment Fund being kept in
parity with the Unemployment Fund of
Great Britain. It is in this way that we
can secure for our people the same benefits for the payment of the same contributions as insured persons receive throughout Great Britain. But parity in the
Funds involves my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, in further
liabilities. He is required to put up at
the end of each year our insured population proportion of any surplus earned by
the Unemployment Fund of Great
Britain in that year.
When the original Estimate was prepared it was expected that the Unemployment Insurance Fund of Great
Britain would earn a substantial surplus.
In effect it earned £3,000,000. This is
more than was anticipated, and the result
is that our Exchequer becomes again involved in an additional liability on
behalf of the Fund of approximately
£80,000.
I have already stated that our
experience of employment and unemployment has diverged, to some extent, from
our expectations. We have had heavier
unemployment than we anticipated
amongst the insured classes, and part of
the sum asked for under sub-head B goes
to meet this cost.
On the other hand the contribution
income of the Unemployment Fund has
exceeded our expectations by about
£15,000. This sum represents a substantial amount of extra employment,
although, strange to say, employment
over the year has been much better and
unemployment rather worse.
This seeming contradiction can be best
explained in this way. There has been
a substantial increase in our insured
population. Between July, 1934, and
July, 1935, the population rose by about
8,000 apart altogether from the addition
to the insured classes made by the lowering of the minimum age of entry into
insurance to correspond with the schoolleaving age. This additional income I
have referred to of £15,000 requires a
further State grant or contribution from
the State to the Fund of £5,000.
Our original Estimate assumed that the
unemployment assistance scheme would
be in full operation throughout the whole
financial year.

EDUCATION ACT (SECTION 10).
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether it is the duty of the
Ministry or the Regional Committees to
carry out the provisions of Section 10 of
the Education Act; whether any of the
Regional Committees have carried out
these provisions and to what extent; and
whether he can state the attitude of
Down Regional Committee in this
matter.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): It is the duty
of the Regional Education Committee to
carry out the provisions of Section 10
of the 1923 Act.
All the committees have made provision of the kind specified in the Act
to a greater or less degree. Each application is considered by a committee on
its merits and dealt with accordingly.
In the case of County Down Regional
Education Committee a recent application by certain voluntary schools for the
provision of materials for handwork was
refused on the ground that their financial
position did not justify them in making
a grant.

EXPORTS OF MAIN CROP
POTATOES.
10. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked
the Minister of Agriculture whether he
can state the number of tons of main
crop potatoes exported to Great Britain
from Northern Ireland in the season
1935-36, and how many tons of the quota
allowed under
under the Potato Marketing
Act can still be exported.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): From the
the 1st
September, 1935, to the 29th February,
1936, 121,847 tons of main crop potatoes
were shipped from Northern Ireland to
Great Britain as compared with 50,682
tons in the corresponding period of the
year 1934-35. As I have explained to
the House on previous occasions, there is
no formal quota in respect of shipments
of potatoes from Northern Ireland to
Great Britain. The position is that we
came to a friendly arrangement with the
Potato Marketing Board for
for Great
Britain whereby we agreed to limit our
shipments to 200,000 tons whenever the
United Kingdom crop was in excess of
home consumption requirements and
there were no imports from other
countries. At present, as the hon. and
gallant Member is aware, imports from
abroad are taking place and, therefore,
there is no restriction, voluntary or
otherwise, on the quantity of potatoes
that may be shipped this season from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Thank you.
COMPENSATION FOR PART-TIME
VETERINARY SURGEONS.
11. Mr. FRYAR asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether veterinary surgeons who were only part time in the
service of local or sanitary authorities,
and who, on account of their age, were
not appointed as veterinary surgeons
under the recent Act of 1934, are entitled
to receive reasonable compensation for
loss of employment in such duties as they
performed in the Counties of Down and
Armagh for the County Councils;
whether their financial loss on the
average during the last three years of
such services amounted to over £300;
and whether Section 4 of the Diseases of
Animals Act, 1934, was specially put
into the Act to enable County Councils
to pay such compensation.
Mr. HANNA: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answers to the first and last parts
of the hon. Member's question are in
the affirmative. As part-time officers
are not normally covered by the Superannuation Acts the section mentioned by
the hon. Member was inserted in the
Diseases of Animals Act, 1934, in order
to meet their case. I am not in a
position to say what the average financial loss of such officers has been, but
the cases of a number of them are at
present being considered and suitable
compensation will be awarded at a very
early date.

In reply to the first part of the
question, I am not yet in a position to
give the information asked for by the
hon. Member.

AMENDING WORKMEN'S

13. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Midgley)
asked the Minister of Labour whether he
will consider the advisability of introducing an amending Workmen's Compensation Bill to remove anomalies and
injustices in existing Acts.
Mr. ANDREWS: The law on workmen's compensation is similar throughout
the United Kingdom, and it is desirable
that this uniformity should continue.
The British Home Secretary has recently
appointed a committee to inquire into the
working of certain aspects of the Acts,

amendment is made in the British Acts

introduced here.

Mr. ANDREWS: Allegations have
been made from time to time that the

importance, and I want to know what
the right hon. Gentleman is going to do.
There is a sum of £680,000 on the
Vote on Account for Educational Services. Is it not quite true that notwithstanding the great teachers that we have
in Northern Ireland, and notwithstanding that the children are now being
looked after better than ever before,
there is no work for them when they
leave school? The Minister of Labour
puts on the hoardings, "Buy Ulster
Goods," in order to help to find employment for some of the 25,000 children
who leave school every year and to take
them out of the queue at the Labour
Exchange. The right hon. Gentleman
said that of the number leaving school
only 3,000 were able to secure employment.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is not so.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the right
hon. Gentleman tell me the percentage
of the 25,000 for whom employment is
found. My contention is that the
Minister of Education and the Minister
of Labour ought to do something to
assist those children who are leaving
school with no hope of getting employment.
It is an appalling thing that you
should give these children a better education and not try to find work for them.
It is quite true that the Minister of
Labour has a training centre in Alfred
Street, and I notice that he has started
a training centre in the loyal town of
Portadown. But what he should do is
to find work for these children. Has he
ever thought of introducing something
that will enable these children to secure
employment when they leave school?
Mr. ANDREWS: May I point out to
the hon. Member that as regards these
children more than half obtain work.
About one-fourth of them remain in the
school after the fixed school age has been
passed, and of the remainder a very considerable number go home to help their
parents in their homes. Really very few
of them remain unemployed.
Mr. HENDERSON: I can assure the
right hon. Gentleman if he saw the
number of children who have left the
school, and who are signing at the exchanges, it would amaze him. Has he
paid visits to the Juvenile Employment
Centres? Has he not seen thousands-
Mr. ANDREWS: Not thousands.
Mr. HENDERSON: I will give the
right hon. Gentleman the opportunity of
telling the exact number of unemployed
youths who are attending the juvenile
training centres. When he has done
that he will hardly realise his own
figures. Other hon. Members will likely
deal with that matter. It is not my
desire to detain the House, but there is
one important matter I would like to
refer to. Will the right hon. Gentleman
tell me why this Government set up a
Royal Commission to look into the question of poor law administration? A large
sum of money was spent on getting
expert advice from all the municipalities.
in regard to reforms that were necessary
to prevent over-lapping. Will he tell me
why nothing was done with regard to
putting into operation the reforms that
were suggested in that Commission's
report? The Minister of Home Affairs
or his representative is not here to
answer this question and perhaps the
Minister of Labour would reply. This
Commissioner got expert advice which if
followed would have revolutionised the

administration of local government

It has been pointed out to me time and

law system was not reformed. The Corporation are doing one part and the
guardians another part. Why this overlapping? It is the same thing all over
the country. I challenge the right hon.
Gentleman to tell me one solitary reform
that has been carried out.
Mr. ANDREWS: Medical benefits.
Mr. HENDERSON: That was not
one of the reforms suggested. I was
talking about reforms in regard to local
government administration in order to
prevent the over-lapping that now takes

medical benefits. Is it not true that
since the introduction of medical benefits
panel patients are not getting the services
they are entitled to?
Mr. ANDREWS: Absolutely untrue.
Mr. HENDERSON: When a doctor
attends to a panel patient and pays halfa-dozen visits does he not suggest: "You
will have to go into a hospital."
Mr. ANDREWS: That is a very good
thing.
Mr. HENDERSON: That is wrong.
It is a good thing for the doctor to get
rid of the patients that the State pays
him to look after, but it is not a good
thing for the shy man who does not want
to go into hospital and who thinks he will
be better quicker amongst his own family.
I suggest that the Minister should look
into that matter. Now that the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs has come in I suggest that
the Ministry should take drastic action
against those local authorities who are
not carrying out schemes that would
help the workers in the way they ought.
I do not mean progressive authorities
like the one the hon. Member for Mid-
Antrim is connected with. I am speaking of the local authorities composed of
old die-hard farmers who would not spend
a bean on the construction of footpaths
or roads or sewers. No attempt has been
made by the Ministry of Home Affairs to
get the water supplies of the Province
co-ordinated. There is the Silent Valley
where great employment could be given.
I do not know the number of gallons of
water that go into the Silent Valley, but
I know there has been no serious
attempt at a distribution of that water
throughout Northern Ireland. The
Ministry of Home Affairs are doing
nothing, and with all respect I say it is
time there were some changes there.
They have ample opportunities and great
scope for creating employment.
The roadways throughout Northern
Ireland are in many instances virtually
death traps. What do you find outside
the city of Belfast, leaving main roads
out? Narrow lanes with no footpaths.
They are a danger to mankind. Yet the
Ministry of Home Affairs take no action
in these matters at all. They should
send some of their staff on a journey
round the countryside and see what the
people require. They never do that.
The Minister of Home Affairs is very
seldom in this House. Unfortunately I
was absent yesterday and great notice
was taken of the fact. I feel that the
Minister is responsible for the apathy
that exists in all parts of the
Province with regard to the unsanitary
conditions under which the people have
been compelled to live. Take the constituencies represented by the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna) and the
hon. and gallant Member for East Down.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: May I
correct the hon. Member? In East
Down, at least three schemes of water and
sewerage have been introduced in the
last three years.
Mr. HENDERSON: Notwithstanding these particular schemes, the old
village pump and bucket still exist. If
there has been a little reform in East
Down I suppose the hon. and gallant
Member played his part in getting it
carried out. I suggest he should use his
influence with the Minister of Labour to
get the village pump taken off the main
street of Newtownards. The village
pump is still in Shrigley; it has not been
removed. The village pump still exists
in the town represented by the hon. Member (Mr. Gordon).

can usefully employ

Members will have appreciated that the
two Clauses are merely declaratory that
the pre-valuation position is to be maintained. Mr. Speaker has, however, indicated to me that he would have felt it
incumbent on him on the Report Stage
of the Bill to require these two Clauses
to be omitted as being outside the ambit
of the long title of the Bill.
The only
alternative to this would have been an
amendment in the title of the Bill itself as
I cannot controvert his view that the
Clauses are, in fact, outside the title of
the Bill; such an amendment, however,
might alter the whole character of the
Bill.
A word of explanation is necessary from
me as to why the Clauses were inserted
seeing that in point of fact, their omission is of no importance. They were inserted by the Government in order that
the full effects of revaluation on all enactments might be within the cognisance of
the House, and nothing go by default.
The general tenor of the Bill is to place
all statutory enactments where valuation or poundage is mentioned in the same
position after revaluation as before. It
would, therefore, in my opinion have
been quite improper for the Government
to bring a Bill before the House which
purported to do this and yet failed to
call the attention of the House to any
omissions which were proposed to be
made on general grounds. Accordingly,
the Government decided to bring to the
notice of the House by means of these two
Clauses the fact that it did not intend to
make these two enactments, where
poundage rate is involved, conform to the
general amendments which the Bill will
bring about. This could, of course, have
been done by a mere statement by my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
on the Second Reading of the Bill, but it
was considered fairer to the House that
the point should be directly referred to in
a declaratory Clause in the Bill itself. It
was, in fact, realised that their scope was
somewhat outside the title of the Bill, but
it was considered that this objection was
outweighed by the advantage of publicity.

if it is the intention of the Northern
Government to introduce legislation to
compel Cabinet Ministers to resign their
directorships of private companies during
their tenure of office and thus keep step
by step with the British Parliament.
The PRIME MINISTER: In the unavoidable absence of the Minister of
Finance I propose to reply to this
question myself.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): As the hon. and gallant
Member is doubtless aware my Ministry
merely acts. as agents for the Irish
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour.]
Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust, which
is an Imperial Service. I have, however, made inquiries and am informed
that so far as the Trust is aware there

cottages must feel.
I have also been informed that full

I observe that the hon. and gallant
Member refers to an "economic" rent.
The rents charged by the Trust do not
include any sums either by way of interest
or sinking fund in respect of the capital
cost of the cottages, as would be the case
if an "economic" rent were charged, but
merely includes such sums as in the
opinion of the Trust will cover with certainty the necessary expenditure on
maintenance of the cottages, administration charges and provision for vacancies,
bad debts, insurance, etc.

4. Rev. PROFESSOR CORKEY asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
is aware that in some districts much
drunkenness and misery are caused by the
consumption of an intoxicant known as
"Red Biddy"; whether this drink is
manufactured in Belfast, and whether
the Government will take steps to control more effectively the sale of this drink.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Before this question
is answered I desire your ruling as to
whether the expression "Red Biddy" in
this question is parliamentary? I do not
know what it is derived from. I cannot
find it in any authorised dictionary.
Some hon. Members at least do not know

some-
Mr. SPEAKER: In this and other
Houses of Parliament words are
times used that are not to be found in
the Oxford Dictionary. I think in this
case it is a familiar term and most of
us understand it.
Mr. CAMPBELL: It is certainly not
Irish.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Actually there is no
wine manufactured or sold under the
name of "Red Biddy," but this term is
commonly applied to cheap British-made
wines. The greater part of these cheap
red wines is, I am informed, imported,
but there is one refinery in Belfast which
produces a wine of this class.
The question raised by the hon. Member is one which has already been the
subject of investigation and continues to
be carefully watched.
The analyses of this wine which have
been made from time to time go to show
that the wine is in itself harmless, but
I am informed that undoubtedly the
wine is sometimes drunk after it has been
fortified with methylated spirit or other
deleterious spirit, and in such conditions.
the mixture has a very highly toxic effect.
It is illegal for any person on licensed
premises to sell or have or supply any
liquor mixed with any alcohol other than
ethyl (that is, the ordinary alcohol contained in whisky, etc.), and under the
Intoxicating Liquor Act of 1927 a publican guilty of this offence is liable to forfeiture of licence. This provision,
together with the restrictions on the sale
of methylated spirit contained in our
Intoxicating Liquor Acts, has had a very
salutary effect, but, of course, confirmed
dipsomaniacs will always find some means
of satisfying their appetite, and instances,
no doubt, do occur where the law is
broken in this respect.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

SALE OF METHYLATED SPIRITS.
5. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that there is in some districts in
Northern Ireland an intoxicating mixture composed largely of methylated
spirits and sold under the name of
"Surgical Spirit"; whether any licence is
required for its sale, and whether it is
necessary to keep any record of the
quantity sold.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Surgical
spirit, which I understand is composed
of methylated spirit, castor oil and
boracic acid, and which is exceedingly
unpalatable, is intended for external use
only. No licence is required for its sale;
neither is any record of sales necessary.
From inquiries which I have made, I
have ascertained that there are no
grounds for believing that the sale of this
spirit generally is anything but small;
neither, I understand, is there any reason
to fear that (except possibly in some individual instances) it is used for human
consumption.

PERSONS SUFFERING FROM
TUBERCULOSIS.
8. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
the number of persons suffering from
tuberculosis in Northern Ireland, and
what special steps the Government are
taking to combat this terrible disease.
Sir DAWSON BATES: According to
the latest returns available, there were,
at the close of the year 1934, 9,937
persons on the registers of the tuberculosis committees definitely diagnosed as
suffering from tuberculosis.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, there are special committees in
each county and county borough for the
purpose of providing treatment and
taking measures to prevent the spread of
the disease, and half the net expenses
of these committees is recouped by the
Government.
I might add, to show the effectiveness
of the measures taken, that the death
rate from this disease has declined
steadily since 1901, and that the chief
tuberculosis officer in his last annual
report to the Corporation (to which the
hon. Member belongs) referred to the fact
that the death rate for the year (0.96 per
1,000) was the lowest ever recorded in the
city, and showed a fall of 53.4 per cent.
on the figure for the year 1914 (2.1 per
1,000).

that during the past few weeks searches

Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to
the first part of the hon. and learned
Member's question is in the affirmative.
These searches were carried out under
the provisions of the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act, and no warrants
were, therefore, required. I am not prepared to give the hon. and learned Member any information as to the results of
these searches, except to say that ten
persons have since been prosecuted, and
in each case convicted of having seditious
documents in their possession.
I am satisfied that every care is taken
not to cause unnecessary inconvenience
or alarm to those residing in or present
on the premises during the search.
I can assure the hon. and learned
Member that these searches are only
carried out after senior police officers
are satisfied that there are full and
adequate reasons for doing so, and I do
not accept the suggestion that the police
are acting on information invented by
spiteful individuals.
The answer to the last part of the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware that these searches were conducted

TOTAL YIELD OF FLAX.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
'TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked to reply.
The produce of the flax crop in
Northern Ireland in the years 1934 and
1935 was 3,677 tons and 6,892 tons respectively. The average price per stone
paid for flax in the agricultural year
commencing on the 1st October, 1934,
and ending on the 30th September, 1935,
was 9s 11d. The average price per stone
for the period commencing on the 1st
October, 1935, and ending on the 29th
February, 1936, was 9s 03d per stone.
In view of the lower price received by
farmers for flax grown in 1934, and particularly in view of the slower demand
and lower prices in the spring of 1936,
as compared with the demand and prices
in the spring of 1935, it is possible that
the acreage under flax in 1936 will show
some decrease.

Mr. CAMPBELL: The Second Reading of this Bill gives one an opportunity
for a short survey of the régime at
present in operation in our area. It is a
régime that causes considerable anxiety
to numbers of people in Northern Ireland. They fear that in a very short
time they will be visited with heavier
burdens of rates and taxes. Those
burdens are looming in the very near
future. Revaluation is now on the eve
of being put into operation. It will hit
thousands of people all over the area,
and hit them hard. As a result of that

£420,000, we find that the British
Treasury will be subsidising Northern
Ireland in this coming year-I think the
facts I am giving are right and that the

Ireland in the coming year a sum of
