the
In every domain of administration the
same peaceful penetration prevails. And
yet numbers of the minority when the
blast of war blew showed something more
than mere lip loyalty, something more
than conditional loyalty. A careful investigation was made by a careful
observer and computator-a member of
the staff of the "Irish News"-in regard
to 21 houses in Nelson Street, in a
Catholic area which was stricken sorely
in the Belfast troubles. This investigation revealed that of the 21 Catholic
families living there not one but has had
at least one member of the family in His
Majesty's Forces. In all 65 members of
those 21 families served in the King's
Forces, which is an average of three for
every family. Of those 65, there were
55 who served in the Army, the Navy, or
the Mercantile Marine during the Great
War. Ten, including a boy not 16 years
of age, gave their lives, and one died of
illness contracted on active service. Of
those 21 families, six members lost their
lives during the progrom of 1920-22, and
two had their deaths hastened by illtreatment received during the recent disorders.
Another matter to which I wish to
call attention is that in recent months
innocent households in Belfast have been
harassed and alarmed by searches made
by armed bodies of men, apparently on
unreliable and flimsy
and flimsy information. I
use the word "innocent" households,
because they are composed of lawabiding respectable citizens. Many of
those searches have proved futile, because
nothing incriminatory was ever found.
The forcible and precipitate entry (of
armed men into a quiet home is a matter
of gravity. The intrusion of an armed
body into a quiet home is calculated to
inspire alarm and terror, and it may do
irreparable harm to the health of delicate
people. The danger is very real that in
the exercise of the arbitrary powers
vested in the Executive under the Civil
Authorities Act these searches can be
made an engine of torture of innocent
political opponents. I do utter a word
of warning against that danger, and I
protest anything in the nature of haphazard and indiscriminate use of those
powers.
The last topic I wish to deal with is
the attitude of the Ministry of Education to the Irish language. A recent act
of that Ministry, which ranks Irish as a

and obscurantism that are almost
unthinkable. There are 10,000 children
learning Irish in the elementary schools
of Northern Ireland. Over 5,000 are
learning Irish in the city of Belfast;
over 1,200 pupils are learning Irish in
the secondary schools of Northern Ireland, so that all told between 11,000 and
12,000 children are and have been for
some time receiving instruction in Irish.

I would remind the House that 90 per
cent. of the place names in Northern

The names in use in Northern Ireland
can only be properly appreciated by a
person with a knowledge of Irish. I was
glad to see that last week his Grace the
Governor gave an Irish name, Lisnagarvey, to the new wireless transmitting
station. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I was very glad to see that. That name
has a true Irish ring, but it conveys
nothing to a man who does not know
Irish. To a man with a knowledge of
Irish it has a delightful ring and flavour
about it. I was delighted to see that the
name was adopted. The Celtic language
had entered Ireland by way of the northeast corner, and from that corner it had
gone across to Scotland. Only Philistines
and withered pedagogues would try to
degrade Irish. The gaucherie of the
Ministry reminds me of Sydney Smith's
classic story of Mrs. Partington. I am
sure you all recollect the reference. Mrs.
Partington lived upon the beach at Sidmouth, and in a violent storm she was
seen at the door of her house vigorously
pushing away the waves of the Atlantic
Ocean with her mop. It was a very
unequal contest. Mrs. Partington was
excellent at a puddle, but she was helpless in a storm. The Atlantic beat Mrs.
Partington. I think the Irish people
need not despair at the attitude of the
Ministry of Education of Northern Ireland. They will survive it-undoubtedly
Irish scholars will see to that—and they
will in time defeat the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education.

In regard to the prisons, and I want
this borne in mind by the right hon.
Gentleman, no High Court decision can
be carried into effect in view of the
present prison accommodation in Northern Ireland. Under the Prisoners Act,
1886, a prisoner has the right to see that
the sentence imposed upon him by the
judge is properly fulfilled. When a
prisoner receives five years' penal
servitude how do you carry out that
sentence? You put him into a shortterm or local prison, and you torture him
by keeping him in that short-term prison
for his period of detention. A prisoner
sentenced to penal servitude is entitled
to open-air exercise, and he has to do
work of a suitable kind. He cannot get
that here. The very boots supplied to
the prison officials here are brought from
London. You say, "Push Ulster goods"
and buy the boots for your prison officials
in London.
The next thing I have to say about the
prison service is that when a prisoner
makes a complaint his word is never
accepted. A civil servant, whose name I
will not mention, goes from Stormont
and sits to hear the complaint of the
prisoner. In 99 cases out of 100 the
prisoner is treated by him as a noted
liar. But that is not the final result of
the inquiry. In 99 cases out of every
100 the civil servant from Stormont prescribes punishment for the complainant.
Just imagine. A civil servant is
empowered to go up there and listen to
the complaint, knowing perfectly well
that the complaint is against a member
of the staff or against the Civil Service
itself. How can you, in those circumstances, expect justice to be carried out
between the prisoner and the official?
I suggest that the sooner a Prison Board
of representative people is appointed the
better it will be for the administration of
the prison service in Northern Ireland.

Another point mentioned by the hon.

with our prisoners and convicts. It is a
very, very serious matter. At the present time we have only one modern jail,
which was never intended for convicts.
In the old days convicts went to one

Ireland. We have to house in that
prison not only the convicts but first
offenders, juveniles, and prisoners who
are in for short terms. We do the best
we can.
We have something like thirty

Mr. BYRNE: I just want to mention

We are most anxious that our children

We are, and always have been, anxious

Under the present Act we have a very

it is the duty of our priests to erect

of the poor in order to try to erect schools

splendid schools, but I say that we have
as good a right to get the cost of our
schools from the Government as any
other denomination. We are determined

not to hand over our schools to any

I want to call attention to the fact that

I think the Minister of Home Affairs
should take more notice of the existing

a dangerous pace are prosecuted.
I appreciate, and I am sure every

to take this opportunity of paying a

There is another matter about which

It is very hard for women and children

I am not in favour of any illegal

are
May I say in conclusion that I do not
agree, as some people know, with the
Government in all the little details
brought forward, or with all the Bills
they put through, but I say that the
Government are entitled to our support
and encouragement. They have done
good work for the community. As far
as I am concerned I am prepared to give
the Prime Minister and the Government
my whole-hearted support so long as they
give equal treatment to all people,
irrespective of religion, whether Roman
Catholics or Protestants, in the matter
of conditions, grants and social services.
I congratulate the Government and all
concerned on what they have already
done. I look forward with a great deal
of optimism to the future. I believe if
we could only settle down together,
leaving all sectarian questions outside,
and work for the common weal we could
make this place a great deal brighter and

probably is.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): This Measure, to which I
have the privilege, on behalf of the Government, of asking hon. Members to give
a Second Reading to-day, is one of farreaching importance, affecting as it does
in various ways every member of our
community. As hon. Members know,
the first Unemployment Insurance Act
passed by the Imperial Parliament became law in 1911. It applied to a few
industries only in which it was considered
there was most likelihood of unemployment, and brought within its scope
approximately 2 million workers. The
1920 Act greatly extended the scheme
and provided insurance cover for over
11 million workers, or, in other words,
for practically all the industrial workers
in the United Kingdom, with the exception of those engaged on the land and
domestic service. These two classes were
excluded; land workers because of special
difficulties, and domestic servants because
of the absence of unemployment in that
occupation. I have felt for some years
that it was an anomaly that farm workers
were left out of our Unemployment Insurance Acts, especially as they are
insured under our Health and Pensions
Acts under exactly the same conditions,
including rates of contributions and
benefits, as other industrial workers. I
am glad that the time has come to remove
that anomaly and right the wrong.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We should remember to-day that
farming is our oldest and still our most
important industry-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-and that in most instances
our farms are being tilled by men, both
as employers and employed, whose
families have been associated with the
land for generations, and who understand
its cultivation, and the aim of the Government is to help in every way possible.
both sections of those whom I may call
the farming community. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, and
his distinguished predecessor, have, in
co-operation with His Majesty's Imperial
Government, promoted many schemes of
very great value to our farmers, and
this Bill is being introduced mainly, but
not entirely as I will show later on, to
assist their labourers when out of employment through no fault of their own.
This Bill, which corresponds to the
Measure which is passing through the
United Kingdom Parliament, is largely
based on the Report of the Statutory
Committee set up under the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1934. I feel that
it is of great benefit to Northern Ireland
that it is so ably represented on the Committee by my right hon. Friend, Captain
Charles Craig. The Bill will bring into
unemployment insurance all employees

between 16 and 18, 2d; girls between 16
and 18, 1d; boys who have not attained
I am gratified that the principle of
insurance for those engaged on the land
as labourers has met with universal
approval, and that the only difference of
opinion seems to be about the amount of
benefit to be paid to those who are willing
to work but cannot get it. It has been
said that the rates of benefit are too low,
and that they should be the same as in
the general insurance scheme for industrial workers. The answer to that
criticism is twofold; first, the higher the
benefit rates the higher the contribution
rates, and we must be careful not to put
too heavy a burden on either our farmers
or their labourers. Secondly, the wages
paid to farm labourers are in most
instances lower than to workers associated
with our other industries.
On the other hand, it has been urged
that the benefit rates proposed are too
high; the Government do not take that
view.
I do not think, for example, any
reasonable person will feel that 14s per
week is too much to support an adult
man, or 7s too much to give him to support his wife (not many of us would like
to try it, I admit); nor will an excessive
birth rate be encouraged by a dependant's
allowance of 3s for each dependent child,
with a maximum payment, as I have said,
of 30s, no matter how many dependants
he may have. Beside, as regards the
rates of benefit, it should be remembered
that the average weekly payment over a
period of unemployment will be less than
the rates provided in the Bill, because,
as in the general scheme, a claimant will
have to serve his "waiting week" at the
beginning of each period of unemployment, unless there has been an interval

,708
Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
of less than ten weeks since the last period
of unemployment. This will reduce, considerably, the average weekly amount
which he will receive during short spells

I think there are misconceptions in
many quarters on several aspects of the
scheme. It has been suggested, for
example, that the benefit provisions are
so ample that labourers will be disposed
to throw up their employment in order
to draw benefit, and that farmers will
not be able to get the men they need to
work the land. I want to say here and
now that there is no foundation in the
Bill for suggestions of this kind; quite
the contrary, the duration of a man's
title to benefit will be governed strictly
by the ratio rule set out in Clause 5, and
it will depend entirely on the number of
unexhausted contributions standing to
his credit at the beginning of his benefit
year. It is true that under Clause 4 of
the Bill a claimant will be able to qualify
for benefit on showing the payment of 20
contributions during the two years before
he makes his claim, provided, of course,
he satisfies the other general conditions
for benefit. In return, however, for
these contributions, and assuming that he
has no more than these 20 contributions
unexhausted when he opens his benefit
year, he will be entitled to no more than
42 days' benefit at the most. Take, for
example, the case of a man who is employed continuously between the date
when this Act will come into force and
the date when benefit will first become
payable; the maximum number of contributions he can receive for that period
will be 26, and the maximum amount of
benefit those contributions will entitle
him to receive will be ten weeks' benefit.
One newspaper correspondent has suggested that a farm labourer need only
work 65 days in the year in order to
qualify for the remaining 300 days of the
year. Actually if the 65 days represented.
ten weeks' work the man would have only
ten contributions to his credit and could
not receive benefit in that year at all, as
he would not satisfy the contribution condition. If in the following year he again
worked for only ten weeks he could satisfy
the first contribution condition at the end
of that ten weeks, but the maximum
benefit he could receive would be 42 days'
benefit. On the other hand, the steady
worker who keeps his employment will
find a very helpful standby in the scheme
if he falls out of work through no fault
of his own. A full year's regular employment will tide him over 23 weeks' unemployment, when he is capable of work and
is available for it but cannot obtain employment. The scheme, in fact, provides every
inducement to a man to work while he
has the opportunity, so that, if he does
fall out of employment he may have the
greatest possible number of contributions
to his credit to tide himself and his
family over the period of enforced
idleness.
It has been said that farmers will
stand-off their men unnecessarily during
the "dead" season of the year. I do not
think that this will be done to an
appreciable extent. I have always found
that farmers are willing to play the game
-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and
that they realise the importance of keeping their permanent hands happy, contented, and interested in their work, and
that they are not willing to take the risk
of losing them. On the other hand, it has
been suggested that farm labourers will
seek idleness in preference to employment.
In my experience, now extending over
many years, I have never found this to
be the case as regards our working people;
besides, as I have already pointed out, if
a man does not work he will not have the
contributions to his credit, and will not
be entitled to benefit. I think these fears
are, therefore, largely groundless. Besides
in this connection it should be
remembered that the fund will be the
fund of the contributors-the farmers, the
labourers, and the State-and if throughout the United Kingdom it were
subjected to unnecessary burdens it would
mean, of course, that contributions would
require to be higher than would otherwise be the case.
Before I leave this question of rates of
contribution and of benefit I wish to say
that the Government is convinced that in
these respects, as in others, our scheme
must stand on all fours with the scheme
in the other parts of the United Kingdom. As I have already pointed out,
agricultural insurance will share equally
with industrial insurance in the great
benefits of the Reinsurance Agreement
with the United Kingdom Government.
That Agreement is founded on the basis
of equality, and hon. Members will

realise that if we were to depart from

operation in Great Britain we would

Parliament had not been established, and

indefensible to deprive our farm labourers
-our poorest people-of this advantage
simply because we have a Parliament of
our own. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I want to mention now briefly some
other matters. In the first place, apart
from having to show 20 contributions
paid during the two years before he makes
a claim, a man, in order to qualify for
benefit, will have to satisfy the other conditions that are in force under the
industrial scheme. For example, he will

that he has made his application in the
prescribed way; and, lastly, that he has
been resident in the United Kingdom
for a period of five years before the date
of his claim. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Apart from these conditions, which are
common both to the agricultural and the
general scheme, there are certain provisions in this Bill relating specially to
the agricultural scheme to which I should
refer. In certain parts of Northern
Ireland there is a practice of yearly and
half-yearly hiring of farm labourers, and
for the benefit of both farmers and
labourers working under this system
Clause 9 of the Bill gives power to make
regulations providing for a rebate of contributions at the same rates as in Great
Britain, that is 25 per cent. in the case of
yearly hirings and half that amount in
the case of half-yearly hirings. The
rebates will be payable when the term
ends, provided that notice of the hiring
has been given within 28 days after the
employment began, that the hiring has
continued for the full term agreed on,
and that application for the rebate is
made within the prescribed time.
Clause 10 deals with the case of
labourers who at times may be employed
in agriculture and at other times in industries insured under the general
scheme. The Bill lays down the broad
principle that in such cases a claimant
may draw successively, but not concurrently, to the extent of his full rights
under each scheme. It is fully appreciated
that difficulties may arise in connection
with these "mixed" employments, and
for this reason the Clause provides for
regulations to be made to deal with the
matter. I need hardly say that it is my
intention that the regulations here will
coincide with those in Great Britain, and
it will be my duty to lay them before
both Houses of Parliament so that each
House will have an opportunity of considering them.
Clause 11 of the Bill, although rather
lengthy, is largely concerned with matters
of administrative detail. The Clause
provides for regulating the position in
insurance of persons who are employed
partly in agricultural work and partly in
industrial work; for treating as insurable
under the general scheme employment
which though prima facie agricultural in
character is, having regard to the conditions under which it is performed, so
similar to industrial employment that it
ought to be treated as such, and vice
versa; and for ensuring that employment
in agriculture which is ordinarily carried
on as a subsidiary employment only, and
would, therefore, not be insurable, shall
be treated as being insurable in the case
of any person whose principal employment it is or who is normally employed
in some other kind of insurable work
either agricultural or industrial.
One other special feature in connection
with Agricultural Insurance is the provision in Clause 13 to deal with the case
of the man who comes to the United
Kingdom year after year, not to make his
home with us, but merely to engage in
seasonal harvesting work, returning to
his home after the harvest is over. The
Statutory Committee recognised that contributions should be required from the
man who employs these labourers, so
that he should have no inducement to
employ them in preference to our own
workers (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
but that, as these men do not reside in
the United Kingdom, they should not
qualify for benefit. Accordingly, the Act.

provides that any person employed in

This brings me to one other matter
which I will briefly mention, and, that is,
that the reciprocal arrangements, which

Great
Britain in connection with the

Britain in exactly the same way as if the

Britain; and similarly a Northern Ireland worker can qualify for agricultural
benefit here on agricultural contributions
standing to his credit in respect of farm
work performed in England, Scotland, or
Wales a recognition of the fact that
labour is mobile throughout the United
Kingdom.
We hear a great deal at the present
time about getting people back to the
land. The best way, in fact the only way
of promoting that, in my opinion, is to
help the farming industry to reach as
profitable a basis as possible along the
lines the Government has been pursuing,
and to secure for the labourers during
unemployment a provision against the
poverty which has been all too general in
the past.
This Measure should help materially to
reduce the drift of workers from the
country to the towns in order to find work
in industrial occupations. How serious
this drift is may be realised, I think,
when we contrast two sets of figures.
According to the statistics collected
by the Ministry of Agriculture the
number of workers on the land has fallen
by 3,836 between 1932 and 1935. On
the other hand, the number of men aged
21 and over who are connected with
occupations insurable under the general
scheme has grown between the same years,
1932-1935, from 137,000 to over 149,000,
an increase of nearly 10 per cent. In
some areas the increase has been as much
as 30 per cent.
I need hardly point out that those who
turn from the land and get work in
industrial occupations diminish the
chances of employment of those who have
been brought up all their lives to look
to industrial employment as their means
of livelihood. The drift from the land,
therefore, is neither in the interest of
agriculture nor of the community as a
whole. On this ground alone, therefore,
I am sure hon. Members will support this
Measure. By removing an anomaly that
cannot be justified on any ground of
equity, it will redress a grievance of a
most valuable group in the community,
the farm labourers, whose skill is essential
to the successful carrying on of agriculture.
If any hon. Member is in doubt about
how he should act to-day, may I suggest
that he should think of the thousands of
lonely little cottages, where the resources
are the slenderest, scattered over our
countryside, from which the dread of unemployment is seldom absent, and where
want and suffering on its account are undoubtedly frequent. When he pictures
these humble little hearths and their
straitened circumstances, the homes of
many of the finest of our citizens, his
doubts will disappear and he will see
clearly the course that he ought to follow
in order to bring confidence and comfort
into these Ulster homes.
are

wealth
may be; no matter how satisfactory our trade returns, we cannot feel

of the sufferer, unrelieved.

do not claim that this is the last word in

Once you admitted the principle of insurance regarding town labourers, you could
not indefinitely shut out the farm

The drift to the towns is a most saddening feature of modern civilisation.
The strength of almost every nation lies
on the land, and the nations that are
going down the hill are the nations that
have left the land and congregated in the
towns, with the great mass of the population living in urban surroundings and in
urban conditions of life. Anything that

not

Oral Answers to Questions.
BY-PRODUCTS FROM POTATOES.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the result of the recent experiments
which have been carried out in England
in regard to the manufacture of certain
commodities from potatoes, and whether
he is aware that wines, scents, etc., can
be produced from potatoes; and whether
his Department is carrying out any experiments of a similar kind to encourage
the Ulster farmer to grow more potatoes.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I am not aware of
the results of any recent experiments of
the nature to which the hon. Member
refers. I know, of course, that numerous commodities, including farina,
industrial alcohol, etc., can be manufactured from potatoes. Only last
month my Ministry, in conjunction with
the North of Ireland Potato Marketing
Association, the Ulster Farmers' Union,
and the Ministry of Commerce, was in
conference with a London concern
interested in the use of potatoes for
manufacturing purposes. The difficulty
was that for such a purpose no
than 25s a ton could be paid to the
farmer, whereas the actual cost of production is at least £2 a ton. Quite
obviously, farmers would not produce
potatoes at such an uneconomic price.
more
With regard to the latter part of the
question, no experiments are necessary
to encourage our farmers to grow more
potatoes. It is all a question of price.
Our present policy is to work in conjunction with the Potato Marketing
Board in Great Britain to secure
a stabilised economic price to the producer. As to encouraging further
production, I would like the hon. Member to bear in mind that at present our
farmers produce about half-a-million
tons of potatoes over and above what is
required for human consumption in
Northern Ireland and for export to Great
Britain.

widening of Dee Street Bridge has been
submitted to the Ministry, but if such

that it will receive my sympathetic consideration as I fully appreciate the
desirability of widening this bridge.
With regard to the proposed widening
of the Holywood Arches, a sketch plan
and summary of estimates indicating an

for widening and reconstructing the

suggest, but the Corporation have been
asked to furnish some evidence in sup-

FIRES OUTSIDE BELFAST.
3. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state what steps, if any, the Government are taking to prevent serious
loss of life in the event of fires in the
areas outside Belfast owing to the insufficiency of the fire fighting appliances.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Local authorities are empowered by their bylaws to
see that all buildings are properly constructed so as to minimise danger from
fire.
In the case of hotels and boardinghouses special requirements as to fire
escapes are prescribed by Section 29 of
the Local Government Act (Northern
Ireland), 1934.
In the case of factories safeguards are
prescribed under the Factory Acts.
It is the duty of the local authority
to see that these requirements and safeguards are provided, and I have no
cause to apprehend that they neglect
their duties.
All urban authorities have full power
to establish a fire brigade provided with
all necessary equipment, but, of course,
in the case of smaller towns it is not
generally practicable to maintain a fulltime staff or the most up-to-date equipment, but in such cases it is usually
possible to arrange for obtaining assistance from a neighbouring town, and I
am glad to say that such co-operation has
proved of material service.

Gentleman aware that there is no Coordination in so far as fire fighting services in Northern Ireland are concerned?

Lieut-Colonel GORDON: I rise to continue the debate on this Bill from yesterday. The speech of the Minister of
Labour clearly showed the justice of the
extension of unemployment insurance to
farm labourers. He also explained
clearly to the House the factors which,
of necessity, limited the scope of the Bill
as regards benefits so as to maintain it
within the bounds of practicability and
keep it within the Unemployment Insurance Agreement recently made with the
United Kingdom. Both the Members for
Dock and Pottinger in their speeches
seemed primarily concerned with what
was the origin of this Bill. They claimed
on behalf of themselves that they, and
they only, were the originators of the
scheme. To my mind the important fact
is that it is a Government which is not
Labour, but National in outlook, which
has lifted this scheme from the realm of
talk and Royal Commissions and has
brought it forward and put it on the
Statute Book.
We on this side of the House have
been twitted with a lack of interest in
this Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Frankly I will give the reasons which
make me support this Bill, and I may say
for the information of the hon. Member
for Dock (Mr. Midgley) that for the last
two years on public platforms, in my
area, I have advocated this insurance
scheme. I have been told that it was
not necessary and that the time was not
ripe for it. I will now, as I say, give the
reasons which made me consider that the
labourer was fully entitled to come under
a scheme of insurance when he was unemployed.
Some time ago a deputation of farm
labourers came and saw me, and this is
the case they put up. They said their
wages on the average were 12s a week and
meat from the farmer. Out of that they
said they had to keep a wife, and if they
had children they had to feed and clothe
them. They had to pay rent of 2s a
week if they lived in a rural district
cottage. They had also to provide school
books for the children. They had to do
that, they said, on a wage of 12s, and
if they were thrown out of employment
they received nothing. They went on to
say that next to some of them in the
cottages are men who work in the brick
works and are now drawing unemployment benefit of 30s a week, while they,
the agricultural labourers, had nothing.
They said further that on Saturdays when
the meat cart came round it had to pass
their doors, because they could not afford
to buy meat. That is the case which
made me realise that the agricultural
labourer wanted security in his life just
as much as the industrial worker.
think that everyone in this House, having
heard this statement, will agree that this
Measure is only just and right.

it, and I would like to deal with this

We, in Northern Ireland, as agriculturists, cannot, on Monday, claim our full
membership of the United Kingdom and
on Tuesday, as such members, accept
subsidies for cattle we have received, in
subsidies, £377,000, for milk £288,000,
and for wheat £74,000, making a total
of £739,000 from the taxpayer in Great
Britain-we cannot do that and then, on
Wednesday, deny the labourer, who has
helped to produce this stock and products which earned this £739,000, a scale
of benefits equal to his brother labourer
in Great Britain. The obvious answer
is, if you are not prepared to accept this

Ireland in an inferior position to that in

I am certain no one in this House
payer.
is going to advocate that line.
a
It has been said further by the Farmers'
Union that this Unemployment Insurance
Bill will mean an influx of cheap labour.
The Minister explained yesterday that a
man has to have his card stamped for five
years before he can claim benefit, unless
he is a normal or ordinary resident of the
United Kingdom. That is a safeguard
against an influx of labour. It has
further been said that these labourers
would come in and work at a very cheap
rate. The Government, if that happens,
have the remedy in their own hands.
That remedy is the introduction of wages
boards. They would cure that evil.
Next, I would like, shortly, to examine
the finances of the Bill. The contributions from the State, the employer, and
the labourer are annually £23,000 each,
making a total of £69,000, and the expenditure, based on an unemployment of
11 per cent., is estimated by the Minister
of Labour at £100,000 a year, with
administrative charges of about £8,500,
which gives a deficit of £40,000 a year, to
be made up by the State under the
Reinsurance Agreement for equalisation
grants and the British Exchequer. I
regret the scheme is not self-supporting,
but in view of the fact that the scale of
contributions is 44d, that is not possible.
If you further examine and go deeper into
the question of State support, you must
link this Bill with the coming into force
of the Second Appointed Day, when the
administration of relief for those outside
unemployment insurance is taken over by
the State, aided by a small contribution
from the local rates.
When the Second Appointed Day comes
the administrtaion in regard to the unemployed who are outside unemployment benefit will be undertaken by the
Public Assistance Board. It is obvious
that if this Bill is not on the Statute
Book the burden of providing for the unemployed farm labourer would fall on the
State when the Second Appointed Day
comes; therefore, this Bill is going to
relieve the Exchequer of a sum equal to
that paid out in benefits, which the Minister gave as £100,000. So while the State
is going to lose a deficit of £40,000 on
the "swings" by insuring the farm
labourer, it is going to save £100,000 on
the "roundabouts " of the Second
Appointed Day.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is a very good
juggle.

he, as an insured person, has the benefit-

hired for twelve months there is no such

on spuds and buttermilk, and I hope they
will always be available to fall back on.
We provide a clean milk supply, and
supply our workers with fuel, potatoes and

arrived at. If we follow on those lines,

I feel that a great deal can be said for
and against unemployment insurance. I
propose to deal with the case for unemployment insurance and to compare our
experiences of these Acts in the past. I
am in agreement with the general principle of industrial insurance so far as
unemployment is concerned, and I mean
by that a genuine scheme whereby there
is an insurance fund that is in a liquid
state of finance and that is calculated on
a contributory basis to stand by itself.
But when I take into account what has
happened in the past under these various.
Acts I question the advantages which
agricultural insurance will bring on the
basis of an extension of the present
scheme. I believe that in the original
scheme of Mr. Lloyd George, so far as
unemployment was concerned, there were
many things that were based upon this
promise as to the liquid finances of these
schemes standing by themselves.
But
our experience of the Acts since then
has been very much the reverse, and so
far as I see this Bill follows on the old
vicious lines-I do not say they are entirely vicious but there were many things
which had to be amended and which
have not been fully amended even to-day
-without righting the glaring wrongs
under which the workers have laboured
with regard to insurance. Possibly hon.
Members will tell me that to remedy
those evils might kill the patient. That

on continuing the unsatisfactory position
as it is to-day and as it will probably
be to-morrow, and, so far as agriculture
is concerned, there will be no difference.

813- Unemployment Insurance
26 MARCH 1936

Committee
Unemployment Insurance (Agriculture)
[Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That for the purpose of any Act of
the present Session to include employment in agriculture among the employments which are insurable under the
Unemployment Insurance Acts (Northern Ireland), 1920 to 1935, and to
make modifications in the provisions of
those Acts in their application to such
employment, and other consequential
modifications in those provisions, it is
expedient to make provision for any increase attributable to the passing of the
said Act of the present Session in the
sums payable out of moneys provided
by Parliament by virtue of sub-section
(3) of section five and sub-section (1)
of section forty of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, 1920, as amended by
subsequent enactments, and by virtue
of section three of the Unemployment
(Agreement) Act (Northern Ireland),
1936. - (Governor's recommendation
signified-Mr. Barbour.)

Second Reading
Canals Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Canals and Inland Navigation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): The brief Measure to which
I now invite the attention of the House
is largely self-explanatory.
From time
to time one or other of the Canal undertakings in Northern Ireland has discussed
with my Ministry the question of powers
to carry out some relatively minor work
of improvement, but has been deterred
by the expense involved in the promotion
of a Private Bill. The primary object of
the Bill before the House is, therefore,
to simplify the procedure by enabling the
owners of a Canal undertaking to make
application for a Provisional Order for
the purpose of repealing, altering or
amending the provisions of any local or
private Act of Parliament relating to the
undertaking.
The general lines of procedure by way
of Provisional Order are, of course, well
known to Members of the House, there
being ample precedent in the public
health code and in the statutes relating
to harbours, for example. Briefly, the
applicants are required to give public
notice of what they propose to do by way
of Provisional Order. Where there are
any objections the Ministry is empowered
to appoint a competent and impartial
person to hold an inquiry, and it is not
until after that stage has been reached
that a Provisional Order can be made.
Then, before the Order comes into effect
it must be embodied in a Confirmation
Bill and submitted to this House, where
any interested party may petition against
the Order. A somewhat simpler procedure
is provided for an application in respect
of the fixing of tolls and charges, and
advantage has been taken of the present
Measure to repeal the Canals (Continuance
of Charging Powers) Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, for the continuance of which
it has been necessary to make provision
annually in the Expiring Laws Continuance Act.
We have in Northern Ireland six
canals, or inland navigations—the Lagan
Navigation, the Newry Canal, the Upper
Bann Navigation, the Lower Bann
Navigation, the Coalisland Canal, and the
Strabane Canal. These waterways serve
a useful purpose, though a not inconsiderable proportion of the traffic formerly
borne by them has been transferred to the
roads.
Two further matters call for mention.
If hon. Members will turn to Clause 4
they will observe that provision is made
for the special rate now levied on
specified areas to meet a deficit on the
operations of the Upper Bann Navigation
Trustees to be treated in future as a
county-at-large charge. I understand
this course meets with the approval of the
three County Councils concerned, namely,
Armagh, Down and Tyrone. Clause 5
deals with a rental charge of £300 per
annum payable by the Lagan Navigation
Company to the Ministry of Finance.
The origin of this charge is historically
interesting. The construction of the
Lagan Canal was undertaken in the year
1753 at a cost of £43,304. This amount
was raised by a local tax on beer
and spirits which was levied on
the inhabitants of the district through
which the canal passes. Subsequently
the canal became derelict, but it was
revived in the year 1843 and vested by
Act of Parliament in the present company
subject to the payment of a yearly rent
charge of £300 to the Government in
consideration of the sum originally
raised by local taxation for the construction of the canal.
The Royal Commission for Inland
Waterways recommended its abolition in
the year 1906, and this recommendation
has been constantly pressed, first on the
Treasury, and later on the Northern
Ireland Ministry of Finance.
As a palliative the Derating Act of
1929 provided for its payment, not to the
Exchequer but to the Freight Rebates
Fund. As this fund will be wound up
on 1st January next under the provisions
of the Local Government (Finance) Bill
recently before this House, it is proposed
to abolish the rentcharge simultaneously.
I beg to move, "That the Bill be now
read a Second time."
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for Tuesday next.
The remaining Orders were read and
postponed.

ESTATE DUTY FILES.
1. Mr. O'NEILL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he can state to what extent correspondence of taxpayers with Income Tax
Departments are available to the officials
of the Estate Duty Office, Ministry of
Finance; and whether the Estate Duty
files are open for public inspection.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The statutory provision
in this matter is contained in Section 53
of the Imperial Finance Act, 1927, which
allows officers of the Commissioners of
Inland Revenue to disclose, under the
usual obligation of secrecy, to officers of
the Northern Ireland Estate Duty Office
such information as is necessary to enable
liability to Death Duties to be properly
assessed.
The reply to the second part of the
question is in the negative.
WIDENING OF ARDOYNE ROAD.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state why the inspector, Mr. Bates, who
presided at the inquiry held in the City
Hall, asserted that he was not supplied
with proper plans and details in connection with the proposed widening of
the Ardoyne Road; whether he can state
if this scheme was turned down to hinder
Mr. McKibbin from developing his
estate on proper town planning lines.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): No such assertion
as the hon. Member alleges was made
by the inspector at the inquiry in connection with the widening of Ardoyne
Road.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, the scheme put forward by the
Corporation provided for the construction, at the expense of the Corporation, of a 60-foot roadway from the
Crumlin Road, on the line of the existing Ardoyne Road to a point some considerable distance from the Ballysillan
Road. As the hon. Member is no doubt
aware, the Ardoyne Road does not afford
any connecting link for traffic between
the Crumlin Road and the Ballysillan
Road, and is nothing more than a track.
It was,
no doubt, suggested at the
inquiry that the Corporation might
at some future date carry on the
road to meet
meet the Ballysillan Road,
but no definite evidence on this
point was produced, and the application
which formed the subject of the inquiry
was limited to the particular road on the
Ardoyne Estate. Consequently, my Department was being asked to sanction
an expenditure of £18,625 for the construction of a 60-foot road which would
be a cul-de-sac, ending in a field at the
boundary of Mr. McKibbin's property.
It is unnecessary for me to point out
that it is the duty of my Department
to examine every application for sanction
to a loan received from a local authority
in order to ensure that the ratepayers
are not being called upon to bear the
cost of schemes which are not primarily
in the public interest.
I am satisfied that in this case the
benefit, if any, which would have accrued
to the ratepayers generally would not
have justified the expenditure involved.
There is absolutely no foundation for
the allegation contained in the hon.
Member's question that the scheme was
turned down to hinder Mr. McKibbin
from developing his estate. On the contrary, the decision arrived at does not
in any way prevent Mr. McKibbin from
developing his estate, including the construction of such roads as he considers
necessary.

Mr. BLACK: I do not think this
matter is so obscure as it has been made
to appear.
Under this first Clause it is
provided that employment in agriculture.
shall be insurable employment. There
is no difficulty in deciding what is
employment in agriculture, because
before this Bill becomes law you will
have to decide what is employment in
agriculture in order to find out whether
a man is acceptable under the present
Unemployment Insurance Act. When
the question comes to be considered as
to what employment in agriculture is,
you are driven to the definition Section,
and there it is defined in these words:-
"Agriculture" includes horticulture
and forestry.
Therefore, you start with this broad
proposition, that the Bill is prima facie
designed to sweep in under agriculture
people engaged in horticulture—that is,
people who are engaged in the ordinary
care of gardens. There is an exception
which is to be found in Clause 2 of the
First Schedule, but I see the Minister
of Labour has on the Paper an Amendment which is intended to bring it in
under Clause 16. The purpose of that
is to include within the scope of the Bill
the private gardener, who is defined as
"a person employed in horticulture
otherwise than in any trade or business
carried on for the purpose of gain." So
that if a man is engaged privately as a
gardener and not engaged in a business.
carried on for the purpose of gain he is
excluded from the Act. Any jobbing
gardener who comes to my house once a
week to trim my garden is excluded.
Similarly, if I was
a rich man and
employed one, two, or three gardeners
in whole-time employment and they
looked after my roses and glasshouses
they would be excluded from the Act.
Even if a man who has a gentleman's
place sells some of his surplus produce
his gardeners would still be excluded
from the Act, because this proposed
addition to Clause 16 says a private
gardener means "a person employed in
horticulture otherwise than in any trade
or business carried on for the purpose
of gain," so that unless the employer
organises his garden in the way of a
trade or business I do not think his
employees would be insurable. A man
who employs two or three gardeners and
sells roses and peas and lettuce would
not have his gardeners swept within the
ambit of the Act unless he so organised
his garden that the selling of those roses
and peas and lettuce, in the words of
this proposed Clause, constituted a trade
or business. If he really makes it a
trade or business in which he is in competition with nurserymen his gardeners
would be included in the Act. I
think the distinction is quite clear.
Exactly where the line should be drawn
is another matter. It has been drawn
in the Bill and there is no obscurity
about it.
The phrase "trade or business" is a
phrase that has been used
for many
years in the Income Tax Acts, and the
income tax authorities have had to consider time and again whether certain
activities were so organised as to amount
to a trade or business. I think the
result of it is this; that if the Bill is
passed in its present form the ordinary
private jobbing gardener will not be included, and a gardener employed about
a gentleman's place will not be included,
if that
gentleman sells produce
occasionally and in an incidental way,
but if he does organise his garden in
the way of trade or business his
gardener's employment will then be
insurable.

class, I state that no person in the

Things should be faced
reason at all.
from the economic point of view mainly.
What is there in the economics of the
agricultural worker that demands 2s a
week reduction? The only argument I
heard put forward in this Committee by
one of the country representatives that
seemed to have any solid foundation, was
the argument that, generally speakingand this is not always true-rents of

the economic point of view, the price of

agricultural worker, whether he is lowpaid or not, whether he is in employment or is unemployed, has got to pay
the same for his commodities as a person
in town. Why then should dependants'
benefit be 2s a week less?
Furthermore, why should there be a
maximum of 30s a week for an agricultural labourer? In my opinion this is a
far-reaching Clause. The maximum
implies two things, or we can infer two
things from it. One is that it is tacitly
admitted that the standard of living, as
measured by wages, is substantially
lower in the country than in the towns.
If that is the claim, it admits the case we
have always made out, that the country
people are underpaid. Secondly, the
dangerous thing about it is that it draws
a permanent line of demarcation between
one section of the working classes and
another, and as a representative of the
working class, I mean the organised
working class, the articulate working
maximum.
The idea that we should use our powers
inside the House of Commons to lay it
down in the law that one vast section of
the working-class population is to be for
ever separated from the other, is something which passes all comprehension.

Over a year ago, at the request of the
local authority, I imposed a speed limit
of 20 miles per hour in the town of
Antrim, and the effect of this is being
carefully watched with a view to determining how far a speed limit is effective
in Northern Ireland, where towns are, as
a rule, much smaller than in Great
Britain. So far the operation of this
speed limit has not proved very conclusive, as during the period of its operations the number of traffic accidents
reported actually increased, although
none of the accidents which occurred was
in any way due to speeding.

(NORTHERN IRELAND), 1935.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY ΤΟ THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. GORDON): I beg to
move: "That the Order in Council made
by the Governor of Northern Ireland on
the 29th October, 1935, under Section 18
of the Unemployment Act (Northern
Ireland), 1934, for increasing the amount
of the unemployment benefit payable in
respect of dependent children, be hereby
approved."
Power is given to the Governor by
Section 18 of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1934, to
apply to Northern Ireland, with necessary
adaptations, any Order amending the
Unemployment Insurance Code in Great
Britain, made by the Minister of Labour
there on the recommendation of the
Unemployment Insurance Statutory Committee, to secure the solvency of the Unemployment Fund or to dispose of a
surplus. One of the matters on which the
Statutory Committee may make recommendations for these purposes is the rate
of benefit in respect of dependent
children.
On the recommendation of the Com-
Imittee the Minister of Labour in Great
Britain made an Order on 25th October,
1935, increasing the weekly rate of unemployment benefit in respect of a dependent child from 2s to 3s, with effect from
31st October, 1935. This increase was
applied to Northern Ireland, with effect
from the same date, by the Order for
which the approval of Parliament is now
sought.
In the absence of approval by Parliament the Order would lapse on 31st
October next, that is, on the expiration.
of twelve months from the date on which
it came into operation, and the former
rate of 2s per week for a dependent child
would again become effective in Northern
Ireland. I am sure no hon. Member in
this House would like to see that take
place. Consequently, I beg to move that
this Order be approved.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to mention to the Minister of Home Affairs a
matter of which I have only received
notice myself. A very serious position
has been created in the city of Belfast by
the Belfast Board of Guardians making
drastic cuts in outdoor relief grants.
A
rent strike is threatened if
some redress is not granted.
would like the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary to take serious note
of the poverty of the people who are
affected. A very large number of people
have been depending on the Second
Appointed Day being declared at a very
early date. They have been very
I
anxiously waiting for an improvement in
their condition, but the Second
Appointed Day is very far off at the
moment as far as they are concerned, and
instead of an improvement taking place
their position has been worsened by a
drastic cut in the meagre amount of outdoor relief they were receiving.
Meetings are being held in regard to
this matter, but I do not think that outside meetings will be effective. Perhaps
men in dire necessity may go to extremes
they would not go to in normal circumstances. I want to see the peace of the
city maintained, but I also want to see
the people of the city getting the
amounts agreed upon by the Minister of
Home Affairs with the deputation which
waited upon him in 1933. For reasons
best known to the Belfast Board of
Guardians last Friday 200 men were
turned away. Every other man was
turned away and was told to come back
on the following day at 11 o'clock. The
result was that a very serious cut took
place in the allowances.
The result is very serious at the
moment, and I appeal to the Minister of
Home Affairs to take immediate action
to find out the real cause of the large
reduction. Just before I came into the
House I heard of a man who had 4s a
week, and he actually received 2s 7d.
That is a very bad policy for the
Guardians to pursue, to make such a
reduction without due notice or regard to
the circumstances of the individual.
Other applicants have wives and young
families dependent upon them. They
were getting 20s or 22s and now they are
getting 12s. I would like to know what
has come over the Guardians or by what
authority they are acting.
I am inclined to think there is something in regard to the Second Appointed

fit who are now getting relief from the
Belfast Board of Guardians. Is he going

I look through the Estimate and I find

Minister a real separate one or only a

Finance, Commerce, Home Affairs, Agriculture and Education are all separate
Departments. Is there in reality a
separate Department of administration
known as the Prime Minister's?
The tradition in Irish life is that no

they are invariably losers at the end in
everything but reputation. That applies
also to public men in Great Britain.
I was greatly struck when I read the

in any brain of his time, except Mr.

of time, could stick the job for fifteen

All rock excavations under the contract have been completed. The four
sluice gates at the Cutts, a similar
number at Portna, together with fish
passes, improvements to salmon cribs,
new fish house, and so forth, are complete; the maintenance period has expired.

bank.
The past winter has been very severe
with periods of heavy rainfall. The
sluice gates at the Cutts, Portna, and
Toome have been operated to the
maximum extent possible without
endangering the safety of the contractor's dredging craft now at work
between Portglenone and Portna, and
records show that we have been able to
discharge down the Lower Bann approximately 50 per cent. more flood water
than would have been possible in precontract days with the same Lough
levels. There has been very little flooding around Lough Neagh which can be
Public Works and Buildings 976

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
attributed to the high level of the Lough.
Technical opinion is that without the
benefits achieved from the partially completed works Lough Neagh would have
attained a maximum level of nearly two
feet higher than the maximum at which
it was controlled last winter, and the
period of such high level would have been
much longer. In spite of unsettled
weather the operation of the sluices and
the discharge possible through the
partially completed channel succeeded in
reducing the level of Lough Neagh to the
normal summer level of 52 feet above sea
level by the 1st March. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I have given notice
along with the hon. and learned Member for Central that we would raise this
question of the outdoor-relief workers
who are receiving grants under the
special distress scheme. Yesterday when
I raised the matter I had not sufficient
data at my command to put before the
Minister to impress upon him the necessity for his taking strong action. But
he was ready in his reply to stab me
right away for my failure to comply with
Parliamentary etiquette, might I say, in
not forewarning him of my intention of
raising the question. But I had protected myself in my first few remarks by
saying I had only got notification and
had not had time to do so, and I was
pleased to see that Mr. Speaker came to
my assistance.
The Minister has now had ample time
at his disposal to consider this allimportant matter. It is not a question
of whether the Belfast Board of
Guardians is a democratically elected
body or not. It is a question to my mind
whether there is anything behind this
attack on the most helpless class of the
community. I feel since yesterday that
something unforeseen must have happened
whereby 1,500 odd people have been told.
within 24 hours that their grants will be
subject to a reduction. I am quite aware
that the Government give a lump sum
in lieu of these distress payments. I
want to know have the Government got
any representation made to them that the
amount they passed for relief of distress
has been eaten up to such an extent that
the authorities who administer it would
be compelled to reduce the grants if the
Government did not come to their
assistance. That is the first point I want
to know if you had any notice of this
amount being eaten up. If not then what
other reasons can I suggest would be the
cause of cutting down the grants some
20 per cent., some 30 per cent., and in
one case actually 50 per cent.
I had an influential-they were influential because they were citizens—a
large body of these poor souls who have
wives and families dependant upon them
appeared in my office and presented the
amounts of money they received, and
presented their family budgets. They
had their budgets made up to the figure
they were receiving from James Street,
and they were left this week high and
dry. The amount they were getting
would not pay the amounts due, which
meant that the few goods from the grocer
had to go behind, the rent could not be
paid, the necessary things for the family
could not be got, and they were in an
awful plight. Poverty was staring them
in the face. Desperation also seemed to
lurk at the back of their eyes. I said to
them: "I am deeply sorry for your predicament, and I am more than sorry that
anyone should make an attack upon you
at such short notice, but I do feel that
there is something other than the Board
of Guardians not having sufficient money
to meet the requirements of the grants
they allow. I will take it upon myself
to inquire from the Government how far
they are responsible for this drastic cut
that has taken place, because I assisted in
Adjournment-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
passing a large sum of money for paying
out these special grants to the people who
have passed the tests for receiving
them."
I do not want to suggest anything that
might be responsible for it. I want the
Government to be open in the matter.
I want them to be frank. I do not want
unemployed relief workers to be the
victims of any ill-feeling, or any dispute,
or any misunderstanding that has arisen
between any public boards and the
Government. Here is what one man
says:
I served twelve months in prison
because I got into trouble due to want.
I was released 10-1-36. I was granted
the sum of one pound for four weeksthis to keep my wife, five children and
myself, after which I was turned down
completely. Luckily a friend found me
work on the 9-1-36, but I had to live
for nine weeks and keep seven of us
on £4. I hope you mention this case
as one of the cases whom our friends
the right hon. Gentlemen think are
being treated fairly.
The name and address are given. Now
I think many other Members on
this side of the House, and I presume
Members on the other side of the
House, had representations made from
these people who were cut. I want
now to try to solve the mystery
of this lightning cut in grants which
were brought down from the least possible for anyone to exist on. I feel that
the number here, 1,458 people feel that
they are the victims of a certain set of
circumstances over which they have no
control, and to which they were not a

Gentleman must understand for no
political, Press, or other propaganda
stunt. I am not desirous of this being
made a political or party matter at all.
It is a bread-and-butter matter for those
who are suffering and those who are looking to this House for some assistance to
tide them over a difficult period.
I do feel that the reduction at this
period is unfair, and as to the lame excuse
of the Belfast Board of Guardians that
after investigating into the family circumstances in the cases referred to the
reductions were made in accordance with
those circumstances, I want to say here
were
and now that in 100 per cent. of the cases

the home are exactly the same as they
on the first day the grants were

to speak for them, to portray their

of these poor people reconsidered in a most
sympathetic way. This reduction means
ever so much to some of these people. For
instance, a reduction from 28s to 20s or
21s in the case of a married man with a
family, or, in the case of a single man, a
reduction from 14s or 15s to 7s or 8s a
week probably means all the difference
between being able to struggle along and
being reduced to a state of semi-starvation.
I do not want to cast any reflection on
the Board of Guardians, or to impugn
their bona fides or honesty, but I think it
is a serious matter that, at a time like
this, without any warning or notification
whatever, such a drastic step should have
been undertaken by this particular Board
without any consultation with the Ministry. I think that is a very regrettable
step. The saving that will be effected
will not be very great. Probably the step
was dictated by motives of economy, but
we should be very sorry to see economy
practised at the expense of the very
poorest and weakest class in the community. I ask the Minister, and I hope
not in vain, to exercise the influence and
good offices he possesses in the direction
of having the claims of these people reconsidered and, as far as it is consistent with
justice and the public interest, met in a
sympathetic spirit.

as my experience goes I have always found

that the Guardians would be justified in
dealing even harshly with these people,
even if they were paid for doing nothing.
We know that is not the case with these
people. They are paid a subsistence allowance because they can get nothing to do,
and on that account I think there would
be no harm done to the community as a
whole if the Guardians in their general
policy were a little more generous. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
If all industry can secure from
the masses of the unemployed all
the labour that it needs there would
be no injury whatever done to the

anything to do in a degree of physical
efficiency. I would not like to dictate or
Adjournment-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

give the impression that I was dictating.
It is a rather surprising thing that in this

has increased by, perhaps, ten times the

done, and it would be destructive to the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have read

Antrim are not erecting labourers'

Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a
fact that the Rural District Councils of
Antrim are not erecting labourers'
cottages. Five out of the seven Rural
District Councils in the county
already initiating building schemes under

are
The
Neither is it a fact that the cottages
already built are in a deplorable condition and not being repaired.
Rural District Councils carry out repairs
from time to time as required, and the
Ministry's housing inspectors make regular inspections with a view to seeing that
any necessary repairs are carried out.
In these circumstances I do not consider
an inquiry necessary.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the Minister

Sir DAWSON BATES: I was
referring to labourers' cottages built
under the Acts for which the rural district authorities are responsible. I do
not believe that the condition of affairs
referred to by the hon. Member exists
in regard to these cottages. It may be
that certain farmers have let cottages
which are in a very unsanitary condition.

AIRCRAFT AND ARMAMENTS
FACTORIES IN BELFAST.
6. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the result
of his recent representation to the
Imperial Government to have aircraft
and armament factories established in
Belfast; and whether he can state what
steps the Government are taking to secure
for the Belfast Shipyard a share of the
Admiralty work.
The PRIME MINISTER: The British
Authorities have been kept thoroughly
informed from the outset of this Government's willingness to assist in every
way in our power any schemes that may
be found necessary for the national
defence, and Ulster's potentialities have
been fully explained to the various departments concerned.
As the details are necessarily of a
strictly confidential character, it would
not be in the public interest to give
further information.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the Prime
Minister aware that very large contracts
have been entered into with other parts
of the Empire and Ulster has not been
considered yet?
7. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he would be prepared
to set up a committee to investigate the
possibility of securing new industries for
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
Whilst the Government is at all times
open to any suggestion designed to bring
about the establishment of new industries
in Northern Ireland, they do not consider that this purpose would be usefully
served at the present time by the setting
up of a committee as suggested by the
hon. Member.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
fact that industrial development has been
a failure and that no new industries have
been created, does the Minister think it
advisable to appeal to the employers of
Northern Ireland to take the matter up?
The Government have failed, and only an
eggshell factory has been established.

1937, to defray the Salaries and Expenses

Services, Registration, Loan Services,

(N.I.), Land Law Acts, collection of

Mr. BARBOUR: This Estimate will
be found on page 10 of the Book of
Estimates. In introducing this very
comprehensive Estimate I do not propose
to enter on the subject of the numerous
activities of the Ministry, which are set
out in detail in Part I of the Estimate,
and it will suffice to begin my statement
with a description of the changes in staff
organisation for which it is necessary to
provide in the forthcoming year. The
total number of staff shows an increase
of fifteen, and this is the principal reason
for the increase in the total of the
Estimate.
Apart from a small addition to the
centralised duplicating and calculating
machine staff, the staff increases are confined to the Works Branch of the Ministry, and are due to the intensified
building programme which is now taking
place. Schools, police barracks, employment exchanges, not to mention the reconstruction of Government House and
the construction of the R.U.C. Depot at
Enniskillen, all make considerable
demands on our Works Division, and it
has been necessary, in the interests of
efficiency, to make certain additions to
the staff. In the technical branch there
is an additional assistant architect and
two more temporary assistant quantity
surveyors. In the engineer's section provision has had to be made for two more
assistant engineers and three
temporary engineers. Finally, there is
an extra temporary assistant engineer for
the Bann drainage site staff.
more
Apart from the additional staff, there
are various small increases due to full
consolidation of salaries and to increments. There is also part provision for
a special gratuity to the Director of
Works as some indication of the valuable
work he has done over a number of years
in connection with the Bann drainage
scheme. The arrangement to signalise
the special responsibility attaching to

of the present position of these works.
when dealing with the Works Vote.

Ministry of Finance
7 APRIL 1936
In connection with the provision for
Land Purchase staff, appearing on page
12, a few figures will show the efficient
manner in which the collection of land
purchase annuities is administered. In
1935-6 the amount to be collected is
£956,720, of which only £15,000, or
1.57 per cent., is estimated to be in
arrear at the end of the year. I am glad
to say that the amount in arrear shows a
considerable decrease compared with
1934-5, when it was 2.08 per cent. of the
total. The cost of the staff necessary to
deal with 124,300 accounts involved is
only .56 per cent. of the amount collected,
slightly more than half of one per cent.
It will not be out of place for me to pay
a tribute to the admirable way in which
the great majority of land purchase
tenants fulfil their obligations. They regard the payment of the annuities as an
honourable obligation to be punctually
fulfilled.
Sub-head D for legal charges, on page
16, is up by £750. In this sub-head provision is made for out of pocket legal
expenses incurred in connection with
guaranteed loans and Government loans
activities. It is obvious that the
Estimate for this sub-head must be
largely conjectural, but it is based on the
most accurate forecast that can be made
in the circumstances. There is still a
tendency for the number of Government
loans to decrease as the larger borrowers
find it cheaper to obtain money from
sources other than the Government Loans
Fund. Of the total provision on this
sub-head £600 is in respect of possible
expenses in connection with loans guarantee cases, £900 in respect of general
charges, and £750 in respect of the
Government's costs in the appeal to the
Privy Council regarding the education
rate. The last item accounts for the
increase on this sub-head over last year.
The expense of Ulster Savings Certificate administration, which will be found
under sub-head H, page 17, shows a
small increase due to full consolidation of
salaries.
The money provision for the Registrar-
General's office requires no comment; the
increase is simply due to full consolidation of salaries, plus certain increments.
However, as on previous occasions, I am
sure the Committee will be interested to
hear some account of the work of this
office in the past year. To those hon.
Members who are specially interested in
the registration service I can confidently
recommend the Registrar General's
annual report for 1934, which gives a
very interesting survey of the registration arrangements and the state of the
service.
In the matter of vital statistics, it may
be of interest to note that in the year
1935 both the general death rate was
somewhat higher than usual and the
birth rate established a new low record.
Unfortunately, partly owing to a serious
epidemic of measles in the early part of
the year, the infantile death rate equalled
the highest hitherto recorded in the
history of the Northern Government. A
more encouraging feature, as shown from
the year's records, is that the marriage
rate is the highest of the present century,
with the exception of the two years
immediately following the war, and to
some extent at least one may, perhaps, be
justified in concluding that this reflects
a higher standard of prosperity amongst
the population as a whole.
As has already been announced in
another place, the Government decided
that no census of population should be
taken in Northern Ireland this year. In
the meantime, with the cessation of
emigration, it appears that the population has been increasing slightly over the
past few years. The question as to
whether a modified form of census of
population shall or shall not be taken in
1937 is under consideration.
During the past year another issue of
the Ulster Year Book has been made and
the sales indicate that this publication
serves a public want.
Turning lastly to Sub-head M, the
receipts appropriated-in-aid, two items do
not recur-the repayment in connection
with engineering staff services on county.
council drainage schemes, as no schemes.
are anticipated next year and the agency
fee for enemy property services, an excrescence which now disappears.
The Committee will notice that there
is an increase of £2,650 in the receipts
from the British Government on account
of reserved agency services. Owing to
the delay in certain large works, such as
the telephone exchange and to the stoppage of the internal painting at Stormont,
the receipts on this account for 1935-6
were over-estimated to the extent of some

Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will
find this Estimate on page 20 of the
book. They will note that there is
another substantial decrease on this Vote
on account of the completion of the
major portion of the general revaluation.
Apart from the normal year to year work
of the valuation staff there is still a considerable amount of work to be done in
connection with appeals. When the
latter are completed a further reduction
in valuation staff may be anticipated.
Hon. Members will see that in subhead
A the valuation staff has been reduced
by 43 per cent. That is on page 21.
As my hon. Friend the Member for
Mid Antrim (Mr. Crawford) recently
raised the question of the return of
valuation staff to normal, I should like
to make some remarks on this point.
When the Valuation Bill of 1932 was
going through the House hopes were
expressed from this Bench that when the
first revaluation was completed the staff
would return to normal. I fear that this
was too optimistic. Experience shows
that quinquennial revaluations mus
mean a permanent addition to the staff.
What that addition will be I cannot forecast now, but I anticipate that in twelve
months' time the Estimates for 1937-38
will show what the stabilised staff costs
are likely to be.
The increased provision for the
Ordnance Survey Staff is maintained for,
1936-37. As I explained in introducing
this Estimate last year the staff in connection with this branch of the Ministry's
activities had for the past ten years been
kept considerably below the strength
necessary to keep pace with the work;
the effect of this was accentuated by the
necessity for employing the survey staff
on mapping work for revaluation purposes and the result was that ordnance
survey work fell considerably in arrear.
Hon. Members may have noticed that
the necessity for keeping ordnance maps up
to date has recently been stressed in Great
Britain by a committee specially appointed
to examine this problem, and although
building developments here do not bring
about such drastic changes in the
countryside as they do in Great Britain,
yet in many respects the changes here in
the vicinity of centres of population are
very marked.
The reduction in travelling expenses
follows on the reduction in valuation
staff, while the reduction in postage is
due to the fact that last year we had
amongst other things to provide for the
posting of 350,000 revaluation notices.
The provision of £1,000 in sub-head D
for legal charges in connection with
valuation appeals is of necessity conjectural, the amount required depending
considerably on the number of cases
settled by agreement at the last moment.
Finally, the appropriations in aid show
a substantial decrease due to the reduced
amount to be received from counties as
their contribution to the cost of revaluation. I may say, in reply to my hon.
Friend the Member for Mid Antrim,
that the county authorities are almost as
interested in revaluation and valuation
work as the Government. Of course, it is
on the valuation that the rates are
collected and the whole finances of the
counties are based. Therefore, I am
afraid I cannot hold out any hope to my
hon. Friend of any substantial reduction
in the charges from time to time to the
counties for the work done by the Valuation and Survey Department.

Mr. BEATTIE: I am sure most Members of this Committee have come in contact with the staff for whom we are asked
to provide in this Estimate. I myself
had the sorry experience of meeting one
of the officers estimated for here.
notice that we have grading as far as
these officers are concerned, Temporary
Valuers Grade 1, and Temporary
Valuers Grade 2. I think I met one in
Grade 2, because he came to the house in
which I have taken up my abode and
his knowledge of the valuation of that
house was nil. I want to be quite
candid. He had an English accent. The
tenants of the house did not know what
he was talking about. He said that, of
course, the valuation was too low, that
Northern Ireland had not been paying
its quota in comparison with Great
Britain in regard to valuation. Why he
said that I do not know.
Then another officer came out. I presume he was in Grade 2. He measured
up the house and after I had learned
how the valuation chief had made up his
figure, I found that my house was overvalued about £10. As I said here before,
my house was valued before it was built.
How he knew it was going to be built I
do not know. All I could think was that
he had seen the builder's plans in the
Corporation, and that from those plans.
he actually fixed the valuation of the
house. To-day the area I refer to is a
disgrace to the Valuation Department of
Northern Ireland. One house fronting
the Upper Newtownards Road with
beautiful accommodation-three roomshas been valued at £35 while the houses
in the back street have a valuation of
£44, and they have only two rooms.
That is a standing disgrace to the Valuation Department, and the result is that
five of these houses in the back street,
which has only been made about twelve
months, are now up for sale or to let.
People thought that that would be a
little area in the country to which they
could go to live, but they are being
driven out of the homes they were trying
to purchase owing to the maladministration of the Valuation Department. I
know the Commissioner and I give him a
hearty invitation to see for himself. I
will not say one word about him, but if
he comes with me I will show him what
is a standing disgrace to this Estimate,
and will always remain a great injustice
to the persons who purchased property in
that area or rented houses there. I am
not putting this down to the head of the
Department.
I believe he is as competent to carry out the work of valuation as the head of any other Department.
I know it is utterly impossible for him
fully to realise the thousands of
anomalies that have been created by the
staff which he was given with which to
carry out this revaluation. I do not
grumble about our old staff, nor about
the local officials who understood the
conditions, but I certainly do grumble
and feel very resentful in regard to those
Englishmen who were brought here to
increase the valuation of property about
which they did not know the first thing
so far as Northern Ireland was
cerned. I did not appeal myself, and I
have no intention of appealing. The only
alternative left to the whole of us is to
get out. Therefore, we do feel very resentful that a Department paid out of our
pocket should put its hand into our other
pocket and take out more than we are
able to pay.
con-
I fully realise that the revaluation of
Belfast and Northern Ireland was
essential, and I agree with the Valuation
Act to a certain extent in so far as the
rateable value of Northern Ireland was
far below that of any other part of the
United Kingdom in accordance with its
size. But surely that was not the time
to make an attack on new property
without the enhanced value of ground
rents being taken into account. That is
where the damaging factor comes in, and
a very severe blow has been struck at
individuals who are compelled to pay
very heavy rents to ground landlords.
The Valuation Department have not
taken that matter into consideration at
all but have increased the valuations
irrespective of ground rent charges. I
disagree altogether with that method and
principle of valuation. I see a reduction
in the number of temporaries has taken
place. All we can say to that is "Thank
God they are away.”
