Let me illustrate this in my own way.
At the age of 21 apprentices in the shipbuilding, engineering, and other trades,
have qualified as journeymen. In the

CLASS II. No. 9.
PUBLIC RECORDS AND ANCIENT
MONUMENTS.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £3,013 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1937, to
pay the salaries and expenses of the
Public Record Office of Northern Ireland
(13 and 14 Geo. V. (N.I.), c. 20), and
the cost of administration of the Ancient
Monuments Act (16 and 17 Geo. V.
(N.I.), c. 12). (Note-£1,500 has been
voted on account.)
The PRIME MINISTER: There is very
little variation from last year's Estimate.
Salaries are slightly increased through the
operation of normal increments.
Under Subhead C there is a re-vote of
£200 set aside for a proposed grant to
Carrickfergus Urban District Council for
work affecting the outskirts of the Castle.
This has not yet been commenced by the
Council in view of their general improvement scheme, which will not only affect
the vicinity of the Castle, but the seafront for some distance to the eastward.
It is, however, expected that the improvement beside the Castle will be effected
very shortly.
As Members may not be
aware of the Ministry's plans so far as
the Castle is concerned, I may say that
its intention is to preserve permanently
the unimpeded view of the front and both
flanks of the Castle and of the sea from
the town, which has been opened up by
the demolition of a number of modern
War Department excrescences under the
Castle walls. An agreement has been
made with the Urban Council that in consideration of the proposed grant these
northward fringes of the Castle, after
allotting a space for a much needed road
Estimates-
Public Records
7 APRIL 1936
widening, shall be grassed over by the
Council and maintained as small parks. I
may say I went down myself to see the
place and I was very interested in the
progress that is being made. Should the
larger projects of the Urban District
Council take effect, care will be taken that
the immediate amenities of the Castle are
not impaired.
An increase will be noted in the charge
for maintenance, etc., of ancient monuments under Subhead D. This item varies
from time to time according to the nature
and number of the monuments requiring
attention. The total number of monuments now in charge of the Ministry is 42.
During 1935 three were taken over,
namely, Ballylumford Dolmen in Islandmagee, which stands beside a main road,
and is probably familiar to many; a small
but complete stone circle at Drumskinny,
near Kesh, Co. Fermanagh; and a very
remarkable set of prehistoric stone burial
chambers at Cregganconroe, near Pomeroy, in Co. Tyrone.
The vote under Subhead E-Acquisition of Historical Documents, including
the purchase of original documents by the
Public Record Office, and the cost of copies
and photographic facsimiles made for itremains at the same figure, but I am glad
to say that each year more use is being
made of this provision, and it is increasingly better known and more generally
accepted that the Record Office is the most
suitable place for the deposit, either in
original or transcript, of any manuscript
relating to the history of Ulster or Ulstermen. A notable discovery of this kind
during 1935 was a fine volume in private
ownership of original State accounts,
dealing largely with payments to King
William III's army in Ireland, of which
a complete copy has been made and
deposited as a record. An account of
the contents will appear in the next
annual report of the Record Office.
Under Sub-head H, a small increase
appears in the travelling and miscellaneous expenses of the Ancient Monuments Advisory Committee.
This provision is intended to meet expenditure
likely to be incurred in connection with
the Committee's project of making a preliminary survey of the whole of the ancient
monuments of the Six Counties. Various
members of the Committee, with the help
of private individuals, have made themselves responsible for collecting material
from the different counties, and in view
of the fact that they will be giving their
services gratuitously, the Ministry considers it only right that they should be
recouped for any extra expenditure incurred in travelling to view the monuments.
The editorial work, which is likely to
be exacting, will be done in the Public
Record Office, and the Ministry of Finance
has undertaken the publication, the cost
of which has been partly defrayed by subscription.
Under Sub-head I., page 47, the provision for archæological investigation has
been reduced from £500 to £300. As
hon. Members will remember, the basis
of this scheme is that the Government is
prepared to pay 60 per cent. of the wages
of unemployed men who receive work in
the course of these operations. As this
works out in practice the total cost of
the work, including supervision, implements, etc., is shared almost equally between the State and the individuals or
learned bodies promoting the excavations.
On the experience of 1935 it is considered
that not more than £300 per annum is
likely to be provided in Ulster from non-
Governmental sources for archæological
research.
During 1935 the following schemes
were put in hand:-The "raised beach"
at the Curran, Larne, was excavated to a
depth of 26 feet by the Harvard
University Archæological Expedition to
Ireland. These deep diggings produced
over 10,000 flint implements, the study of
which and the framing of the conclusions
to be drawn therefrom, have, it is understood, occupied the American scholars for
the whole of the past winter.
At Doonroe, in the mountains to the
north of County Tyrone, Mr. C. Davies,
Lecturer in Roman History and Classical
Archæology at Queen's University, commenced the excavation of a very remarkable prehistoric burial cairn. In
the course of this work Mr. Davies discovered six cists, one entire and containing a food vessel. This excavation was
not concluded at the end of the year and
is to be renewed.
At the Doon, Larriban Point, near
Ballintoy, Professor Gordon Childe, of
Edinburgh University, excavated a headland fort in which he found objects not

Public Records

only of bronze and amber but of glass,
leading him to the conclusion that the
site was inhabitated not only in the prehistoric period but also as late as 700-

At Portbraddon, Whitepark Bay, Mr.
A. McL. May has commenced the investigation of a large shore cave, 21 feet wide
at the entrance and 90 feet long. He has
found fire-places and occupation layers
beneath each other and sometimes under
marine deposited matter. The work is
still proceeding. I beg to move.

see these cover fees for admission to

per

1935-36. There are two new subheads in
this Vote. Provision of £400 is made for
remnant expenditure in connection with
the railing and so forth, round the vault
of the late Lord Carson. The new subhead G, entitled Unclassified Expenses,
is intended to include any small items of
expenditure which cannot be classified
under any of the other subheads of the
Votes for which the Ministry of Finance
accounts.
The non-recurrence of provision for
turbary schemes requires some explanation. There are two types of turbary
scheme. The first is that which is required principally to preserve tenants'
rights when an estate is being sold under
the Land Purchase Acts. Being definitely connected with Land Purchase, such
schemes are drawn up by the Land Purchase Commission and administered as a
reserved service. The second type of
scheme is that occasioned, say, by the
necessity for redistribution of turbary or
scheme falls within the functions of the
Ministry.
Up to the present owing to the operation of the 1925 Land Act, schemes of the
first type have been more numerous, and
for the comparatively small number of
schemes of the second type the Ministry
has made use of the staff dealing with
turbary matters in the Land Purchase
Commission on an agency basis. Since,
however, the work on turbary schemes
arising out of sales of land under
the 1925 Land Act has almost
been completed, and the Land Purchase
Commission itself will soon be closed
down, it has been decided that the
Ministry will hereafter assume direct
responsibility for the administration of
turbary, as the second type of turbary
scheme, to which I have referred, continues to provide work of considerable
volume. Provision is accordingly being
made in the Ministry of Finance main
estimate for the appropriate expenditure
on staff, which replaces the cost of the
agency service formerly borne on this
Vote. The Land Commission staff hitherto
engaged on this work is being taken over
by the Ministry, and will work under the
supervision of the superintendent of
Ordnance Survey. It is hoped that
turbary schemes which were previously
delayed by reason of the priority of the
Land Purchase work will now be considerably expedited.
The only other item calling for comment
is the provision in Sub-head A for the
payment of the balance of the fee for
the preparation of the second edition of
the Index to the Statutory Rules and
Orders affecting Northern Ireland up to
31st December, 1935. The actual payment made for this work in the year 1935-
36 was £200, and a sum of £70 is included to cover the remainder of the
work, which it is expected will take
another three or four months to complete.
I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: According to the
notice I gave I intend to put as briefly as
possible the question which I put at the
opening of the House. I have in
my possession certain documents from
recipients of outdoor relief. My whole
case on their behalf is against the Advisory Committee appointed to deal with.
the outdoor relief grant. When this
Committee was being appointed I opposed
them strenuously. The right hon. Gentleman, who is responsible for the appointment of this Advisory Committee, has
allocated to them the right of administering the amounts which applicants shall
receive or of reducing those amounts. The
Government handed over to the Belfast
Board of Guardians a grant plus an
amount from the rates and the Minister
Exceptional Relief Grant 1058
Adjournment-
7 APRIL 1936
gave them the right of appointing a committee to govern the funds. I claim that

been dealing with poor-law administration

such that this class of work should not
have been allocated to them. From that
point of view I was opposed to their getting any control over these special relief
grants.
Unfortunately the Minister of Labour
stands firm by that body, and I hold him
responsible for the action of the guardians
last week in reducing the amounts that
recipients were receiving. I apportion the
blame in the right quarter. The Minister
of Home Affairs is responsible for Local
Government services, and he is not the
subject matter of discussion now. This
Advisory Committee acted in a highhanded way at an important period of the
year in making a reduction of anything
from 20 to 50 per cent. in the meagre
amounts they doled out. What have we
done to assist the outdoor relief people?
We have abolished over £100,000 or
£170,000 of that grant. Has this money
all been eaten up? I say that 75 per
cent. of the people who are claiming are
those who will be taken over
on the
Second Appointed Day. The responsibility for keeping these people until that
day arrives is on the Minister of Labour.
Hence my reason for putting the question
to the Minister of Labour and asking him
to abolish the Advisory Committee and
take away from the Board of Guardians
the administration of this special relief,
and establish a Committee that will work
more in conformity with public opinion
in the giving of grants to those requiring
them.
There is the case of a man and his wife
with a family of five who are asked to

paper over to the proper authority to see

the financial assistance necessary to keep

the case of the man with a wife and
family of four who was asked to live for
nine weeks on £4. Those are illustrations

which I spoke. There is no justification

Fund.
In regard to the Minister of Home

Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member has raised a question in regard
to the administration of the Customs
Acts. I think he is under a complete
misunderstanding in regard to the whole
matter. May I explain to the House
that up to a short time ago something
like 113 police officers were detailed
specially to deal with Customs
along the Border. Their duty was confined to Customs and nothing else, and
they received the usual warrants to enable
them to make arrests under the Customs
Acts.
Mr. BEATTIE: Arrests only?
cases
Sir DAWSON BATES: Seizures, if
my hon. Friend will permit me. It was
found in practice that these 113 men,
who did no work except Customs work,
were entirely insufficient to deal with the
situation that arose. Apart altogether
from that, it meant a great deal of waste
labour on the part of the ordinary police
along the Border, who were not armed
with similar powers to those conferred
upon these 1'13 men. As a matter of fact,
everybody in this House will agree that
nothing could be worse for the community
than that smuggling should be allowed
to continue as it has been in the past.
The result of all this was that we had
a conference with the Customs people
on the other side of the Channel.
We pointed out to them that it was rather
an absurd situation that a limited number
of police should deal with Customs cases,
and that the rest of the police should look
on while cattle were being smuggled. That
is really what took place. The result is
that the police generally have the necessary authority which up to that time had
been conferred only on a limited number
of police. In other words, in addition to
the ordinary duties of the police not only
along the Border but elsewhere, a further
duty has been imposed upon them, and
that is of enforcing the law in relation to
the Customs.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 8th April, 1936.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Notice of Questions.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before proceeding
with the business of the House I would
like to address hon. Members very shortly
on the subject of questions asked in this
House. Strictly speaking, Standing
Order No. 8 says that notice of questions
shall be given by Members in writing to
the Clerk at the Table, but owing to the
habit of this House of having an
adjournment over a long week-end, I
have always instructed the clerks to
receive questions by post or otherwise
during the week-end. That would be for
the convenience of hon. Members. If
the House would agree I am quite prepared to continue the relaxation of the
strict Rule as laid down by the Standing
Order. However, I would like to make it
clear that I would not be prepared to
extend that relaxation to any longer
period than an adjournment over the
long week-end. It is obvious that during
an adjournment of for instance, two or
three weeks, some 150 or 200 questions
might accumulate, if they would be sent
by post throughout that period, and that
would create a condition of affairs with
which I would not be prepared to cope.
Therefore, if the House is agreeable, any
questions which hon. Members wish to
send in during the Adjournment on this.
occasion should be handed in on 28th
inst. when the House is sitting. Perhaps the House will continue to approve
of the relaxation as regards the sending
in of questions by post or otherwise over
the long week-end in order to suit the
convenience of hon. Members.
Oral Answers to Questions.
WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION
АСТ.
1. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Midgley)
asked the Minister of Labour whether
he is prepared to consider sympathetically the advisability of amending
the Workmen's Compensation Act so as
to make it compulsory upon every
employer, including farmers, to insure
against liability to pay compensation for
injuries received; whether he is prepared
to consider that the minimum amount of
such insurance should be not less than
£500; whether he is prepared to make
it an offence of a grave nature for an
employer not to be so insured; and
whether he will recommend that it be
compulsory for an employer to produce
evidence of such insurance to the
Ministry's inspectors.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): As I informed the hon.
Member in reply to a question which he
put to me on the 12th March, the Workmen's Compensation Code is uniform
throughout the United Kingdom, and it
is desirable in the interests of all concerned that this uniformity should continue.
No representations have been made to
me on the subject of compulsory insurance, but if the hon. Member has any
information which he would like to bring
to my notice with regard to hardship
having been caused as a result of the
absence of insurance, I am prepared to
consider the matter in consultation with
the Government Department concerned
in Great Britain.
BURGLARIES IN BELFAST.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Midgley)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware that a serious outbreak of house burglaries has taken place
in Belfast lately; whether it is a
fact that scarcely a week passes but
dozens of citizens are complaining of
heavy losses as a result of the activities .
of those engaged in robbing workingclass houses; whether he is satisfied that
adequate police supervision is being
given to working-class districts in order
to detect the offenders; whether he is
aware that the usual practice is for the
miscreants to effect an entry by utilising
the back passages between two streets,
and whether, in view of this apparently
well thought out campaign of house
breaking, he is prepared to make representations to the local authority to affix
gates to such back passages wherever
practicable.
Oral Answers
Bills Presented
8 APRIL 1936
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am unfortunately
only too well aware that the number of
cases of house-breaking reported is still
very considerable, but I am glad to be
able to state for the information of the
hon. Member that this number has
recently shown a decrease, and that
taking the last quarter compared with
the same quarter for the previous year
there is a reduction of almost thirty. I
realise that a large number of these
cases relate to the type of house which
the hon. Member has in mind, and I
think that he will agree that this type
of house is more easily accessible to
evilly-disposed persons than is the case
in less thickly populated areas.
I might add with regret that in my
view a very considerable proportion of
these offences are committed by
juveniles. I have been in consultation
with the Inspector-General and I am
satisfied that all possible supervision is
being and will continue to be given to
this type of crime. I am not prepared to
make representations on the lines suggested by the hon. Member as I believe
if carried out his suggestion would
cause great inconvenience to the
residents, and in my view the remedy
lies in other directions.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether it is
a fact that the majority of these crimes
perpetrated in the North of Ireland are
due to the police being taken off ordinary
police work to attend Customs work, and
whether it is a fact that Northern
Ireland owing to the change over to the
British Customs of the police has become
a paradise for burglars?
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is not
the slightest foundation for the suggestion made by the hon. Member. For
example, in Belfast, where a great many
of these offences take place, not a single
policeman has been taken to increase the
staff at the Border.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not also due to
the fact that large numbers of police in
the city of Belfast are now performing
duties other than ordinary street police
duty!
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. There is
no foundation for that either. One of
the most important duties of the police is
to prevent the crimes to which my hon.
Friend refers.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman refer to the last question I
asked in this House and the figures
which he gave of the policing of the city
of Belfast, and will he state whether it
is a fact that the number is far below
what Belfast is entitled to have for police
work?

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 APRIL 1936
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 9th April, 1936.
The House met at Twelve Noon of the
Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
INSURANCE OF NON-MANUAL
WORKERS.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Labour whether the Government
propose to extend unemployment insurance to "black-coated " non-manual
workers earning from £250 to £400 a
year.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The question of extending
the Unemployment Insurance Scheme to
non-manual workers who are in receipt
of salaries not exceeding £400 a year
has been examined by the Unemployment Insurance Statutory Committee,
and their report is at present under
consideration. If such an extension is
made it will be applied uniformly to
Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the Minister
be surprised to learn that owing to the
depression of recent years considerable
insecurity prevails among this class of
worker?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am
aware that
there has been insecurity, but my answer
points to the fact that the matter is
having active consideration.
NEW UNEMPLOYMENT
ASSISTANCE REGULATIONS.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can give an
assurance that the new Unemployment
Assistance Regulations will not be delayed
beyond this Session, and that these
Regulations will not sanction any Means
Test which would break up families.
Mr. ANDREWS: I can assure the
hon. and learned Member that the
Regulations are receiving active consideration, and that they will be brought
into effect here on the same date as in
Great Britain. I cannot obviously at
this stage indicate the provisions which
they will embody, but there is no desire
on the part of the Government that they
should have the result suggested in the
question.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Could the Minister
say when the appointed day will arrive?
Will it be far short of doomsday?
Mr. ANDREWS: I do not know that
that arises out of this question, but, in
any case, I cannot say.
Mr. CAMPBELL: If the Minister
does not know could he tell me who does
know?
Mr. BEATTIE: As a supplementary
question I would like to ask the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to recommend to the Committee which drew
up the regulations on the Means Test,
that the age should be set out classifying males and females as self-dependent
persons, and whether he is aware that
that is a very important aspect of the
matter before the House at the moment?
Mr. ANDREWS: If the hon. Member
will let me have his proposals in reference
to the matter I will give them careful
consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that a girl of eighteen,
or a boy of nineteen, is generally
classified as a self-dependent person, and
that those persons are now being expected
to live upon the earnings of their fathers
and mothers?
Mr. ANDREWS: Many circumstances
arise in deciding the matter.
CENSUS OF UNEMPLOYED.
3. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he is prepared to have
a census taken of the unemployed persons
in Northern Ireland, in order to ascertain
the exact number unemployed.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply to this
question.
The registers of the Employment
Exchanges show the number of persons
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
who are unemployed and who attend at
the Exchanges, not alone to receive
unemployment benefit or assistance, but
also in order that they may be considered
for vacancies notified to the Ministry.
Having regard to the difficulties and
the cost of doing so, the Government
is of opinion that no useful purpose will
be served by endeavouring to ascertain
the number of additional persons who
are unemployed and who do not avail
themselves of this opportunity of obtaining
employment.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that thousands of
single men who have been signing for
years have now stopped signing owing
to the refusal of the right hon. Gentleman's Department to give these young
men employment? If the right hon.
Gentleman would take this census people
would know exactly how matters stand
in Northern Ireland in regard to unemployment.
Mr. ANDREWS: It appears to me
that that is merely a repetition of the
question, and the answer I have given
obviously applies.
PROVISION FOR EX-SERVICE
MEN.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state when he
intends to carry out the promise which
he made to the ex-Service men of Northern Ireland who served during the Great
War that he intended to have erected in
Northern Ireland a home or hospital
similar to the one in Chelsea.
The PRIME MINISTER: The circumstances under which I expressed my
intentions in the direction indicated were
entirely personal and in no way involved
the Government or public funds; consequently the matter is not one in which
I can be questioned in my official
capacity. However, out of courtesy to
the hon. Member, I will nevertheless
explain that, although the original
scheme was abrogated in its stead, the
36th Ulster Division Patriotic Fund was
established through the generosity of the
people of Northern Ireland and friends
elsewhere, with a financial foundation of
£60,000 since when the voluntary committee has been discharging its beneficent
work among deserving cases of ex-Service
men and their dependents, in harmonious co-operation with
with analogous
organisations.
Mr. HENDERSON: I thank the
Prime Minister for his kindness in
answering my question. As he will
remember he made that promise in the
old House of Parliament on one occasion
and it was my intention to look it up.
In view of the fact that the ex-Service
men who belonged to the Ulster Division
rendered great service to their King and
country and that many of them are now
in a state of starvation will the right
hon. Gentleman take the earliest opportunity to fulfil his promise?
The PRIME MINISTER: I rather
resent questions which affect me personally, but not in my official capacity. It
is up to any hon. Member to help the
ex-Service men in any way he can.
Having had such close touch with the
Ulster Division I personally concentrated
my efforts in that direction and have
done all I possibly could. I think the
way in which the Committee carry out
their work day after day in striving to
help deserving cases is sufficient justification for the generosity of the people.
Mr. HENDERSON: Does the right
hon. Gentleman not think that these ex-
Service men who served Ulster and the
Empire deserve a better fate than to be
left in the poorhouse? The right hon.
Gentleman says this is a personal
matter-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must not debate this matter on supplementary questions.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the noble Lord was this promise an
election pledge?
The PRIME MINISTER: No, not at
all.
SCHOOL CHILDREN SUFFERING
FROM TUBERCULOSIS.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
number of children attending elementary
schools in Northern Ireland who have
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
9 APRIL 1936
been diagnosed as suffering from tuberculosis, and what steps are being taken
to have modern sanatoria erected in
Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: According to
information compiled from the reports of
the school medical officers for the year
ended 31st March, 1935, the number of
school children found to be suffering from
tuberculosis was 228.
I should, however, say that while this
figure may be taken as representing substantially the state of affairs, it is not
absolutely accurate as there are one or
two districts not covered by these reports.
Sanatoria have been erected by the
County Councils of Armagh and Tyrone
and by the County Borough of Belfast,
and there are, in addition, a number of
private institutions-as, for example, the
Forster Green Hospital-which are available to local authorities. I have had no
reason to think that these arrangements
are inadequate.
I
may
add that the Belfast Corporation
has under consideration the reconstruction of its sanatorium at Whiteabbey.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that there are hundreds
and hundreds of school children attending
elementary schools every day and that
they are using the same pens and pencils
as children diagnosed as suffering from
tuberculosis? There is no room in the
hospitals for these children, and in view
of the seriousness of the situation will the
right hon. Gentleman take immediate
action to have something done?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think if the
hon. Member would direct his remarks to
the Belfast Corporation, of which he is
a member, it would be much more to
the point.
Mr. HENDERSON: I have already
done that, and I find them as slow as the
right hon. Gentleman's Department.

UNSANITARY.

being erected in Northern Ireland.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my hon. and learned Friend,
the Parliamentary Secretary to
Ministry of Education, to reply.
the
The Ministry, through its inspectors,
is at present engaged upon an investigation into the circumstances of any public
elementary schools which are regarded
as unsanitary or as otherwise unsuitable.
In the absence of full information-which
is not yet available-I am unable to
reply to the first part of the question.
To reply to the remainder of the
question, it would be necessary for the
Ministry to communicate with every
education authority or individual school

say that since the establishment of the

of new schools and the improvement of
existing elementary school accommodation. Up to the end of 1934 approximately 140 new public elementary schools
had been erected.

Cabinet Ministers and replying for
Departments he knows nothing about.
(Hon. Members: Order, order.) Very
well, I congratulate the hon. Member

PAY AND CONDITIONS OF PRISON
STAFFS.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
if it is a fact that in 1919 the pay and
conditions of the prison staffs in Ireland
were assimilated with those obtaining in
the Prison Service of England and Wales;
whether the latter have had two increases
in their basic rates of pay which have
been denied to the staffs in Northern
Ireland; and whether the Northern Irish
prison officers receive less pay by about
3s to 4s per week than the prison staffs
in England and Wales.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a fact
that in the year 1919 the pay and conditions of the Irish Prisons Service were
assimilated to those of the Prisons
Service in England. In the year 1924
the conditions of the Service in England
were revised and an increase in pay was
given. Subsequently, in the early part
of this year, the English rates of pay
were again revised and certain ranks
received additional increases. Neither of
these revisions was followed in Northern
Ireland, where the rates are still those
applicable when the Government of
Northern Ireland was set up, aíthough,
in certain specific cases, salaries have
been revised and increased. The statement as to the difference in pay between
the two Services is approximately correct.
I can assure the hon. Member, however, that I have not lost sight of the
matters which he has brought under my
notice.

the cause of the delay in settling the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware that any delay has taken place in

which have been acquired by the Northern Ireland Transport Board, and I can
only refer the hon. Member to my

and gallant Member for St. Anne's

Gentleman aware that many of these men

PAYMENT OF BENEFITS BY
APPROVED SOCIETIES.
Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Labour whether it is a condition or otherwise that an approved
society under the Health Insurance Acts
is called on to pay the benefits to which
the insured person is entitled, and
whether some approved societies cannot
fulfil this condition because they have
not sufficient funds.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): An approved society is
required by law to pay the statutory
minimum benefits to which its members
are entitled in accordance with the provisions of the Acts and Regulations, and
the finances of the scheme provide
societies with sufficient funds for this
purpose. Benefits additional, however,
to the statutory minimum benefits are
payable only in the case of those societies
which the Government valuer ascertains
on valuation to possess disposable surpluses available for supplementing the
minimum benefits.
Major McCORMICK: I appreciate
the answer of the right hon. Gentleman
as to statutory benefits, but I would
like to ask him, supposing a young person
wished to have teeth attended to by a
dentist would that be termed an
additional benefit, and has an approved
society the right to refuse it?
Mr. ANDREWS: That would be an
additional benefit, which would only be
payable if the funds of the society warranted it and if it was selected as one
of the additional benefits which the
society were in a position to pay.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that the time has arrived when centralisation should take place as far as
approved societies in Northern Ireland
are concerned, and in view of that time
arriving will he make overtures to the
Government to take over this service and
give equal service to all members of
approved societies?
Mr. ANDREWS: No; it would be a
great disadvantage to Northern Ireland if
such a course was taken here until it is
taken in Great Britain.
Mr. HEALY: Can the Minister say
how many approved societies in Northern
Ireland are not in a position to pay
additional benefits?
Mr. ANDREWS: No. I would like
notice of that question.

Milk and Milk Products Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): This Bill does not
propose any drastic amendment of the
Milk and Milk Products Act of 1934,
nor is any change of principle involved.
As a result of the operation of the Act
a few minor points have arisen in conan amendment
nection with which
appeared desirable, and this Bill has
been introduced for the purpose of dealing with these points. As hon. Members
are aware the Milk Industry Assistance
Grant which we receive from the United
Kingdom Exchequer has been extended
for a further period of eighteen months,
namely up to September, 1937. This
amendment also is included in the Bill.
milk
With regard to Clause 1, in addition
to those creameries in Northern Ireland
which are registered under the Marketing of Dairy Produce Acts, there are
other undertakings which also engage in
the manufacture of butter from
supplied to them by local farmers, and
which would, if they were in Great
Britain, receive the full benefit of the
assistance which has been given by the
British Government. These undertakings have not hitherto obtained any
benefit by way of equalisation payment
for the purely technical reason that they
churn whole milk instead of separating
the cream first. Two creameries in this
position, the B.B. Farm and the Gleno
Dairy, have made very strong representations to me to the effect that it was
unfair that their suppliers should be
deprived of the advantages which have
accrued to other creameries as a result
of the Act. It seemed to me, after consultation, that these suppliers had a
strong case and the Bill, therefore, proposes to make provision for equalisation
payment on the same basis as the other
creameries have received it. It is not
anticipated that any creameries other
than the two mentioned will be in a
position to benefit under this Bill.
It is proposed that the equalisation
payment shall be made retrospectively to
these undertakings at the same rates as
those at which payments have been
made to the other creameries. Subclause (3) of Clause 1 is designed to
enable this to be done with the least
possible interference with the somewhat
complicated financial arrangements
under which equalisation payments are
made.
Hon. Members will recall that Section
11 of the 1934 Act provides for the payment out of the Milk Fund of the
expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
and the Joint Milk Council in
administering the Act. It has been
found, however, that Departments other
Milk Products Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
than the Ministry of Agriculture also
become liable for defraying expenses
which arise as a result of the operation
of the Act, for example, the expenses of
the Ministry of Finance in providing
accommodation for staff engaged in the
administration of the milk scheme and
the liability in respect of the pensions of
civil servants employed in connection
with the scheme.
Clause 3 re-enacts with certain
modifications the provisions for repayment under the 1934 Act, that is to say,
moneys which have been advanced to
creameries under the Milk Industry
Assistance Grant are repaid under certain
conditions.
Under the original section the period
for repayment ran from the 1st April,
1936, to the 31st March, 1938. In view
of the fact, however, that equalisation
payments have been extended for a
further eighteen months the period for
repayment has been similarly extended.
No question of repayment can, of course,
arise in any month unless the average
price for that month exceeds 6d. per
gallon in the case of a summer month
or 7d. per gallon in the case of a winter
month.
The original section has also been
modified to meet the case of prescribed
undertakings to which payments may be
made under Clause 1 of this Bill. Such
undertakings will make repayments on
the same basis as the other creameries,
and no claim for repayment can arise
unless the average price paid by those
creameries exceeds the rates specified in
the Clause. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. MINFORD: Do I understand
that this Bill is for the purpose of

price for butter and cream all over
Northern Ireland?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I did not quite
catch the hon. Gentleman's question.
Mr. MINFORD: Is this Bill to enable
the Board to establish fixed prices for
butter and cream all over Northern
Ireland?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: No, Sir.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill, accordingly, read a Second time,
and committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
Marketing of Eggs Bill.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: On a point
of order. I would like to draw the
attention of the Government to the fact
that this Bill was read a First time on
the 8th of April, and from the 8th of
April till the 25th of April hon. Members were not in possession of copies of
the Bill. To-day is the 28th and we are
now asked to discuss the Bill when it
has only been in the hands of hơn. Members for two days. I do not propose to
discuss the Bill. On the face of it it is
a very wide and far-reaching Measure,
and, to my mind, to ask hon. Members
to discuss it without having had an opportunity of going thoroughly into the
details of it is not fair. In passing I
may say that the Bill appeared in the
Press on the 15th of April, and yet hon.
Members did not receive their copies
until the 25th.
I may add that I was rung up last
night by one of my constituents who
asked me had I seen the Bill. I said
yes, that as a matter of fact I was at
that moment engaged in reading it. He
said: "Do you propose to discuss this
Bill seriously on Tuesday?" and I replied: "Yes. It is down for Second
Reading on that day." He said: "How
can you discuss it when you have not
even seen it until now?" As I say, it is
a very far-reaching Bill, which is going
to affect every little village in Northern
Ireland, and yet to-day, without having
had an opportunity to consider the Bill,
we are asked to discuss it and to pass it.
I do not think it is fair or right that
we should be asked to do so.
Mr. MINFORD: Would I be in order
in saying a word or two on that also?
Mr. SPEAKER: If the hon. Member
wishes to raise a point of order he can
do so.

sequences to every person in Northern

involved.
The Bill, to which I am now asking
the House to give a Second Reading,
marks another and very important stage
in the development of our great poultry
industry. Sometimes, because of the
very humble nature of the domestic fowl,
we are apt to lose sight of its importance
as a contributor to the wealth of our
Province. The value of the output of
our poultry industry amounts to approximately £3,500,000 per annum ; it
constitutes the largest single item
of our agricultural income and as
such exceeds in value the output of our
cattle industry or our dairying industry.
Of the £3,500,000 no less than £1,000,000
is represented by the value of our eggs
exported to Great Britain.
Since
Hon. Members will recall that the
Ministry, with the co-operation and
guidance of egg merchants and producers, first sought the approval of the
House in 1924 in an effort to improve
the conditions of our egg trade.
that date several amending Acts have
been passed and the Ministry and the
interests concerned have done everything
they can to improve the quality and
appearance of our eggs and the marketing methods of our egg industry. Concurrently with the improvement in our
marketing methods the Ministry, in conjunction with the County Agricultural
Committees, has carried through an
intensive educational campaign amongst
producers, and has provided facilities and
incentives for increased production.
I
can best illustrate the success of all these
combined efforts by mentioning that in
1924, when these efforts commenced, the
poultry population of the Province was
6,814,418, and that in 1935 it had expanded to 10,084,670.
That, of course,
is an indication of the general prosperity
of the industry, because no producer
would increase his stock unless he felt
that it was to his advantage to do so.
I have previously told the House that
Marketing of Eggs Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
at one time the price of Northern Ireland
eggs was the lowest in the British
market, but at the present moment it
is the highest price paid for any imported
eggs and compares favourably with that
small and very select portion of the
British supply marketed under the
National Mark. It is no exaggeration
to add that the success which has
attended the development of our egg
industry is one of the principal factors
which has enabled our small farmers to
weather the eight years of intense depression through which the agricultural
industry has passed.
The principles upon which the existing
legislation is based are:-
(1) making it an offence for a producer to offer or expose for sale
any stale or dirty eggs; and
(2) the fixation of high standards of
quality in respect of our eggs
shipped to Great Britain, the
grading on a weight basis of such
eggs, and shipment in standard
non-returnable cases.
""
All eggs which do not reach the high
standard of quality required for fresh
laid eggs have had to be marked as
"Seconds.' The chief method of control has been the inspection of supplies
prior to shipment, the prosecution
of unsatisfactory shippers, and, finally,
if the shipments have continued unsatisfactory, the removal of their licences.
In order to ease the responsibility thus
cast upon licensed merchants the Ministry at their request, and with funds provided by the trade, has conducted an
intensive educational campaign amongst
producers during which every individual
producer in Northern Ireland has been
visited at least once and the proper care
of eggs and marketing efforts explained
to them.
The Ministry has, however, always
realised that the principles underlying
the existing legislation were not ideal.
They were, however, the best that could
be devised and operated at the time,
but it has always been obvious that
until the producer could be induced by
way of monetary reward to market fresh
eggs it would be difficult to achieve the
degree of improvement and the elimination of losses and waste which are SO
essential to the proper well-being of all
concerned.
Hon. Members are, I am sure, fully
aware of the fluctuations which take
place in the price of eggs in accordance
with the season of the year. Briefly,
after the period of heavy spring
production prices from May onwards
rise until the month of December,
when prices fall until they reach
a low level during the peak of
the spring season production. Producers are, of course, fully conscious of
this and during June, July, August and
September, the very season of the year
when it is most desirable that eggs
should be marketed as rapidly as possible, there exists the tendency to hold
back supplies for rising markets. The
trade pays a flat rate for all eggs purchased from producers, adjusting the
price in accordance with anticipated
losses due to second quality. Thus the
producer who regularly markets nothing
but fresh eggs receives exactly the same
price as the producer who markets a substantial proportion of what are really
second quality eggs. In addition to that
the merchant who may feel that action
should be taken against a producer
because of the bad eggs he is supplying
may hesitate to take that action for fear
of losing his supplies. There is, however, a further repercussion. As prices
are good during this season and the price
margin between first and second quality
eggs very marked, there is another
temptation on the part of shippers to
lower their standard of testing during
these months. The Ministry has as a
consequence found it necessary to increase
its dock inspection staff. Every year we
have had to issue strong letters of warning to the trade threatening drastic
action if these malpractices continued.
This year, in order to support the
position of our eggs on the London and
other cross-Channel markets, we found it
necessary to carry these threats into
effect on a more extensive scale than
previously.
We can, of course, continue to operate
under existing legislation, but after discussing the position fully with the trade
and with producers I have come to the
conclusion that it would be much
sounder if we could secure conditions and
organisation whereby there would be a
direct incentive to producers, dealers and
shippers to market supplies as fresh as
possible in other words, make mone-
1117 Marketing of Eggs Bill-

28 APRIL 1936
Second Reading
tary reward the incentive to improvement instead of the Criminal Court.
This Bill, therefore, provides for the
purchase of eggs from producers on a
quality basis and for the fixing of prices
to producers for first and second quality
eggs by a joint committee of the trade
and producers. Fortunately, the main
item of the necessary machinery already
exists, as an identification system has
been in operation for some years whereby each individual producer's supply is
identified through to the shipper's store.
At this stage, in case there should be
any misunderstanding or misapprehension, I ought to make three points
perfectly clear. First of all, there will
be no serious interruption in payments
to producers. The collectors will pay a
week in arrears. After the first week
payments will flow normally as in the
past, and in so far as the sale of eggs
is a credit against the purchase of
groceries, etc., from the collectors there
will be no interruption.
Secondly, the producer will not be left
at the mercy of the shipper with regard
to the determination of quality. Just as
in the case of the grading of pork carcases the Ministry will undertake the
onerous responsibility. The third point.
I should like to make perfectly clear is
that this Bill does not in any way affect
the producer who retails the eggs he himself produces to the consumer.
And now I want to turn to other
important provisions of the Bill, namely,
those concerned with the internal trade.
Up to the present the control of quality
and freshness within Northern Ireland
has been limited to the provisions which
make it an offence to sell or expose for
sale stale
a
egg. Hon. Members will, I
am sure, realise that there are several
shades of quality between new laid and
stale. I feel certain that it will be the
general view that the consumer in Northern Ireland is entitled to the same
guarantee with regard to the freshness
of his egg supplies as the consumer in
Great Britain. Whilst, therefore, this is
a move in the interests of the consumer
it is also in the interests of the producer
as it will create confidence and lead
directly to increased consumption. And
here may I state that all studies into the
diet of the people agree in the conclusion
that milk and eggs in particular are two
of the products in which consumption is
lamentably low. Increasing prosperity
bringing in its wake increased purchasing power will, I hope, lead to a much
greater consumption of eggs to the
mutual benefit of the health and wellbeing of the people of Ulster and the
prosperity of the poultry farmer.
The immediate source of supply for
eggs sold retail is mainly of a two-fold
character. Certain grocers buy their
supplies from a merchant holding a
Class A licence who has alreday tested
and graded his supply. Others, however, buy directly from producers at the
various country markets. The latter will
be required to pay the producer on a
quality basis in the same way as the
Class A merchants.
Both classes of
grocers will-with
certain exceptions have to sell on a
quality basis also, and it consequently
will be permissible to offer only newlaid home-produced eggs to the consumer
in Northern Ireland without a mark.
All imported eggs must be marked
"Imported."
Home-produced eggs,
unless they are "New Laid" must bear
the word "Seconds" stamped on the
shell.
Finally, the Bill makes financial provision for carrying these reforms into
effect. At present, part of the cost is
borne by the Ministry and part by the
trade through the medium of the licence
fees and the levy of d. per case on all
eggs shipped to Great Britain. Under
the present Measure practically the
whole of the cost will be borne by the
industry. All retailers of eggs will in
future be licensed. The small trader
who ordinarily sells less than, say, 60
dozen eggs per week will pay a consolidated licence fee of £2 per annum.
Other retailers will pay a fee of 10s. per
annum, together with a fee of d. per
dozen in respect of all eggs sold by retail.
Where, however, a retailer purchases his
supplies from a Class A merchant
arrangements may be made whereby the
fee of d. per dozen will be paid by the
Class A merchant instead of by the
retailer. A fee of 1d. per dozen will also
be paid by merchants and grocers selling
imported eggs, who will thus be required
to pay their share of the cost of giving
to the consumer an adequate guarantee
of the freshness of his supply.

I need not emphasise to you how vital
it is for us to beat on a quality basis
every competitor on the British market.
Last week I visited some of the most
important merchants in London, and I
saw eggs from every part of the world,
including South America. They were
competing against ours. I am glad to
say that the Northern Ireland egg is
holding its own. We are in a unique
position for capturing that quality
trade, and I think it is essential that
every measure should be taken to keep
and, if possible, enhance the quality, so
that the confidence which I mentioned
before shall continue on the other side.
Every move that we make is watched with
the greatest keenness and interest by
those who are our competitors. I will
mention one point to illustrate this. A
short time ago the Ministry's investigators discovered that when eggs
were packed broad-end down in the cases
a high proportion of them gave the
appearance when tested in Great Britain
of being second quality, and that when
packed in this way the eggs did not keep
so well. The Ministry, therefore, made
it compulsory to pack all eggs broad-end
up. Within a year our lead was followed
by South Africa and practically_every
country sending eggs to the British
market. Again I would ask the Members of the House to give this Bill their
very earnest consideration from the
point of view of another move in the
direction of helping the whole of the
agricultural industry. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I think I may
assume that it will be in accordance
with the wishes of the Committee if I
follow the procedure which has been
adopted in recent years and if, in introducing the Vote for the Ministry of
Home Affairs, I at the same time refer

which my Ministry is responsible and
which are the subjects of the subsequent
Votes.
In dealing with the Estimate for this
Ministry, I cannot refrain from referring
to the irreparable loss which the Ministry, and the whole Civil Service of
a
Ministry of Home Affairs 1130
Northern Ireland, has sustained in the
past year in the untimely death of the
Permanent Secretary to the Ministry,
Major George A. Harris. Major Harris was
man of great gifts and outstanding
personality. His experience of administration generally, and of local government administration in particular, was
of invaluable service to the Government.
He devoted all his great abilities with
untiring energy to the services of the State,
and in addition to his administrative
qualities, he enjoyed a remarkable degree
of personal popularity in the highest
sense of the term, and his loss will be
deplored not only by his colleagues in
the Service, but by everyone who has
had the privilege of being associated
with him either personally or officially.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In the Vote for the Ministry there is
nothing that calls for special mention,
but a slight increase in staff has been
rendered necessary by the increasing
pressure of work falling on the Roads
Branch of the Ministry, an increase
which, indeed, is long overdue.
I should like, however, to refer in
passing to one item in the Estimate, and
that is the establishment of the Arbitration Tribunal under the Road and Railway Transport Act. As no doubt hon.
Members are aware, the Hon. Mr. Justice
Megaw has accepted the chairmanship
of this tribunal, and Mr. J. B. Morrison
and Mr. J. H. Fitzsimons have consented to act as members. I think the
Committee will agree that the personnel
of this tribunal will carry the unqualified confidence of the community, and in
expressing my gratification that these
gentlemen have accepted appointment to
the tribunal, I should like in particular
to refer to the debt of gratitude which
we owe to the Hon. Mr. Justice Megaw
who, notwithstanding his other heavy
judicial responsibilities, has agreed to act

order, which is naturally of primary
importance, I regret I cannot regard the
position as entirely satisfactory.
have in this House during the past few

unhappy disturbances which took place
in the city last summer, and while I
cannot avoid making a passing reference

to those deplorable occurrences, I wish

There have been from time to time outrages and acts of intimidation, to which
I need not refer in detail, but which

The Committee will recall that during
the consideration of the Estimates for
my Department last year I drew
attention to the fact that an increase
in the number of cases of juvenile crime
was becoming apparent, and I suggested
that while there were many contributory
causes for this state of affairs I considered that the main remedy lay with
the parents themselves, who in many
cases which had come under my notice,
had exercised little or none of that control which may be expected of them.
This increase in juvenile crime has unfortunately continued to grow, and hon.
Members will, I am sure, have seen that
His Majesty's judges have found it necessary to call the attention of the community to this serious state of affairs.
May I say at once that this evil is not
confined to Northern Ireland, and I am
sure that hon. Members must have seen
many references to the growth of juvenile
crime which have recently appeared, not
only in the Press of Great Britain, but in
that of other countries as well. The rise
in the number of juveniles charged with
indictable offences in Northern Ireland
will indicate the alarming extent of the
increase. Whereas in 1930 the number
of such cases was 270, the corresponding
figure in 1934 was no less than 439, and
although the figures for 1935 are not yet
available it is evident that a further
increase has taken place in that year.
I have made it my business to go very
carefully into the types of offence with
which these children and young persons
are mostly charged, and to take the year
1934, in which, as I have said, there were
439 youthful offenders charged with
indictable offences. I find the following
facts:-302 boys and 7 girls were under
the age of 14 years; and 129 boys and 1
girl were aged between 14 and 17 years.
The great majority were charged with
simple and minor larcenies, but there were
no fewer than 84 cases of breaking into
shops and 30 cases of housebreaking, and
in addition, some 47 cases of malicious
injury.
Only a few weeks ago an hon. Member
on the opposite side of the House raised
in this House the question of taking
further measures to combat the increasing number of housebreakings which have
occurred, more especially in workingclass areas, and, while I am glad to
inform the Committee that since then
a number of detections of this form of
crime have been made, the figures I have
quoted unhappily go to show that much
of the responsibility lies with juveniles.
Approximately one-quarter of the cases
in which juveniles are convicted of indictable offences were dealt with by the young
people being placed under the care of a
probation officer; 93 were sent to an
industrial school, and 42 to a reformatory,
while the remainder were dealt with by
way of fine. In only two cases did the
court think that an appropriate punishment would be the cane.
The figures for other years show that
the proportions of young persons charged
with the various types of crime which
I have mentioned are very much the
same. In spite of this increase I find
that the numbers of children and young
persons committed to reformatory and
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
29 APRIL 1936
industrial schools have steadily decreased
year by year from 629 in 1922 to 381 in
1935. I think when these figures are
considered that it is open to question if it
may not be that we have gone too far
in our natural reluctance to impose
punishment on young persons, and are,
perhaps, giving them too many chances
and making a too extensive use of the
probation system. I may say at once
that I have the very greatest regard for
and fully realise the great value of the
probation system, but it may be that the
courts as one of His Majesty's judges
has recently pointed out-will have to
take sterner measures.
Of the number of youthful offenders
sent to the Borstal Institution during the
year 1934, twelve had one previous conviction, eight had two previous convictions, three had three previous convictions,
and one had six previous convictions.
In nearly every one of these cases these
boys had been given previous chances, but
neither they nor, I am afraid, their
parents, had paid attention to the warnings they received.
It seems to me to be the general trend
of the present generation to leave the responsibility of looking after children to
the school teachers, but I maintain that
it is the home and not the school upon
which the moulding of character primarily
depends. Only too many children have
in the end to be committed to industrial
schools and reformatories because they
will not attend school and are not made
to do so by their parents, and I know it is
the experience in these schools and also
in the Borstal Institution, that in a great
many of the cases the children who are
committed are almost illiterate or of a
very low standard of education, which, I
think, is proof of the lack of interest their
parents have taken in their education.
This idea, as I have said, so prevalent
to-day, of leaving education to the State,
is all very well so far as it goes, but the
State can never take the part of the
parent.
I know that the criticism has been made
that committals to such schools for two
or three years cost the taxpayer and the
ratepayer money. At the same time, I
venture to suggest that no individual
ratepayer or taxpayer who has visited
these schools and knows the splendid work
which is carried on, and the results
achieved would suggest that money spent
on helping these boys and girls to become
decent citizens is other than money well
spent.
There is one point which I think
deserves to be mentioned when dealing
with the question of juvenile crime, and
that is the extraordinarily good work
which the various youth organisations,
such as the Boy Scouts, the Girl Guides,
the Boys' Brigade, and others are doing,
and I only hope that their good influence
may be widened and extended, as I feel
that the habits of discipline and the
training given by these organisations may
. become a very valuable factor in keeping
the youth of the present generation from
falling into the habit of lawlessness. The
reason I deal with this matter at such
length is that I realise the seriousness of
the situation, and I feel everybody should
know exactly what is going on.
This whole question of juvenile crime
is a matter which, as I have said, is
causing great concern not only here and in
Great Britain, but throughout the world,
and I can only hope that it may be a
passing phase. I have no doubt that the
committee recently appointed by meand of which my hon. Friend, the Member for North Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn),
very kindly consented to take the onerous
position of chairman-to inquire into the
existing provisions of the law relating to
young offenders, will, in its deliberations,
take into account this aspect of their
problem, and I need hardly say that any
recommendation which may be made by
that committee, or indeed from any
source which has for its object the reduction of this wave of juvenile crime, will
receive my most earnest consideration.
Before leaving the general subject of
law and order, I might, perhaps, refer
very briefly to the effects of the operation
of the Summary Jurisdiction Act. The
Act has not yet been in operation
sufficiently long for its full benefit to have
been experienced, but the experience
which has been gained all goes to show
that the reforms inaugurated by that
Measure have greatly tended to the convenience of the public, and to the proper
administration of justice. The change of
system has been effected without any disorganisation of the business of the petty
sessional courts, and the gloomy anticipations of those who were opposed to the
Bill have not, I am glad to say, been
realised.

With regard to the prison service, it
will be recalled that during the debate
on the Estimates last year there
certain criticism-and I am glad to
acknowledge at once that it was made
in a most helpful spirit-of the cost of
our small service, and, indeed, it was
suggested that we should consider closing
down the female prison in Armagh. I
should like to assure those hon. Members who take an interest in this matter
at once that every suggestion put forward has received my personal consideration.
I should very much like to be able to
have a separate convict prison in Northern Ireland, but, I am glad to say, our
convict population is very small and the
expenses of such an institution would be
excessive in the extreme. The fact that
at Belfast Prison we have to accommodate some six or seven different types
of prisoners-for example, we have convicts, prisoners undergoing hard labour,
contempt of court prisoners; prisoners
on remand and awaiting trial; juveniles;
adults; and so on-means a great deal
more work for the staff than would be
the case if only one type of prisoner was
accommodated in each particular prison.
For this reason I suggest that it is not
fair to work out comparisons of cost as
between prisons in Great Britain and
those in Northern Ireland, because of
the fact that we have all these different
types of prisoner in Belfast, and because
it is essential, as no hon. Member will
dispute, that we should segregate these
types as strictly as possible. As a result
it is necessary, perhaps, to have
slightly larger staff than would be the
case in other circumstances. Moreover,
in considering the question of the cost
per prisoner, the fact must not be forgotten that luckily our prison population.
is relatively small. If the numbers in
a
our prisons were greater-which, I am
sure, is the last thing any Member would
desire-we could, no doubt, show a substantial decrease in the per capita cost,
but inasmuch as the overhead charges of
a prison must necessarily remain to a
large extent constant, the fact that our
numbers are small runs up the per capita
cost.
As to the suggestion that Armagh
Prison, where the female prisoners are
accommodated, might be closed and a
part of the Belfast Prison reserved for
females, I have already explained the
difficulty which arises in Belfast Prison
from the fact that we have necessarily
so many different classes of prisoners
confined therein for whom, even at the
moment, the facilities for segregation of
the various classes during exercise and so
on are not as good as I would wish, and
not
certainly do
compare with the
amenities that the prisoners of a similar
class enjoy in Great Britain. While,
therefore, it would be true to say that
there would be adequate cell accommodation in Belfast Prison to accommodate the
female prisoners who are at present in
Armagh, apart from the other difficulties which would arise in the administration of a prison common to both sexes,
it would be impossible to provide these
prisoners with the other necessary

and so on.
May I say in passing that I am very
glad that recently an hon. Member in

being done by Mr. Watson, the governor,

I cannot leave the subject of the

help and assistance rendered to the

The majority of the items are

and expressed the hope that the following year would see a great revival in

Housing Act of 1923 was passed. During

While claiming credit for the Government, I cannot omit the part played by

I may now briefly refer to a series of
grants to local authorities of great importance from the point of view of the health
and well-being of the people. They are
contributions towards the expenditure of
local authorities in special public health
services. I am sure no one grudges such
expenditure and my only regret is that
we cannot afford to give greater assistance to the local authorities who carry
on such valuable work. We owe a great
deal to the general practitioner, and our
dispensary system, which brings medical
aid within the reach of everyone in case
of illness has done much for our people;
but concentrated effort, directed specially
to the prevention and elimination of
those diseases which are more largely
responsible for ill-health and incapacity,
is likely to be most effective in the
building-up of a healthy and vigorous
population. For this reason these special
services are particularly valuable.
over
For example, as the result of such
effort the death rate from tuberculosis
in Northern Ireland, which was
3 per 1,000 of the population at the
beginning of this century, has been
reduced to slightly over 1 per 1,000.
That is to say, it has been more than
halved, and infant mortality has been
reduced from 150 per 1,000 births at the
beginning of the century, to 70 last year.
A matter which still gives cause for
grave public anxiety is the continued toll
of road accidents. I regret to say that the
number of such accidents in Northern
Ireland steadily increases in spite of the
various measures adopted to reduce them.
Last year there was an increase of 140
over the previous year, resulting in
injuries to 2,155 persons and 124 deaths.
Ministry of Home Affairs 1142
Estimates-
29 APRIL 1936
The only bright spot in the returns is
that there were 8 fewer people killed
last year than in the preceding year-
124 as against 132.
The main causes of these accidents may
be classified under three headings:-
Negligent driving; careless pedestrians;
careless cyclists; and each has shown a
consistent increase during past years.
Roughly, 85 per cent. of the accidents
are due to these causes. Of the 455
accidents due to negligent driving, it is
significant that 244 occurred at road
intersections, and 83 were due to
skidding. Both these figures suggest that
a little more care and a slackening of
speed at dangerous points would assist
appreciably in reducing the number of
accidents.
While the figures for Northern Ireland give cause for anxiety, they compare favourably with the statistics published for Great Britain. On the basis
of the number of vehicles in each area,
we find that last year there were 47
accidents per 1,000 vehicles in Northern
Ireland, as compared with 76 in Great
Britain. Again, on the basis of population, we find that the ratio per 100,000
of population is 158 in Northern Ireland
to 425 in Great Britain. If we take the
mileage of roads in each area the figures
reveal 15.2 accidents for each 100 miles
of road in Northern Ireland, as compared with 107 in Great Britain. Conditions admittedly vary considerably in
Great Britain, but nevertheless these
figures suggest that the toll of life and
the number of persons injured in Northern Ireland as a result of road accidents
is comparatively less than in Great
Britain.
One of the saddest features in connection with this question is the number
of cases where young children have been
the victims of road accidents. Last year
no fewer than 30 children under 15 years
of age were killed and 564 received
injuries. In almost 90 per cent. of these
cases the children themselves were at
fault. It is no doubt impossible to expect children to exercise the same degree
of prudence that is to be expected from
adults, but a good deal more could be
done by parents and teachers in training.
young people to exercise due care while
on the public thoroughfares. The police
have done much in this direction, and
particularly in escorting children across
the road whilst going to and coming from
school. The teachers are actively cooperating by impressing upon the
children the need for care. I should like
to make this further suggestion to the
teachers, that possibly they might, on
the occasion of school breaking up, check
the children as they leave and prevent
them, in their enthusiasm at getting free,
from rushing across the street without
waiting whilst the constable holds up
the traffic. I throw that out only as a
suggestion.
Every effort is being made to bring to
the notice of all classes of road users their
responsibilities in the use of the roads and
certain requirements which will conduce
to their safety are being imposed by regulations. Road improvements of various
kinds have been carried out, and warning signs erected with the co-operation
of local authorities. In this connection
it may be mentioned that "Major Road
Ahead" signs are being erected all over
the Province with the object of avoiding
the too frequent occurrence of accidents at
cross-roads. A Highway Code has been
prepared and is at present with the
printers, which will be available for every
member of the community. It is hoped
that the valuable advice contained in the
little booklet will be studied and observed
by all concerned.
By a spirit of co-operation and a
friendly recognition of the rights of other
road users much can be done to reduce the
number of road accidents, but I have been
forced to the conclusion that in the
present circumstances the main weapon
at our disposal with which to fight this.
evil is the imposition of heavy penalties
and, in particular, the cancellation or
suspension of drivers' licences in the case
of those who have been convicted of
serious road offences. The hardship
involved in the cancellation or suspension
of driving licences may, in individual
cases be heavy, but I do suggest that the
innocent public must be protected (hear,
hear)—and it is only by the imposition
and rigid enforcement of substantial
penalties that those who accept the responsibility of driving motors will be
brought to a realisation of what that responsibility involves.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does that apply to
the police?
Ministry of Home Affairs 1144
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may say
that I have been surprised at the number
of cases where applications for the restoration of licences, cancelled or suspended
by the court for offences such as drunkenness in charge, dangerous driving, etc.,
have been supported by individuals who,
I am sure, are quite as anxious as we all
must be to do everything possible to make
our roads reasonably safe, and who, if
they thought twice, would refuse to be
associated with such applications.
I
think that in most of these cases a little
consideration would show that whatever
one's feeling of sympathy for the individual concerned may be, it is essential,
from the broad view of the public
interest, that every motorist should
realise to the full that if he transgresses
the law he cannot hope to escape the due
punishment for his offences, and that the
law-abiding road user must be protected
from such irresponsible drivers.
There is one other way in which I think
liability to accidents on the roads might
be reduced, and that is by the improvement of the roads themselves-by widening dangerous corners and providing
alternative or by-pass routes to relieve
roads where undue congestion exists. It
is not, perhaps, generally known that the
mileage of roads in Northern Ireland is
relatively far greater than that in Great
Britain. The actual figures are:-The
mileage of roads per 100,000 of populain Great Britain is 395, whereas in
Northern Ireland the comparable figure is
1,015, that is to say, our mileage on a
population basis is nearly three times as
great as in Great Britain.
Moreover, it must be remembered that
prior to 1922 the roads in Great Britain
had been brought to a high state of perfection, whereas in Northern Ireland the
roads had been scandalously neglected by
those in authority. It will be seen, therefore, that as compared with Great Britain
we started with a very heavy handicap.
Notwithstanding the handicap, very good
work on our roads had been accomplished,
and a tribute is due to the local authorities for the great improvement which has
been effected, but, I must say, that much
still remains to be done in this respect.
I am glad to say that this year we have
been able to approve of the advance of
some 600 miles of Class III roads into the
Class II category, thus qualifying them
for a 30 per cent. grant instead of 15 per
cent., and next year the grant for Class
II roads will be increased to 40 per cent.
grants. In addition, we are pursuing a
policy of widening dangerous corners.
All such improvements will have their
effect in the reduction of accidents as the
improvement in Class III and Class II
roads will naturally tend to relieve the
congestion elsewhere.
In speaking of by-pass roads, I think
I might here appropriately refer to the
proposed widening of part of the Newtownards Road, a road which is one of the
main traffic arteries in Belfast and which
suffers from the congestion inevitable to
a road which carries traffic from Bangor
and Newtownards, and so on. Naturally,
before approving of a scheme of widening
this road, which would have involved
very heavy expenditure, we had to give
the whole question very careful consideration, and we came to the conclusion that
although this particular widening might
possibly effect some improvement in
traffic conditions, it would never prove a
satisfactory solution of the problem as a
whole. The real solution of the difficulty in these main arteries is a definite
diversion of all traffic for Holywood and
Bangor from the Newtownards Road by
way of a by-pass road. We are now exploring such a scheme, and I may take
this opportunity of expressing my indebtedness to the Belfast Harbour Board for
the way they met me in the earlier
negotiations. I have great hopes that we
may, before long, be able, at all events,
to contribute something to make that very
congested area of the Newtownards Road
a little bit safer. I must apologise for
taking up the time of the Committee, but
I have tried to deal fully with the various
points.
Mr. GRANT: The criticism which I

I hope the
Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary,
if they do not agree with everything I

Now I want to touch briefly on
another question which I have already
raised in this House on several occasions,

Street area on 11th May last year.
were promised an inquiry into that

Midland Railway to Henry Street, they
erected barricades across the streets.
Time and again I have appealed for the
removal of those barricades, but no
attention has been paid to my request,
and those barricades have now been up
for almost a year.
Then we are told we should not say

live in those streets forget the events of
last year
when every time they come

living in Abyssinia. In addition, I want

It is also time that common sense was

What were those barricades put up

The boy was without a stain on his

Sir DAWSON BATES: It
shorten the discussion if I explain the

Mr. BEATTIE: I am very pleased to
have that answer from the Minister,
because since I was a very young boy
that place has been a real menace. The
condition of the road at Dee Street
Bridge exists from the time of Paddy's
Box, which was a little lane from the
turnstile across the railway line to
Queen's Island. Now that that matter
has been taken in hands and will be
remedied I am very pleased. The last
item to which I wish to refer is prisons.
I believe the policy of the Government as
far as prisons are concerned should be
changed. The policy of keeping prisons
open in Armagh, Derry, and Belfast is
not what I would call the best way to
house our prisoners. The housing of
prisoners is a very important factor as far
as the reform of the prisoner is concerned,
and the policy that houses all prisoners
-juveniles, hard labour prisoners,
remand prisoners, and convicts-together
is not a wise one for the Ministry to
follow. Juveniles should not be domiciled along with hard labour prisoners.
They should not come in contact with
adult prisoners at all. Remand prisoners,
who on being tried are sometimes found
innocent, should not have to face the
ordeal of mixing with convicted prisoners
and others in the Crumlin Road.
A special place should be set aside for
those two classes, and the female prisoners
from Armagh should be housed in the
Crumlin Road. Provision could be made
for them for the purpose of exercise in
part of the new gardens. It is no excuse
to say that the question of exercise prevents you from bringing the female
prisoners from Armagh. It is no excuse
to say that that is one of the reasons why
you must keep life prisoners in a shortterm prison. No argument has been put
forward by the Government to justify
such a state of affairs, and I am going to
continue to draw the attention of the
Committee and the House to the matter
so long as such a state of affairs exists
in Northern Ireland, which is classified
as a Christian country. I feel compelled
to make this protest once again with a
view to having the Minister take the
question of the housing of prisoners into
consideration at the earliest possible date.
With regard to the Borstal Institution,
I wish to add my tribute to what the
Minister has already said. The work of
the Borstal Institution for juvenile
offenders is excellent, but with regard to
the industrial school end, while the work

1923. At the moment they come under

would ask the Minister to transfer those
