the Education Act of 1923. The only
other matters in these Estimates on which
I wish to comment are matters of administration, and I leave them until the
proper time arrives.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I am deeply disappointed at the statement of the Minister of Home Affairs this afternoon with
regard to one matter of urgent public
importance. That is the question of
motor traffic regulation in Northern
Ireland. The Home Office is fast asleep
on that point. The public, especially the
working-class public, are becoming
aroused to the increasing massacre on our
roads. The question has grown in grim
significance every year. I think the
people of Great Britain are beginning to
wonder whether a death roll of 6,500 per
year is not too high a price to pay for
swift motor transport, and the people of
Northern Ireland are also beginning to
wonder whether a death roll of 125 a year
is not too high a price to pay for the same
result in their own area.
The people who suffer most by the
increasing peril of our roads are the
poorer classes. Richer folk hardly realise
what it means to the home of a poor man
when the breadwinner of the house is

in

the road accidents in Great Britain during

the past two years the greatest reduction

It means delay. It means less speed.
While in England they have 23 cars to

only seven owing to their vast territory,
in England, with the lesser number of

I differ from the Minister in this respect
---you cannot expect much care from
children between four and ten years of
age. I understood him to impute in
some degree blame to parents. No
amount of teaching in our schools, and
no amount of guidance by police constables will prevent young children of
from four to ten running loose on the

humanity. You cannot make children
other than children. They will be
children to the end of the chapter even

I totally dissent from the doctrine that

When he speaks like that the Minister
is simply tinkering with this problem.
I submit that speed is the root of the
motor car trouble at the present time,
and I submit that sooner or later the
Ministry will have to face the imposition
of a speed limit for Northern Ireland.
It is inevitable. It will come, perhaps,
sooner rather than later. I admit that it
will not suit some people. It will not
suit the harum scarum motorist who will
break through at all costs and regardless
of all peril to others. It will not suit,

lives, and I submit to this Committee

test of this question.
I am bound to admit as a matter of
truth that the large majority of motor
car drivers in Northern Ireland are careful, skilful, and humane, but there is a
minority who are not careful, who are
not skilful, and who are not humane,
and who are a positive nuisance if not a
positive danger to the whole community.
I saw quite recently a poster issued by
the Pedestrian Association giving a
warning to motor car drivers. It showed
a photograph of a little dead child lying
limp in the hands of a police constable,
and above that photograph were the
words, "It may be your child next."
Many a father and many a mother send
their children out to school, and they do
not know whether those children will
come home safely. All day long during
their absence the mothers are in trepidation and in apprehension. Beneath that
photograph are the words, "Driver,
6,500 were killed last year. Don't take
a chance." I see that the Chief Constable of Aberdeen has ordered a supply
of these posters for his district, and I
hope that the Inspector-General of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary will order a
supply for Northern Ireland. They are
on exhibition in London.
The same Association has many records
of the slaughter caused on our roads. There
was one case that pained me very
greatly. Two little girls were playing
outside their mother's gate-one aged
five and the other aged eight. The little
one aged five called the mother out as
the elder girl was injured. The mother
found the elder child lying dead at the
gate, crushed to death by a speeding car
which had mounted the pavement. How
long is young life to be sacrificed in that
way to this fetish of speed? What do
they gain by this speed? If they arrive
at Portrush five minutes or ten minutes
sooner what do they gain? How long is
this modern massacre of the innocentsfor such it is to go on without any
determined effort to end it?

On that I wish to make only one comment. Those disturbances were grave
enough to justify a most searching
investigation. The loss of life alone would
justify that investigation. There were
historic precedents for such an investigation. The minority sought it. Such an
investigation was given by the British
Government in 1865 in Belfast after the
disturbances of 1864 and the result of
that commission of inquiry was the dissolution of the local Police Force and
the introduction into the city of the
Royal Irish Constabulary. A second and
minor result was the system by which
one of the resident magistrates in Belfast
was to be a member of the Catholic
persuasion.

The Unionist Government of the late
Lord Salisbury in 1886 granted a commission of inquiry into the disturbances
of 1886. I will say this that
reports of the two commissions, one in
1865 and one in 1886-the last one presided over by an eminent English High
Court judge-showed that the disturbances in those years at least were not
due to the causes suggested by the Prime
Minister in this House when refusing an
inquiry into the 1935 disturbances. They
were not due to those causes. I do think

CASTLEDERG NEW P.E. SCHOOL.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Gamble)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education whether he can
state the reason for the delay in sending
out plans of the new Castlederg Public
Elementary School to the Strabane and
Castlederg Regional Education Committee.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The plans
referred to by the hon. Member were
returned to the Regional Education
Committee on the 25th April, only three
days after they had been received in
the Ministry subsequent to their examination by the technical advisers.
I regret that there has been some
delay, but I find that it was due to the
general pressure of building work which
usually occurs in the spring and to
special difficulties over the plans of this
particular school.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I ask the
hon. and learned Gentleman is he aware
of the very unsatisfactory arrangements
existing at present and will he do his
best to assist the Regional Committee to
get the new school erected at as early
a date as possible?
Mr. ROBB: I am aware there is a
great demand for this new school and
every assistance will be given by the
Ministry to the Regional Committee.
UNEMPLOYED ELEMENTARY
TEACHERS.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry
of Education whether he can state the
number of unemployed elementary
teachers in Northern Ireland, and what
is the likelihood of their being employed
at an early date.
Mr. ROBB: It is not possible to
furnish exact figures of the total number
of unemployed teachers as there may be
Oral Answers
Ministry of Education
30 APRIL 1936
some former teachers who have resigned
from the service but who are now anxious
to obtain re-employment.
It is presumed, however, that the hon.
and gallant Member has more particularly in mind those young teachers who
have not yet been able to obtain
positions.
Of the students who completed their
training at the three recognised training
colleges during the past six years, 69
were unemployed on 31st March, 1936,
but of this number seven women have
married since finishing their training.
Only 30 of these ex-students have never
at any time been in employment.
Moreover, 39 finished their training
only last summer and, as the hon. and
gallant Member will realise, vacancies in
the schools occur, not at one period
only but throughout the year.
PLANS FOR NEW LABOURERS'
COTTAGES.
4. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he has
promised to prepare plans to guide local
authorities in the erection of labourers'
cottages, and whether the delay in
issuing these plans is keeping back this
urgent and necessary work.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The reply to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is in the affirmative, and I may inform
him that the plans are in course of
preparation and they will be ready for
issue shortly.
I am not aware that in any rural
district the schemes have advanced to the
point where plans are actually required.
As the hon. Member will appreciate,
there is much to be done in the way
of selecting sites and obtaining the necessary statutory powers before building
can be started.

To return to the Estimates, Vote 1,
at £66,166 shows a trifling increase over

There are little ups and downs, but
nothing striking under the various subheads, any small increases owing to
normal awards of increments to the staff
and to the small adjustments due to consolidation of Civil Service salaries being
off-set through the saving effected by
the changes of personnel following the
recent retirement on pension of Mr.
W. A. Houston, the Assistant Secretary
in charge of the Higher Education
Division. I may be allowed to express
the Ministry's sense
of loss at the
departure of this officer, whose ripe experience of intermediate and secondary
schools gained in the post of Assistant
Commissioner of Intermediate Education
in Dublin for over a dozen years proved
of the highest value in the starting and
developing of the Ministry's educational
policy. Provision is made in the Estimate for one additional clerk in the
elementary education division, but no
increase in the Vote is entailed, as the
cost is met by a reduction in the amount
required for overtime and occasional

An executive officer continues to act
as bursar in Stranmillis Training College,
and his salary, which is paid out of the

and
under Subhead E as

an
The net increase in Vote 2, for Educational Services, is merely nominal,
amounting to £334 in a sum of
£1,937,209, but there are subheads which
show fairly large increases, as well as
others which show decreases.
The chief increases in the Vote are in
the grants for secondary education and
in the cost of teachers' pensions; the sum
required for the grant to the education
authorities is also up by £2,500. On
the side of the savings, £1,455 less is
needed for the training colleges, and we
anticipate that elementary teachers'

Ministry of Education
salaries will be lower by £10,000. These
decreases are almost entirely due to a
small falling-off in the school attendance,
to which I will refer in a moment.
With regard to the cost of the training colleges, there is first a saving of
£1,000, due to the ending of the terminable annuity hitherto payable to St.
Mary's Training College under the
arrangement made by the Imperial
Government 25 years ago as a contribution towards the capital expenditure required for the erection of the building,
a liability which fell upon our Ministry
on its taking over the recognition of the
college in 1923. The last payment of
this liability was made last year. Next,
we expect to spend £830 less in respect
of capitation grants, as it is anticipated
that a smaller number of new admissions
of students will be made for the coming
session. I have frequently referred to
the difficulty of estimating with any precision the number of new teachers that
will be required at a date two or three
years hence.
This figure has, of course a relation to
the number of teachers retiring or resigning for various causes, and this number
was substantially less in the last eighteen
months than in any similar period before.
Hence there is at the moment a certain
amount of unemployment amongst the
students who left the colleges last July,
and it seems desirable to lessen the
number of admissions next session. There
is, it is true, a certain element of risk
in this course of action, seeing that the
requirements of the schools cannot be
accurately gauged in advance, and an
increase of even one per cent. in regularity of attendance, a desirable and I
believe by no means an impossible
eventuality, would at once call for about
forty new recruits. The Ministry much
regrets that any students should be
delayed in finding employment, but it is
a temporary phase and may be expected
to disappear in a short time. Some relief
may be found through a permission.
recently given to our ex-students to accept
posts as schoolmasters in the Army,
Navy, and Air Force, in which it is
understood that there are vacancies.
Under the head of training of teachers
the Ministry is making provision for
vacation courses for teachers in a wide
range of subjects, such as English teaching methods, speech training, drawing
Ministry of Education 1194
Estimates-
30 APRIL 1936
and craftwork. These courses are intended
to be of an inspiring character and to
give teachers fresh ideas and so enable
them to keep abreast of modern developments in several branches of instruction.
It is hoped that many teachers will avail
themselves of the opportunities thus provided, and if the experiment proves
successful the courses will be held
annually. The importance of such
courses is fully recognised in England,
where a large number are organised by
the Board of Education. A sum of £375
is set down under this head, in addition
to the sums already assigned to the
summer courses in horticulture.
The average number of pupils on the
rolls of the public elementary schools
during 1935 was practically the same as
in 1934, but at the end of last December
there was a decrease of over 3,000 as
compared with that date a year earlier.
The decrease was fairly evenly distributed
over the two county boroughs and all the
regional areas, and it is not possible to
say that the schools of any one district,
or of any one class, showed any appreciable difference in feeling the decline.
addition to the fall in enrolment, attendance was less regular than in 1934; this
falling-off in regularity was not, however, to be found in the Antrim, Ballymena, Cookstown, and Strabane regions.
It is difficult to account for this decrease,
except that weather conditions were not
favourable during a good part of last
winter.
In
I fear much of it must be ascribed to
a certain laxity on the part of some
regional committees in enforcing the law
of compulsory attendance, especially
where part-time attendance officers are
employed, and I would earnestly request
all committees to look into this matter
and see whether greater regularity of
attendance cannot be secured. For some
years now the percentage of regularity of
attendance in Northern Ireland has been
practically stationary at 85 or 86 per
cent. of the enrolment, and it is disappointing to find that no improvement
is being made. This is surprising when
we remember that so many unsuitable
and unsatisfactory school buildings have
been closed and so many fine new ones
erected in the last dozen years. While
the decline in enrolment may be
attributed to a decline in birth-rate, the
falling-off in regularity has no such cause
and should be remedied.
As under the regulations the results
of a decline in attendance do not affect
staffing for some months, it is anticipated.
that even if the numbers now become
stationary somewhat fewer teachers will
be required in 1936-37, and a saving of
approximately £10,700 is expected on this
account. This sum, however, represents
much less than one per cent. of the salary
bill.
I may refer to an interesting change
made in the system of payment of
teachers during the past year. Hitherto,
as most hon. Members are aware,
principals of schools received a capitation
payment dependent on each pupil in
average attendance, and this payment
formed the chief extra emolument payable to the headmasters and head
mistresses. It has now been arranged
that in the case of all new appointments
to principalships no further capitation
payments will be made, but a lump sum,
varying with the size of the school, will
be paid instead. For this purpose the
schools have been divided into classes,
according to the number of pupils in
attendance. The amount of the grant
has been fixed so as approximately to
represent the average sums received in
capitation, and there is no expectation
of savings being effected by the change.
It will, however, obviate fluctuations in
salaries through every trifling alteration
in the attendance.
Coming to secondary education, there
is a steady and continuous increase in the
number of pupils at our secondary schools.
This has now risen to 13,165, the highest
figure yet recorded. This, of course,
necessitates a corresponding increase in
the capitation grant payable to these
schools, for which the Estimate is £1,000
higher, and there is also an increase in
increments amounting to £2,550, making
a total rise for secondary education to
£178,300. No branch of our system
shows a greater advance since the settingup of the Ministry than secondary education, the attendance, as well as the cost,
having risen by nearly 60 per cent. in the
last ten years. The Ministry is not, however, satisfied that parents in all cases
send their children to secondary schools
sufficiently young. It has been frequently pointed out that pupils ought
to enter these schools under thirteen
years of age, if they are to have sufficient
time to take the full course provided, but
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
little improvement in this respect has
taken place, and as a result some schools
are forced to condense a five-years' course
into four years, with evil results in overpressure on the pupil. Less than 25 per
cent. of pupils who enter secondary
schools from elementary schools do so
under thirteen, and more than one-third
delay the transfer until they are over
fourteen. This practice is not only detrimental to the best interests of the children
but unfair to their teachers, who have to
crowd the work of two or three years into
one, especially in subjects which are new
to the pupils.
It is satisfactory to find that the
number entering for the certificate
examinations is increasing and that the
great majority take these examinations at
the right age. For many years past the
Ministry has made monetary awards
based on the results, but there is a substantial and growing body of opinion that
awards of this kind should, for weighty
physiological reasons, especially in the
case of girls, be deferred until the senior
certificate stage is reached.
No alteration of outstanding importance has taken place in the past year in
the technical schools. The enrolment is
about the same as for several years past,
the only section of the work showing
definite increase being the day work in
the form of junior technical and commercial schools. I may remark, however,
that several technical school principals
will soon, in the ordinary course of
events, have to relinquish their posts in
favour of younger men. These principals
have been chiefly responsible in the past
for the success of the technical schools,
and it can only be hoped that those who
follow them will prove equally successful.
The local education authorities continue to be active in promoting education
throughout the Province. Building of
new schools is still proceeding steadily,
both in the city of Belfast and in the
districts outside, and eight large new
schools were opened last year, bringing
the number of new schools provided by
these authorities to 117. The medical
inspection service continues to progress,
and valuable work is being done by the
school doctors throughout the Province.
The question of giving increased attention
to physical education has been much in
evidence of late, and the movement to
provide playing-fields and opportunities
for exercise and recreation is receiving
more attention but much remains to be
done. Conferences with the Ministry and
the education authorities and teachers
have taken place in regard to the best
means of saving children from road
accidents, and with the assistance of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, picked members of the Police
Force have given valuable lectures on
road dangers in several of the elementary
schools.
One further matter to which I should
like to refer is the opening of the Hay-
The
park Special School last month.
buildings have now been completed and
equipped in a most satisfactory manner
for the boarding and education of
mentally defective children, and a competent teaching staff has been appointed.
The school will deal both with boarders
and day pupils. It was opened in the
middle of March last with an attendance
of about thirty pupils of both sexes,
drawn from all parts of the Province. It
is hardly necessary to say that the number
of children in Northern Ireland who
would benefit from the care and training which can be given in this school
is considerable, but we have found that
a great many parents hesitate to send
children to it, apparently through a
natural dislike to entrust them to
strangers so far from their homes. I can
quite understand their reluctance, but I
would urge those who may have influence
with such parents, the teachers, medical
officers, members of education authorities, and the public generally, to use that
influence to overcome those feelings and
to point out to them that in opening and
maintaining this school the Government
and the education authorities are anxious
to provide for these young people, who
are, through, perhaps, various causes,
somewhat below the average in intelligenco, suitable opportunities for overcoming, or at least alleviating, their
defects and for turning them into men
and women capable of becoming useful
and self-supporting members of the community. I would invite hon. Members
who are interested in this work to pay a
visit to the institution and see for themselves the way it is carried on and the
advantages it offers. I can speak with
confidence of the care and attention that
have been bestowed on the fitting-up of
Ministry of Education 1198

the premises and the organisation of the
school, and I feel that it would be a great
pity if its capacity to serve our people
were not fully availed of.
There are of course many aspects and
details of our education system upon
which I am not touching in presenting
these Estimates. I do not desire to take

Mr. BEATTIE: The brief summary
of the Estimates given by the Parliamentary Secretary is welcome on this
side of the Committee? With reference

I hope that all classes of the community

children.
As I know other speakers desire to
follow I wish to make my comments on
this Estimate as brief as possible. I
regret that the Parliamentary Secretary has presented to the Committee a
very black outlook for those who are
responsible for the education of the
children in so far as the decline in the
child population of Northern Ireland is.
concerned. That decline brings a very
black outlook to the homes of many
young people who have qualified for the
teaching profession, and to the large
number of young teachers who are unemployed in Northern Ireland to-day. That
number is far above what it has been for
the last ten years, and next year the outlook is not going to be any brighter. I
regret that that position is appearing in
Northern Ireland, but I think that, in
the consultations which take place
between the Ministry and those who
carry out their services in the schools,
the matter could be dealt with by a conference on the question of how best the
schools could be staffed, and the advisability of having a register compiled
setting out the requirements of the
school population of Northern Ireland,
and regulating the training of teachers
in accordance with those requirements.
I am not so sure that one per cent. of an
increase in the school population would
employ forty teachers. That is one statement made by the Parliamentary Secretary which I would question very much.
If that were so we would have our ups
and downs of employment and unemployment and would know where we
stand.
The services rendered by the teachers
of Northern Ireland have been recognised by the Parliamentary Secretary
and his Department. Anyone who takes
the trouble to read the Report of the
Ministry of Education and realises the
high standard of the teaching profession
in Northern Ireland-a standard which
they have maintained through all their
troubles, trials, and difficulties-must be
proud of the teaching profession of this
Province. It has been described by those
best able to judge, as the cream of the
teaching profession in Great Britain or
Ireland. I would like to go further and
say "Yes. It has been maintained at the
cost of a very high sacrifice by the
teachers of Northern Ireland in so far as
they have applied themselves to the
education of the child, in so far as the
environment of the home has not been
suitable for education purposes, and in
so far as the conditions of the home, due
to other causes, have really taken all incentive for learning from the child."
The teachers have been able, despite all
these troublesome conditions, to maintain a very high standard of efficiency
in the education of working-class children
in Northern Ireland.
I feel that I am justified in saying that
the teachers have been looked upon as
having no grievances, no troubles of their
own. It cannot be denied that their
whole lives are devoted earnestly and
sincerely to the advantage of the children
of the Province. After saying that, and
after giving credit where credit is due,
I ask, have the Government done justice
to that hard-working class of the community. Have the Government treated
the teaching profession in Northern Ireland in the same way as the Government
of Great Britain have treated their
teachers? We all know that at the
present moment education is going onand let no one stand in the way of

years—but

Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, by amalgamation. As you know in the past the local

In 1930 it was stated that there were

to which I refer, but I challenge anyone
to say that there are more teachers
employed to-day than there were at that

purposes. I am inclined to say now, not

has turned out very highly efficient

and it was only what you might call
three back rooms knocked into one. But
in that little school a child was watched
from its creeping days until it left school

understood the little difficulties with
which the child had to contend as far as
learning was concerned. The teacher
really was the guardian of the child from.
its early days till its school leaving days,
and by that process I am inclined to
think that the child was as well equipped
as the children are to-day.
I know opportunities were not as open
as they are now-I admit that but I
am not so sure that a school of 350
children would not be large enough for
an all-in school. Senior and junior
schools, in my opinion, are not the best
provision for the educational services
which we require in Northern Ireland. I
know that in England, in Lincoln,
Southampton, and other places, the local
authorities now say that senior and
junior schools are not really the best for
their purposes, and the Lincoln Council
has made a proviso that no school shall
be built to accommodate more than 350
pupils. I give that information to the
Parliamentary Secretary for his serious.
consideration and, if he thinks it worthy
of consideration, to be passed on to the

As I say, in those savings and in the
building of these large schools the
teachers have been the sufferers. I was
commenting on the conditions surrounding the agreement. Surely it is time now
that the teachers had restored to them a
salary sufficient to maintain themselves
in decency and comfort, and to give
them that contentment and ease of mind
that are necessary for the work they have
to perform. To-day to the outside public
I declare that the life of a teacher under

any industrial worker in Northern Ireland. He has to serve five years, and

First and foremost, our people want

few words on this Vote before the debate
ends. As one who mixes very much

Protestant population, and at the same

serious matter for us, and one we will

as that injustice continues to be perpetrated upon us.
It is all very well for you to say,

get the same treatment as other people."
The Protestant schools that have not
been transferred are rapidly decreasing in number, and I believe that
in a very short time all those schools
will have been handed over. But,
as this Committee is well aware, the
Catholic people will never hand over their

the control of the religious teaching of

University (Prof. Johnstone), but also the

gallant Member for East Down (Colonel
Gordon), the enthusiastic rhetoric of the
hon. Member for Dock (Mr. Midgley),
and the complaints we are accustomed
to hear every year from those representing

would like to deal with a few of the
matters that were raised.
There is one matter I am reluctant
to refer to, but I do not think it should
be unanswered, and that is the complaint
made by the hon. and learned Member
for Central and the hon. Member for
Falls that their community is placed
under some handicap or disadvantage.
You would almost think it was some kind
of tyranny. Such is not the case. When
one throws one's mind back to the state
of education in Ireland before the establishment of this Parliament one can recollect that education suffered from two
curses. One of these curses was the lack
of money, and the other was the extraordinary denominational split which
rocked education from top to bottom. On
the one hand there was not enough money
to build schools, and, on the other hand,
through this excessive denominationalism,
there were small Methodist, Presbyterian,
Roman Catholic and Church of Ireland
schools. It was a system which any wise
man could see at once was not a good
system. Accordingly, when our Ministry
of Education took the matter in hand it
had to do something that was obvious,
and that was to build schools which had
fallen behind 50 or 70 years. It was
necessary to have new schools, and the
only way they could be provided was out
of public money.
It was also obvious that it would be
a foolish thing to apply public money
in the building of Presbyterian,
Methodist, Roman Catholic and Church
of Ireland schools, and accordingly it
was decided that the local authorities
should have charge of the building of
schools, which should not be provided
for one denomination alone, but for the
whole community. The immediate
interests of the community were safeguarded, because it was expressly provided by the Act of 1923 that it should
be the duty of the education authority
to afford opportunities, according to the
religious denomination of the children,
for the priest or pastor to come in and
give instruction to the children of his
own denomination. That was done, in
my opinion, adequately. Take the case
of the enthusiastic minister of the
Methodist Church who would say, "It
is not enough to have that opportunity in
the school. I want to keep control of
the school myself," or the Presbyterian
minister who would say, "I wish the
Shorter Catechism to be taught by the
teachers in the school," or the Church of
Ireland minister who would say, "This
is a Church school, and I want to keep
it a Church school, and I want the
Church Catechism and Creed taught
there." The Government allow these
people to keep their schools. They pay
the teachers in those schools and say, "If
you insist on having religious control of
the school you will not expect us to provide for the school in the way that the
local authority provide for transferred
schools."
The Roman Catholic Church is in no
different position from the Presbyterian
Church, Methodist Church, or Church
of Ireland in that regard. If they wish
to have their particular tenets taught
in any school, and wish to retain that
school, they are entitled to do so, but
they cannot come in and claim that
while retaining control of their schools.
the local authority should pay all the
expenses of working and equipping them,
and that the Government should pay the
cost of the teaching staff. When they

schools. They should not claim to have
the teaching of their Church provided at
the public expense any more than the
teaching of the Shorter Catechism is to
be provided at the public expense or the
teaching of the Church of Ireland catechism or the Church creeds at the public
expense. I will now come back to matters
which, perhaps, are of more importance
educationally, because that controversy
has been closed so far as Northern Ireland
is concerned. The hon. Member for Dock
made a striking speech, full of rhetoric,
which I enjoyed-
Mr. MIDGLEY: And full of facts, I
hope.
Mr. BLACK: The whole burden of the
speech was that we fall short in Northern
Ireland of what is being done in England
and other parts of the Empire.
Mr. MIDGLEY: That is correct.
Mr. BLACK: In the first place, I
would suggest to the hon. Member for
Dock that he cannot leave out of consideration the fact that we were only set
up here in 1921, fifteen years ago, and
that when we were set up educationally
we were 40, 50 or 70 years behind the
times-
Mr. MIDGLEY: Agreed.
Mr. BLACK- -and that much has
been accomplished during the last fifteen
years. I do not say that much does not
remain to be accomplished, but much has
been accomplished. The hon. Member
for Dock drew a comparison between the
state of things in Belfast and in the
country districts. I do not know whether
that is a just comparison or not, but if he
draws a comparison between the state of
things in Belfast now and the state of
things in Belfast before the war, he will
have to acknowledge that much has been
done.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Hear, hear.
Mr. BLACK: A man who intends to
build houses first sits down and calculates
the cost, and if he wants to build a palace
he gives the matter much longer thought,
and when the hon. Member speaks of
the reforms which he has visualised he
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
30 APRIL 1936
should have presented to the Committee
something in the nature of a calculation
of the cost. It is very easy to say, "Get
this or that" without informing the
people who have to pay for it how much
they will have to pay. He suggests that
we should bring in a Bill to compel the
local authorities to do this, or that, or
the other thing, but you cannot fairly
bring in a Bill directing the ratepayers
to do this, or that, or the other thing,
without telling them what the cost would
be, and if it meant 2s, 3s, 4s, 5s, or 10s
or more in the £ on the rates, though
they might be very desirable reforms, the
ratepayers might not approve of them.
You cannot go further than you can with
the material before you. Before any such
reforms as have been suggested could be
considered the cost must be calculated.
Now, amongst the matters he suggested
-I do not know that some are entirely
wise was the building of a municipal
secondary school. Personally I have some
doubts about the wisdom of that. I am
quite as keen as the hon. Member for
Dock that every boy who can take advantage of secondary education should be
given an opportunity of getting it, but
to build a municipal secondary school in
Belfast would, I fear, lead to the position
that it would be regarded as a school for
working men's children, and there would
be some sort of distinction drawn between
it and the existing schools, and that
people would consider they belonged to
a better class socially. That would be a
mistake. I think the better way to go
about that problem is the way it has been
tackled up to the present, that is by
providing scholarships for working men's
children, who can take advantage of a
secondary education, and let them go
into the existing schools. No class distinction should be drawn between school
and school.
With regard to elementary education,
I think one blunder was made here.
Everyone who knows anything about
elementary education in Belfast knows
that in the suburbs there is great reluctance on the part of parents to send their
children to public elementary schools.
That is a misfortune. There are, no
doubt, some good private schools, but,
taken as a whole, I think the instruction
given in the public elementary schools
is superior to that given in the private.
schools.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Hear, hear.
Mr. BLACK: I would like if it were
possible-one would not make any compulsion about it that all children in
Belfast should attend a State school run
by the State, and that the small private
schools should be wiped out. I believe
that would be good for education, but
you may find it difficult and at the
moment impossible to do that. I think
on the whole it would work out well in
the suburbs if public elementary schools
were established. They need not be free
schools, but fee-charging schools. Let the
people who can afford it in that way pay
for the education of their children, but
still let the children have the advantage
of the education in the State schools,
which are better staffed and better run
in every way than the average private
school.
or
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to ask

me, what is the moral difference
between a municipal secondary school,

by public funds, and a public elementary

there not be the same objection to the

Mr. BLACK: Before the Government of Northern Ireland took over in
Belfast there were a number of feeand there
charging schools, and
difference between them and other
schools. The boys from the one met the

was felt. There were undoubtedly

who would not have been willing to send

is that it was a mistake to do away with

about a change you would still have got
in the elementary schools a number of
Ichildren who have been lost to them.
I only make these remarks, by the way,
in dealing with the matter of the
municipal secondary school which the
hon. Member mentioned. He referred
Ministry of Education 1248

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
again to the question of scholarships, and
contended there were not sufficient
scholarships from the elementary to the
secondary schools. He says he was informed by someone that the secondary
schools do not want working-class boys.
Mr. MIDGLEY: No. Not a bigger
percentage.
Mr. BLACK: I take it this is a matter
on which persons connected with secondary schools ought to be able to give an
opinion, and they gave to me what I
think was a quite candid and unbiased
opinion on the matter. They find that
with the existing system of scholarships
the boys who take the lower places in the
city scholarships are just on the margin
of being able to take full advantage of
secondary education, and when you get
below that line they think, taking one

would not be able to take full advantage
of secondary education. That may or
may not be so, but it does suggest that
the question cannot be settled in general
terms, but that the facts must be ascertained from those competent to give
advice; that is the teachers in the secondary schools who get the pupils from the
elementary schools and are able to gauge
their capacity to take advantage of
secondary education.
So much with regard to those matters.
There is one other matter which has been
touched upon, and which, I think, is of
great importance. That is with regard
to the salaries of public elementary school
teachers. These teachers suffer under a
sense of injustice. It is a great pity that
they should suffer under that sense of injustice. They suffer under a particular
sense of injustice in the respect that the
last cut has been restored to other public
servants-it has been restored, I think,
to the police-but it has not been restored
to the teachers. It is a bad thing for the
teachers to have that feeling, and it is
also a bad thing for the community. If
a promising boy or girl is minded to become an elementary school teacher he or
she will naturally take advice from some
other elementary school teacher. If a
boy wants to become a lawyer his father
will get in touch with some lawyer and
ask him all about that profession. If a
boy wants to become a doctor his father
will get in touch with some doctor and
ask him all about that profession. But
if a boy wants to become an elementary
school teacher and his father gets in touch
with a teacher he is sure to receive discouragement. He will be told, "We have
not been treated fairly. This is not a
service in which you are treated fairly.
I would not advise you at all to put your
boy into this profession." It is a bad
thing if you are discouraging boys from
going into the profession. The profession
ought to set out to try to attract the very
best, but so long as there is this uncertainty and feeling of unfairness it will
react most detrimentally on the standard
of education in the community. From
that point of view I think something
should be definitely settled, and settled
as soon as possible, to let the teachers
know where they stand and not leave
them in the position in which the matter
has been left up to now.
The hon. Member for Pottinger has
touched upon another matter, as, indeed,
did the hon. Member for the University
(Professor Johnstone). That is the inspection system. I have heard a great deal
of criticism of the inspection system, and
the general impression left by the
criticism I have heard is that there is
too much inspection. I do not think
that is what is wrong with the system
at all. What I think is
with
wrong
the inspection system in our public
elementary schools is that there is too
little inspection. I think the fault of
the present system is that the Ministry
has not a big enough staff, and that an
inspector can only visit a school at very
rare intervals, once in two or three years.
I think the system would be greatly improved if you had a staff sufficiently big
that an inspector would be quite a
frequent visitor to the school, that he
could come in two or three times in the
year, and so get to know the teachers
better, and be able to weigh up the staff
better. If an inspector had an opportunity of getting into much closer touch
with the school, and of getting to know
the capabilities of the teachers better
through more frequent visits, I think a
great deal of the objection to the present
system would disappear. The objection.
to the present system is that the inspector
is apt to fix the merit marks arbitrarily.
If both the inspector and the teacher had
greater opportunities of meeting each
Ministry of Education
Estimates-

30 APRIL 1936
other and of seeing each other at work
I believe the greater part of that objection would disappear.
There was one other matter raised by
the hon. Member for Pottinger with
regard to the danger of a man being
reduced in class and rated as inefficient.
Everyone knows that as a man grows
older he may become lazy, or even something worse may befall him, and a man
who starts life as an efficient man may
become inefficient. In professions such
as medicine or the law that is easily
found out. Why should a teacher who
becomes inefficient be kept in something
like a privileged position?
Mr. MIDGLEY: What about the civil
servant?
Mr. BLACK: If a civil servant becomes inefficient he ought to be thrown
out of the service too. The same with
any other man. He ought not to be
retained in his position, whatever it may
be, whether he be a teacher, a civil
servant, a lawyer, or anything else. To
determine whether a teacher is efficient
or not there must be some inspection
system. Whether the present system is
ideal or not I do not know, but I think
the real remedy is, as I say, not less but
more inspection.
Professor CORKEY: It is always a
pleasure to hear the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education, and
I think on this occasion he may congratulate himself that those who have spoken
in this debate, however they may have
criticised the general policy of the
Ministry, have not to any extent directed
their criticism towards the administration
itself. As far as administration is concerned everyone seems to be fairly well
satisfied. In regard to policy there will,
of course, always be differences of opinion
where you have a Government that is
anxious to secure popular control of the
schools, and I am afraid, having regard
to that matter, difference of opinion is
inevitable.
The hon. and learned Member for
Willowfield has dealt faithfully with that
subject, and if the hon. and learned
Member for Central (Mr. Campbell) feels
a little bit sore as a result I would like
to comfort him by saying that, so far as
religious education is concerned, I agree.
entirely with him in principle. As an
occasional visitor to one of our own
schools, I would like to testify that
magnificent work is being done by our
teachers in this department of education;
and in all transferred schools it is being
done by the teachers voluntarily. It is
a great delight to go into these schools
and hear the children singing their
hymns, repeating their prayers, and
manifesting a knowledge of the moral
principles and ideals in the grand stories
of the Bible as they are explained to
them by these teachers.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the hon.
Member is he perfectly content with the
Bible instruction in transferred schools?
Professor CORKEY: So far as I have
had any evidence in regard to the character of that teaching it is exceedingly
efficient and satisfactory? At a moment
when the very foundations of our civilisation are subject to a great deal of
criticism I consider that this element
of education is of tremendous importance,
and our Government might go
further in the direction of making compulsory for all children who are subject
to their rule in Northern Ireland lessons
on the broad principles of the civilisation
which we have inherited and which we are
determined to retain. For example,
even
lessons might be given on such subjects
as the value of honourable and useful
work, of free speech and liberty, the
worth of individuals, on the character of
governments and local authorities, and
on international duties. Those are
elemental principles-I would almost say
elemental moral principles-which it is of
importance to have implanted in the
minds of our children if we are to retain
our civilisation. There are other things
which I would have liked to have said,
but at this hour I forbear.

REMOVAL OF STREET
BARRICADES IN BELFAST.
1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
considers that in the interests of good
order, and for the furtherance of trade,
the time has arrived to remove the metal
barricades in many of the streets of
Belfast.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am just as
anxious as the hon. and gallant Member
is, and for the same reasons that he
mentions in his question, that these
barriers should not remain longer than
is necessary, and I can assure him that
I will have them removed as soon as
I am satisfied that this can safely be
done.
Mr. GRANT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the municipal
elections in the city of Belfast are
approaching and it will not be possible
for the different candidates to get in
touch with their constituents unless the
barricades are removed?
SEARCHES OF HOUSES IN
FIVEMILETOWN.
2. Mr. STEWART asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that on 1st April, 1936, raids took place
by members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary on at least two Catholic houses
in Fivemiletown, County Tyrone, and
whether he can state on what information these raids were ordered.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that certain searches were carried out by
the police on the 1st April last in Fivemiletown, but it would not be in the
public interest to give the information
sought by the hon. Member in the latter
part of his question,

Sir DAWSON BATES: The man
referred to, Thomas O'Neill, was not
discharged by the medical officer of the
hospital, but it would appear that a
nephew of his wrote to the Guardians
requesting their permission to take
O'Neill out of the hospital. O'Neill
himself expressed no wish to leave, and,
having regard to his weak mental condition it devolved upon the Guardians
to decide the matter as seemed to them
the best in the old man's interests, and
in all the circumstances they decided

ST. BARNABAS' SENIOR
VOLUNTARY SCHOOL.
4. Mr. GRANT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he will reconsider his
decision to close St. Barnabas' Senior
Voluntary School, Belfast; and whether
he is prepared to concede to the trustees,
managers, and the parents of children
attending a Protestant voluntary school
the same rights to continue such voluntary school as are accorded under similar
circumstances to trustees, managers, and
parents of children attending Roman
Catholic voluntary schools.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The position
is not quite as represented in the
question. The action of the Ministry in
the reorganisation of the school referred.
to has arisen on account of arrangments
proposed by the Belfast Education Committee for the improvement of educational facilities in this district of the
city of Belfast.
Two schools have hitherto been recognised-St. Barnabas' Infants and St.
Barnabas' Senior-and it is intended
that these schools shall in future be
organised as a junior school with approximately the same number of pupils as
in the two existing schools. The senior
pupils will, however, attend senior
schools in the district, under the Belfast
Education Committee, which are suitable
and available for their instruction.
The Ministry regrets the necessity for
interference with any existing public
elementary school, but, in view of the
superior facilities now provided for the
education of the senior pupils, it considers that the arrangements proposed
are most desirable on educational
grounds. It is perhaps unnecessary to
point out that satisfactory arrangements
for religious instruction are provided in
the schools at which the senior pupils
will attend in future.
way
The circumstances are in no
similar to those applicable to schools
under Roman Catholic management, as
it is well known that the parents of the
children in such schools are not prepared
to send their children to senior schools
under the management of the Education
Authority.
Mr. GRANT: Is the Parliamentary
Secretary aware that St. Barnabas'

MILK AND MILK PRODUCTS ACT.
5. Mr. YOUNG (for Mr. Christie)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he can state the amounts levied
on (1) Grade "A" milk producers; (2)
Grade "B" milk producers; (3) Grade
"C" milk producers; since the Act came
into force; whether he can state the total

the sum paid to creameries by way of
subsidy.
Oral Answers
Ministry of Commerce
5 MAY 1936
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke); During the period
since the Milk and Milk Products Act
came into force up to 31st March last,
the following amounts have been received
in respect of licence fees levied on milk
producers:-
Grade "A"
Grade "B"
Grade "C"
...
...
£722
15,805
50,558
Total £67,085
The total cost for the same period of
administration of the Act, together with
veterinary and laboratory services, was
£44,591, which includes the sum of
£4,329 for veterinary inspection for part
of a year.
Up to 31st March equalisation payments in respect of milk delivered to
creameries amounted to £288,853, and
in addition bonuses totalling £23,361
were issued, all but a negligible fraction
of which went to "C" producers. A
total of £312,214 has thus been paid to
creamery suppliers.
In connection with the hon. Member's
question he may be interested to learn
that of the 12 million gallons sold on
the liquid market 1,300,000 gallons is
"A," 6 million gallons "B," and 3
million gallons "C," so that we are now
within measurable distance of the whole
of the liquid milk supply being either of
"A" or "B" quality.
SCHOOLS UNDER ROMAN
CATHOLIC MANAGEMENT.
6. Mr. STEWART asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education what proportion of the one
and a quarter million pounds expended
by his Ministry since 1921 has been
given to schools under Catholic management.
Mr. ROBB: I presume that the hon.
Member refers to expenditure from
public funds upon the building of new
schools and the enlargement, reconditioning or improvement of existing school
premises which expenditure, I may say,
has now reached almost one and a half
million pounds.
Of this sum the amount spent in
grants from the Ministry is £142,989, of
which 84 per cent. (£120,282) was paid
in respect of schools under Roman
Catholic management.
In addition, schools under Roman
Catholic management have received
£14,960 (or 75 per cent.) of the £19,940
granted by local education authorities
under Section 16 of the Education Act.
The balance of the total expenditure
referred to above was spent by local
education authorities upon the erection
of provided schools as well as the enlargement, reconditioning and improvement of transferred schools.

CLASS VII. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF COMMERCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £13,564 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1937, for
the salaries and expenses of the Ministry
of Commerce (14 and 15 Geo. V. (N.I.),
c. 21; 15 and 16 Geo. V. (N.I.), c. 3,
s. 4; and 16 Geo. V. (N.I.), c. 4).".
(Note-£7,000 has been voted on
account).
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Committee will
observe that the total provision for the
services included in this Vote is £20,564,
which represents a decrease of £105 as
compared with the amount provided last
year. This decrease is due to the reduction, by one, in the number of the staff;
the saving effected by this reduction being
offset to some extent by the award of
annual increments.
Last year, when presenting the
Estimate of my Ministry, I referred to
the advance towards prosperity made.
during 1934, and on this occasion I think
that I can fairly state that in spite of all
the difficulties that beset the international
situation, this advance has been maintained. International trade, although
still hampered by tariffs, quotas, and
currency restrictions, has, according to
Ministry of Commerce 1260
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
the statistics collected by the League of
Nations, shown slight signs of improvement during 1935.
The United Kingdom, whose fortunes.
we share, has, I am glad to say, shown
a further increase in trade, the value of
imports having risen by 3.5 per cent.
over 1934 and the value of exports by
7.6 per cent. The average number of
insured persons employed in Great
Britain during 1935 was 10,371,000, the
highest since the war. In Northern
Ireland the Ministry of Labour estimates
that there were 11,800 more persons in
insurable employment on the 23rd March,
1936, than on the 25th March, 1935.
Mr. BEATTIE: What is the total
insured population?
Mr. BARBOUR: I cannot give the
hon. Member that figure. So far as concerns Northern Ireland's external trade
I am in a position to estimate the extent
of Ulster's trade during the past year.
The total trade amounted in value to
over £92,000,000, as compared with
£88,500,000 during 1934. Imports,
which totalled some £47,000,000, during
1935 increased by over £1,500,000 on the
1934 figures, while exports, which
amounted to £45,000,000, increased by
over £2,000,000. This development was
not unexpected in view of the steady
increase in the volume of trade passing
through our principal port. The imports
and exports which passed through Belfast
harbour in 1935 amounted to 3,630,000
tons, the highest figure since 1913.
For
the first time in the history of the port
the tonnage of shipping cleared passed
the four million mark, the total being
4,181,000 tons-an increase of 6 per cent.
over 1934.
Another satisfactory feature of 1935
was the increased activity of our shipbuilding industry. The improvement in
1934 was continued during the year just
ended, and the tonnage of ships launched
amounted to almost 102,000 tons. We
are proud to know that the two largest
ships launched in the world during the
year were launched in the Lagan. There
is, I am glad to say, ground for the belief
that the increased activity of the past two
years will be maintained in 1936.
Our linen industry has experienced a
year of some difficulty. Raw material
prices have been rising, and this has
hampered the development of trade, particularly in view of the fact that other
textile products have not had to contend
with an equivalent increase in the cost
of their raw materials. Nevertheless,
the value of exports of linen goods from
the United Kingdom increased by 6 per
cent. over the value exported in 1934,
while piece-goods, which constitute
almost 67 per cent. of our export trade,
showed the satisfactory increase of 9 per
cent. over last year.
I am glad to be able to inform the
Committee that this improvement has
been maintained during the first quarter
of the present year, when the export of
linen goods increased in value by 12.7
per cent. over the corresponding quarter
of 1935, and represents the highest export
for that period in any year since 1930.
Correspondingly, the value of the linen
piece-goods exported in the first three
months of this year increased by 15.1
per cent., and was the highest for the
first quarter of any year since 1928.
In former years the linen industry
depended mainly on foreign markets to
absorb its products. The high tariff
policy of the United States of America,
however, the continued depression in that
country, and exchange and tariff diffi
culties in other markets, have led to a
reorientation in the markets of the linen
trade. The home market has now become
of major importance to the linen
industry, and British markets overseas
have been steadily increasing their purchases of linen. The result of this
change has been that the decrease in
foreign trade has been compensated to
no small extent by the increase in the
home and dominion markets. Indeed,
the value of the exports of linen piecegoods to British countries overseas has
increased to the extent of 60 per cent.
since 1931. As the value of exports in
1935 was the highest since 1930, I think
that we can congratulate the linen industry on having so successfully combated
the many and perplexing difficulties
which confronted it during the past year.
It would be foolish to blind ourselves
to the fact that the competition from
certain quarters abroad which our linen
trade has to meet in overseas markets is
increasing in intensity, and it is more
important than ever that the trade should
strive after, and seek to maintain, the
Estimates-

His
highest pitch of technical efficiency, by
which means alone our hold upon our
markets can be assured, let alone extended. Convinced of the urgency and
importance of this matter, the Government proposes to continue the financial
assistance given to the Linen Industry
Research Association. Last year the
attention of hon. Members was directed
to the conference of Research Associations which was called by the British
Government early in 1934, and which
was attended by representatives of the
Linen Industry Research Association and
of my Ministry. The Research Associations were asked to prepare for the next
five years schemes of work of increased
scope, and were assured that
Majesty's Government would help them
to meet the extra expenditure involved.
During the past year the association.
has effected considerable internal reorganisation and has notably extended
the scope of the research programme.
has been decided to continue the flax
processing experiments in Norfolk on a
commercial scale, and a sub-station of the
Research Institute has been establised on
the Sandringham Estate for carrying out
agricultural, botanical and fibre processing investigations. I should like here to
pay a tribute to the public spirit of those
firms in the linen trade who have provided the capital necessary for the processing factory and plant, and those who
have guaranteed the funds of the
Research Association against loss on the
commercial operations.
It
During the year extensive experiments
and investigations have also been made
at the institute on materials and methods
used in spinning, weaving and bleaching.
The institution of research work on sisal
fibre at the Linen Research Institute has
necessitated the establishment of a new
department which will confine its
activities to problems concerning the
utilisation of sisal and its waste products,
and the development of a larger field of
use for this fibre. The cost of work on
sisal is financed separately by a grant
from the Board of Trustees for Sisal
Research. I mention the matter merely
to indicate the increasing scope of the
activities of the association.
With regard to the public supply of
electricity, the promotion, regulation
and supervision of which are included
amongst the statutory duties imposed on
my Ministry, I have again to report
another year of remarkable progress,
which has vindicated once more the policy
of the co-ordination of public supplies.
The returns which have just been received
show that the total number of units sold
by statutory undertakers has risen from
114 millions to 142 millions, or 24.5 per
cent., and this following on a year in
which an increase of over 30 per cent. was
recorded. The most gratifying feature
of this development is the fact that it
is due partly to a general improvement
in trade and industry, and partly to the
manner in which supplies of electricity
for all purposes are being made available
in the smaller towns and country districts
which had not previously enjoyed the
advantages of a supply of electricity at
all or
were dependent on small local
plants, which could not hope to provide.
supplies at reasonable rates for heating
or cooking or to large power users.
and
The growth of the demand in rural
districts may be gauged from the fact
that during the year 1935 the Electricity
Board purchased about 263 million units
from the Belfast Corporation
320,000 units from the Londonderry
Corporation, as against approximately 16
million units purchased the previous year,
while the Antrim Electricity Supply
Company, who are responsible for the
transmission of supplies to the towns in
County Antrim and South Derry, purchased from the Larne generating station
4,710,000 units last year as compared
with 3,903,000 units purchased in the
previous year.
Members of the Committee are aware
of the commercial services which my
Ministry undertakes on behalf of Ulster
exporters. Information on tariff changes,
exchange restrictions, foreign agents and
importers, is collected in the Ministry
and disseminated to interested firms in
Northern Ireland, and I am glad to be
able to inform the Committee that the
close contact with the commercial community and the assistance which we have
been able to give manufacturers and exporters in the manifold problems which
confront them, have not only been maintained, but intensified, during the past
year.
on
I have expressed
many
occasions the view that the utility of my
Ministry to the commercial community
continues to increase in direct relation
to the extent to which that community
Ministry of Commerce 1264

utilises its services, and I believe that
both traders and trade associations will
bear me out when I say that the experience of the past year has amply demonstrated the truth of this contention.
I need hardly remind the Committee
that my Ministry continues to keep a
close watch on trade negotiations with
foreign countries in order to safeguard
and to further Northern Ireland's trade
interests wherever these may be affected,
and at the same time my Department
endeavours to keep exporting firms in
touch with the latest developments in
foreign markets not only, as I have
stated, by the circulation of market information, but also by arranging periodic
visits of His Majesty's trade represesentatives abroad for the purpose of
interviewing interested firms.
I should like also to emphasise here
that, in our efforts to keep firms in
touch with trade openings abroad and
with general market developments, my
Ministry endeavours to aid all classes of
trade whether the industries concerned
be large or small. The results of the
Ministry's efforts in this direction cannot, of course, be measured in statistical
terms, but I am convinced that they are
of considerable magnitude.
At the British Industries Fair, which
closed in February last, my Ministry
again organised a comprehensive display
of Northern Ireland food products, cooperating in the case of bacon with the
Pig Industry Council. The display of
bacon and hams at the Fair is
undoubtedly extending into Southern
British markets knowledge of the
developments which are taking place in
the Northern Ireland trade. Provision
is made in the Estimate for participation
on similar lines in the Fair which will
be held in 1937. Hon. Members will, I
am sure, recognise the necessity of bringing Northern Ireland products to the
notice of potential purchasers and that
participation in these exhibitions is one
of the most effective and most economical
means of achieving this end.
Hon. Members will observe that, in
conformity with the established practice
of the Imperial Government to take a
census of production in Great Britain at
five-year intervals, provision is made.
for such a census in Northern Ireland in
respect of the year 1935, very much on
the lines of that carried out by my
Ministry for the year 1930. Similar
inquiries, but on a more restricted scale,
have been undertaken by my Ministry
on behalf of the Board of Trade in
respect of the years 1933 and 1934 under
powers contained in the Import Duties.
Act, 1932. The cost of these inquiries
was, of course, defrayed by the Board
of Trade but the information so collected
has constituted a valuable addition to
the statistical information at the disposal of my Ministry.
The 1935 inquiry, covering as it will
a wider field than that covered by the
inquiries relating to 1933 and 1934, will
be conducted under the joint powers conferred by the Census of Production Acts
and the Import Duties Act, 1932. The
greater part of the cost of that portion
of the inquiry which falls under the
Import Duties Act will be defrayed by
the Board of Trade. The entire results,
so far as Northern Ireland is concerned,
will, however, be available here and a
report based on them, covering the
entire field of production in Northern
Ireland in 1935, will be published
expeditiously as possible.

In speaking of fisheries in the course
of my speech on last year's Estimates I
was obliged to paint a somewhat sombre
picture. The year 1934, as hon. Members may be aware, proved to be almost
a total failure in so far as herring fishing
was concerned, and it is the herring fishing which makes the difference between
success and failure in the year's operations for a large number of our fishermen. On this occasion I am glad to be
able to report a more satisfactory state
of affairs. Herring in the summer of
1935 were unusually plentiful on the
grounds accessible to our fishermen and
the main difficulty which confronted the
men was to secure a local market for all
the herring they were able to catch.
That, unfortunately, is a difficulty which
is always liable to arise during the early
portion of the season when the herring
are too immature for the purposes of the
curer. Last year this difficulty was more
accentuated than usual since the herring
continued to be indifferent in quality
well beyond the usual time at which they
are fit for curing. This, of course, is a
factor beyond human control, and when
it is present to last year's degree our
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce

fishermen are necessarily obliged to rely
for their market on home consumption
alone. It is in such circumstances that
the Herring Industry Board is able to
exercise useful control, and the Board,
through its Northern Ireland Area Committee, can prevent excessive gluts on
the local market, with the consequent
undue depression of prices, by restricting
the fishing on particular nights or,
alternatively, by limiting the number of
nets which may be used by each boat.
From what I have said it will be gathered
that curing operations were possible on
only a small scale, but even if the size
of the fish had been sufficient to allow
of curing starting early in the season,
there would still have been the difficulty
of finding an outlet for the cured
herring on the restricted Continental
market. Some of our local boats,
I am glad to say, were able to supplement their earnings from local herring

fishing quite considerably from
herring fishing off Maryport during

be
the year as a whole 1935 can

on
Escallop fishing, which, it will be
remembered, was heralded as a useful
addition to the activities of many of our
fishermen along the County Down coast,
continues to afford increasingly satisfactory results. This class of fishing can,
of course, be prosecuted only during the
winter and spring months, but it does,
nevertheless, offer a valuable alternative
to whiting fishing when prices for
whiting are unusually low in the English
and Scottish markets.
The catches of salmon, both in the
rivers and, with a few exceptions, at the
coastal stations, during 1935 were
exceptionally good and the prospects,
judging by the number of spawning fish
observed in the upper reaches of the
rivers during the late autumn, are
equally good for the coming season.
Salmon fishing, as hon. Members are
aware, represents a substantial commercial enterprise, and Northern Ireland
salmon have the highest possible reputation across the Channel.
In November of last year elections for
new Boards of Conservators, in accordance with the provisions of the Northern
Ireland Fisheries Act, 1934, were held
in each of the four conservancy districts.
I am glad to be able to report that the
new procedure for the holding of elections established by that Act worked
smoothly throughout, that the members
of the new Boards are taking up their
duties with zeal, and I am hoping that
their work will result in the proper safeguarding of the fishing interests in our
area.
From year to year when submitting
this Estimate, I have referred to the
duties undertaken by my Ministry in
connection with the business of Industrial Assurance-that system of life
assurance where premiums, rarely
exceeding a few pence in amount, are
collected by agents in person at weekly
or monthly intervals. This type of
assurance is largely favoured by the
poorer members of the community to
make provision for funeral expenses and
similar charges, which often constitute
a serious drain
upon their slender
resources. Its magnitude may be gauged
by the fact that in 1934 the total
amount paid in premiums in Northern
Ireland was over one million pounds. It
will be appreciated that in the conduct
of a business of this nature, disputes
may frequently arise between policyholders on the one hand and companies,
societies, and their agents on the other,
and it is particularly in the solution of
these difficulties that the Industrial
Assurance Commissioner and his staff
render valuable service.
During the year 1935, 622 cases in dispute were referred to the Commissioner
and in 81 of these it was ultimately
found necessary to arrange for formal
hearings. Of these 52 were heard in
Belfast and the others in such provincial
centres as Londonderry, Omagh, Newry,
Portadown and Enniskillen. I beg to
move.

to

we should do everything we can to ensure that the North of Ireland shall not

With regard to the scarcity of flax, it
is a great pity that in this Committee,
and, indeed, wherever I see or hear the
subject discussed, it is nearly always.
talked about by those who have flax to
sell rather than by those who in the
conduct of their business are under the
unfortunate necessity of having to buy
flax, and so, may be, the great difficulties which undoubtedly lie in the way of
guaranteeing a price for flax are not
brought to the notice and to the understanding of the Committee in the same
way as is the hope of the farmer that he
may be able to obtain what seems to him
an adequate reward for the trouble of
growing flax. And, of course, there are
differences of opinion as to what would
be adequate. But I think I may say
beyond all question that the flax spinners
are sympathetic towards the farmers.
They have shown that in the past by the
establishment of the Linen Industry
Research Association, and I think even
the farmers will admit that the flax crop
has been made very much more attractive
by the great improvements introduced
by that Linen Industry Research
Association and also by the Ministry of
Agriculture in Northern Ireland in
respect of the strain of flaxseed and the
great increase in yield per acre of fibre
produced. It is in that direction really
that I think the best hope for the farmer
lies. The more you can increase the yield
of fibre per acre-there is greater scope
for hope in that direction than in
attempting to fix any guaranteed price.
I am greatly interested in the experiment which the Irish Free State are
making in this direction and shall watch
it with a great deal of interest, but I am
glad it is being made at their expense
and not at the expense of the Government of Northern Ireland.
As regards the supply of electricity,
the object of the Government was to
provide a supply of current so cheaply
that we would bring it within the means
of nearly every consumer. The whole
scheme of the Electricity Board was
designed to ensure that it should be run
on business lines, and, so far from this
House at the time considering that any
political intervention in the conduct of
its affairs would conduce to its efficiency,
they actually stipulated in the Act of
Parliament which set it up that no
Member of Parliament should be
appointed as a member of the Board. It
is supposed to stand on its own feet and
to be self-supporting financially. I only
regret that it cannot be brought within
the reach of every user, but that is too
great a thing, and so the Board have to
see that in the meantime they confine
their supplies and their connections to
such consumers as make it a profitable
proposition.
snowstorm
With regard to the failure of the
electricity supply, I have the greatest
sympathy with the hon. Member for
Mourne. In the ordinary way one could
hardly have imagined such catastrophic
results as he has revealed to us this
afternoon, but this year we were
undoubtedly visited by a
which more nearly approached the conditions of a blizzard in the United States
than anything of which I have had
previous experience. In giving this
service we must necessarily rely upon
methods of distributing the electricity
throughout the country as cheaply but
as efficiently as possible. Therefore, we
are bound to depend upon aerial transmission. To put these lines underground
would be entirely out of the question. I
must say personally, although I am connected up with this supply and suffered
by the failure, when I saw the conditions
prevailing I thought the inconvenience
I had to suffer was as nothing in comparison with what the members of the
Electricity Board's staff-to whom, I
think, we all should be grateful for the
way. in which, under great difficulties,
they restored the connections in a
surprisingly short space of time-had to
face. We must remember that the snowstorm which brought down the electric
wires also brought down the telegraph
and telephone wires and so deprived
them of means of communication just at
a time when those facilities would have
been most valuable. I am hoping, however, that even failures of this kind may
be rare in the future.

Considered in Committee under
Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That it is expedient to provide for
the removal of the limit of time in
relation to the giving of guarantees by
the Ministry of Finance under section.
twenty-nine of the Electricity (Supply)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1931, in
respect of loans raised by the Electricity Board, and to charge upon the
Consolidated Fund or
the growing
produce thereof such sums as the said
Ministry may require, by reason of the
removal of the said limit of time, for
fulfilling guarantees given under the
said section. (Governor's recommendation signified.-Mr. Barbour).
Mr. BARBOUR: The Resolution
which stands upon the Order Paper is
the preliminary to a Bill which is
designed to enable
enable the Ministry of
Finance to guarantee the principal and
interest of any loan which may be raised
by the Electricity Board without limitation in point of time. Hon. Members
will remember that under the Act of
1931 the Government guarantee was
limited to a period of five years from the
date of the establishment of the Board,
it having been intended at that time to
limit State liability to the initial period
of the Board's operations.
Hon. Members may recollect that the
Electricity Board was established on 1st
June, 1931, so that the undertaking
completes five years of life in a month's
time. The period which has intervened
since the setting up of the Board has
been largely concerned with development
work, the Board having in commission
at the end of 1935, 457 miles of extra
high tension lines, and 339 miles of low
tension distribution mains. At the same
date a supply was being given in 93
towns, while 26,212 consumers' premises
were connected to the Board's system.
These figures are indicative of the
progress which has been made, but
perhaps a better index is to be found
in the total number of units sold by the
Board. In the year 1932 the sales
amounted to 3,048,000 units; in 1933 to
7,195,000; in 1934 to 13,910,000; and in
1935 to 23,333,000 units.
Thus far the Board has financed its
operations mainly by short term loans
made under a guarantee by the Government. Now, in accordance with the
terms of the Act of 1931, the power of
the Ministry of Finance to guarantee
borrowings expires on 1st June, 1936.
The Board has, therefore, been discussing
with financial interests the question of
funding its indebtedness, and I am glad
to say that the discussions indicate that
the credit of the Board stands high, and
that an issue of stock is likely to be
possible on favourable terms. In the
course of these discussions, however, it
has been pointed out that as the Government is closely associated with the
establishment of the Board, it might be
desirable for a Government guarantee to
be given in respect of the new issue, since
such a step would mean a substantial
saving in interest, and the Government,
after giving careful consideration to this
question, has agreed that the interests of
Northern Ireland industry-including, of
course, agriculture-would be served by
an extension of the powers of the Ministry of Finance to enable a long-dated
guarantee to be given. This Resolution
is accordingly submitted to the Committee.
I may remind hon. Members that the
total borrowings authorised by Statute
are £2,000,000, although power is given
to the Ministry of Commerce, in consultation with the Ministry of Finance, to
increase the maximum borrowing power
to £2,500,000.
Hon. Members will have noticed from
time to time from the Parliamentary
Returns which have been submitted to
the House that the guarantees of the
Ministry of Finance have already issued
in respect of short-dated loans up to a
figure of £1,850,000. Under the proposal to fund this indebtedness the
contingent liability of the State under
the existing guarantees will cease and a
new liability, covering a longer period
of time, will be substituted within a
maximum limit of £2,500,000, being the
limit of the borrowing which may be
exercised by the Board under Statute.
I beg to move.
