Mr. BARBOUR: Following on a series
of earlier statutes increasing the powers
of the Ministry of Finance within which
the Ministry was empowered to issue
guarantees in respect of capital undertakings creating employment, Parliament
in the year 1931 imposed a statutory limit
of thirteen million pounds. The Act pro-
Ivided that this maximum limit should be
related to the aggregate amount of the
guaranteed loans outstanding at a given
date, that is to say, amounts repaid could
be deducted in arriving at the total.
was expected at the time that, allowing
for the operation of repayments in the
shape of annual or bi-annual instalments
of principal, it would not have been necessary to seek an extension in the amount
of the maximum limit. It falls to me
to-day to ask this Committee to assent to
an increase from thirteen million pounds
to fourteen and a half million pounds, a
fact which reflects the very welcome revival in our shipbuilding industry.
It
In 1931 our yards were practically
empty, since when, assisted by this Gov-

Committee
ernment's credit facilities, new construction programmes of great magnitude have

Mail Steamship Company, and this Resolution is, in fact, necessitated by an extension in the large building programme
of that great company.
The additional programme of work involved exceeds three million pounds in
value, and in stating that our shipyard

the extent of a maximum figure of
£2,062,000, I need make no apology on

Having regard to the magnitude of

cent. of the total contract price, it is
not surprising that it should make inroads upon the margin within which the
Ministry is statutorily empowered to give
guarantees, and in order that the Ministry of Finance shall not be debarred
from continuing its present policy the
Committee is asked to agree to the proposed extension of the maximum limit.
Such extension will provide a reasonable
margin for the future, as substantial repayments may be expected at no distant.
date. It would not, in fact, be incorrect
to look upon this increase as a provision
for "peak" conditions.
The Loans Guarantee Act of 1935 provided for the continued operation of the
Loans Guarantee Acts until the 31st
March, 1937; that is, for a period of two
years. One year has elapsed, and the
occasion of this legislation is being taken
to extend the period by one further year;
that is, to the 31st March, 1938.
The Committee will, doubtless, expect
from me some general observations on

which have already been given, and I am
quite expecting that my hon. Friend the
Member for Central and my hon. Friend
the Member for Mourne will again

On the last occasion my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, when

abundantly justified itself. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Incidentally this

I am glad to report that two of these

surance
Mr. GORDON: In as few words as
possible I beg to submit this Order to
the House. The Unemployment In-
Statutory Committee set up
under the 1934 Act by the Imperial
Government are required to furnish a

financial position of the Unemployment
Insurance Fund. They have now disclosed that there is a disposable surplus
of roughly £6,500,000, which I think is
very creditable, and goes to show the
upward trend of employment.
The Committee recommended to the
Imperial Government that the contributions of each party to the Fund, except
from insured persons under 18 years of
age, should be reduced by one penny per
week, and this has been accepted. The
Committee examined the position from
many standpoints, and decided that the
best way of dealing with this surplus was
as I have just now stated. This reduction
will have effect from the 6th July, 1936.
We propose by Order in Council to
make a similar reduction in unemployment insurance contributions. This will
reduce the income of the Fund by roughly
£126,000 in a full year, but it will mean
that industry will benefit by £42,000 per
annum, and also that the worker will
benefit by £42,000.

benefit to the extent of, roughly, between
£40,000 and £42,000, and that the employed contributor will benefit to the same
extent by the reduction in the contribution.

interrupt the hon. Member's brilliant

to examine the proposals in the Bill and
the policy underlying it. I would like to
outline what is being done in England to
evolve a scheme for improving and bettering the marketing of eggs, and in doing
this I would quote an article from "The
Times" in which
in which the proposals are
described in far better language than I
can use or have at my disposal. The

I will now give an extract from this

All pro-
These proposals follow broadly the
lines of the Reorganisation Commission's scheme. A producers' board
would be set up to administer a scheme
under the Marketing Acts, the country
being divided into areas with one packing station for each area.
ducers with some exceptions would be
bound to sell their eggs to the area
packing station, where eggs would be
candled and graded, the board fixing
national minimum prices, varying with
the supply and demand situation, at
which packing stations should sell the
different grades of eggs.
I will now proceed to quote an extract
giving the opinion of Mr. Elliot, the
Minister of Agriculture in England:-
Mr. Elliot has never pressed the
industry to adopt the Commission's
scheme. Time and time again he has
said that it is for the industry itself to
decide on the form that the improvement in marketing arrangements should
take.
The article goes on to say:
The question which producers
naturally ask is, "If we do not accept
this compulsory scheme, will the
Government do nothing to afford our
industry proper protection? Is this
scheme the price of protection?" The
Cabinet alone can give an answer, but
it is clear that Mr. Elliot, for his part,
does not regard the present proposals
as essential. He has told a deputation
of the N.F.U. and N.P.C. that he saw
no objection in principle to the alternative plan on voluntary lines, by
which an extension of standardised
grading and packing was to be secured
by offering a bonus to producers who
contracted to supply packing stations.
The question to be decided now, however, is whether a compulsory marketing scheme is wanted. The proposals
should be considered on their merits.
There are about 500,000 producers with
25 hens or more, many of whom
are small people, and many of
whom are farmers' wives. If they
feel that this is
an undesirable
plan it would be folly for the
N.F.U. and N.P.C. to saddle them
with this scheme in order to get the
industry within the framework of the
Marketing Acts.
These extracts from this illuminating
article which I have quoted give the
House a very clear and precise indication
as to how the proposals are being dealt
with in England. I may say that to my
mind they are a very striking contrast
to the attitude of compulsion which is
being proposed by this Bill. The whole.
question whether or not the egg industry
is to be stabilised lies first and foremost
on the policy of the Imperial Government.
Until it is decided that this industry is
to be protected or not, and until compulsion or voluntary methods are adopted
in England, this Bill, in my opinion, is
premature and should be postponed. No
one is going to quarrel with the Government in their endeavour to have eggs in
this Province marketed in the best
possible condition, but are the proposals

in this Bill practical? That is for the

In fixing prices as it is proposed by
Clause 1 can the Minister get away from
the axiom "To fix prices you must have
control of the markets.' As I have
already stated stabilisation can only be
obtained by a policy of protection and
that is outside our province and outside
the scope of what we can do here. How
can we guarantee to fix a price for eggs
and maintain it? May I point out that
in the first quarter of 1936, 5,365,000
great hundreds of eggs were imported.
into Great Britain, and that is 1
millions more than for the similar
quarter of 1935. I cannot understand
how anyone can attempt to fix a price
that will not be affected by the conditions I have stated. In my opinion it
will be a most dangerous experiment.
The English proposals, whether compulsory or voluntary are to be worked
by a producers' board. In this Bill the
producers' board to my mind is a farce.
It is just a dummy board and has no
executive powers whatever. It cannot
appoint its own secretary and has no
control over the levies which the producers must pay. If you refer to Clause
4 you will see set out in some eight lines
the whole powers the board possesses.
They are purely advisory and
executive. It places the whole industry
lock, stock and barrel under the Government. I again repeat that this is in
striking contrast to the attitude of the
Government across the water.
not
Next let me deal with the question of
licences. I understand that to a certain
extent this is an agreed Measure. To
my mind it is certainly an agreed
Measure as far as the shippers are concerned, because they are going to be
given a virtual monopoly of the egg
trade. To the large provision merchants
and stores where eggs are sold it will
make no difference except that the levy
of a farthing per dozen will be passed on
to the consumer. I may say that I have
been informed on good authority that a
farthing is equal to 21 per cent. of profit
on a dozen eggs.
What about the country grocer who
will be asked to pay the £2 levy or the
10s levy and the d per dozen? These
people want to know why this extra tax
should be imposed upon what they state
is a perfectly legitimate and proper business to carry on. Very few
Very few grocers will
be able to handle eggs on their premises,
and, therefore, under this Bill they are
going to be compelled to buy from the
shippers. What will happen? The eggs
which are now brought to the local grocer
to be sold will be sent to Belfast to be
tested, and then they will be carted back
to the place they came from. This will
mean delay, extra charges, and fewer
fresh eggs.
I would remind the House of the
custom in many parts of the country for
the farmer's wife and the small poultry
keeper to take groceries in place of the
eggs they take in. You are going to
upset the whole countryside if this Bill
goes through as it stands. I am aware
that the Ministry speaks of excepting
certain of these established grocers from
this licensing, but you are going to give
a very great grievance to those who are
not excepted and to create dissatisfaction
between those who pay the levy and those
who do not.
While giving the Government every
credit for trying to improve the egg
trade, I ask why not wait until the
English scheme, which I outlined at the
beginning of my speech, has been settled
and until the policy of protection has
also been settled. I would suggest that
this Bill be withdrawn for the very
strong reasons I have given. That will
give the necessary time for proper consideration and consultation so that we
may work on the same lines as in Great
Britain. It will do the Government no
harm; in fact, it will strengthen their
hands and it will convince all those concerned in the poultry trade that there is
no desire to force this Bill, which is pure
compulsion, down their throats.
Further, as I have said, it is going
to place the whole egg industry under
a Government department. What I have
said here to-day is my own considered
opinion without any outside interference
or, as was suggested the other day, intimidation by anyone, and it is without
advice from any source except the sources
I have quoted in my speech. Since I
came to this conclusion I have been
fortified by a letter which the Farmers'
Union have sent to the Prime Minister
and the Minister of Agriculture on this
matter and which I propose to read. I

Mr. MIDGLEY: I am somewhat
astounded at the complexity of the
reasoning of the hon. and gallant
Member for East Down. If my
memory serves me correctly he has
on numerous occasions inside this House,

be exercised not only by the Minister of
Agriculture in regard to other products,
but he also voted for a measure of control with regard to transport questions
in the North of Ireland.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I was not
here at that time, but if I had been
here I believe I would have voted.
Mr. MIDGLEY: You would have
voted for it-exactly. With that correction the moral which I wish to draw
is completely vindicated. When Members of this House approach a question
like this they do so from the point of
view that they want protection for their
own form of industry and free and unrestricted trade for other forms of commerce. In the present state of economic
affairs I believe there must be certain
elements of control in certain industries,
and the question is how to get that
control with the minimum of hardship
and difficulty. The hon. and gallant
Member made the statement that he was
opposed to bureaucracy and he protested
against this Bill as bureaucratic.
Then
he finished up by stating that the organisation within the industry must be left
to the industry itself. That is syndicalism.
The hon. and gallant Member has had
the privilege of standing on the Government side of the House and advocating
syndicalism. I have read some
very
illuminating leading articles upon syndicalism when it happened to be the coal
mines question, but when it happens to
be eggs we are to have no control or
co-ordination, although we are to have it
with regard to pigs, cattle, transport,
fruit, and all the rest. Quite frankly
I cannot understand the logic of the
hon. and gallant Member who has time
after time supported these Measures and
yet to-day describes this Bill bureaucratic. If I were half as enthusiastic
about this Bill as the hon. and gallant
Member I would do the logical and
correct thing, I would vote against it.
In fact, if I were as well primed on this
subject and as indignant as the hon.
and gallant Member I would move the
rejection of the Bill. I am not
going to move the rejection of
the Bill, but I am going to try
to indicate where I think it might
be improved. I believe in co-operation
and co-ordination-both these terms
mean the same thing-within industry,
and one of the reasons I believe in them
is that there will inevitably come the
time and I hope hon. Members on the
other side of the House will not be
startled by this statement-when owing
to the developments of the economic order
itself the question of socialisation will
have to be considered by the State, and
it will be much easier for the State to

get co-ordinating boards established than
if the industry were left free and untrammelled to the wishes, desires, and
avaricious propensities of the people
engaged in them. I have read the Bill
very carefully, and I have with me all
the correspondence that took place on it.
in the "News-Letter" and "Northern
Whig." During the week-end I read the
Bill at least twelve times, going through
it Clause by Clause very methodically,
and there are some points in it about
which I am in doubt and which present
features of uneasiness to me. I would
like to indicate some of the points that
have occurred to me in connection with
the Bill.
In Clause 1, which indicates the design
of the Bill, the objective of the Minister
seems to be to do what other Bills have
not succeeded in doing, that is, to guarantee under almost all circumstances and
conditions that eggs when they are put on
the market will be sold upon the basis
of quality. The Minister has indicated
in the memorandum prepared by his
Department that the previous Egg Acts
have not succeeded to the extent he
would like. Consequently-because of
the dereliction of duty-of public duty I

the industry, it is necessary to bring the
legislation more up to date and to make
some of the conditions more stringent.
I should like to ask the Minister in
considering the question of quality-I
take it that it is his desire not only to
improve the quality on the export market
but also on the home market, believing
that in so doing he is going to give the

consumer in Northern Ireland a better

-that frequently in Belfast the people

the way, in answer to those who are

applied to the efficacy of the various.
policies outlined is how the market is

industry in eggs is in a more flourishing

true of the home market. In any scheme

of eggs we want to see that it will

eggs may happen to go. That justice
can be secured if we have attention not

We have also to try to guard against
the tendency, which has set in in other
Boards, of achieving an increase in price
of such a nature that the amount of the
commodity to be consumed by the people
in the home market is going to be lessened
because of that increase in price. That
may not sound far-reaching, but I have
had statistics supplied to me as a member of a local authority in Northern
Ireland which would seem to indicate that
in certain sections of the community, on
account of the incidence of price following the setting up of marketing schemes,
there has been a lesser consumption of
certain commodities in consequence of the
price change. I would not like to think
and I hope the Minister will give this

improvement merely for the outside or
export market and have a consequent loss

Northern Ireland.

The purport of the Bill is to ensure
that a better quality of commodity in
the shape of eggs shall be placed on the
British market, in order that we may
not have the spectacle of large producers
of eggs palming off an inferior quality
of eggs to the detriment of our business
and the detriment of the commercial
reputation of the country? That is the
purport of the Bill, and the Minister also
claims that incidental thereto it is the
desire of his Department to see to it that
the consumers share in the same advantages. If you are going to allow a
section of the trade to be absolutely
uncontrolled, unregulated, and uninspected, then you are not giving the
consumers that protection which the consumers are entitled to expect and which
you aim at in this Bill generally.
There are one or two points in which
distinctions are drawn with regard to
the treatment of people in the egg business. The Minister himself knows that
according to this Bill certain small classes
of shopkeeper and certain geographical
districts, which are much more important,

the Bill. In one part of the Bill it says
that certain districts may be exempted
from the operations of the Bill.

I
do not like monopolies. I do not think
the public like monopolies. It may look
strange in your eyes, but monopolies are
hinted at in the great Charter of over
700 years ago, and monopolies in that
Charter are referred to as something repugnant to the freedom possessed by subjects. I do not know whether that
Charter appeals to you very much nowadays. It is suspended in Northern
Ireland. You prefer the Civil Authorities Coercion Act to Magna Charta. It
does not count now.
These monopolies have always been
looked upon with suspicion and jealousy
by the English public. The first great
fight ever fought by the Commons of
England against the Crown was fought
on the question of monopolies, and the
first great victory the
victory the Commons of
England won against the Crown was won

1601. I happened to read quite recently

Men with conviction, men with fair minds

Pork, milk, eggs! I wonder what next?

The way in which the Bill will work
out in one important respect is this. No
grocer will be able to sell an egg in the
future unless he is licensed. No egg retailer will be able to sell an egg unless
he also is licensed. You muzzle both of
them. They, in turn, will not be able to
buy from anybody except from the
monopoly. They are caught on one side.
by the monopoly, and on the other side
they must get a licence before they can

buy an egg. These small traders will be
unaccustomed to these fetters. It will be
their first dealing with State machinery
in the form of Socialism. Imagine a
little trader in a small village, struggling
to keep his head above water, and if he
sells an egg to a customer he has to pay
£2 a year for a licence. To many of these
people that is a matter of very great
stress. A sum of £2 may cover his entire

pay a fee of 10s, and a farthing a dozen
for all eggs sold by retail under this
scheme.
This is regimenting industry. It is
doing it on Prussian lines, and our people
are not accustomed to be dragooned and
regimented on Prussian lines. Their commercial prosperity has not been built up
by that system. It has been built up by
free competition and by the encouragement of individual enterprise. We are
going back on that now and bringing into
the trade a modification of the goose
step. In future the retailer will not go
to the farmer to buy his eggs. He will
cease to visit the country for that purpose.
He will go to the wholesale stores and
nowhere else.
I believe the Bill will mean extra cost
to the producer, and for the consumer it
will mean that eggs will be dearer and
staler. There will be a great deal of delay
owing to the restrictions that will be put
on this trade by regulations regarding
handling processes and other matters of
that kind. That is not for the good of the
trade or the good of the public. Has the
trade been so derelict in its duty as the
Minister suggests when he says he will
not bring it into the criminal court
but will dangle a bait in the form of a
bribe before it? I think the trade
has been in a fine and prosperous way
for years, and I am told that the producers ten years ago got something more
than twice per pound for eggs than they
do to-day. Under this Bill there will
be a small margin of profit to the producers who will be left in Northern Ireland. Then transport will be dearer.
We were told that transport fares under
the new Board would not be anything
higher to the public. That has not
proved to be the experience of the
public. In many instances it has meant
higher fares. Some of us in this House
ventured to say that it would end in

that Bill, and you will find we will get

pay a penny extra." Is that the case today? Transport is made to pay. It must
be an economic service. In that way I
do not blame the Board. They must
deliver the goods and must make the
public pay for what is a more costly
service.

are regimenting and Prussian ising the egg industry in Northern

Boards or Government departments are
concerned the public are never consulted.
I do think it is forgotten that we are a
small community and there is a limit to
these ever increasing costs. The cost of
living is continuously rising, and I do not
know where it is going to end. Whether
it is in Pig Bills, or Milk Bills, or Egg
Bills, the chances are fairly certain that
the Minister may run the risk of killing
the goose that lays the golden egg-or
in this case the hen egg. We have not
such a broad back that we can stand this
all the time. We have not got such a
broad back as the English back, although
we have had matters of revaluation which
give us such a fictitious source of wealth
that we seem to be equal with our
co-partner.
The egg industry, as the Minister of
Agriculture has informed us,, is worth to
us annually in export one million pounds
and home consumption possibly another
half million pounds. I suggest that the
Minister should rest content with the
results already achieved. So far as I
know there has been no demand from
anyone for this "quality" demand, not
even from the producers, who are directly
concerned. There are thousands of small
egg producers, growers or persons who
work hard and whose success is made up by
the reputation they have made in keeping fresh eggs for sale. I am not speaking of mere egg dealers or egg gatherers,
I feel that there will be a tendency even
to keep stale eggs because of the price
for second quality which is being
recognised by the Government. I feel
that in such an important industry there
should be only one quality of egg, and
that is a fresh egg. Doctors and health
experts will tell you that. They do not
speak of second or third quality. We
have eggs for baking purposes.
If there
were eggs for election purposes we might
have fewer Members here in this House to
meddle with Bills of this kind which I
think are not required. I say this Bill
will put a premium on stale eggs. It
does not seek to help the quality. There
is only one grade of egg, and that is the
prerogative of the hen to produce-a
fresh egg.
And it produces that fresh
egg. We seek here to interfere with that
duty of the hen by the encouragement
of stale eggs, instead of persuading the
hen to lay more eggs than one per day.
So far as I can see by the figures this
will cost between £50,000 and £70,000
whether by export or home consumption
and will be borne by the consumer without any benefit or return. The Minister
has truthfully said that the original Egg
Bill of 1924 was brought about by the
Ministry, with the co-operation and
guidance of egg producers and merchants,
in an effort to improve the quality and
appearance of our eggs as a marketable
commodity. It has been a proved success,
but apparently these small people so
intimately concerned with the egg
industry have not been taken into conference about this Bill as it stands. I
feel that is a mistake.
The principles of the 1924 Act were
set down fully by the Minister. They
were, first, making it an offence for a
producer to offer or expose for sale stale
or dirty eggs, and, second, to fix the
standard of quality in respect of the eggs
shipped to Great Britain, to grade on a
weight basis, and to specify standard
cases. I say that is sufficient. To do anything more is to interfere with this
profitable industry to its detriment.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Member

It will be quite obvious to hon. Members

the Ministry visualises the work of this

ago.

I should now like to touch on the
position of the three classes of people
who will be affected by this Bill. First
of all, there is the shipper. The shipper
will be in no worse position than he was
under the other Bill. He will be in this
position, that he will know that the eggs
which he receives are eggs that are fresh,
or, if they are not fresh, he will have
paid for eggs that are of second quality.
Previously he was compelled to accept
eggs of first-class and second-class quality,
and he got those through on to the
English market if he could. He was not
caught by the Ministry's inspectors.
Therefore he will be in a safer and a

As regards the producer, we will take
first of all what might be considered as
a disadvantage to the producer. The
only disadvantage the producer will be
under as compared with his position
under the old Bill will be this. He will
have a lag of one week, and during that
week the eggs which he has sold to a
collector will be tested. He will have his
docket, and these eggs will be tested
under the supervision of the Ministry.
He will have exactly the same guarantee
as to receiving the correct amount of
money for his quality of eggs as the pig
producer receives at the present time,
His only disadvantage is that lag of one
week. His advantage is a very great one
because, as I explained in my Second
Reading speech, a producer was only
paid on a flat rate, the payer having
taken into consideration the fact that
he was getting a very large percentage of
second quality eggs.
Now the producer who sells his eggs
without delay and without waiting for a
rising market will obviously receive a
better price than he got before. On the
other hand, the man who is not prepared to look after his own egg trade
and leaves the eggs in the nest or keeps
them in a badly ventilated cupboard or
house will get a lower price. What we
are aiming at in this Bill is to induce
the producer, by monetary reward, to
put his eggs on the market as first quality
eggs.
With regard to the position of the
consumer in Northern Ireland, he is
given a guarantee which he had not got
before, namely, that he is getting a fresh
egg. I, myself, do not see any reason
why there should be a rise in prices, but
if you are buying a dozen eggs it is
surely better to know that they are fresh
and that you are not getting two or three
that have passed that stage.
May I now turn to the reasons for this
scheme. Some hon. Members have suggested that because we have commanded
the highest price in the British market,

Mark eggs, there is no necessity to go on

be prohibitive. All the inspectors can do
is to check a small number of boxes.
I mentioned before that one of the

TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): This short Bill

It
does not at all affect the principle or policy

has been invited by the Government to

desire and not his intention to receive

Sir Lynden Macassey is an English
barrister practising at the English
Parliamentary Bar, it was felt it was

that many of the Clauses in our Road

the late Prime Minister was over here
from New Zealand, even from so far as

Measures dealing with road transport, for
the very reason that they solved one of
the great difficulties with which the

In other words, they could not get the
advice or the analogous Clauses in
England but had to come here and say,
"Those particular Measures, or parts of
them, meet the difficulties with which we
are confronted in New Zealand." That
shows that if ever there was a Measure
which has been fully justified it is the
Road Transport Measures that have been
passed by this House. It would be very
ungracious of this House indeed if it were
to accept the suggestion made by the

be taboo when everybody who knows

made to date by way of grants under

CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £38,664 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1937, for
the salaries and expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture (15 and 16 Geo. V.
(N.I.), c. 3, s. 4; 16 Geo. V. (N.I.),

on account).
The MINISTER OF
AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The Ministry's Estimates for the current financial
year show an increase over those for
the year 1935-36 of approximately
£3,500, of which sum £2,000 represents
the increased cost of administrative
expenses and £1,500 an increase in the
cost of agricultural services.
I shall later on refer to this small
increase in the cost of agricultural services. With regard to the relatively
small increase in the cost of administration, hon. Members are, I am sure,
aware of the great expansion which has
taken place in the functions and activities of the Ministry, and it is unnecessary for me to go into the various small
adjustments in the several headings
which account for this relatively small
increase.
It is common knowledge that the agricultural industry is passing out of the
lean and very anxious period which had
been its lot for more than seven years,
and I think even the hardest critics of
the Ministry will give it credit for the
fundamental soundness of the policy
which it has pursued despite many
serious obstacles and disadvantages.
Contrary to what has happened in most
agricultural countries, we have pursued
1383 Ministry of Agriculture-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Sir Basil Brooke]
with increasing success a policy of
increasing production, but that has only
been possible because ever since the
inception of the Ministry it has by every
means in its power concentrated upon
the task of improving the quality of our
stock, and our stock products. During
the past year our output in every branch
of the industry has been increased.
Hon. Members will doubtless recollect
that when the Ministry inaugurated in
1933 the present scheme for the development of our pigs and bacon industry I
set as its objective the doubling and then
trebling of our output. Our output of
pigs for 1935 at 590,000 is more than
double the figure of 282,000 for 1932,
and the estimate of our output for 1936
is no less than 700,000. At the present
rate of progress we shall by next year
have trebled our 1932 output of pigs.
During this short period two modern
Wiltshire curing factories have been
established in Northern Ireland with an
output of between 150,000 to 200,000
pigs per annum, and here again we are
within reasonable distance of securing
our objective to have every pig produced in Northern Ireland cured here
other
as to provide, amongst
advantages, the maximum amount of
employment for our own people.
SO
I think I may, therefore, reasonably
claim that the first stage which has
already brought to this small country an
increase in its trade of over £1,500,000
per annum has been successfully accomplished, and I should like to pay my
tribute to the Pigs Marketing Board and
the Pig Industry Council, on which both
curers and producers have co-operated,
for the magnificent services they have
rendered to the country. There are, however, equally important developments in
this industry which must shortly be put
in hand, but it is more appropriate to
deal with them when the time arrives
for inviting the co-operation and assistance of this House.
And now, may I turn to other developments which figure prominently in these
Estimates, namely, the milk industry. I
do not want to weary the Committee
with a detailed account of the progress
made during the past year. I shall
content myself with a few salient facts.
First of all, the milk supply to the
creameries has increased by 30 per cent.,
a figure which includes a very gratifying
increase in the winter milk supply of 50
per cent. As a consequence of this increase the manufacturing costs of butter
have fallen by 6s. per cwt., slightly more
than a d. per lb. This decrease in manufacturing costs, together with the improvement which has taken place in the
world butter price, has reduced the
amount required from the Imperial
Exchequer for equalisation payments
from £165,000 per annum to £70,000
per annum.
Turning to the liquid milk aspect of
the question, the consumers in Ulster have
by far the cheapest milk supply in the
United Kingdom. Belfast and neighbourhood is our dearest area. Nevertheless, milk can be obtained by any person
in this area at a price at which it is proposed by means of a State grant to make
milk available in one of the distressed
areas in England. That fact alone constitutes the finest tribute that can be
paid to the spirit in which producers,
distributors, and consumers have worked
together on the Joint Milk Council.
But there is another aspect of the milk
problem which is of even greater
importance from the consumer's point of
view and, therefore, the producer's also,
namely, the quality of cleanliness. The
improvement in the cleanliness of the
supply has eliminated a great deal of
waste, and has been an important factor
in keeping down costs. Perhaps I can
best indicate the truly remarkable
change which has taken place in the
cleanliness of our milk supply by telling
the Committee that 11 per cent. of our
liquid milk supply is Grade A, 56 per
cent. is Grade B, 33 per cent. is Grade C.
I will only add that our standard for
Grade B is the same as that which until
recently was known as Grade A in
England, and is now known as Accredited.
•
There is one other significant change
in our agricultural industry to which I
should like to draw the attention of the
Committee. Until recently our cattle
shipments consisted almost exclusively of
store cattle for fattening into beef in
England and Scotland. Beginning in a
small way eighteen months ago and continuing with great rapidity during the
past year we are now supplying increasing quantities of beef instead of stores
to the British market. At present the
Ministry's officers are certifying 52 per
1385 Ministry of Agriculture—

7 MAY 1936
Committee
cent. more cattle for beef than they were
doing a year ago, and we have found it
necessary to provide a special certifying
day for the London beef market, a
market on to which beef from Northern
Ireland never before ventured.
con-
This development of the beef trade has
involved a large increase in the consumption of feeding stuffs. If to that is added
the increased consumption as a
sequence of the unparalleled expansion
of our pig population the Committee
will be better able to realise the magnitude of the contribution which the agricultural industry is making to the
prosperity of our towns. And here may
I emphasise that this contribution to our
industrial prosperity is not confined to
our country towns. It is manifest in a
hundred directions in our capital city of
Belfast. Just as the rural population
often fails to realise how important the
industrial prosperity of our capital city
is to them it is just as frequently the
case that city dwellers fail to appreciate
that the milling trade, the distributive.
trade, the machinery, fertiliser and
transport concerns, to mention only a
few, depend for their prosperity upon
the agricultural industry.
In my opening remarks I drew the
attention of the Committee to an increase in the Service Vote of £1,500.
This is mainly due to the provision for
two experiments which, I think, will be
of interest to hon. Members.
The first is in connection with the continuation of our work with Mr.
Spahlinger's dead anti-tuberculosis
vaccine. A full report of the initial
experiment carried out by the Ministry
has been published. I will content myself by reminding you that the results
showed that Mr. Spahlinger's dead
vaccine conferred a very high degree of
immunity against a lethal dose of
tubercle injected into the blood stream
and at least an equally high degree of
immunity against intense natural infection during a period of approximately
two years. Such highly satisfactory.
results raise the question of the compulsory use of the vaccine as a means of
eradicating Bovine Tuberculosis from
our Ulster herds.
As a first step towards this object it is
desirable to clear up two points. First,
whether the application of the tuberculin
test to an animal which has been vaccinated interferes in any way with the
immunity conferred by Mr. Spahlinger's
dead vaccine; and secondly, how long
the immunity conferred by the vaccine
can resist intense natural infection. The
first of these experiments has already
started, and the second, in which a large
number of animals will be required, will
start as soon as Mr. Spahlinger can provide a further supply of vaccine. Before
I leave this subject I should like to tell
hon. Members that our veterinary
research officers have been completely
successful in growing the tubercle
organism in accordance with the method
published by Mr. Spahlinger. I mention
this matter because doubt has been cast
by prominent people on the possibility
of doing so owing to lack of success in
two laboratories in England.
The second experiment is one with a
dead anti-abortion vaccine which has
been prepared by the Ministry's veterinary research officers. Hon. Members
are aware that contagious abortion is
responsible for the greater part of the
losses occurring in our dairy herds. The
estimated losses in the United Kingdom
due to this scourge amount to at least
£5,000,000 per annum, and there is at
present no certain remedy. The
Ministry's research officers have prepared
a dead vaccine and for some time past
have been carrying out experiments with
it on small animals with very satisfactory
results. It is essential, if we are to proceed further, to carry out an experiment
with cattle. The Ministry has, therefore,
rented an appropriate area of grazing
land on which two groups of animals,
one vaccinated and the other unvaccinated will be exposed to infection. I
am most anxious that there should be
no undue optimism and, therefore, I
desire to emphasise that the Ministry
will not have, until this experiment is
completed, direct evidence as to the value
of the abortion vaccine prepared by our
veterinary research officers.
There remain two items in the Estimates to which I should like to direct
your attention. One is an increase in
the grant in respect of the improvement
of agricultural holdings. Under the
scheme small farmers who undertake
improvements such as drainage, the
improvement of ditches, rivers and sea
embankments, the removal of trees,
1387 Ministry of Agriculture-

Committee
[Sir Basil Brooke]
hedges, etc., and employ for that purpose unemployed men through the local
labour exchange, receive assistance up
to a maximum of 50 per cent. of the
wages of the men engaged through the
employment exchange.
The other item is a decrease of £1,000
in money required by the Cattle Diseases
Fund in respect of compensation under
the Tuberculosis Order. This work is
now in the hands of the permanent
veterinary officers of the Ministry, and
I am glad to think that the greater

Before I sit down there is one further
matter to which I should like to refer.
There is a disposition in certain quarters
to think of agriculture as the spoilt
child of the Government. It is, therefore, proper that I should point out that
the net Estimate for the Ministry is
only £183,000, which is practically the
same figure as for the year 1929-30, and
that, therefore, the progress and
developments which have taken place
during the past few years have been
accomplished without adding to the
burdens of the Exchequer. That, I
think, is no small achievement. I mention this matter, first, because I think
that in no country in the world can the
cry of "town versus country" do more
harm than in Ulster. My second reason
is that the governing policy of the
Ministry has been and is that what is
in the real interests of the consumer is
in the true interests of agriculture, and
conversely, whatever is of real benefit to
agriculture is to the advantage of the
consumer. I beg to move.

in

Some years ago we were able in

The
economic position of the workers at that
period allowed that, but to-day the purchasing power of the working class,
spread over the seven days of the week,
would not permit of the same quantity
of food being bought as in 1912 or 1914.
I can assure the hon. Member that the
cost of foodstuffs has gone up very much
on the working class. I do not take the
figures in the Ministry of Labour
Gazette as genuine. The cost of living
so far as it is concerned is based on the
purchasing power of those who buy in

bought in small quantities, the increase
in the cost of living is enormous.
I, as representing the working class,

in the production of their products, but

fully that if they want a market, and
especially a home market, they must not
only pay attention to the producer, but

of the purchasing power and the producing power. If you are going to take too
much away from the purchasing power
you are going to pauperise the cities by
putting on them a burden they will not
be able to bear. Then they will have to
revert to the purchase of the cheap

will have to allow our good materials
which we produce at home to go to the
other markets because we will not be able

Electricity (Supply) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. BARBOUR: In introducing to
the Committee the Money Resolution
upon which this Bill is based, I gave
hon. Members at that time a report of
the progress made up to date in connection with the operations of the
Electricity Board. At the time that the
Act was passed to set up that Board, it
was felt that in view of the interests of
the consumers of electricity in our area,
and in order to tide the Board over the
initial stages of its existence, a Government guarantee should be granted to the
Board to enable it to finance its operations until the time should come when
a public issue could be made.
Under the Act of 1931 the Government guarantee was limited to a period
of five years, and now that period is on
the eve of expiring. It is felt that the
time has now arrived when advantage
might be taken of the present condition
of the money market for an issue to be
made on the London market. It has
been felt that considerable advantages
would accrue if, instead of being limited
to the period of five years, as was fixed
in the Act setting up the Board, the
Government guarantee was unlimited as
regards period in respect of any loan
which the Board might be able to
make. Therefore, this Bill is introduced
to remove the restriction placed upon the
period in the original Act. I beg to
move.
a
Mr. BEATTIE: Of all the things
that have been asked for in this House
I think this is the most serious-an
unlimited period of time to cover
guarantee whereby certain money could
be got for floating the Electricity
Board's undertaking. I, as a representative of the city of Belfast, could not
stand for that. I could not agree to the
goods of the taxpayers being put in
pawn for an unlimited period as a
guarantee for a Board with the working
of which I, at any rate, am dissatisfied.
I certainly could not
agree to the
Second Reading of this Bill. On the
Money Resolution I made reference to
their management, and I do not want to
refer to that matter again. The object
of the establishment of the Board was to
give the consumers of Northern Ireland
power which we thought would benefit
outlying districts to such an extent that
new industries would be cropping up
here and there. That was the real
object, as it was understood on this side
of the House. We also understood that
the representation of this House would
be so powerful that they would regulate
the policy of the Board, but, after the
years that have passed since its establishment, we find that not only is the representation of the House on the Board
ignored, and the House ignored, but that
the majority of its members are directing
its policy to become privately owned.
Mr. BARBOUR: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: The future will
decide whether I am right or wrong.
That is the whole thing to-day. They
are running purely on a profit-making
basis. They are not making a profit at
the moment, and the Board's objection
Electricity Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
to the extension of their activities is due
to its not being a paying proposition. The
profit-making system was never in the
minds of this House when they were
giving authority for the establishment
of the Board. The whole object of the
Members at that time was to give
electricity to every part of Ulster, and
particularly to those areas that were
likely to make use of that power. To-day
we have heard from rural areas that it
is an utter impossibility to have any
extension of the Board's
activities
because of the heavy cost that the necessary plant would entail. I want to say
that as the stock of the Board is so high
in the money market, and as the efforts
of the Board have been so restricted in
Northern Ireland, we should say, "Let
your stock
be the security for your
loan; we will not continue our guarantee
any longer." I think that is the only
way to deal with this Board which has
failed to recognise the object for which
it was founded. It was established solely
for the purpose of giving power to all
parts of Ulster at an economic price.
We are not getting that to-day. Therefore, I certainly do object to
unlimited period for the guarantee to
the Electricity Board.
an
The PRIME MINISTER: I think
the hon. Member for Pottinger has
argued in a way that makes it very difficult for us on this side of the House to
understand exactly
exactly what it is he
objects to.
Mr. BEATTIE: An unlimited guarantee.
The PRIME MINISTER: It is not
unlimited.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is.
The PRIME MINISTER: No, no.
This, of course, had to come before the
Government, and my right hon. Friend
consulted all his colleagues as to whether
it would be better to allow the Electricity
Board to go to London on their own and
borrow the necessary money, which they
could have done without coming to this.
House at all. We went into the matter
very carefully, not for any profit to the
Government, not for any profit to shareholders, because there are
none, but
because we did desire to take every step
that would enable the Board to supply
the whole of its area with current at as
cheap a rate as possible. The whole
essence of this Measure is to enable us
by guaranteeing this sum of money to
reduce the interest charges payable,
which in the aggregate would amount to
something like £7,000 a year. This
House by this Bill is saving the consumers in Ulster £180,000. There is
nothing else behind it, and there is
really nothing else to discuss. I think all
sides of the House should be only too
delighted to know that the Government
by guaranteeing this are really running
no risk whatever on the one hand, and
yet, on the other hand, they are
enabling the Board to supply the Ulster
consumers with current at the cheapest
possible rate, cheaper than probably any
other combination of the kind in the
United Kingdom is able to do.
I may say that from time to time I
have read the reports of some of the
Electricity Boards in England, and in
those reports frequent and most complimentary reference has been made
to the Board established by my right
hon. Friend. They have said that the
time would come when it would be necessary to copy the Ulster system whereby
there is no differentiation throughout the
area at all. The person living in the
outermost parts would in the end have
an opportunity of being supplied with
current at the same rate as those who
are nearest to the generating station.
I really cannot yet grasp what the
hon. Member is objecting for, unless, of
course, which is quite legitimate, he feels
that as a Member of the Opposition it
is his duty to oppose. If that is so,
there is not very much in the argument.
I do strongly recommend the House to
support the Government in doing what
it can to give our farmers and our
traders in the smaller towns, and indeed
the manufacturing side generally,
current at the lowest possible price.
Those are the real reasons for the Bill,
and I do hope that the hon. Member
will understand that this is all for the
good of the people, not for the good of
the Government, not for the good of the
shareholders, of whom there are none,
but for the good of the people, because
they are the real shareholders who will
profit.

For
Mr. ANDREWS: I have seen the

which the hon. Member refers.
several years past, the Corporation
Departments have, in pursuance of a
Standing Order of the Corporation, notified to the employment exchange
vacancies for semi-skilled and unskilled

Under the agreed procedure, the Corporation decide whom they will employ

PROTESTS AGAINST INCREASES
OF RENT.
3. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received
protests from a number of tenants
against the large increase made on the
rents as the result of revaluation;
whether the agents in most cases kept

12 MAY 1936
Oral Answers

Oral Answers
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The reply is in
the negative.
and whether it was the intention of the
Government when they introduced the
Revaluation Bill that the tenants should
pay all increases.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked to
reply.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, has forwarded to me for
perusal the communication referred to.
Revaluation in itself does not increase
rents, but in the case of small house
property where the landlord pays the
rates and recovers them from the tenant
along with the rent, undoubtedly the
tenant will have to pay more in the
total in those cases where the house
occupied has had its valuation increased
by a larger percentage than the average.
With regard to the second part of
the question, the Commissioner of
Valuation sent notification of the new
valuations to agents or occupiers and to
immediate lessors in accordance with
paragraph 3 of the General Revaluation
Regulations (Northern Ireland), 1935,
made by the Ministry of Finance under
Sections 1, 9 and 15 of the Valuation
Acts Amendment Act (Northern Ireland), 1932. I am not in a position to
say whether, in all cases, the agents
advised the tenants of the new valuations.
The answer to the third part of the
question is that revaluation is intended
to ensure that each occupier pays his
fair share of the rate struck by the local
authority. The Government, save to the
extent to
to which it has safeguarded
tenants by the Rent Restriction Acts,
cannot intervene in the arrangements
made between the landlord and tenant
in regard to the payment of rent and
rates combined.

VISITS TO ANCIENT MONUMENTS.
8. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance if he will arrange that
children visiting the ancient monuments
of the Province will be admitted either
free or at reduced charges.
Mr. BARBOUR: In reply to the hon.
Member I may say that an arrangement
along the lines which he desires has
been long in existence. No admission
charge is made for children at any of
our monuments, provided they are
accompanied by adults paying for
admission in the proportion of one adult
to three children. Thus a parent and
three children would get in for the
adult's admission, namely 6d, and two
parents at 1s would be able to secure
the free admission of no less than six
children. A similar concession has been
allowed to parties of children, such as
schools, scout troops, etc. In this case,
if there are not enough adults present
to secure free admission for the whole
of the children admission is allowed to
the remainder at a charge which is based
upon one full admission fee for each
three juvenile members of the party.
This works out at 2d for each child.

Mr. ANDREWS: In presenting the
Estimates of the Ministry of Labour last
year I explained that the policy that
actuated all its activities is the one which
the Prime Minister and his colleagues in
the Government have consistently
followed since the Imperial Government
asked us to undertake the responsibility
of administering the transferred services
in this area of the United Kingdom.
Hon. Members know what that policy is
-equality in the social services throughout the Kingdom-and I rejoice that from
the beginning this House has endorsed
this principle and supported the Government in carrying it into action. It is
now fifteen years since I had the honour
of being called upon to act as Minister
of Labour in Northern Ireland, and looking back upon them, filled as they have
been with many perplexing problems and
some disappointments, I am confirmed in
the opinion I held at the outset, that the
course which we mapped out in 1921 to
follow is the only one that accords with
our place in the United Kingdom, and
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
with our duty to the people of Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is the policy which has been the mainspring of the social services administered
by the Ministry of Labour. Its justice
has also been accepted at Westminster.
This is made clear by the willingness of
the Imperial Government to enter into
the reinsurance arrangements, to which I
shall refer later, and to help in other
ways.
It is because the Governments both at
Westminster and in Northern Ireland
have consistently acted on the footing
that the Kingdom still remains one and
indivisible that the Financial Secretary
to the United Kingdom Treasury, the
Right Hon. W. S. Morrison, K.C.,
speaking in Belfast on the 21st February
last, was able to say that:
:-
"Such discussions as they had had
over financial matters had always been
inspired on the part of both sides with
a feeling that they were trying to make
a family arrangement; that it was not
a question of one side trying to score
at the expense of the other, but of an
apportionment of the national revenue
that would best meet the needs of all
parts of the nation."
This is a principle which should never be
lost sight of, no matter who may govern
here. In my opinion, it is the only one
which is consistent with our constitutional
position.
The year that is past, 1935, was a year
of steady progress towards recovery, not
only in Northern Ireland, but throughout the Kingdom. Our own unemployment figures fell, and the number of
persons in employment rose. The most
convincing evidence of the improved
situation in the United Kingdom is
afforded in a table published in "The
Times" on the 9th March, 1936, which
gives comparative figures year by year
for the last five years under 35 heads of
national production and activity, and I
would commend to all its study.
I have thought it right to deal with these
general matters at some length, because
the Estimates of my Department,
although less by £345,569 than last year,
are very much the largest of the Departmental Estimates, making a net demand
as they do on the Exchequer for
£4,426,873, apart from the contribution
of £600,000 from the Exchequer of the
United Kingdom, which the Reinsurance
Agreement is expected to yield on the
basis of present estimates. But this is
not the total sum which the Ministry of
Labour will be responsible for disbursing during the year. When the contributions to the insurance schemes are taken
into account and sundry other sources of
income, the total amounts to over six and
a half million pounds.
There are those, I know, who object to
the social services, and who assert that
they are ruining the country and demoralising the spirit of our people. I
would ask them to consider how far their
views are consistent with the fact that
the United Kingdom has made in the
words of "The Irish Times," "the most
remarkable recovery of all time" from
the crisis of 1931 when a financial
collapse seemed imminent. For my part
I firmly believe that it is not a mere
coincidence that, during these post-war
years of world-wide unrest and financial
chaos in international dealing, the
nation that has exhibited the greatest
economic industrial and social stability,
and the most marked progress towards
recovery, is the one to which we belong,
the one which has developed the social
services to the greatest degree.
The national value of social services in
this respect is confirmed, in the opinion
of the majority of the American people,
from the President downwards, by the
bitter experience of that country during
the last few years. In their view the
tragic results of the financial crisis that
overtook the United States were gravely
aggravated by the absence of any system,
of what they call social security, to lessen
the shock, and it is now an essential part
of the programme of President Roosevelt
and his supporters to build up in the
United States a system corresponding to
ours, expressly because, in their view,
we owe to our social services our present
stability and relative prosperity.
It is, unfortunately, true that disturbed
international political relations and the
dislocation of international trade by unsettled exchanges and fiscal barriers are
still retarding world recovery. Until
there is a clear and definite determination,
the world over, to remove these handicaps to international intercourse, I fear
civilisation will remain confronted with
the shortage of employment, however
great may be the efforts of individual
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
12 MAY 1936
nations to increase the volume of work
available at home. The policy of the
United Kingdom Government has gone
a long way to improve the internal situation, and we here, as an integral part of
the Kingdom, are enjoying the advantages of their wise action. By our own
local efforts too, through the Loans
Guarantee Acts, the assistance of public
utility works, the fostering of agriculture, the encouraging of industry, and in
many other ways, we have secured
increased employment for our people.
This is shown by the registration figures
at the employment exchanges. Last
month there was a fall of 2,575 in the
number of unemployed as compared with
the previous month, and not only has the
number of persons attached to the industries covered by the general unemployment insurance scheme grown during the
last five years, from which one can conclude that the insured industries generally
are expanding, but there has been more
employment for those in industry. It is
estimated that last month there were
approximately
13,000 more persons
between the ages of 16 and 65 at work
than in April of last year. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is difficult to indicate graphically
and completely the extent of the services
performed by the Ministry's staff in our
exchanges, but the unemployment insurance and assistance schemes make it
possible for me to give, as an example,
a few figures. Last year the local staff
of the Ministry were responsible for
making 2,600,000 individual payments,
involving an aggregate sum of two and a
half million pounds, and errors in dealing with this huge volume of payments
have been reduced to so small a number
that in the net result only £36 was overpaid in the year to applicants for benefit.
and assistance. The number of claims
that were lodged at the exchanges under
the unemployment insurance scheme were
a quarter of a million, the register of
those who are unemployed having a three
to four-fold turn-over in the course of a
year. As I have frequently pointed out
on other occasions, the total number of
persons on the register is not a solid body
of persons permanently unprovided with
employment. Those placed in work
through the agency of the exchanges in
the year were over 21,000.
Hon. Members will observe that the
Estimates provide for continuing our
practice of assisting local and public
authorities to undertake works of public
utility. Nine local authorities in the
country submitted schemes last year
which were approved for grant, but only
one scheme was submitted in Belfastby a hospital authority for enlarging its
accommodation. I hope very much the
Corporation of Belfast will see their way
to resume their previous activity in this
direction during the present year, so that
as many of our people as possible may
obtain employment on improvement
works. Eleven extensions were approved
of schemes previously sanctioned. Altogether, since 1922, with the aid of grants
from my Department, constructional
works, amounting to £9,000,000, have
been undertaken, which have added
greatly to the capital equipment of the
Province, and which have provided most
useful employment, not only to those
directly engaged upon the works-the
direct placings have numbered 87,000but also in the trades concerned with the
manufacture of materials.
The local employment committees continue to be most helpful in urging local
authorities to undertake useful schemes,
in assisting the King's National Roll
organisation for employing disabled ex-
Servicemen, and in facilitating the cooperation of the local education
authorities in establishing educational
classes for young people registering at the
exchanges. Outside Belfast 85 classes
have been provided at 20 centres, and
have been attended by almost 1,900
juveniles. Instruction has been given
both in educational and technical subjects, and cookery and dressmaking
courses have been provided for girls, and
carpentry for boys. In Belfast the
juvenile instruction centre continues to
perform its admirable and much appreciated work. The average daily attendance
is not far short of 600, and since the
centre was opened almost 19,000 juveniles
have been admitted. In addition, the
Belfast Education Committee are providing, this summer, metal-working and
wood-working classes, and classes in
domestic subjects for 180 unemployed men
and women. The powers and duties of
the local education authorities and of my
Ministry to provide instruction for unemployed young people between the
school leaving age and eighteen were considerably extended by the last Unemploy-
Estimates
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
ment Act. Undoubtedly all who have
been in contact with the problems of
juvenile unemployment are convinced of
the value of providing for those young
people facilities for continued education
on sound and practical lines, and I am
sure I shall have the full support of this
Committee in giving effect to the extended powers which Parliament has
entrusted to the Ministry in this matter.
Some of our local employment committees are taking an active interest in
voluntary welfare centres that have been
established for the unemployed of their
localities, and in the garden plot movement. Welfare centres have been
established at Bangor, Carrickfergus,
Lurgan, Newtownards, Portadown, and
Shrigley, and centres are in process of
formation at Coleraine and Londonderry. They have proved to be a very
successful means of helping the unemployed to help themselves, and I am
particularly interested in the garden.
plots which are being run in association
with the centres. I am very gratified
that this voluntary movement has
developed to the extent of leading those
who are actively engaged in it to form a
Central Welfare Council with the object
of encouraging and co-ordinating welfare
work throughout Northern Ireland.
I wish to pass now to other responsibilities of the Department which concern those who are in employment-the
administration of the Factory and Workshop Code, the Workmen's Compensation
Act, the Trade Board system, and the
conciliation duties of the Ministry in the
negotiation of wages agreements. I am
convinced that the most important
portions of the Factory Code are those
concerned with safeguarding the health
of those engaged in manufacturing processes from the effects of unsatisfactory
factory conditions. In fact we have
repeated proofs from our observations of
the working of the health insurance
scheme that the seeds of ill-health, which
may give rise to a deplorable harvest of
illness and suffering, can be sown by
exposure in early life to unfavourable
general conditions and in particular to
dust or fumes in manufacture, which can
be minimised and even in some instances
eliminated altogether. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Factory conditions have
been improved immensely in the last
fifteen years-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear)—and many firms have spent large
sums to achieve this, and in particular to
secure better ventilation and dust
removal. A few firms, however, still
unfortunately lag behind, and they have
been given to understand that the law
must be conformed to without delay.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I referred last year to the importance
of accident prevention. Unfortunately
1935 saw a steep rise in the number of
fatal accidents from 9 in 1934 to 28,
and from 1,818 non-fatal accidents to
2,075. It is not an answer that the
Workmen's Compensation Act provides
sufficiently for the victims of industry.
Money compensation at the best is a poor
substitute for a bereaved home or a
maimed body. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Where an accident is due to a
serious breach of the safety provisions of
the Code our practice is to institute proceedings in the courts, but many unfortunately are due to thoughtlessness or
recklessness often on the part of the
victims themselves. It becomes, therefore, a question of taking every opportunity of urging on all concerned in our
many factory establishments-employers,
managers, foremen and workmen-the
importance of watchfulness and care in
taking every preventive measure practicable.
During the year under review there
took place the very regrettable fire in a
linen warehouse in Belfast when a very
gallant life was sacrificed in helping to
save the workers from disaster, that of
Mr. Powell, whose widow received at the
hands of His Majesty the King, the
Edward Medal of the first class in
silver, which is awarded only for recognised acts of outstanding gallantry.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
Carnegie United Kingdom Trust has also
conferred its highest award, the bronze.
medallion. There are provisions in the
Factory Acts placing upon factory
occupiers the duty of installing and
maintaining satisfactory means of escape.
and the Department has issued to all
local authorities, on whom rests the duty
of supervising the installation of fire
escapes, and to all occupiers of factories,
a circular calling attention to the obligations laid upon them by the Factory
Code, and containing suggestions for
organising means of fire prevention and
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
12 MAY 1936
escape. I am glad to say the circular has
met with general approval. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Industry in Northern Ireland has continued to enjoy its accustomed freedom
from serious industrial disputes, and the
reasonableness and sense of public spirit
shown by both employers' and workers'
representatives have contributed very
largely to this happy result. The industries covered by the Trade Boards,
which give employment to some 50,000
workers, find that the system affords a
satisfactory machine. for negotiating
wages and working conditions. The
existence of standing conciliation
machinery in the shipbuilding and
engineering industries, and in the building, dock, railway and road transport
industries, is of great value. In the
spinning and manufacturing branches of
the linen industry, in which important
wages questions came up for consideration during the past twelve months, the
voluntary negotiating bodies established
under the auspices of the Ministry have
proved very effective and satisfactory to
all concerned.
Now that unemployment insurance
has been extended to farm workers and
those engaged in horticulture, except
private gardeners, and in forestry, it
will be necessary in future to speak of
the general scheme and the agricultural
scheme. The development of the general
scheme proceeds steadily. The increase
in the rates of benefit in 1934, consequent on the Act of that year, was
followed in 1935 by an increase of the
dependent children's allowance from 2s.
to 3s. The conditions of benefit for
seasonal workers have been eased, and to
encourage the continuance of whole-time
education after the age of compulsory
school-attendance has been reached legislation was passed in 1935 with regard to
the crediting of contributions to boys and
girls who remain whole time at school.
Notwithstanding these increases in the
benefits provided by the scheme, it will
be possible as from the 6th July next to
reduce the weekly contributions from
each of the three contributors by 1d.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Hon.
Members, I am sure, will realise the
importance of these improvements. In
fact it is remarkable how, thanks to our
reinsurance arrangements and the
improved position of employment
throughout the United Kingdom, the
financial condition of the scheme in
Northern Ireland has been transformed.
The debts, which the fund contracted
before the original Reinsurance Agreement of 1925 and since, have both been
funded and the United Kingdom
Exchequer has undertaken to assist in
liquidating these obligations, whilst we
have now built up a reserve in the fund
itself represented by investments amounting to £516,000, which we hope to increase this year. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
I understand from what the hon.
Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) said
in this House a few days ago that he
thought the Government wished to wrap
up in mystery the effect of the working
of the Reinsurance Agreement on the
finances of our Unemployment Fund. I
can assure him this is not so; quite the
contrary. The accounts of the Fund are
published every year, and the Public
Accounts Committee, of which the hon.
Gentleman is a Member, have before
them each year the report of the Comtroller and Auditor-General on the Fund
accounts.
Let me try to state the position very
simply. The operation of the Reinsurance Agreement has to be regarded from
two aspects. First, from that of the
Unemployment Fund, and secondly from
that of our Exchequer. First, as regards
the Fund, the Reinsurance Agreement
enables our Exchequer to keep the Fund
in complete parity with the Great
Britain Fund at the same rates of contribution by employers and employees
and at the same rates of benefit. This
parity is secured by the parity payments
made into our Fund by the Exchequer,
the estimated payment this year being
shown in subhead B of Vote 3.
effect of parity to-day is that, as the
Great Britain Fund has a reserve at
present of about £25,000,000, our Fund
has its equivalent reserve, as I have said,
of about £516,000.
The
Secondly, as regards our Exchequer,
in so far as the making of parity payments to the Fund involves our
Exchequer in an excess cost for the
service as compared with the Exchequer
cost in Great Britain, the excess is shared
by the Exchequer of the United Kingdom as laid down in the Agreement.
