Contributions under the agricultural
scheme became payable as from the 4th
of this month, the agricultural benefit
will begin to be payable as from the 5th
November next. Steps have been taken
to bring the details of the scheme to the
notice of as many as possible of those
concerned. Leaflets have been prepared
and circulated to some 27,000 farmers,
notices have been inserted in the Press,
and posters have been displayed at post
offices and police barracks, as well as at
the local offices of the Ministry of
Labour. In addition, in order
order to
facilitate the issue of unemployment
books required for the payment of contributions, 62 temporary centres were
opened at the end of April, bringing the
number of local offices of the Ministry,
at which these books may be obtained
and information given, up to 114.
Between now and the time when benefit
will become payable my Department will
investigate carefully the question of what
additional permanent sub-offices may be
required in order to secure the efficient
and convenient administration
scheme.
of the
Sometimes, when new Acts of Parliament have been passed, I like to see them
in their practical working, and a few
evenings ago, when passing one of our
local offices, where I knew agricultural
workers were obtaining their cards and
necessary information, I went in to see
how matters were progressing. I found
three or four dozen men sitting patiently
and happily awaiting their turn and as
I was passing out of the hall I observed
three who were sitting somewhat apart
from the others. I went up to them and
I said, "Well, what do you think of this
new Measure?'' One of them said, "It
is all right." I said, "Have you three
men ever been unemployed?" and they
said "No." I said, "Well, why do you
think this Act is all right?" and one of
them said, "Well, you see, we never know
the minute, and already it has given us
a contented mind." Another said,
"Yes, sir, if we never get anything out of
it we do not object to giving a few
coppers every week to help those of our
fellow-countrymen who are less fortunate
than ourselves." I could not help
marvelling at the wonderfully unselfish
spirit that that expressed, and I felt that
so long as that feeling existed amongst
our working people Northern Ireland
would be all right.
Hon. Members are fully aware, I think,
that as a result of the continuous legislation of the past sixteen years the Unemployment Insurance Code has become
extremely involved, and they will welcome
the fact that before this year is over
Parliament will be invited to place upon
the Statute Book a Measure to consolidate the law and bring it all within the
compass of one Statute. Health insurance and pensions legislation is also being
consolidated, and this will be a great
convenience in administration.
Turning to the unemployment assistance scheme, I think the belief is
current in certain quarters that it is
entirely in abeyance. Nothing, of course,
is further from the truth. The scheme
has been in operation since January, 1935,
and the Board has already taken over the
bulk of its load. The total number of
payments made under the Board's
assessments have been averaging about
18,500 per week for some months past,
and the total number of cases current on
the 18th April was not far short of
20,000. During the last financial year
over 37,000 fresh and renewal applications for assistance were received by the
Board, investigated and adjudicated
upon, and allowances amounting to about
£950,000 were paid through the employment exchanges on the assessments of the
Board. The investigation of the circumstances of applicants, which has been
carried out by officers of the Board, has
proved invaluable not only in ascertaining that statements with regard to the
circumstances of applicants are correct,
but in disclosing special difficulties and
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
12 MAY 1936
hardships of various kinds which the
Board have been able to lessen. Whilst
there was a tendency at first to regard
the Board's investigating officers with
suspicion, they now find that they are
generally welcomed, for they have not
only been able to assist households with
information in connection with the
services of the Ministry of Labour, but
they have been frequently consulted on
general matters, and, in instances, where
domestic friction or thriftlessness has
brought households into difficulties, they
have been able, in many cases, to restore
harmony by appealing to the self-respect
or family affection of those who have
applied for assistance. From all areas
reports have come into the Board of the
improvement in the condition of the
households visited and revisted by investigators on their daily rounds. They have
seen old furniture repaired, rooms papered
and repainted, the equipment of the
homes improved, and also an improvement
in the physique and morale of those who,
until the unemployment assistance scheme
came into operation, were living very
near the border-line of destitution.
Hon. Members will see that I am asking the Committee to vote £1,040,000
this year in respect of the unemployment
assistance service, and it will be well
spent money, because it will go to homes
where it is undoubtedly required.
The outstanding feature in connection.
with National Health Insurance has been
the recent valuation of the assets and
liabilities of the approved societies employed in the administration of the
scheme. Every five years, as hon. Members may know, an actuarial valuation is
made of the assets and liabilities of these
societies, and in those cases in which the
valuation discloses that a society has a
disposable surplus, the society has to submit to the Ministry or to the Joint Committee in the case of societies operating
throughout the United Kingdom, a
scheme for providing additional benefits
to its members out of the surplus
declared to be disposable. The last
valuation period included some years
when employment was bad and contribution income fell and benefit expenditure.
was high. It is gratifying, therefore,
that of the 19 Northern Ireland Societies,
10 had disposable surpluses, and have
already brought into operation, with the
Department's approval, new schemes of
additional benefits, which will remain in
force for the next five years. The
majority of the United Kingdom societies
have also disposable surpluses, so that
some two-thirds of our insured people
have available for them schemes of
additional benefits that supplement the
standard benefits provided by the statutes,
and provide such benefits as dental and
ophthalmic treatment.
Expenditure on sickness, disablement
and additional benefits amounted in 1935
to over £520,000, and in addition, the
cost of medical treatment and the provision of medicines accounted for
£248,000. Almost 383,000 persons are
entitled to medical treatment, and 524
doctors and 455 chemists are co-operating
in this service. We are assisted in the
medical features of the scheme by the
Department's chief medical officer, to
whom I desire to pay a tribute for the tactful and able way in which he discharges
his responsible duties, and by two wholetime medical officers, and part-time professional assistants. This is by far the
most comprehensive medical service that
exists in Northern Ireland, and it must
be a great source of satisfaction to all
who are concerned in promoting the health
of our people, that it has been possible to
bring into existence, quietly and
smoothly, this great instrument for the
alleviation of sickness, the prolonging of
life, and the education of our people in
the principles of healthy living.
I wish to take this opportunity of
thanking again the medical profession for
their whole-hearted co-operation with the
Ministry in this matter, and I am gratified that year by year we have been able
to provide for certain of the doctors engaged in this scheme a post-graduate
course at Queen's University which has
the enthusiastic support of the Medical
School of the University. I am glad to
know that this is much appreciated by the
profession.
The other treatment benefit I feel I
should refer to briefly is that of dental
benefit. This is one of the additional
benefits, as I have said, which is available for the members of those societies
which have schemes of additional benefits
in operation. Dental treatment is much
sought after, and both the Department
and the profession are anxious to see the
standard of treatment improved. I fear
that in the past there have been too many
Ministry of Labour
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
instances in which some dentists, instead
of trying to conserve and treat the teeth
of their patients, have resorted to extractions, and supplied them with the
unsatisfactory substitute of artificial sets.
I feel that this must stop, and I am confident that I have the support in this of
the leading members of the profession.
The Ministry is assisted in supervising
its administration by a Dental Benefit
Council, comprised of dentists and representatives of the societies affording the
benefit. The activities of the Council
have undoubtedly led to an improvement
in the standard of treatment, as the
Council has not hesitated to report to the
Ministry cases which, in their opinion,
have called for inquiry and action. The
Department will continue to give the
Council its full support in its endeavours
to raise this treatment to a satisfactory
level, and I look to all members of the
dental profession to co-operate in securing a service that will conform to the
highest standards.
I find that the pensions schemes continue to meet with general approval. The
contributory scheme is providing to-day,
in round figures, for 15,400 widows,
almost 10,000 orphans and dependent
children, and about 14,500 persons
between the ages of 65 and 70—a total
roll of nearly 40,000 (39,795), as compared with a total of 12,000 in 1926. It
is a considerable achievement that it has
been possible to establish and build up
within the short period of a few years so
acceptable and necessary a provision for
this large and deserving portion of the
community. In addition, the insurance
qualification acquired under the contributory scheme enables an increasingly large
proportion of those who reach the age of
70 to enjoy the over-70 pension without
the restrictions applicable to the noncontributory scheme. There are 21,143
persons in this group, whereas in 1929
there were less than half that number.
Under the non-contributory scheme there
are 33,328 pensions in
payment.
Altogether, therefore, the two schemes
between them provide for 94,266 persons,
ranging from early childhood to very
advanced old age.
I feel that it is not necessary to say
more in support of these pension schemes
than to mention the relief of poverty
and distress represented by this provision not only to the widow, orphan,
aged, and blind pensioners themselves,
but also to their friends and relatives
who otherwise in many cases woud have
to stint themselves in order to contribute
to their support. We ought also to bear
in mind the sense of security and confidence that these schemes give to elderly
workers approaching the time when they
feel that the burden of active life is
becoming somewhat too great for them to
carry.
I said at the outset to-day that I
estimate that this year the Ministry of
Labour will be responsible for administering some six and a half million pounds
in connection with the five social
services entrusted to the Department,
and I wish to turn now to the financial
aspects of the Ministry's activities. The
Ministry's revenue, being derived not
only from moneys voted by Parliament,
but also from other sources, it seems to
me that I can most clearly explain to
hon. Members the range of our duties
and responsibilities, if I place before
the Committee the main items of a composite account of the estimated receipts
and payments in 1936-1937 of the five
principal social services; namely, the
National Health Insurance scheme, the
two unemployment schemes and the two
pensions schemes.
On the receipts side of the composite
statement, just over a quarter of a
million pounds will come from interest
on investments, and from National
Health Insurance centralised funds and
reserves. £1,835, 500 will be contributed
by employers and employees in approximately equal shares, and the net grants
of the Northern Ireland Exchequer will
amount to about three and three-quarter
million pounds after allowing for its reimbursement under the Reinsurance
Agreement to the extent of about
£600,000 by the Treasury of the United
Kingdom.
Of these receipts we estimate that iu
over five and a half million pounds will
be spent in benefits under the Nationa
Health Insurance and the Unemployment Insurance and Assistance Schemes,
and in pensions to widows, orphans,
dependent children and the blind and
aged. £274,500 will be carried to
reserves. Loan charges including repayments of capital will account
£230,000, and the total administration
for
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
12 MAY 1936
charges of the Ministry, the health
insurance approved societies and the
Unemployment Assistance Board together will amount to £438,000, that is,
7.9 per cent. of the expenditure on
benefits, or 6.8 per cent. of the aggregate
income.
The average ratio of administrative
expenses to income of some of the principal industrial
assurance companies
operating in the United Kingdom and
enjoying an annual income of almost
£57,000,000 in 1933, the latest year for
which figures have been published, was
four and a half times higher, namely,
30.6 per cent. as compared with our
ratio of 6.8 per cent. I feel, therefore,
that our administrative costs are very
reasonable, particularly when account is
taken of the extremely wide range of
these five social services. It is a subject
to which unremitting attention is
given, and I think a fair indication can
be obtained of our measure of success in
this by comparing the position to-day
with that in 1922, when the Ministry
took over its duties for the first time.
There has been during that period a
development of responsibility to the
public in all the services that were transferred at that time to the Ministry. For
example, the unemployment schemes
have expanded, the provision of juvenile
instruction and training in particular
being a development to which I attach
great importance on the ground of its
public value. There have been developments too under the National Health
Insurance scheme, which have added to
the Department's work, and the Factory
Code has seen an enlargement of its
scope. In addition, however, to all these
normal developments which have added
to the activities of the Ministry, responsibility has been laid upon the Department for new services which are of major
importance-the contributory pensions
and the old age pensions schemes, the
medical benefit service, the unemployment assistance scheme, and latest of all
the agricultural insurance scheme, which
has come into operation this month.
The most graphic way in which I can
state the growth of the Ministry's duties
and indicate the administrative cost of
carrying them out is to compare the
figures of 1922 with those of this year's
Estimates. The gross expenditure on
benefits under the only two social
services for which the Department was
responsible in 1922 was £1,868,000. The
corresponding benefit expenditure under
the five social services this year is
expected to be £5,504,500. The administrative cost was £205,500 in 1922
or 11 per cent. of the benefit expenditure
and is £438,000 or 7.9 per cent. to-day.
The percentage of administrative cost to
benefit expenditure has fallen by 3 per
cent. Outside these five social services,
the other administrative costs of the
Ministry amount to £8,800 in respect of
the administration of the Factory and
Workshop Code, the Trade Board system,
workmen's compensation and industrial
conciliation. This cost cannot obviously
be expressed a percentage of any
figure in pounds, shillings and pence,
but when the social and industrial value
of healthy and safe manufacturing conditions for our working people is considered, and the importance to all
branches of industry and commerce of
harmonious industrial relations with
freedom from dislocation due to trade
disputes is taken into account, this small
annual expenditure represents an investment beyond financial measurement.

I feel I need not detain the Committee
by going over in detail the seven Votes
which appear in the summary on page
86 of the book of Estimates. The only
variation between this year's Estimate
and last year's to which I think I need
refer is the decrease of £260,000 on Vote
3. This is accounted for mainly by the
expectation that there will be more
employment in the insured industries
than during last financial year.
I have now completed this explanation
of the Ministry of Labour Estimates, and
I hope I have been able to make it clear
how very wide is the range of our
activities. There is no section of the
community, I think, that has not in some
way or another contacts with the
Ministry, and, whilst we are liable to
human errors, I can assure hon. Members that we honestly try our best to do
the work that Parliament requires of us,
thoroughly, impartially, and sympathetically. In our administration of
these funds we are exposed to criticism
from opposite quarters. There are those
who say we are too lavish: others assert
we are too strict, and say we act as
though we regard it as our duty to save
the funds in every way open to us, good,
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
bad, or indifferent. I have never taken
that view. On the contrary, I feel we
are obliged to see that every applicant
shall receive that which he is entitled to
obtain under the Acts which Parliament
has made this Ministry responsible for
carrying out-no more, and no less.
That is the course we shall continue to
pursue.
I desire, in conclusion, to take this
opportunity of thanking the Parliamentary Secretary, the Permanent Secretary,
and all the members of my staff, both at
headquarters and in our various
exchanges, the Unemployment Assistance
Board and their staff, as well as the local
employment committees, for the valuable
assistance which they have all rendered
to the public and to me during the past
year. And, finally, I desire to thank
hon. Members on both sides of this House
for the very patient and kind consideration shown to me while I was explaining
the Estimates of my Department. I beg
to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I extend to the
right hon. Gentleman my congratulations on his review of his Department's
work. In saying that I would like to
draw his attention to the usual custom
adopted in the presentation of Estimates
which he has, perhaps unwittingly, on
this occasion trespassed against. The
House listened to the presentation of
Estimates for the year under review, and
instead of our being informed of what is
likely to happen in the future we have
had a historical review of what has been
done since the year 1922. Might I put
that down as a grave injustice inflicted
upon Members of this House, and also
a very expensive policy in respect of the
charges upon the finances of this Parliament. Those who presented that report
are the higher grade officials of his
Department, and I am satisfied from the
length and amount of detail extending
back to 1922 that very many hours of

not to be found in Great Britain. I
believe that in Great Britain the proof
necessary for a sixty-five pension is
simpler than in Northern Ireland. Here
the Minister adheres to a very rigid principle in so far as if you do not prove that

contributor, with at least 104 contributions to your credit, you do not qualify
for a pension at sixty-five. He also
gives you a second chance and says that
if you have an average contribution of
thirty-nine in the three years preceding
the date on which you become sixtyfive you qualify. That average test is a
very hard one to fulfil. It is nearly
impossible for a man who is approaching
the age of sixty-five to get three insurance years whereby he can receive thirtynine contributions in each of those years.
It is only about one out of every ten
who qualifies. I want a modification of

unemployment or sickness. I believe that
if the Government take this matter up
we will be able to cope with a large number of people who are now going about

I
What I do in such a case is this:
ask the lady next door to give sleeping
accommodation to the two daughters.
She is a stranger. I go another door up

grants. If the Minister applies himself

great tragedy.

In connection with the unemployment

I was glad to hear the Minister stating
that the numerous Unemployment Insurance Acts which he has introduced into
this House from time to time are to be
consolidated this year.
I am sure every
Member of the House will appreciate the
Minister's action in having this done. I
hope that in consolidating the Acts he
will deal with one or two anomalies that
exist. The Ministry-I am not saying the
Minister on this occasion-have been
very unfortunate in the different phrases
used in connection with the statutory requirements for benefit. For many years
we had the old shibboleth, "not genuinely
seeking work," but eventually we persuaded the Minister to drop it. There
is, however, one used in connection with
a
statutory disqualification that is a
thousand times worse. I refer to the
use of the word "misconduct' when a
person is discharged from employment.
I have had very respectable women coming
to see me when they received such a
notice, and they have been absolutely
horrified at the Ministry daring to suggest that they have committed misconduct. I think that is a very unfortunate
word to use in this way. After all, if a
young woman tells her foreman that she
has to do more work than she is entitled
to do, and is dismissed for saying so,
it is not right that she should receive
a notice from the Department that she has
been dismissed for misconduct. It is not
just the thing that that word should be
used, and I hope the Minister will take
the matter into consideration when bringing in the new Bill to consolidate the
various Acts.
In connection with the investigations

which his Department makes, I was

approximately ten days from the date in

the year they depend upon the goodwill

We go

Once a year the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary get an opportunity,
and they do not always even get it then.
It is almost becoming biennial, this opportunity to state their position. But I do
in conclusion implore the Minister and his
assistant not to minimise the gravity of
the present situation. If there is a Cabinet
Minister or a Member on the Government
side of the Committee who thinks that at
the present moment, industrially speaking, everything in the garden is lovely he
is making a great mistake. The cancers of
unemployment and poverty are still eating
into the vitals of the people. Whether or
not that fact is realised to the extent it
ought to be, the old economic order is not
satisfying the requirements of mankind.
I am not now speaking in the narrow
political sense at all, although you all
know what I am. You all know that I
believe that the coming of socialisation is
inevitable. But I am not now speaking
in that sense; I am speaking in the wider
sense to make an appeal to all. The present social order is not satisfying the
requirements of the vast masses of the
people to the extent that they ought to be
satisfied. It is, therefore, the bounden.
duty of statesmen, not to say that they
thank God that things are a little better
than they were twelve months ago, or to

and the problem for statesmen is,
are things as we find them to-day
what they
they ought to be, are they
giving the promise, the opportunity,

the negative then there is something
fundamentally unsound in our state of
society. I claim that there is and that
the activities of the Ministry of Labour
reveal the deficiencies of the existing
social order.
The best that can be claimed for the
Ministry's work is that it is a useful form
of social ambulance work, performed
under a system in which there are many
casualties through unemployment, poverty
and the shortcomings of an unjust

it does not complete the problem. That

to work and to achieve so that a better

prosperity may accrue to all the sons of
man.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I would
like to make one or two remarks merely.
First of all, I would like to say,
I am sure it is a great joy to
the Minister of Labour to be able
to introduce such a Vote as this. It is
a wonderful thing to be able to ask
in a little Province like ours for a sum of
six and a half million pounds in order
that it may be spent in meeting the necessities of the people who are less privileged.
It is a token I think of the direction in
which our society, with all its imperfections, is moving, and it is an assurance
of the public spirit, and I might say the
Christian sympathy that have been
animating a great part of our legislation
both in this Parliament and in the Parliament at Westminster during the past
thirty years. It is a wonderful thing
when one realises that at the beginning
of this century not one penny of this
money would have been voted for these
services. I, of course, am not satisfied
with the present position any more than
any other Member who has spoken. The
situation in the economic world to-day is
by no means perfect. But the world
makes progress rapidly, and I believe we
are moving in the right direction.
It has been said that it is lamentable
that there is still in our midst a tremendous mass of unemployment. I would
like to call the attention of the House to
a couple of facts connected with this
subject. First of all, it has been calculated that about half our unemployed are
associated with industries which are
engaged in the export trade, which would
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
12 MAY 1936
seem to suggest that the interruptions
which have taken place in the international exchange of goods as a result of
the war and as a result of the perpetuation
of the war spirit in the world has a great
deal to do with the dislocation of many
industries in our country, and a good
deal to do with the fact that a good
number of people are unemployed. It
seems to me mere foolishness to attempt
to laugh this consideration out of court
and to pretend that international trade
is simply an attempt to steal the business.
of other people. It is nothing of the sort.
International trade is just like any other
trade. It is an exchange of utilities between one person and another, between
one set of people and another. And in
the past a great number of our people
have made a livelihood for themselves and
given work by the just, honourable and
desirable trade of this sort.
The other fact I would like briefly to
mention in this connection is this. It
would appear that in communities such
as ours at times there is an excessive
amount of saving, resulting in an excessive amount of investment, both arising
from excessive profits and resulting in an
excessive amount of goods of a particular
and limited nature being produced with
the result that so far as the particular
commodity is concerned the market becomes very speedily glutted thereby discouraging manufacture and tending to
perpetuate these cycles of boom and
depression which have been a great
affliction not only to us, but to all mankind for a considerable length of time.
That is why I am not alarmed at all at
legislation which would seem to involve
increased taxation, for I believe that unemployment difficulties in part, not altogether, have originated in an unsuspected
way from excessive inequalities in income,
resulting in at times excessive saving and
excessive investment, and that would seem
to point in the direction that this world
will not be a good place for any of us
until it is a better place for all of us.

The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Gentleman cannot return to that point, having

Mr. BEATTIE: This is a charge on
the Board's funds, and the Board can
only get funds from one source, and that
is out of the pockets of the travelling

side of the Committee, with one exception,

transport. I am not going to agree with
the Government. The Prime Minister
said on the Second Reading that he hoped
it would be a long time before a Britisher
and an Ulsterman could be separated from
recognition. I only hope that day is a
long way off. He has recognised them
in other spheres. I will give an illustration of it. The Government has failed
to recognise a teacher here as being equal
to a British teacher, as they have not restored the cut. That is one way they
have failed to give recognition.
The only time they will give recognition to a British citizen is when he can
come here to serve the interests of the
governing classes. That is why the
Government wants to bring in an English
barrister who is competent to deal with
all matters pertaining to English railways. They will bring him in under
paragraph (a). He has been a very able
lawyer for the railways, but as regards
road transport I question very much
whether his experience is very wide,
Transport Bill-
Committee
13 MAY 1936
other than that which he has had of road
transport in Ulster. I claim that such a
person coming, as he does, from a nation
with high purchasing power, is not competent to deal with matters in Ulster
where the purchasing power is lower.
We cannot get the travelling facilities
in Ulster to-day that we had twelve
months ago. I have in my possession
very serious charges in regard to the high
increases that have taken place. I have
documentary evidence of instances where
50 per cent. has been added to the
amounts previously charged. Here in my
hand are the cheques of the old caterer
and here is the estimate of the Board,
and I say that the gentleman they desire
to bring over will confirm these new rates,
because they will help the railways. I
can give you the actual cost per mile of
running a bus; the total cost per mile
of a first-year bus, of a second-year bus,
and of a fourth-year bus. I want to say
candidly that the charge in this estimate
which I have in my hand, for a trip to
Dublin, is exorbitant and is not in conformity with the purchasing power of
those who use that form of transport.
How can we expect to get any consideration if we allow this paragraph to
go in and appoint an English barrister
of ten years' standing, who has been
accustomed to regulate the fares to be
paid by people who have a higher purchasing power than we have, and of
whom, at the moment, it is suspected that
his real object is to advance the interests
of the railways, due to the position he
holds in England as a representative of
a big railway concern? That being the
case, how can we expect to have the fares
in Northern Ireland regulated in accordance with what we can pay? I have no
hope of getting them so regulated while
paragraph (a) is in the Clause, but I might
have hope if we could confine the work
of the tribunal to a barrister practising
in Northern Ireland who understands the
purchasing power of the community, their
needs and requirements. The only
recreation some of the workers in
Northern Ireland have is an evening trip,
and if that evening trip is to be 50 per
cent. over and above what it was last
year then there will be no evening trip
for them.
That is the position in which we find
ourselves to-day under the policy of the
Board as at present carried out. We are
going to be prohibited altogether from
having these evening trips, and every
person now using road transport is going
to be driven back to the railways by the
economic circumstances in which we are
placed and because we are not able to
pay the high fares charged. This subclause (a) is a very far-reaching one,
so far-reaching that in my opinion in a
very few years the whole transport
service will be of very little use at all to
the poorer classes. It will only be the
well-to-do classes who will be able to use
that transport. Take the amount of
money spent from the earning power of
the workers in this form of recreation
and take the amount of money that those
companies received in profits. I have
been told in this House that some of the
older companies did not pay. I am informed officially by the owners of some
of the older companies that they did pay.
They were quite prepared to run evening
excursions to the extent of twenty-five or
thirty miles with 34 to 36 passengers for
30s., and to pay a living wage to their
drivers. That cannot be done to-day.
That same excursion will now cost you
over £3, and you will have only a limited
seating capacity in the bus, not thirtysix or forty. You will get your regulated
number and not one additional.
I have no hope of securing a return of
that form of recreation for the working
classes if the Committee pass sub-clause
(a) of this Clause. If we had an opportunity of appealing to a Northerner, a
man who understood the requirements of
the workers, we might have a possible.
chance of getting a reduction of these
fares. But under the Clause as it stands
we have no hope of consideration from
the point of view of cheap travelling
facilities for the class which I represent
in this House. There is the quotation.
The right hon. Gentleman may smile at
it. Other quotations proved to be too
high, and the proof that this was right
is found in the fact that the others were
substantially reduced, proving conclusively that the quotation made by the
Transport Board was too high. I am
going to ask the right hon. Gentleman
now to take this estimate and to get the
accredited officials of the Transport
Board to make the proper reduction in
the amount of it. In the meantime I
will try to the best of my ability to
protect the users of road transport, and
I believe I am doing that in opposing
sub-clause (a) of this Clause.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I beg to move, in
Clause 1, sub-clause (2) to leave out the
words "after consultation with" in lines
4 and 5 on page 2, and to insert instead,
"in accordance with advice given by".
Both in this House and in the course of
discussions which I have had with representatives of producers' organisations in
regard to this Bill the fear has been
expressed that the Egg Marketing Committee which is being set up will not
have independent powers. I should like
to take this opportunity of stating most
emphatically that the Ministry has never
contemplated exercising its power under
sub-section 1 of Clause 1 of the Bill to
fix egg prices otherwise than in accordance with the advice of the committee.
The Ministry will reserve to itself the
right to advise the committee, to warn
the committee, even perhaps to veto the
price recommended by the committee,
but I would assure the House that it is
not, and never was, the intention of the
Ministry to fix a scale of egg prices which
would be at variance with the prices
recommended by the committee. The
Amendment which stands in my name
makes this position clear that any price.
fixed by the Ministry will be a price
fixed in accordance with advice given by
the Egg Marketing Committee.
I am glad to say that this Amendment
fully meets representations I have
received from producers' interests and
is moved with their concurrence
agreement.

I would like to point out to the Committee that the wholesale shippers consider that those who represent the Class
B licence holders are bound to vote on the
producers' side, for the reason that if
there is much of a difference as between
the price paid to the producer and the
price the shipper gets, that is to say, if
the B licence holders do not keep the price
to the producer sufficiently high, immediately there will be an opening for the A
licence holders to send round their collecting cars. At the present time there is
such a small margin between the two that
the A licence holder is quite content to
allow the B licence holder to go round
in the normal course of his duties and
collect the eggs. The B licence holder is
bound to vote for the best price he can
get, otherwise the A licence holder will
collect the district he is already collecting. That is the argument which has
been put forward, and I think it is a
perfectly legitimate and right one.
Then there is this other point in regard
to the Councils. The Pigs Development
Council and the Milk Council are
composed of representatives of all
the interests, and, as the Committee are aware, the Milk Council
can, if they wish, refer the price back to
the Ministry's nominees. They have
done so, and the last time they did so
they made their own decisions. The
tendency is for these committees, representing, as they do, all interests, to get
together and hammer out a sensible policy
to cover the whole trade and the various
interests in the trade, and I think it
would be a great mistake and would create
great difficulty if you unbalance a committee of this sort. It is there and must
be there in the interests of the whole

of the trade, namely the shippers or the
producers, you are bound to injure the
whole trade in general. That is why I
cannot accept the Amendment, because

are satisfied, the Committee, after the

satisfied that this is the right way of
doing it.

eggs will be sold by producers to wholesalers. The functions of the Committee
do not extend to the retail trade which
will be governed by the rules made by
the Ministry under Clause 7 of the Bill.
In these circumstances it does not appear
to be necessary that retailers should be
represented on the Egg Marketing Committee whose deliberations will not
directly affect their interests. Therefore,
it would not be fair to producers and
wholesalers, the persons directly affected
by the Committee, that retailers should
be represented upon it.
I am, however, most anxious that
retailers shall be consulted in regard to
all matters affecting them and in the
exercise of its powers under Clause 7
of the Bill the Ministry will take steps
to ensure that representatives of retailers
are adequately consulted. I have discussed this matter with representatives
of the retail trade, have assured them
that they will be consulted before the
issue of regulations which affect them,
and they were good enough to accept this
assurance. For these reasons I am unable to accept this Amendment.

under this section but whose licence

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE

The total quantities of eggs imported
into Northern Ireland from all countries
except the Irish Free State during 1934
and 1935 were 12,775 cwts. and 13,753

6. Major

from such dangers to health.
Mr. HANNA: In the absence of my

The cause of the forty cases of mild

danger from unsound food.

COUNTY DOWN "B" SPECIAL

is a fact that a retired officer has been
appointed county commandant for
County Down in the "B" Special Constabulary, whether this officer has any
previous experience in the Special Constabulary, and is already in receipt of an
Army pension, and whether a member
of the "B" Special Constabulary or an
ex-officer in Northern Ireland, without
a pension, was not available for this
well-paid post.
Mr. HANNA: The answer to the first
part of the hon. and gallant Member's
question is in the affirmative. The
gentleman in question had not formerly
served in the Special Constabulary but is
an ex-military officer with a distinguished
record. He is in receipt of a military
pension.
In the interests of the efficiency of the
Force the only consideration which can
be borne in mind in making such appointments is to obtain the services of those
who are in every respect best qualified
for the post, and in the present instance
no member of the Special Constabulary
or other person was considered to possess
the necessary qualifications to the same
degree as this gentleman, who is a native
of, resides in, and has a thorough
knowledge of County Down.
PENSIONS OF WAR WIDOWS.
8. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that there
exist in Northern Ireland widows whose
husbands served in the Great War and
subsequently died as a result of ill-health
contracted on active service, but to
whom no pensions from the Army
authorities are payable because marriage
took place after the War; whether some
of the deceased men were compelled,
through unemployment, to become selfemployed and in consequence the widows.
are not eligible for widows' pensions;
and whether he is prepared to recommend to the House the introduction of
special legislation to deal with these
deserving widows and thus relieve them
from utter destitution.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) The circumstances in which
War Service Pensions are payable is a
matter for the Imperial Government.
So far as widows' pensions under the
Northern Ireland Contributory Pensions
Scheme are concerned, I would remind
my hon. Friend that unless the statutory
conditions are fulfilled, I have no power
to grant a pension.
Moreover, for reasons which the hon.
Member is aware of, I cannot undertake,
in advance of the Imperial Government
to introduce legislation to make special
provision in Northern Ireland for the
cases to which he refers.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Ways and Means.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Financial Statement, 1936-37.
Mr. BARBOUR (who was received
with general cheers): Before proceeding
with my duty this afternoon I desire to
express my deep regret at the temporary
absence of my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)—a regret which I feel sure
is shared by all the Members of this
Committee. It is my sincere hope, as I
am also sure it is the hope of the Committee, that he may be vouchsafed a
speedy return to health and that he may
shortly resume the duties to this
Province of ours which he has for such
a long time carried out so conscientiously
and with such great distinction. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The financial year which has just
ended has given us many signs of the fact
that our Province is now participating,
though in a lesser degree, in the recovery
which Great Britain is making from the
industrial depression caused by the
"economic blizzard" of 1931. This
recovery must, I think,
I think, be almost
entirely attributed to the change made
in cur fiscal system by the National
Government and to the cheap money
policy pursued by Mr. Chamberlain.
Agriculture, our chief industry, continues to improve under the stimulus of
the cattle and milk subsidies and of the
various marketing schemes sheltering
within the framework of the new fiscal
system of the United Kingdom. The
shipbuilding industry also continues to
improve and the new defence programme
of the National Government will no
doubt tend to its further improvement.
Whilst the linen industry still remains
somewhat more depressed than agriculture and shipbuilding, nevertheless even
here signs of recovery are not wanting.
The exports of linen goods in March last
showed an increase of £88,000 over
March, 1935, all sections of the industry
contributing to the increase, and a noteworthy feature of the increase being the
substantially heavier shipments to the
U.S.A.
I might perhaps at this point give the
Committee some figures which illustrate
the improvement in our general trade in
the past year.
The value of the total
external trade of Northern Ireland in
1935 was £92,165,000 as compared with
£88,287,000 in 1934 and £76,867,000
in 1933. The value of our exports in
1935 was £45,055,000 compared with
£42,973,000 in 1934 and £35,555,000
in 1933. If the estimated total external
trade of Northern Ireland in 1924 is
taken as a standard, the percentage
decline in the value of our total trade
in 1935 was 29.7 per cent. as compared
with 32.7 per cent. in 1934 and 41.4
per cent. in 1933. This increase in the
value of our trade is no doubt partly
due to the rise in wholesale prices
(itself, of course, a reassuring sign of
recovering trade), but the view that it is
also to a large degree due to a real increase in the volume of trade is supported
by the fact that the tonnage cleared in
the Port of Belfast reached the record
figures last year of 7,612 vessels and
Minister's Financial Statement 1564
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
4,180,981 tons. The figures which I have
just quoted include, of course, the value
of the "transit trade" through Northern Ireland ports from and to the Irish
Free State.
The intractable problem of unemployment unfortunately still continues to
confront us, but even here the position
shows some betterment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Last year when my right
hon. Friend presented his Budget the
unemployment rate for the Province was
26.4 per cent, whereas it is now reduced
to 22.6 per cent. The improvement in
the unemployment position is particularly marked in the shipbuilding
industry, where the rate is now 18.4 per
cent. as compared with 31 per cent. this
time last year. This improvement in
employment in the shipbuilding industry
is one which is in no small degree due to
the unremitting labours of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance in the
administration of the Loans Guarantee
Acts. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
When on the subject of unemployment
I must also refer to what was to us the
major financial event of the year, namely
the new Unemployment Reinsurance.
Agreement between the Imperial
Treasury and the Government of Northern Ireland. The ratification of this
Agreement by both Parliaments will
remove permanently, it is hoped, the one
major cause of instability in our financial
framework as well as securing that those
of our people who have the misfortune
to be unemployed shall always enjoy
similar benefits to those who are unemployed in other parts of the United
Kingdom. It is no exaggeration to say
that without this new Agreement the
further growth in our social services,
namely the insurance of agricultural
workers, which comes into effect shortly,
could hardly have taken place. The
finances of the Agricultural Unemployment Insurance Scheme will come within
the ambit of the new Agreement and our
Exchequer will accordingly be safeguarded against abnormal expenditure
caused by disproportionate unemployment amongst agricultural workers in
our Province as compared with other
parts of the United Kingdom.
I might here, perhaps, give the Committee some figures relating to the unemployment finance of last year which will
to
further illustrate the value
the
Province of the new Agreement. During
the year a supplementary provision of
£275,000 was required for unforeseen
expenditure on unemployment, a provision which would have upset all the
Budget calculations if the operation of
the new Agreement had not enabled us
to get from the Imperial Exchequer an
increased contribution of £109,000 above
the original Budget estimate for the
year.
With this short preface I will now
proceed to the more prosaic duty of
describing briefly the outcome of our last
year's finances, showing how closely my
right hon. Friend's anticipations of a
year ago have in general been borne out
by the results. On the whole the results
for the year cannot be considered
unsatisfactory, though it is rather disappointing that our transferred revenues
are not yet, at any rate, exhibiting that
degree of buoyancy which was the
characteristic feature of the Imperial
Chancellor's revenues. I am not yet in
a position to say how far the buoyancy
of the revenues from Customs and Excise
and Income Tax in Great Britain will
exhibit a similar feature in our reserved
revenues in the past year, though I am
exceedingly hopeful that the final figures
of reserved revenues will show a not
unsubstantial increase over the Estimates.
If hon. Members will turn to the
upper portion of Table I. of the White
Paper which has been circulated they
will find statements comparing the estimated with the actual outturn of last
year's finance. My first duty will be
mainly directed to that Table, but if
hon. Members wish to see the items in
greater detail they may do so if they turn
to Table II. for the outgoings and
Table III. for the income.
Expenditure, 1934-35.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure, we find that Consolidated Fund
Services, apart from the Road Fund and
the self-balancing item of the Milk
Industry Assistance Grant, accounted
for £400,819, or £3,181 below the
Estimate.
ROAD FUND.
The Road Fund payment of £651,774
represents the net yield of motor vehicle
Minister's Financial Statement 1566
The Budget-
14 MAY 1936
duties and fines in respect of motoring
offences after the deduction of the luxury
tax of 25 per cent. of the yield of the
duties on private cars, which was
imposed by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance in his last Budget.
The full amount of the luxury tax on
private cars was £81,037, but as hon.
Members will recollect my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance allowed
credit to the Road Fund for the annual
£50,000 which is due by it until 1940 in
respect of borrowings for distress relief
works, so that the net amount retained
in the Exchequer in respect of the luxury
tax was £31,037. I would remind hon.
Members in this connection that in Great
Britain one-third of the yield of motor
vehicle duties on private cars is retained
in the Exchequer as a luxury tax. The
payment of £651,774 to the Road Fund
is £27,774 in excess of the Budget
Estimate a result which hon. Members
will agree is very satisfactory.
MILK GRANT.
The expenditure out of the Grant
from the Imperial Government in aid of
our milk industry was £151,354.
SUPPLY SERVICES.
The Budget Estimate for supply
services was £9,327,000, to which should
be added approximately £500,000 for
supplementaries, mainly on account of
increases in the cost of unemployment
services, including the cost of the special
grants to local authorities by way of
compensation for the postponement of
the Second Appointed Day under the
Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934,
making a total estimated expenditure on
our departmental services, after deducting the contributions made by our local
authorities towards the cost of educational services, of £9,827,000.
The actual expenditure for the year
was £9,608,821, a gross saving of
roughly £218,000. Part of the saving is
due to the fact that the full amount of
the supplementary provision sanctioned
in respect of unemployment and old age
pensions was not required. Despite this
fact my right hon. Friend was able to
defray nearly half of the supplementary
provisions required in the year out of
savings made on the various Votes.
DEDUCTIONS FROM RESIDUARY SHARE.
We repaid to the Imperial Government sums collected by us from the local
authorities in repayment of loans made
before we took over control (£64,000),
and also collections of "New" Land
Purchase Annuities (£302,000), making
£366,000.
The expenditure of the Imperial
Government on the Reserved Services
which they control, such as the cost of
collecting Income Tax, Post Office,
Customs, etc., has been provisionally
maintained at the same figure as the
Estimate for last year,
namely,
£1,908,000.
The total net expenditure, therefore,
of the Province last year, after deducting the amount of the local contribution
towards the cost of educational services,
amounted to £13,086,768, and I shall
now refer briefly to the sources of
revenue for meeting this expenditure.
Revenue, 1935-1936.
TRANSFERRED TAXES.
The revenue from transferred taxes
imposed by our Government produced
£1,165,200, that is, £190,200 more than
the Budget Estimate.
This large increase in the yield of
transferred taxes over the Estimate is
almost entirely due to the estate duty
received from one very large estate, the
duty on which was approximately
£296,000. Apart from this windfall, the
yield on estate duties was, I regret to
say, on the whole, somewhat disappointing, especially having regard to the
appreciation in capital values to which
the Imperial Chancellor attributed the
record yield from these duties in Great
Britain last year.
Stamp duties also contributed to the
increase in the yield of transferred taxes
over the Estimate with the relatively
small but reassuring sum of £8,000.
Excise duties, despite the reduction in
entertainments duty made in the last
Budget, also show a small but welcome
increase of £3,000 over the Estimate.
Motor taxation, as I have stated above,
produced £682,811.
RESERVED TAXES.
The Budget Estimate for reserved
taxes collected by the Imperial Govern-

ment was £7,630,000. The receipts are

NON-TAX Revenue.
There are two items of non-tax revenue
to which I especially desire to draw the
attention of the Committee namely the
payment of £150,000 from the Reserve
Fund and the receipt of £132,545 in
respect of recoveries under the Loans
Guarantee Acts. The payment of
£150,000 made from the Reserve Fund
last year to help to balance the Budget
has practically absorbed the resources of
that Fund.
The receipt of £132,545 in respect of
arrears under the Loans Guarantee Acts
is one which must be particularly pleasing to my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, as it justifies the "nursing"
policy which he has adopted in this particular case. The receipt represents a
portion of arrears of interest payments
in default which had been met out
of the Exchequer. There is every reason
to expect in this particular case an early
repayment of the outstanding principal.
The amount received from the Imperial
Government under the new Reinsurance
Agreement was £752,000, a figure which
exceeds the Budget Estimate by
£109,000. The reason for this increase
is that the Estimates of unemployment
were rather more optimistic than events
subsequently provided.
Other items of non-tax revenue are set
out in Table I and are, in general, so
close to the Estimates that it is unnecessary for me to weary the Committee
by quoting items and figures in detail.
In all, the non-tax revenue (including
the self-balancing items in respect of
local loans repayments, "new" land purchase annuities, the appropriation from
the Reserve Fund and milk industry
assistance grant from the Imperial
Government) amounted to £3,623,355,
bringing the total revenue available from
all sources last year to £13,101,366.
If
we deduct from this the total
expenditure for the year, already
mentioned by me, £13,086,768, we are
left with a balance of £14,598 as the
provisional amount available for surplus
and Imperial contribution.
Although this surplus is not large, and
is subject to adjustment by the Joint
Exchequer Board when the final figures
of reserved revenue are available, nevertheless it represents a record of which
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, may well be proud, as it is his
fourteenth successive Budget surplus-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-an achievement which I am certain is without
parallel in post-war Europe.

To save Members of the Committee
searching for these figures I may say they
do not appear there. This is the first

I have fixed my Estimate of estate
duties at about £180,000 less than the
actual yield for last year, because, as I
have already explained to the Committee, the receipts for last year were
unduly inflated by reason of a windfall
from one large estate. I have taken an
optimistic view of the probable trend of
the business on the Stock Exchange and
increased my Estimate of the yield from
stamp duties by some £7,000. The
Estimate for the excise duties remains
at exactly the same figure as last year.
I have provided for an expansion of
£26,000 in the yield from the motor
vehicles duties.
Hon. Members will be aware from
statements which have already appeared
in the Press that the Government is
unable to agree to any alteration in motor
taxation, and they will not expect me to
develop the reasons which my right hon.
Friend, the Prime Minister, has already
fully advanced publicly and to deputations. I am, however, happy to be
able to state that, as the result of the
representations made by the Royal Automobile Club, and our own local motoring associations and Chambers of Commerce, my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, proposes to
accept the plea that it is unfair that the
owners of new vans and lorries, when
they have just taken delivery from the
manufacturers, should be required to pay
in respect of the first police examination
the full licence fee prescribed in the
regulations. In future a merely nominal
fee of 1s will be charged for this initial
examination.

economy proposals were made.
therefore, a somewhat remarkable coincidence that I should be privileged to
make the proposals which I am

desire at the outset to say that I have

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
now
Hon. Members are aware that the
various economy cuts which were made
in the salaries of our public servants
came into force some six months earlier
than the corresponding cuts in Great
Britain. Hon. Members are also aware
that the full restoration of the cuts in
Great Britain was made in two stages,
the first half being restored in the
summer of 1934 and the second half in
the summer of last year. That it would,
of course, have given my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, much
pleasure to have kept precisely step by
step with Great Britain in this matter
goes without saying. He was, however,
prevented from doing so by the stern
necessity of our financial position. The
financial position has now, I am happy
to say, been materially altered by an
unexpected and gratifying improvement
in our reserved revenues for the present
year which, it is hoped, will continue.
in future years and which is unconnected
with the special increases arising out of
the additional taxation imposed by Mr.
Chamberlain for the purposes of national
defence.
My first proposal relates to the
teachers. Although strong representations have been made to the Government
for the full restoration of the cuts in
teachers' salaries, the Government is
convinced that there is certainly a feeling amongst a section of the public that
teachers at any rate, public elementary
school teachers are sufficiently remunerated at their existing salaries,
having regard to their general conditions
of service.
-
Mr. BEATTIE: Who says that?
Mr. BARBOUR: The general public
in large measure.
Mr. BEATTIE: No. It does not.
Mr. BARBOUR: At the same time,
the Government have to recognise the
fact that when the economies were made
in 1931 it was indicated that the Government hoped that these economies would
only be temporary. Furthermore, the
economies were accepted by the teachers,
as well as by other officers affected, in a
public-spirited manner. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The proposal I am about
to make attempts, therefore, to hold the
balance evenly between the interests of
the general body of taxpayers and those
of the teachers. It is not possible to
institute an exact comparison between
teachers salaries here and in Great
Britain as there are various scales in
force there, while, on the other hand,
here special payments are made for
certain qualifications, etc., which have
no counterpart in Great Britain. Generally speaking, however, we might regard
it as definite that the restored British
salaries gave
teachers there on the
average higher emoluments than in
Northern Ireland, but half the cost of
the salaries in Great Britain is borne
by the ratepayers. To restore the salary
scales for all classes of teachers to the
pre-1931 level of remuneration would
cost about £130,000 in a full year. I
do not think, however, that our resources
are permanently capable of meeting this
sum, and I am of the opinion that the
equities of the teachers' claim will be
satisfied by the setting aside in a full
year of the sum of about £65,000, which

On the present reduced scales a man
teacher in an elementary school starts
at £148 a year and a woman at £134 a
year. The former can by increments
reach a salary of £318 a year, and the
latter £259 a year. But on top of this
each can by reason of special efficiency
reach a point of £357 in the case of a
man and £284 in the case of a woman.
Nor is that the end, for if the teacher
is a principal he obtains another £16 a
year in the case of a small school and up
to £185 a year in the case of a large
one by gradual progression according to
the number of pupils.
Mr. BEATTIE: Of what scales are
you speaking at the moment? Super
normal or normal?
Mr. BARBOUR: The present reduced
cales. These salaries cannot surely be
regarded as unreasonable, and now, with
the proposed reconstitution of the scales
of salary and other
payments, the
average salary for a properly qualified
teacher will be £340 per annum in the
case of men and £243 in the case of
women. The actual details of the reconstituted scales will be brought to the
notice of the House in due course by
means of the presentation of the usual
Statutory Rule.
Teachers who have retired since 1931
will also have their pensions recalculated
in accordance with the new scales of
salary, so that the temporary financial
sacrifice which they willingly made in
1931 may not adversely affect them for
all time. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This proposal will cost the Exchequer
about £2,000 per annum.
a
Simultaneously with the foregoing
proposals, I I propose to introduce
further benefit, namely, an amendment
in superannuation conditions sought by
the teachers to give them on retirement,
in addition to pension, payment of a
lump sum allowance on the same lines as
civil servants. This concession will be
conditional on the teachers themselves
paying a further 1 per cent. contribution to pension charges, bringing their
contribution to 5 per cent. as in Great
Britain, where, however, local authorities also bear a further 2 per cent. Much
as I would like to make this benefit
retro-active--that is, to allow past service to reckon towards it-I regret that
I am unable to do so as it would throw
an inordinate burden on the Exchequer.
This concession will, therefore, operate
only in respect of service given from the
1st July next. The cost of the superannuation proposal will be about £1,500
per annum, gradually rising to £40,000,
towards which the teachers will have contributed the percentage I have just
mentioned. The detailed arrangements
involved in this superannuation proposal
will be embodied in Regulations which
will be submitted to the House in due
course.
The proposals which I have just outlined to the Committee for the reconstitution and stabilisation of the
teachers' salaries and superannuation
benefits give rise to the question as to
what should be done in the case of other
salaries which participated in the
economies of 1931, and in respect of
which no restoration of cuts has yet been
made. As hon. Members will recollect,
my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance in the case of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary made a restoration of cuts
comparable to those made in Great
Britain, that is to say, they now make a
pension contribution of 5 per cent. instead of the 10 per cent. put into operation in 1931. There is no intention, of
course, of bringing this 5 per cent. to
the figure of 2 per cent. which operated
up to 1931. He also in his last Budget
restored the cuts made in the fees paid
to panel doctors. The other salaries and
allowances affected by the economies of
1931 in respect of which no adjustment
has since been made may be divided into
three groups:
(1) Parliamentary.

(2) Members of the Cabinet and
Parliamentary Secretaries, and other
Members of the Government.
(3) Civil
servants on inclusive
salaries and part-time Government
employees, and certain grants, etc.
I propose to restore the salaries and
allowances in each of the first and third
of these groups to the levels which
existed prior to the economies of 1931.
The estimated cost in a full year of this
proposal is £5,000. The proposal will,
however, come into effect contemporaneously with the proposal relating to
the teachers' salaries-that is the 1st
July-and the cost to the Exchequer in
the current year is accordingly only
£3,000.
The voluntary cuts in the statutory
salaries of Cabinet Ministers, Parliamentary Secretaries and other Members of
the Government will, however, continue
in force.
The total cost to the Exchequer of all
the proposals which I have just outlined
is £50,000 in the current year.
I have now two proposals to make
regarding the Royal Ulster Constabulary
and the Special Constabulary which,
although they do not affect my Budget
figures, will involve some additional
expenditure. I am hoping that it will be
possible for me to meet this additional
expenditure, which amounts to £14,000
in a full year, by means of savings in
the various Votes. Supplementary Estimates relating to the proposals will be
submitted to the House in due course.
Turning first to the Royal Ulster Constabulary. Representations have been
made for a number of years that in the
matter of rent allowances the Royal
Ulster Constabulary was in a position
much less favourable than that enjoyed
by police forces in Great Britain and
that, in fact, the allowances were far
below what the members of the Force on
the average had to pay for housing
accommodation. Last year it was agreed
between the two Departments concerned
to set up an inter-Departmental Committee to investigate this matter.
committee have now reported and have
recommended certain increases in the
amount of rent allowances. To give
effect to their recommendations involves
an increase in the annual cost of these
allowances of approximately £10,000.
The
The Government has decided to act upon
the recommendations of this Departmental Committee, which will have the
effect of placing the Royal Ulster Constabulary, broadly speaking, on identical
standards of remuneration with those in
operation in Great Britain.
As regards the Special Constabulary, I
propose that the economy cuts made in
1931 on the salaries of the whole-time
members of the Force shall be restored in
full as from the 1st July next. I also
propose to increase as from the same date
the bonus paid to members of the reserve
classes of the Force in respect of training
and musketry practice. The estimated
cost of these proposals is £4,000 in a full
year.
As hon. Members are aware,
established civil servants salaries were
consolidated last year. This consolidation also applied to the prison service,
but representations have been made
recently that, in view of the onerous
nature of their work, some further
improvement in the emoluments of
prison officers was desirable. I am able
to say that in the course of a few weeks
improved rates of pay for the prison
service as a whole will be promulgated
with effect from 1st April last.
The balance now remaining in the
account would normally represent the
amount available for Imperial Contribution and Surplus. We have, however,

of £92,000 is proper to be met out of the

Fund designed to perpetuate our terminable revenues,
and that the amount
available for Imperial Contribution
should be abated accordingly.
Pending a decision of the Joint

in all, as being available for Imperial

hon. Members will be able to infer that

Minister's Financial Statement 1580

I have now completed my survey of

and who knows but that next year, if

The next point is probably a matter
of greater public interest. It relates to
a proposal to amend the law relating to

a
in
Minister's Financial Statement 1582
The Budget-
14 MAY 1936
regard to their contents which is of
almost vital importance for the purpose
of the quinquennial revaluation which
must now be a feature of administration
in Northern Ireland. As hon. Members
will be only too well aware, prior to the
recent revaluation it was necessary under
powers conferred by the Valuation
(Amendment) Act of 1932 for the Commissioner of Valuation to issue forms to
every occupier of house property in
Northern Ireland requiring him to
supply certain particulars in regard to
the tenure of his property. For the same
purpose it is very often of importance
to know the price at which property has
changed hands. To issue these forms at
every revaluation and to provide staff
for their ultimate digesting, or to require
a house-to-house visitation by officials in
order
to obtain the information,
obviously would increase the cost of every
revaluation to a figure which this House
might well criticise. In addition the
local authorities, who under statute have
to bear part of the cost of revaluation,
would have good grounds for restiveness.
In order to avoid this the Government
considers that much of this staff increase
and the annoyance of the public being
flooded with forms every five years will
be avoided if solicitors, estate agents and
others are in future required, when lodging any conveyance or lease of property
for stamping, to lodge with it at the
Stamps Office for permanent record either
a copy of the document or a form setting
out the salient particulars in regard to
such matters as the term of the lease,
the rent, liability for maintenance and
so forth. Alternatively, it would be
open to them if they preferred, to leave
the document with the Stamps Office for
a period not exceeding forty-eight hours
in order that the Stamps Office may
themselves abstract the requisite particulars. I am sure that, having regard
to the object to be achieved, no objection
will be raised to this modest requirement. I may say that the Commissioner
of Valuation has discussed the proposals
with the Incorporated Law Society for
Northern Ireland and with the various
bodies representative of estate agents in
Northern Ireland, and they have
indicated that they will offer no objection to these suggestions if carried into
law.
The remaining points relate to estate
duty. The first which is proposed is on
the lines of a proposal already before the
Imperial House of Commons in connection with their Budget there, and is
designed to stop evasion of death duties
arising out of the fact that estate duty
is not chargeable on personalty abroad,
where it has been the subject of a gift,
of a joint investment, or of a foreign
settlement. This exemption is apparently being abused by persons domiciled
in Great Britain, and although such
cases are likely to be extremely rare
amongst persons domiciled in Northern
Ireland, it is considered desirable to
follow British legislation, which proposes
to treat personalty abroad in this respect
on the same footing as personalty at
home.
The second point is one which, subject to Parliamentary
Parliamentary approval, the
Government has agreed with the India
Office to bring into operation. Under
the recent Government of India Act provision was made that as far as Great
Britain was concerned estate duty would
not be chargeable in Great Britain on
annuities paid out of certain Indian
Pension Funds. These Funds in the past
were held in India, and no question of
estate duty arose in the United Kingdom, but under that Act these Funds are
now being transferred to Whitehall, and
normally questions of estate duty would
arise. In the event of any person
domiciled in Northern Ireland being entitled to share in benefits from these
Funds it is proposed to grant to them
exemption from duty.
The last point relates to a method of
evading estate duty which, I am afraid,
is somewhat common in Northern Ireland,
namely, two parties deposit moneys in a
bank on a joint deposit receipt. On the
death of one the asset is not brought
into the statement of the estate of the
deceased, although in law it should be.
The matter has been under the consideration of the Ministry of Finance for
a long time past, and was the subject of
discussion with representatives of the
banks, but it was felt that it would be
difficult to do anything in Northern
Ireland if legislation on the same lines
were not enacted in the Irish Free State,
as it would merely lead to Northern
Ireland residents opening accounts in
branches of the banks in the Irish Free
State. Last year, however, after con-

the Irish Banks, legislation was

of estate duty. It is now desirable, in

in parts. It cannot be wholly condemned
as not sound to the 100 per cent. mark.
My condemnation of the Budget is due
to several points. Unemployment in
Northern Ireland is now a permanent
fixture. The normal unemployment
figure is 22.6. What was the previous
normal unemployment figure before the
Northern Government took possession of
the employment market? It was 12
per cent. of the total employment.
Mr. ANDREWS: No. That is quite
incorrect.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is correct
according to the statistics. I am speaking of the time before ever you became
Minister of Labour. I am speaking of
the normal unemployment when unemployment insurance was first brought in.
That was the unemployment basis on
which it was calculated under the
British Government, of course. I am
sorry to say that has never been returned
to since, and it is not likely, according
to the statement of the right hon.
Gentleman, ever to come back to
Northern Ireland. Hence my reason for
saying we are going to have an unemployment figure of 22.6 always presenting itself, because at the moment we have
no employment where these unemployed
can be housed. We cannot find places
for any other employable men at the
moment. Every unit of industry is filled
up, and for every job we have at the
moment ten men waiting to take it.
What is the solution? I thought the
Minister would have provided some new
industries for Ulster or made some provision out of the money at his command to
absorb into industry those who are unable to find employment owing to
scientific methods adopted in every production. No real effort has been made
by the Government in the Budget Statement, because we are going to plod along
as usual upon unemployment with which
the Minister and the Government seem
satisfied.
Mr. ANDREWS: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: That, in my opinion,
is a downward policy, and one which, if
pursued, will bring about the downfall
of the right hon. Gentleman's Cabinet.
That could not come too soon. (Laughter.)
There is no hope in the Budget Statement for the unemployed, who are now
compelled to depend upon the poor-law

There is no sign of hope of any kind for
that class of the community. What

Oral Answers to Questions.
IMPORTED EGGS OF INFERIOR
QUALITY.
1. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Midgley)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether, in view of the dangers arising
from the use of imported eggs of inferior
quality or unsatisfactory condition, and
in view of his policy as expressed in the
Egg Marketing Bill to improve the
quality of Northern Ireland eggs for the
home and export markets, he is prepared
to take immediate steps to protect the
public against such dangers.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The protection of the public from dangers arising
from the use of foods which are unfit
for human consumption is a matter for
the local sanitary authorities and Parliament has armed these authorities with
adequate statutory powers for dealing
with all foodstuffs unfit for human consumption. Moreover, imported eggs
must, if offered for sale, be marked either
with the name of the country of origin
or the word "Foreign" or "Empire,"
and this in itself affords a considerable
degree of protection to the public, since
it enables intelligent consumers to form
an opinion as to the freshness or otherwise of the eggs which are offered to
them.
INCREASE IN JUVENILE CRIME.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he will inquire into
the relation between the absence of
definite religious teaching in the provided
and transferred schools and the increase
of juvenile crime in Belfast voiced by
a distinguished educationist, Canon
Pratt, at the General Synod on the 12th
instant.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The answer
is in the negative.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask does
that answer reflect the mind of the
Minister or his own mind in dealing in
such a light-hearted manner with such
a serious subject?
Mr. ROBB: I cannot conceive that
a prima facie case has been made out
for any such inquiry as asked for. So
long as the principles common to all
Christian Churches and so long as that
great Commandment, "Thou shalt love

thy neighbour as thyself," are taught

which are nowadays common to all

LIABILITY OF HUSBAND FOR
WIFE'S TORTS.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Attorney-General whether the Government propose to introduce legislation to
abolish the liabilities of husbands for
slanders or other torts committed by
wives before or after marriage.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Government propose in the near
future to place the law in Northern Ireland as to the liability of a husband for
his wife's torts on the same basis as the
law in Great Britain, in so far as it is
expedient to do so, and the matter is
now being considered by the Government's legal advisers.

Question of Privilege.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I wish to raise a
question of which I have given you
notice and to ask for your ruling in
regard to a matter of privilege. In this
House on Thursday last-Budget daythere came to my knowledge that at
least one newspaper circulating in Northern Ireland had received an advance
copy of the Budget statement at about
ten minutes or a quarter-past two on the
day the Budget was to be presented to
this House, and that the other newspapers circulating throughout Northern
Ireland received advance copies of the
Budget statement not later than fifteen
minutes past three o'clock. All the
newspapers of Northern Ireland were in
possession of the proposals contained in
the Budget long before these proposals
were made known to the Members of
this House. As a matter of fact, I am
informed that the wires between Great
Britain and Ireland were humming with
the news contained in the Budget and
that the proposals were known in the
streets of Great Britain, through the
newspapers, before hon. Members here
had an opportunity of hearing them. In
the circumstances, I would ask for your
opinion with regard to this matter of
privilege and ask definitely is it not a
distinct breach of privilege that outside
authorities should be placed in possession
of the facts relating to the finances of
Northern Ireland before hon. Members
had an opportunity of having the facts
presented to them.
Mr. SPEAKER: The province of the
Speaker on a matter of this kind is to
decide whether there is a prima facie
case to come before the Committee of
Privileges. In this instance, after hearing what the hon. Member for Dock
has said, I think it is desirable that the
matter should be inquired-and, in fact,
the whole question of releasing information should be inquired into by the
Committee of Privileges. I think, therefore, there is a prima facie case, and I
would ask the hon. Member to move
accordingly.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to move,
"That this matter be referred to the
Committee of Privileges."
Question, "That the matter complained of be referred to the Committee
of Privileges for investigation and
report," put, and agreed to.
Ordered: That the Committee have
power to send for persons, papers, and
records.

Resolution reported:
"That it is expedient to amend the
law relating to certain duties of excise
and death duties; to require the delivery

""
Question proposed: "That the House
