Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In rising to
speak on the Resolution before the
House which is the result of the Budget
opened on Thursday last, I would like to
join with those who have already spoken
in referring to the absence of the Minister of Finance and regret very much that
he was not here to take his place.
During the past fifteen years he has most
carefully nursed the finances of the
Province, and I am sorry that he was
not here on this occasion when after
a period of lean years he was able to
show a good surplus.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Commerce on the very able manner
in which he put before this House the
finances for the past and for the coming
year. The opening statement of the
Minister of Commerce dealing with the
state of trade and commerce in Northern
Ireland was most comprehensive, and the
most striking part of it, I think, was the
tonnage returns for the port of Belfast,
because they are the most certain and
sure guide of the life and movement of
trade in this Province. The figures of
our exports over the last three years were
quoted, but no corresponding figures were
given for our imports, and I would like
to compare those two sets of figures. In
1935 exports in round figures amounted
to £45,000,000, and in that year our
imports came to £47,200,000; in 1934
our exports were £43,000,000 and our
imports £45,300,000, and in 1933 our
exports were £35,500,000 and our imports
£41,400,000. These figures give a very
fair statement of the way in which our
trade has picked up during the three years.
In dealing with the main item of our
revenue, taxes which are imposed by this
House, I would like to point out that
motor duties have increased very considerably during the past number of years.
In 1929 motor taxation produced
£430,000 and in 1936 £682,000, an
increase of £250,000 in eight years, or an
average increase in these duties of nearly
£30,000 a year. It will be interesting
to note if the elimination of redundant
road transport by the Road Transport
Board will result in a decrease in this
source of revenue from lorries and buses.
With regard to motor car taxes, I would
like to say that in my opinion a motor
car is now in very many cases a business
necessity and not a luxury, and owners of
motor cars will continue to press for
equal taxation with Great Britain, and I
hope that will be granted.
The next large item in the taxes
imposed by this House is estate duties.
The Minister in his Budget speech expressed disappointment with the degree
of expansion in this form of taxation.
If you examine the returns of this taxation for the past eight years they will
show that from 1929 to 1932 on an
average £675,000 was taken out of estate
duties, then there was a very sharp drop
from 1932 to 1935 of £140,000 a year, the
average being £535,000. Last year's
exceptional windfall of nearly £300,000
mentioned in the Budget speech must
surely be abnormal. Northern Ireland is
a small area, and I very much doubt if
the State is going to get such a large
windfall again.
I would like to ask the Minister if the
incidence of this form of taxation has
been worked out and considered by the
Government from the angle of the exhaustion of the goose that lays the golden
eggs, so that it can now only produce
small ones. It is a striking thing that
in eight years a sum of no less than
£5,100,000 has been taken out of capital
by this form of taxation. The effect of
this loss of capital in terms of trade,
current revenue, income tax, and employment must be very considerable, and I
would like to ask the Minister what is
his view of the "life" of these duties at
the present high scale of taxation. To
take £5,000,000 out of capital must
surely have a resulting effect in lessening
the real financial resources of any country.
1599 Ways and Means-Report-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Budget Resolutions
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
The Minister next referred to the repayment or recoupment of £132,000 under
the Loans Guarantee Acts. This sum
was credited to revenue to make the
account balance. In this connection I
would like to remind the House that in
the past three years we have taken from
the Reserve Fund £450,000 to meet
practically equal payments from the Consolidated Fund on account of issues under
the Loans Guarantee Acts. I think in
future, so long as we are able to show a
surplus, that if we take any recoupments
they should be placed to the credit of the
Capital Fund. In this connection I am
glad to note that this year £270,000 is
being taken out of revenue to meet any
liabilities we may have in the Consolidated
Fund under the Loans Guarantee Acts.
As regard the Sinking Fund for
terminable annuities mentioned last year,
I might again remind the House that the
year before £100,000 was taken from the
Fund to increase our revenue. It is
most important that for the future
revenue of this Province an annual sum
be placed into this reserve. I am glad
to say that £90,000 has been provisionally
earmarked for this service. The credit
of this Fund on 31st March, 1935, was
£1,630,000. That may seem a large sum,
but it has to be built up so that when
the land annuities expire the interest will
bring in a sum equivalent to the present
amount we get in revenue from that
source. The Budget forecast for this
year's revenue and last year's returns of
customs and excise-the expansion being
£550,000-show, I think, the very large
part which the policy of Protection has
played both in restoring the national
finances and also our finances here.
I would like to deal with income tax.
In the Minister's statement regarding
inland revenue, that is income tax, I was
struck by the comparatively small increase
in this form of taxation. The expansion
is £445,000, of which £130,000 is due
to the 3d increase in income tax for
defence. At 4s 6d in the £ the normal
increase is £315,000, and the Minister
said that this was on the new valuation.
This rather confounds those critics who
stated that our revaluation Schedules A
and B would bring in half a million. The
fact is, that the increase of taxation,
based on the new valuation and the
normal expansion of this service, is only
making an expansion of £315,000, and I
would further like to ask the Minister
if he could inform the House how this
expansion compares with Mr. Chamberlain's forecast of the expansion of inland
revenue in Great Britain.
Next, I would like to discuss the surplus disclosed after taking into account
the sum provisionally earmarked for the
terminable annuities, that is, land
annuities and church temporalities, and
the cost of the restoration and partial
restoration of cuts. The figure of
approximately £400,000 was given by the
Minister. I would like to point out that
of this figure £210,000 is due to the 3d
on income tax and 2d on tea. This gives
you a net figure of £190,000 as the surplus under taxation at the normal rate
and with no extra tea duty. You will
remember that this year's supply services
show a net reduction of £232,000, due
to a welcome decrease of 4 per cent. in
unemployment. When you consider that
our net surplus is £190,000 and remember
that the 4 per cent. reduction in unemployment has saved £230,000 this year,
the inference is obvious. Our real margin
of surplus is small and there can be no relaxation of vigilance on behalf of the
Exchequer in watching expenditure.
As regards the partial restoration of
the 1931 cuts in the teachers' salaries, I
wish to congratulate the Government on
their action. It should remove a feeling
on the part of the teachers that they have
been badly treated. Now when we have
got a surplus the Government has met
the teachers and partially restored their
cuts, and I think they were quite right
in doing so. I am sure all the teachers
hope they will get the full 7 per cent.
back, and are really grateful for what has
been done for them in giving them 31
per cent. I am sure they are extremely
grateful that the Government intend to
build up a fund for lump sum payments
on retirement. In this connection I
would like to mention that this lump
sum on retirement will only affect new
entrants to the teaching service, and it
might be wise-it certainly would be
advisable to consider whether or not
the older teachers should not be allowed
to come into the scheme on the payment
of a certain sum, representing, as it were,
arrears.

I profoundly disagree with the right
hon. Gentleman. I am not stupid

The point I wish to make is that the right
hon. Gentleman is putting the saddle

generally of trade in Great Britain in so

Government, that is the National
Government-and incidentally you were

He has a right to talk about it, but
the only way to avoid war is to be armed.
If Abyssinia had been armed instead of
disarmed she would never have had to
fight at all. It was because she had no
arms she was attacked. If Britain-and
the old country is not done yet-is to
hold her place she must be armed. We
are part of Great Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) She must be armed.
If everybody thought as some of us think
about arms it would be all right all
over the world, but the amazing thing
is that the people who are going about
now calling for war had been for years
advocating and calling for Britain to
throw down her arms. I am not referring to anyone in this House. If you
want war you must be armed. That is
the spirit of the world at the present
time. I saw an Italian troopship about
ten days ago at Port Said. There was a
contingent of the Australian Navy on the
ship I was on. The men on the troopship were hurling threats at the navymen.
Their conduct was most disgraceful. I
only mention that to show the spirit
prevailing on the Continent. There are
not enough arms in the hands of the
British people.
I remember when the last war broke
out that the soldiers, because they had
no arms in stock, were drilling without
them. If they had had arms it is doubtful if the last war would have taken
place. Not alone should there be arms,
but there should be gasmasks actually
on sale just the same as you would buy

As far as we can see the time is coming

to rise to the occasion and put a stop
to it, with the result that many valuable
lives were lost. I contend that something serious will have to be done to
give the Ulster people more confidence
in the Ministry of Home Affairs and in
those responsible for maintaining law
and order. A good deal of the trouble that
broke out throughout Northern Ireland
was due to the fact that many appointments were made of persons who were
not competent to lead the police under
their control. It would have been far
better for the country as a whole if the
leaders of the police could have been
selected from the ranks of the police
themselves.
I want to say this in the presence of
the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Home Affairs. I sometimes
have the pleasure and the honour of
going to the Ministry on behalf of some
of the taxpayers of Northern Ireland,
and I very rarely can get in touch with
anyone who can give me the satisfaction
or the information I require. It is very
seldom there is anyone of any importance
there. Of course the same thing applies
to many of the other Departments. On
Friday afternoon I had occasion to ring
up the Ministry of Agriculture. The
Minister of Agriculture was not there. I
would not expect him to be there. Then
I asked for the Minister's deputy. He
was not there. Then I asked could I
have a few minutes' talk with the gentleman below the deputy. He was not
there. I went on down the list till I had
gone through seven persons, and I finally
said, "In the name of heaven is there
anybody there who can tell me something
about agriculture." That was on Friday
afternoon. That shows you the way the
country is being run. I say the Prime
Minister of this country must take
definite steps to bring about reform in
the administration of its affairs.
I quite agree with those Members who
state that we should at least pay a contribution to Great Britain for Imperial
services in the event of war, and we are
going to contribute £400,000 this year.
It is also quite true that Great Britain
might ask the mothers and fathers of
Northern Ireland to contribute 400,000
human lives for the defence of the
Empire. But if the people of Ulster,
who are loyal to the core, are prepared
to give to Great Britain that loyalty which
she expects, and which she always receives from Ulster, would you not have
thought that before this day in the year
1936 the British Armaments Committee
would at least have made an announcement of what they are going to give
Ulster in the way of aircraft factories or
the manufacture of armaments? Instead
of that all the loyalty is expected from
Ulster, and apparently she is going to
get very little in return from Great
Britain, notwithstanding the fact that
in the near future there are likely to
be 70,000 people unemployed in this
country. And I want to say definitely
here that if a census were taken of the
persons unemployed in Northern Ireland
you would find that it would be away
over 70,000.

It is quite true to say-make no mistake about this that Great Britain
thinks there is no place in the world like

If the Prime Minister will come to

people to get my nomination papers

a little boy. She was dying from a

terrible disease, and she could not afford

Agriculture should make it their business

Thousands of acres could be reclaimed.
The late Member for Central always
said in this House that there should be a

out.
That is quite true. I happened to
have had the pleasure of being on an
excursion, and I noticed that the Free
State people are carrying out afforestation.
to a greater extent than we are here.
(Hon. Members: No, no.) Yes, they

are behind the times. The country

increased the foodstuffs of the population.
You have absolutely destroyed any happiness that existed amongst the working
people and have prevented them by the
introduction of the Transport Board getting outside their own small towns. I
defy the Prime Minister or any other
Minister to refute my statement, that this
is the most socialistic State in the world.
The Northern Government, which
claims to be a Unionist Government, is
the most socialistic government in the
world. I defy contradiction on that.
There is hardly a thing that humanity
needs that is not controlled by this Government to the detriment of the people.
Take the Transport Board, for which certain sums are allocated. What happened?
A working man was formerly able to go
to the seaside on a mystery tour. Since
the Transport Board was set up these
mystery tours have stopped. Working
women during June and July used to be
able to go down to Millisle, Donaghadee
and Bangor for most of the day-

established holiday camps.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: For conscripts.
Mr. HENDERSON: No, not for
conscripts.
Mr. GORDON: Slavery.
Mr. HENDERSON : No. Those
children can go there if they like, and
they have special instructors to teach
them all sorts of games and to see that
they are fed properly. It is not the
same system as devised by the Minister of
Labour when he allowed a certain gentleman to take the workers' children to a
tent. It is not one of those camps where
certain people take men down to their
estate, get them to fell trees, dig trenches,
perform manual labour to the detriment
of the unemployed workers, feed them on
bully beef and potatoes, and then call
it a holiday. No. I do not want our
Ulster children to have to depend on the
North Belfast Mission, or on people like
the hon. and learned Member on the
other side of the House who takes a deep
interest in these affairs. I do not want
collectors to be running about with flag
days for this and for that. I want the
State to step in and give those children
the holidays they are entitled to as the
sons and daughters of loyal law-abiding
citizens.
If the Minister of Labour desired he
could establish a camp in Northern Ireland at which even young men who receive no unemployment benefit could
attend. You agree that the training
centres which you have set up
are
serving a very useful purpose. These
training centres have served a very useful purpose. It is quite true that the
Minister of Labour has turned out fine
amateur boxers in his training school,
but that sort of thing is not going to help
the youth of the country to keep their
parents. I suggest that the Minister of
Labour should organise holiday camps
for these young men and women, so that
they can have for a fortnight the enjoyment that falls to the lot of those who
live in a wealthier sphere. As an
Independent Unionist, I am suggesting
this to the Socialist Government that is
sitting opposite.
The Government, practising what they
preach, should bring in a Measure to
give to the children of the working people
of this country some happiness, in view
of the fact that their parents are too
poor to provide them with the necessary
travelling expenses. But the Government will go on and on, and nothing will
be done. Through the operations of the
Transport Board those children are going
to be denied the right to have a holiday
at the seaside. I demand, therefore,
that the Government set up a proper
holiday camp, supervised by intelligent
people, and that the boys and girls should
have an opportunity of the same enjoyment in life as the sons and daughters
of other people. But I need not ask the
Government to do that. That state of
affairs will not come about until the
intelligent people of this country realise
that a properly constituted Government
with brains could bring this about with
no great disadvantage to the finances of
the country. In any case, I suppose I
will have to leave that in abeyance until
the new order of things in a couple of
years, and the right hon. Gentlemen are
sent by the electors into oblivion.
Take
the conditions that exist in Northern
Ireland. What is the true position? The
true position is that we are never going
to have a new industry of any importance.
Two of the hon. Members for the County
of Antrim will admit that the Ballymena
Sunsheen Company was established.
What was wrong that it went bankrupt?
Mr. CRAWFORD: That factory was
not in Ballymena.
Mr. HENDERSON: Well, outside
Ballymena. That is only a quibble,
worthy of a schoolboy quibbling about
marbles. That was a new industry that
was going to work wonders in absorbing
the unemployed.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Did you object
to it?

against what is contained in these estimates. For the prevention of tuberculosis
in Northern Ireland the Government is

Mr. ANDREWS: One branch.

There
is
Rev. Professor CORKEY:
only one point in the Budget to which
I wish to refer, and I will do so in a
word. Comment has been made upon the
fact that we are to make an Imperial
contribution this year of some £400,000,
and it has been suggested that that money
will be spent on munitions. Complaint
has been made by more than one speaker
that any of our money should go in that
direction. This is, perhaps, rather an
affair for the Imperial Parliament, but
at the same time as the 3d on the income
tax extends to Ulster I think in connection with our Budget we are probably
in order in making a brief reference to
this matter. This is a question on which
I think very few people can think truly.
I would like to say I have no sympathy
with the merely passivist position. I
have no belief in the theories of those
who imagine a system of law, either in
the civil state, or in the international
world, can obtain and continue to exist
without force. It cannot be done.
Mr. BEATTIE: Do you say that
seriously?
Rev. Professor CORKEY: Nevertheless I have just as little sympathy, and
just as little approval for the mere
militarist, who imagines that we should
throw overboard all attempts to establish
a collective system, and simply build up
a big navy and a big army of our own,
and depend upon force alone.
I am
proud to think that the Imperial Government, to which we are making this
contribution of £400,000, has laid it
down that the sheet-anchor of their
Imperialistic policy is the League of
Nations, I believe that the only hope of
the world lies in a policy which puts the
force of the world behind that collective
organisation. The world has tried for
2,000 years to maintain peace by
means of national armies, every nation
attempting to be stronger than every
other nation, which is a mathematical
impossibility. What the world needs is
an international court of justice to settle
disputes that arise and will arise, human
nature being what it is, between individual nations, and I think unless, in
addition, we come to realise that that
court must have force behind it, if it is
to win respect and to continue to exist,
I can see no hope for civilisation. I
trust that our Imperial Government,
using our money, will make no attempt
to re-organise the League of Nations in
the immediate future, so as to take out
of it all reference to, and all possibility
of sanctions, making it thereby a mere
worthless debating board.

for the University is going rather wide
of the Budget statement. I have allowed
him to refer to the subject matter of his

Budget surplus is going to the Imperial

see that there are to be increased bonuses

the present time it is a voluntary effort

There is one other item I would like
to refer to. Hon. Members will remember that last year the Minister of Finance
in introducing the Budget, as a sort of
sop to Members of Parliament when they
were not getting the 15 per cent. cut
restored, introduced an entirely new
system of paying Members attending
Committee meetings £2 2s a day. Personally, I think now that the 15 per cent.
cut has been restored to Members this
special allowance of £2 2s should be
abolished. After all, we are human
beings, and the fact of being paid £2 2s
for attending Committees leads to a
temptation to lengthen out the meetings
for another day's sitting. The hon.
Member for Pottinger quite clearly agrees
with me in that, because on Thursday
when the Budget was introduced he said,
referring to the restoration of cuts to
Members of Parliament, "I am not too
delighted about having the full restoration." He went on to say further, “I
believe I do my work better when I am
not getting paid than when I am paid.
I feel that when I go into work in detail
I am looked on as one who wants to
prolong the business I am engaged on."
Further on in his remarks he said, "I
think it would be better sometimes if we
were not paid." That is a remark I
quite agree with. Speaking for myselfand I am sure for other Members-I
would feel much more comfortable sitting
on Committees if I were not paid two
guineas for attendance. There is a sort
of impression left on the public that if
the Committee sit for a day or two longer
they are doing it for the purpose of
getting paid two guineas.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I have heard every
Budget presented in this House, but I
never listened to one with greater pleasure
than the one we had introduced on
Thursday by the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Barbour). From my standpoint
there are few things to criticise, and I
feel I should say nothing at all, but I
would like to stand behind my hon.
Friend (Rev. Professor Corkey) in expressing my regret that the Minister had
to say that a sum of £400,000 would be
given for increased armaments. I am
sorry that at this late stage in the history
of the world the principles of the Prince
of Peace have not even greater force over
the whole world than they have at present. It is no mere pleasure for a person
like myself to be placed in the position
to say that we must to some extent
provide armaments sufficient to make our
defences sure. Personally, I would much
rather see this contribution given to
reduce the debt on the nation incurred
as a result of the last war, and that it
was not necessary that through ignorance
or the jealousy of other nations any of
this money should be spent on armaments.
I am not saying that in a critical way.
I simply desire to express the feeling that
I stand for peace, but we must under the
circumstances provide sufficient armaments to preserve our defences. I congratulate the Minister on bringing in a
Budget which is of a satisfactory nature
and meets with the approval of the
people.

intend to detain the Committee by

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I beg to move
in Clause 6, page 10, line 5, at end of
Sub-Clause (5) to add-" Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions of this subsection, the additional sum shall not be
payable in respect of eggs sold by the
holder of a retailer's licence who is also
the holder of a Class A licence under
section one of the principal Act, where
the eggs are sold for use in manufacture."
In the course of their trade wholesale
dealers naturally find a large number of
second grade eggs left upon their hands.
The only method of disposing of these
eggs is to sell them to bakers and other
confectioners. I should emphasise that
the eggs are perfectly edible eggs,
although they do not comply with the
high standard which is prescribed for
"Fresh" or "New Laid " eggs.
Technically such sales to bakers and confectioners on the part of Class A licence
holders are retail sales. If, however, a
licence fee of d per dozen were imposed
upon these eggs the effect would be to
increase the incentive on the part of
bakers and other confectioners to purchase imported liquid eggs. I am sure
that no Member of this House would wish
to see the extension of this class of sale.
The object of the Amendment is to prevent any such incentive arising.
Amendment agreed to.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: This Clause
gives the Ministry rather extensive
powers. What it purports to do is this:
There are various classes of licences,
Class A, Class B, and retailers' licences.
This Clause roughly means that a person
who is now engaged in the retail trade
and also in the wholesale trade may be
refused one or other of the licences to
carry on his legitimate business either as
a wholesaler or as a retailer. The Minister may say, "I am not going to give you
a wholesale licence. You must be a
retailer," or he may say, "I am going to
give you a wholesale licence but not a
retailer's licence." It is rather unfair to
say that a man who is already trading is
not to be allowed to carry on his business
because the Ministry objects. The reason
the Ministry objects is that there are
many persons in the egg trade who carry
'on a retail and a wholesale business in
conjunction. Such cases may give rise
to administrative difficulties, and the
Ministry has taken power to refuse more
than one licence in cases where such difficulties may arise. Because of administrative difficulties a man is to be deprived
of part of his livelihood. I think that is
wrong and, therefore, this Clause should
be deleted from the Bill. To say that
simply for administrative reasons a man
who may have carried on business for
years is to stop it is rather arbitrary.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am quite unable to accept this Amendment. I consider it is in the highest degree important
and eminently reasonable that where a
person is a holder of more than one licence
under the Marketing of Eggs Acts the
Ministry should be empowered to impose
special conditions with regard to the conduct of his business. I may say that in
the past it has not been the practice of the
Ministry to issue Class A licences and
Class B licences to the same persons; such
licences have been separate and distinct.
If, as the hon. and gallant Member suggests, Class A licence-holders were able
to obtain a Class B licence without restriction, it is not too much to say that
the whole administration of the Acts
would become impracticable. I cannot
help thinking that in putting down this
Amendment the hon. and gallant Member has not appreciated its far-reaching
effects, and the fact that it is, in effect,
attempting to abolish the distinction
between Class A and Class B licenceholders, which was distinctly laid down.
in the Act of 1931.
I may just elaborate that by showing

carry on the work.

1, to leave out the word "Ministry" and

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I regret that
I am unable to accept this Amendment.
To do so would, in effect, mean that the
administration and control of the Egg
Marketing Fund established under the
Act would be placed in the hands of a
Committee which would not be accountable to Parliament. I feel sure that the
vast majority of hon. Members will agree
with me that it is preferable that funds
of this kind should be controlled by a
Department of the Government which is
responsible to Parliament and should not
be placed under an independent body
over which this House could exercise no
control whatever. I may add that this is
not exactly on a par with the Pigs
Marketing Board. The Pigs Marketing
Board actually carry on trade as a Board.
In this case the Committee will not carry
on trade. The Minister must be in a
position to answer for the administration
of the fund in this House, and obviously
the Ministry must have control of the
fund.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The right
hon. and gallant Gentleman has clarified
the position by his explanation. I quite
agree that the fund should be under

NEW CLAUSE (Inspection of foreign
eggs).
The Ministry shall provide by regulations for the inspection at their port
of arrival of all foreign eggs imported
into Northern Ireland. (Major
McCormick).
Brought up and read a First time.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: On a point of
order, I should like your ruling. As I
understand the Amendment which the
hon. and gallant Member has put down,
it would in effect interfere with trade,
and this Government, under the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, has no power
to interfere with trade.
The CHAIRMAN: I have carefully
considered this point. The Amendment,
as it stands upon the Order Paper, proposes that-
The Ministry shall provide by regulations for the inspection at their port
of arrival of all foreign eggs imported
into Northern Ireland.
It provides for nothing more than inspection. It does not even provide for
grading or for rejection on the ground
that they are not fit for human food. I
will allow the hon. and gallant Gentleman to discuss the New Clause, but as it
is obvious that it merely provides for
inspection, and does not provide for any
consequences, its effect will be almost
nugatory.
Major MCCORMICK: I beg to move,
"That the Clause be read a Second
time. This New Clause deals with the
inspection of foreign eggs, and has nothing
to do with the importation of eggs.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. and
gallant Gentleman has not quite caught
the point. Under this Bill the Ministry
already have the right of inspection.
Major McCORMICK: Not of foreign
eggs. I say that under this Bill the
Ministry are seeking to regulate our own
egg production, but they have no right
to prevent the importation of foreign
eggs, which are imported in many cases
against our wishes. We can only make
our protest against their importation;
there it begins and ends. I say that we
should protect ourselves against strong
rival competitors who send in foreign
eggs, whether in shell or in liquid form
in cans or containers. We have no say
in the importation of these eggs, but I
think we should have the right of inspection.
The CHAIRMAN: Would the hon.
and gallant Gentleman help me? Does
he merely propose inspection, and that
these eggs can still come in without let
or hindrance?
Major McCORMICK: I am on the
question of inspection of what does come
in. I have inquired into this matter,
and I find that into the port of Belfast
there are imported something like 688
tons of tons of foreign eggs, Chinese,
Finnish, or Danish. I am dealing with
eggs as we understand them. If many of
our people knew of the quantity of these
eggs being imported, or thought that
they were partaking of them, they would
be amazed.
The CHAIRMAN: I may point out
to my hon. and gallant Friend that the
mere inspection of these eggs, without
the power to prohibt their entrance for
the purposes of sale, would be absolutely
futile.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: May 1
point out that what the hon. and gallant
Member seeks is inspection only. If on
inspection these eggs are found to be
bad, the inspector is then in a position
to send to the local sanitary officers and
have them taken away.
The CHAIRMAN: That is not provided for in this Clause.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: It is the
law. If they are bad it is the duty of
anyone who knows to notify the sanitary
authority.
Marketing of Eggs Bill-
Committee
20 MAY 1936
The CHAIRMAN: That may be a
high moral duty, but this new Clause
lays no such injunction on anyone.
Mr. MIDGLEY: It should be borne
in mind that the local public health
authority has power of inspection at the
present time.
The CHAIRMAN: I have already
pointed that out.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to
stress the point that once a thing comes
within the confines of our municipality
we have existing power to deal with it,
provided that the inspection reveals a
certain class of badness. I will have
more to say about this matter on the
Motion for the Adjournment, when I
raise a matter of which I have given the
Minister notice. I should like to ask the
hon. and gallant Member for St. Anne's,
what kind of inspection does he mean?
Define the word "inspection."
The CHAIRMAN : That is what I
have been inviting the hon. and gallant
Member to do.
Major McCORMICK: I think I still
have the floor. In reply to the Member
for Dock, I say I would have those eggs
inspected by an analyst in the ordinary.
way. I understand that foreign eggs in
any form are not allowed to enter the
Irish Free State, and I respectfully
suggest that what is not good for our
Southern neighbours should not be
allowed to enter this country. It seems
an extraordinary thing that after we
have cultivated our egg production in
this country we should be faced with this
strong competition in the form of foreign
eggs. In a report on a test of Chinese
eggs published by "The Scientific
Poultry Breeders Association Ltd." it
is stated:-
That after thawing and attaining
normal temperatures, and although
protected from atmospheric contamination, marked bacterial multiplication
occurs, resulting in the putrefaction of
the product and rendering it unsuitable for use.
The CHAIRMAN: Will the hon. and
gallant Member look at Clause 13, paragraph (2), and he will find that this
Bill has not anything to do with liquid
eggs.
Major McCORMICK: I am not speaking of liquid eggs, but of foreign eggs.
The CHAIRMAN: But the hon.
Member is giving to the Committee a
reason for this new Clause, that reason
being liquid eggs, and he will find on
looking at the Clause I have mentioned
that this Bill has nothing to do with
liquid eggs.
Mr. NIXON: With your indulgence,
Mr. Chairman, and the indulgence of the
Committee; I might be able to clear up
this entire matter. It is a very extraordinary thing that this new Clause
comes from the Government benches.
There is a reason for all that. The
Government at the present time are very
unpopular.
The CHAIRMAN: But surely-
Mr. NIXON: Give me a chance.
The CHAIRMAN: But the hon.
Member must confine himself to this new
Clause.
Mr. NIXON: I have heard it said
that there is a large consignment of
rotten eggs ordered for the next election,
and the object is to keep out those eggs.
The CHAIRMAN: I thought the hon.
Member got up to clarify the position.
(Laughter.)
Mr. NIXON: The people want rotten
eggs to throw at the Government Members at the next election, and this new
Clause is brought forward to keep out
those rotten eggs, and I am not going to
support it. Let the people pester them.
as much as they like. They deserve it.
The CHAIRMAN: It is an agreed
case that so far as imports and exports
are concerned this House has no control
over them. It is also an agreed case that
so far as eggs may be unfit for human
consumption the remedy is already provided for under another Act, and is in
charge of another Ministry. What I
want the hon. and gallant Member to tell
me is how he proposes to carry out inspection without any consequential results
whatever, because that is not provided.
for in this Clause.

Major McCORMICK: There are eggs
other than liquid eggs imported into this
country in shell form, and I base my
case on that. I think the recent poisoning cases to which attention was drawn
in the Press, where the poisoning of
forty or fifty young persons was
attributed by the public health authorities to foreign eggs-whether in liquid
or shell form I do not know-justifies
this Committee in dealing with the
matter. Steps of some kind should be
taken to inspect these eggs, and I beg
to move the new Clause.
Mr. MINFORD: I support this new
Clause, and I think it is one the Minister
should incorporate in the Bill.
The CHAIRMAN: But is this a competent new Clause? How is it to be
operated? That is the real point.
Mr. MINFORD: The object of this
Bill is to provide and make sure that the
people of Northern Ireland and Great
Britain get nothing but good fresh eggs.
No less than 800 tons of foreign eggs
are imported into Belfast annually. Do
you think they are brought in to throw
at Members of Parliament or for food?
The CHAIRMAN: This House has no
control over exports or imports. That is
reserved to the Imperial authorities.
This new Clause provides no method and
no punishment.
Mr. MINFORD: I know we have no
power to prohibit imports, but surely we
have power to say imports that are bad
should not be given to our people for
food.
The CHAIRMAN: That is provided
for under another Act.
Mr. MINFORD: This is a very
important Clause, and it is unfair that
these foreign eggs should come in without
inspection.
The CHAIRMAN: That will not put
this new Clause in order.
Mr. MINFORD: The Member for
Dock said the local authorities had power
to deal with this matter, but they only
take action when cases are reported to
them. If anyone visiting the port sees
a crate of eggs broken they stand as far
away as possible. If the Minister is
anxious to give the public nothing but
good fresh eggs he will agree to have
these foreign eggs inspected. In the case
of foot and mouth disease the Ministry
control the movements of cattle, and yet,
because this Clause seeks to do the same
in the case of eggs you rule the Clause
is not a competent one.
The
CHAIRMAN: Perhaps the
Minister of Agriculture will help us to
elucidate this point.
as
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I understand
that the control of the Public Health
Acts is in the hands of the Ministry of
Home Affairs. It does not come under
my Ministry. The Ministry of Agriculture can inspect imported eggs
suggested by the hon. and gallant Member, but after that their function ceases
and they cannot do anything more. As
I have already explained to the House,
each imported egg must be marked on
the shell with the word "Foreign" or
"Empire," or the name of the country
of origin. Any consumer who has
suffered from the effects of eating foreign
eggs should have learned his lesson and
should in future buy only fresh eggs
that are produced in the United Kingdom. Inspection will not accomplish anything, and the power to inspect already
exists but is not vested in this Ministry.
Mr. MINFORD: Surely it is not too
much to ask the Minister to inspect
foreign eggs when it is remembered that
many cases of food poisoning have been
attributed to these eggs. If the object
of the Clause was to prevent people
poisoning themselves by alcohol or by
other means we would pass it without
question.
The CHAIRMAN: It is now time to
make a definite ruling, and in my judgment this is not a competent Amendment. What it seeks to do can already
be done under existing Acts, and in fact
it could not be done by this Ministry.
That ruling does not debar the hon. and
gallant Member from having a further
run for his money. If he feels aggrieved
by my ruling he can submit the new
Clause again on the Report stage and
obtain the ruling of the court of appeal
upon it.

Mr. NIXON: Regarding this question
of old age pensions, the Minister of
Labour knows, of course, that a lot of
us entertain the opinion that something
more will have to be done for the old
age pensioners in Northern Ireland than

Estimates-
Old-Age Pensions
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. NIXON: I accept that ruling,
but regarding the administration of old
age pensions I am going to touch a point
on which I had the support of the
Minister himself on a former occasion,
but the Minister weakened in his support
through the intervention of the Minister
of Home Affairs. It has been a wellknown fact for a considerable time in
Northern Ireland that when old age
pensioners were compelled through illness
to go into hospital they were robbed, and
that was established. And I want to
know what steps are being taken even
now to see that that practice is not being
continued.
Very queer and peculiar things have
happened in Belfast in that respect even
in the last seven or eight months. I
wrote to the Minister on this question
in the month of July some two or three
years ago. When an old age pensioner
was taken to the infirmary at that time
the pension book was seized and the pension was confiscated and went into the
pockets of officials. In other words they
were being robbed. I had a fair idea of
what was going on, and I wrote to the
Minister about it, and he expressed great
sympathy. He sent me a letter for
publication in the Press to let old age
pensioners know that anybody in the
hospital had a right to their pension
without their consent.
Mr. ANDREWS: No. The other
way.
Mr. NIXON: Yes, you did.
Mr. ANDREWS: You put it the
wrong way.
Mr. NIXON: I stand to be corrected.
I repeat it again. The purport of the
Minister's letter was that when an oldage pensioner went into hospital the
hospital authorities could not take his
pension without the consent of the
pensioner.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is right.
Mr. NIXON: That is what I meant to
say if I did not say it. I am obliged
to the Minister. When it was pointed
out to the Minister that the consent was
being obtained under duress, that a document was put round to the pensioner and
he was asked to sign it, and the pensioner,
a poor old person lying in bed, did sign
it. And there again the Minister was
sympathetic, and the Minister sent an
official to the house to see that the
pensioner got fair play. But this great
Board of Guardians took exception to the
presence of the official in the house and
the Ministry of Home Affairs—although
there was no open breach between the two
Ministries-sided with the Guardians and
the robbery continued, until a gentleman
in a very high financial position was
arrested and prosecuted and convicted
and sent to jail and let out and liberated
and appointed, with the consent of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, to a high
financial position in another public
service. Does anyone challenge that fact,
because we know, by a recent Act of
Parliament, no public body can appoint
an
official without the authority and
approval of the Minister?
The most remarkable thing is that a
certain gentleman, a Guardian who led
the opposition to the Minister's officials
going in to see that these old-age
pensioners would get fair play, is the same
gentleman who is the leader and at the
head, to a certain extent, of the Board
that appointed this convicted thief to a
high financial position in another public
service. It is worth coming back from
Australia the whole way to expose that
job in this House, if I never did anything
else. I want the Minister-and I have
not any doubt at all about the sympathy
of the Minister and the honesty of the
Minister, and I hope the strength of the
Minister-in future to see that there is
no more of this brow-beating and robbing
of old-age pensioners in these institutions.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am much obliged
to the hon. Member for Woodvale in
bringing this matter before me, and it
shall receive my attention.
Question put, and agreed to.

headquarters there are 23 clerks." Let

I am coming now to the huge amount

do we find? We find that the largest percentage of house-breaking in the history
of the Province has taken place. We find
that Belfast has been subject to annual
disorders, and heavy cost has been put

police force seething with discontent.

That is only one factor. The other is

to visit South Derry, a very nice place,
a very nice constituency, and a very nice
people, represented by a very admirable.
representative from the Tory party point
of view.
Mrs. PARKER: You did not say that
in Maghera. (Laughter.)
Mr. MIDGLEY: I told the people in

although the hon. Lady is admirable from
the Tory point of view I think the constituency would be better represented by
a Labour representative. I told them

right to do that as the hon. Member
herself has to come to the city of Belfast
and ask the electors here to support certain

continue to do that.
Mrs. PARKER: I did not indulge in
personalities.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I very seldom use
personalities because the force of my logic
is so strong and my arguments so indestructible that I do not require to deal
in personalities. The hon. Member knows
that. She has already paid a tribute to
me because of what I did in South Derry
in that connection. When I was in
Maghera there was a policeman taking
notes. I have seen policemen taking notes
before. I hope they are always able to
read their notes, because I am told that
shorthand is a very difficult subject to
decipher sometimes. The meeting in
Maghera was a purely peaceful one of
ordinary Labour propaganda within the
limits of a constitutional political party,
recognised as such by all sections of the
community not only here but in Great
Britain. I found when that feeling was
voiced that some of the people in Maghera,
being used with only one kind of political
meeting, were being driven to accept the
viewpoint that the very presence of the
police indicated that there was something
wrong either with the organisation under
whose auspices the meeting was being held
or with the personality of the people who
were addressing the meeting. I merely
raise this question in order to indicate
that at meetings such as ours, when that
is so well known to the responsible authorities, I think it is not necessary at all
for this expensive representation at public
meetings, particularly in country places.
Country people do not understand the
Labour movement, and they do not know
it so well as the townspeople, because the
industrial centre has its trade union movement to a much greater extent than the
rural areas. When you have a meeting
in a country place, and you have present
several policemen, some of whom
taking notes, it has an effect upon the
psychology of the people that it does not
have in a democratically controlled community such as ours.

Some hon. Member sitting

with my party, got up and asked if the

right hon. Gentleman would answer the

Sir DAWSON BATES: It might satisfy

Mr. MIDGLEY: But there were people

That is the kind of meeting which some

There cannot be a very narrow conception

methods, but that they wish to seek to
sent.
bring about a change by democratic and

I am recognised in this city as an

Having asked him for that apology,

as they sometimes do. I do not hold a

and for their control. I would like that

and have some regard to the nature of
the meetings. I know there is a fundamental difference between holding a meeting in Dock Ward during a general
election and during a trade dispute,
because in one case passions are somewhat

who were on strike is indicative of what
I am trying to get at.
On that occasion there was no necessity
for a parade of force, because the people
under whose control the demonstration
was held were people whose public reputation in this city is a hundred per
cent. for the observance of law and order,
and they have the respect and confidence
of the people of Belfast generally. Surely
we who represent people who are protesting against starvation wages-about which
we shall hear more next Tuesday—have a
perfect right to organise any lawful
assembly in order to focus public attention
on their grievances. That is one case
where a great deal more commonsense
should have been brought to bear. I know
it is very hard to dogmatise. I realize
that the feeling in Belfast may change.
from day to day, and that a particular
district may be the centre of antagonism
this week, and that the following week,
and for a long time afterwards, it may
be as calm as the Pacific.

I recognise that fact, but if the police

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sorry the
hon. Member for Dock should have taken

week. He will, of course, appreciate that
the police have a great responsibility. It

and even riot, as unfortunately he and I

Member to accept my assurance that I
would be very sorry to suggest that he
would take part in any illegal meeting
which had for its object the destruction
of our Constitution. The hon. Member
talks about the psychology of the people.
Psychology is a wonderful word, and if
there is no objection I am not sure that
it would not be a good thing to have
classes on psychology. I have heard of
mass psychology and other forms of
psychology.
I want to assure the hon. Member that
we desire that our police force should be
absolutely impartial and no matter what
an individual's politics may be he is
entitled to the protection of the law
through the police. I can assure the hon.
Member that I did not for a moment
intend to suggest that he would take part
in a disloyal meeting. The police cannot
divest themselves of the ultimate responsibility for the good conduct of public
meetings. If a meeting called for a
lawful purpose is started in an orderly
manner and subsequently becomes riotous
it is no excuse for the police to say they
thought it was going to be a peaceful
meeting. I hope the hon. Member will
accept the assurance I have given him.
Question put, and agreed to.

like the right hon. Gentleman to take

to keep on repeating the fact that the

Although he may be a criminal in the

Mr. MIDGLEY: In conformity with
the notice which I gave the Minister of
Agriculture, I now wish to raise a
matter of public importance. The
Minister in reply to a question a few
days ago-Tuesday to be precise-on the
question of the importation of eggs of an
inferior quality and unsatisfactory condition gave the following reply :—
The protection of the public from
dangers arising from the use of foods
which are unfit for human consumption
is a matter for the local sanitary
authorities, and Parliament has armed
these authorities with adequate statutory powers for dealing with all food
stuffs unfit for human consumption.
Moreover, imported eggs must, if offered
for sale, be marked either with the name
of the country of origin or the word
"foreign" or "Empire," and this in
itself affords a considerable degree of
protection to the public, since it enables
intelligent consumers to form an opinion
as to the freshness or otherwise of the
eggs which are offered to them.
If that were literally correct, in the working out it might offer to the public all the
protection which the public thinks it
ought to have, but, strictly speaking,
that is not exactly the position.
Under the Public Health Act of 1878,
Sections 132 and 135, powers such as the
Minister has defined in his reply, are
given to the local authorities, but when
you come to the question of eggs, what
do you find? You find that the public
health inspection with regard to eggsand that is why I asked the Member for
St. Anne's what he meant by inspection
-means, in effect, that the local
authority being the public health
authority has not the power to seize these
eggs unless they are physically loathsome,
putrefying or absolutely obnoxious to the
public taste. As a matter of fact, the
main thing which is overlooked in regard
to the inspection of eggs is that the real
test is a bacteriological test, not the test
of your nose. I remember an officer telling me once to watch out for gas, and on
asking him how I would know, he said I
would smell it. It is the same with eggs.
The only basis on which the local public
health authority can seize these eggs is if
they are unpleasant to the nose and eye
-if they bear the obvious and visible
signs of putrefaction. The eggs, however, that come in tins and containers can
look all right to the eye, as far as broken
eggs can look at all, and yet they can bear
within themselves the seeds of disease. I
am speaking as a member of the public.
health authority, and in this capacity I
warn the citizens and ask the Minister to
face up to this that we have submitted
liquid eggs to our city bacteriologist, and
twelve months ago we got a completely
adverse report with regard to the standard of eggs which were permitted to come
in and which satisfied the requirements of
the Public Health Act. Bacteriologically,
they were unsound, and contained within
themselves the seeds of
many diseases.
The Member for St. Anne's, who
referred to a recent outbreak of disease,
is strictly correct in regard to the incidence
of that disease in Belfast. We are very
loath on the public health authority to
pillory any local merchant if we can
Imports of Foreign Eggs 1720
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
possibly help it, but we must protect public health. As a member of that
Committee I know where the pastries
were made; I know the firm; and I
know that the ingredient used was the
white of Chinese eggs.
We have inspections carried out at present, and the
reports are adverse. They are proving
that these liquid eggs come into Belfast
no matter how they pass the test provided by the Public Health Act of 1878,
while they will not pass the best of all
tests, the bacteriological test. What is
the inference to be drawn? It is that the
Public Health Act, in so far as it affects
the importation of eggs of physical
imperfection visible to the eyes and nose,
is an impracticable Act. It is inadequate
to the situation. What is really required
is complete prohibition of the import of
these rotten commodities altogethercommodities that are coming in in the
spirit of commercialism to enable somebody to make a bigger profit in the manufacture of pastries Eggs which are a
detriment to public health should be
excluded.
If we have not power within the framework of Parliament to take steps what
ought to be done is for the Minister of
Home Affairs or Minister of Agriculture
to get in touch with the Minister of
Health in Gt. Britain. Local authorities like Liverpool have carried out
examinations in the same way as Belfast
and have been able to prove as a result
of the bacteriological test of eggs that
unsound eggs are a menace to public
health. There may be an outbreak of

contagious disease any time, and yet
under existing legislative powers we are
helpless to take the steps we would like
to take. You should ask the authorities
on the other side to face up to the
question of public health against commercialism, and public health implies
prohibition.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
hon. Member who has raised this point
does not fully appreciate that under the
Public Health Acts ample power is given
to the local authority, which, in this case,
is the Belfast Corporation, to take proceedings in regard to the sale of unwholesome food. I cannot understand how the
Belfast Corporation, of which he is a
distinguished member, have not taken
steps to prosecute the vendors of such
commodities.
In regard to the other question, which
is an entirely different thing, the importation of eggs from abroad and other
matters, that does not come within the
purview of this House. I would suggest
that the hon. Member should make
further inquiries in regard to the steps
the Belfast Corporation are taking, and I
can assure him that so far as my Ministry
are concerned we will do all we can to
assist the Belfast Corporation in putting
an end to the sale of unwholesome food.

Marketing of Eggs Bill.
As amended considered.
NEW CLAUSE (Amendment as to
revocation and suspension of wholesale
dealers' licences).
Paragraph (b) of sub-section (1) of
section one of the Act of 1931 (which
relates to the revocation and suspension of the licences of wholesale
dealers in eggs) shall have effect as if
the following proviso were added
thereto :
"Provided that the Ministry shall
not revoke or suspend a licence granted
under the said section unless the
holder thereof has been convicted of
an offence against the principal Act,
or it is proved to the satisfaction of
the Ministry that he has habitually
failed to pay for any eggs purchased
by him, or, if he is the holder of a
Class A licence, that he has failed to
pay-
(i) any prescribed sum payable by
him in accordance with this
section; or
(ii) any additional sum payable by
him under sub-section (5) of
section six of the Marketing of
Eggs Act
Act (Northern Ireland),
1936."
Brought up and read a First time.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): This new Clause,
and the Amendment which I shall
shortly be moving, seek to implement
the undertaking I gave to deal with the
question of revocation of licences. This
matter was raised on the question of
retailers' licences, and it seemed to me
only right that the same principle should
apply to shippers and collectors, that is
A and B licence holders, and that is what
the new Clause is designed to do.
I should like the House to clearly
understand that the procedure set out in
this new Clause is precisely in accord
with the method the Ministry follows in
administering the existing egg legislation. It is quite true that the Ministry
could have revoked licences before
obtaining a conviction in the courts, and
the fact that it was not our practice to
do so makes it reasonable to frame the
provisions in accordance with what is
our established practice. I beg to move,
"That
the Clause be read a Second
time."
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause accordingly added to the Bill.
NEW CLAUSE (Saving for sale of
eggs for refreshment purposes).
Nothing in this Act shall apply to
the sale or offer or exposure for sale in
an hotel, boarding-house, restaurant
or other place of refreshment, of eggs
intended for consumption as part of a
meal or refreshment provided at such
place.

NEW CLAUSE (Inspection of foreign
eggs).
The Ministry shall provide by
regulation for the inspection at their
port of arrival of all foreign eggs
imported into Northern Ireland, and
may report to the proper authority
eggs which, in the opinion of the
Ministry, are unfit for human consumption.
Brought up and read a First time.
Major McCORMICK: I beg to move,
"That the Clause be now read a Second
time." While recognising the difficulties
that surround its inclusion in the Bill,
I think I have the sympathy of the
House with me in its object, and its
relationship to egg legislation generally.
I need not go into the whole matter
of health that lies beneath the Clause.
As the hon. Member for Dock yesterday
on the Adjournment dealt in a most
exhaustive and clever manner with that
phase of it, it is needless for me to add
to it. As we know it is not in our power
to prohibit the importation of foreign
eggs, especially Chinese eggs, yet I
think I may be pardoned if I point out
how very impotent we are in such a
vital matter-vital to the health of the
community and dangerous to the
real objects which this Bill has in
view. After all, that is the object of
the Bill we are now discussing. If
foreign eggs of any kind are allowed into
England, it may be right, I say advisedly
it may be right, to allow them in, yet I
claim that the importation of eggs affects.
us as an agricultural area more than it
affects England.
I feel we ought to take congnisance of
that fact. I take into account the differences in our population and trade, and
I say that we should in some way, such
as by representation to the Imperial
authorities, claim the right to prohibit
such eggs from entering Northern Ireland.
I desire to press this matter, and if I
get the Minister's consideration I shall
feel I have gained something even if
I do not get the Clause through. This
Bill ostensibly provides for the betterment
of the egg industry and for obtaining
eggs of better quality. Yet we are in the
ludicrous position of allowing unfair competition from eggs that are of such an
inferior quality that they are a danger to
the health of the community. On these
grounds I press this New Clause.
Question, "That the Clause be read a
Second time" put, and negatived.

The principle of the Bill is that in
future eggs are to be sold on the basis of
quality. There we are just getting down
to the key that unlocks for us the great
British market. The key to unlock the
British market is quality, and it is no use
Ulster simply producing as good produce
as can be got in England, Scotland, and
Wales. If we want to remain at the top
of the market we must turn out products
of just a little bit better quality that will
make people say, "Ah, you may get good
eggs here and there, but if you want the
best eggs, then buy Ulster eggs." That
is the object of this Bill, and I commend
it to the House.

element to be considered certainly the
consumer would pay more, but it is sometimes possible, under schemes of coordination, to place on the market a
better product which commands more
universal respect and custom so that there
is no consequent increase in the charge
to the home consumer. If the hon. and
gallant Member used ordinary elementary
commonsense he would be bound to arrive
at that conclusion. Does the hon. and
gallant Member or any other Member
think that I, as a member of the Labour
Party and as a member of a trade union,
would deliberately and with malice aforethought, come here merely to support
Measures because they coincide with a
political philosophy of mine regardless of
the economic consequences?
Major MCCORMICK: I would not be
surprised.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I do not think you
would be surprised at anything. I
would not be surprised, indeed, at anything you do or say. In approaching this
question you have to remember that
stupid people have arrived at the conclusion that things in the time of their
grandfather are still the things of to-day.
There are people in this House who talk
glibly about the rights of the small man
as if the small man in the community
bore the same relationship to economic
fashions as he did in the time of the
industrial revolution. They do not
realise that economic conditions have
changed. It is because they have
changed that great Conservative leaders
in Great Britain are now supporting
Measures which it is said savour of
Socialism. Any time they support coordination in regard to marketing or
farm produce or anything like that, they
do it because they expect something more
will be done than can be done within
the ambit of the present system. The
Prime Minister said that when you could
not get the Ulster farmers on a voluntary basis to co-operate to the general
good it was essential to bring in compulsion by legislation in order to achieve
what he considered was for the good of
agriculture collectively speaking. If you
cannot because of the selfish impulses of
some men get this co-ordination which
is required in the national interests, then
you have to have it by legislation.
Do not think that this Bill is Socialism
It is not Socialism. It is not Socialism
in so far as co-ordination and making
the commercial unit the whole Parliamentary area are concerned. It is Socialism
so far as the objective is concerned, but
not in its actual working. Socialism,
let me point out, means collective ownership not only of the means by which
the product is put on the market, but of
the product and industrial fruits generally. I am hoping as a result of the
schemes of co-ordination we will be able
to begin the task of doing something
which has not been done yet. I hope
that by united marketing we will make
our home market as well as our export
market as good as they ought to be, and
that we will begin to remunerate labour
in the agricultural districts in the way
I would like to see it remunerated.
The Prime Minister said if the agricultural community was badly off so was
the industrial community. The opposite
is more true. If the industrial unit is
depressed you are bound to have depression in agriculture. The end is the
same from the economic point of view.
If you want to co-ordinate your industries you have to do it so that economic
fruits will accrue to the hewers of wood
and drawers of water. I am as much
1753 Marketing of Eggs Bill

21 MAY 1936
Estimates
against certain aspects of exploitation of
consumers as anyone. The question is-is
the market not as good as it ought to
be; is the market permanently abused
because of some commercial practices by
certain people? The alternative to that
is to provide a better system of coordination whereby the proper product
will be put on the market and there will
be a common ground for trade for our
own people. That is sound commonsense and good economics.
May I commend this thought in conclusion? It ought to be the bounden
duty of every person here to see to it that
schemes which are brought forward in this
community are not considered on a basis
of prejudice, bad feeling, bad temper, and
lack of knowledge. Schemes brought forward, whether they are in regard to transport, eggs, milk, or anything else ought to
be considered from the point of view of
how they are going to affect the economic
interests of the people involved, and how
they are going to work out with regard to
the wellbeing of the whole community.
Question put, "That the Bill be now
read the Third time."
Mr. SPEAKER stated that he thought
the Ayes had it; and on his decision being
challenged it appeared to him that the
Division was unnecessarily claimed, and
he accordingly called upon the Members
who supported and who challenged his
decision, successively, to rise in their
places, and he declared that the Ayes had
it, two Members only, Major McCormick
and Mr. Henderson, who challenged his
decision, having stood up.
Bill accordingly read the Third time,
and passed.
Ordered, That the Clerk do carry the
Bill to the Senate and desire their
concurrence.

Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to raise a point
on this Estimate for my own guidance.
In the details of the headquarters' staff
in Part III I find there are eight employees given. I want to inform you, sir,
that that is not a true return of the
numbers employed in the headquarters of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary. There
are 43 additional people employed there,
and there is no account of them under the
detailed heading. I would like you to see
that we have the true cost of all those
employed at the headquarters presented
to us in the Estimates next year. This
item says there are only eight persons
employed there when there are 51.
Mr. SPEAKER: It is clear to me that
a question of that kind should be raised
before the Public Accounts Committee.
The notice of the Comptroller and
Auditor-General should be drawn to any
point which the hon. Member thinks is
not in order.

that every penny piece of expenditure in
connection with the Police Service
appeared, and properly appeared, in its

usual and proper place in the Estimate.

Oral Answers to Questions.
CONTRIBUTORY OLD AGE AND
WIDOWS' PENSIONS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of applicants for a contributory
old age pension at 65 disallowed during
the five years ending 1st May, 1936,
and the total number of claims for
widows' pensions which have been disallowed during the five years ending 1st
May, 1936.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In reply to the hon. Member's question, in the five years preceding
31st March, 1936, which is the latest
date for which figures are available, 2,682
applications for old-age pension at 65, and
2,694 applications for widow's pension
were disallowed. These figures include,
however, a number of applications which
were subsequently admitted and a number which are at present the subject of
appeal.
OPERATIONS OF TRADE BOARDS.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the result
of the operations of Trade Boards in
Northern Ireland; whether they have
tended to improve the conditions of the
workers covered by such Boards; and if
he can state the effect upon the relationship of employers and workers operating
in industries covered by Trade Boards.
Mr. ANDREWS: In those trades in
respect of which it has been found
necessary and desirable to establish
Trade Boards, I understand the Boards
have given general satisfaction.

do not allow of the delivery of goods by

any building.

any restriction, such as the hon. and
gallant Member indicates, in the Workmen's Compensation Act or Regulations.
Major McCORMICK: Will the Minister take it from me that to my knowledge goods which have been delivered-

LABOURERS' COTTAGES IN
MOIRA.
5. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that a large number of labourers, including ex-Servicemen, have applied to the
Moira Rural Council for cottages and
that up to now no action has been
taken.

(Sir Dawson Bates): 43 applications for
cottages have been received by the
Moira Rural District Council.
The Council have not yet indicated
what action they propose to take in connection with these applications, but the
Ministry has no reason to believe that
they do not intend to give them the
necessary consideration.

the total number of promotions to the
rank of sergeant which have taken place
in the Royal Ulster Constabulary in the
two years ending 1st May, 1936, and
the number of constables who received
promotion by a qualifying examination
as laid down by the regulations.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number
of constables promoted to the rank of
sergeant in the two years ending the

1st May, 1936, was 76. Of this number 46 had passed the technical examination; 20 were promoted in accordance

were filled by special promotion without

Every constable who had qualified for

KIDNAPPINGS IN DERRY.
7. Mr. MURPHY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has seen
reports of the recent kidnappings in
Derry of two children from their Protestant foster-parents, and whether he
can state if the Government propose to
restore these children to their fosterparents and to prevent the recurrence
of such kidnappings.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts so
far as known are at present before the
Attorney-General, who is considering
what action can be taken in the matter.
DERRY SHIPYARD AND
ARMAMENTS PROGRAMME.
8. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he
can state
what representations, if any, the Government have made
to the British
Armaments Committee in order to have
the Derry Shipyard reopened for the
construction of ships, etc.
The PRIME MINISTER: As I explained to the hon. Member in answer to
a question on April the 7th last, communications with the British Government relating to National Defence are
necessarily of a strictly confidential
character and cannot be made public.
I may add that the hon. and learned
Member for the Maiden City, and Sir
Ronald Ross, its distinguished Imperial
representative, are constantly engaged in
watching over the interests of their constituents and that their efforts are fully
appreciated and supported by this Government.
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the right
hon. Gentleman tell me exactly what
are the efforts that are being made on
behalf of the unemployed of Derry?
REPORT OF COUNCIL FOR CIVIL
LIBERTIES.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON (by private
notice) asked the Prime Minister if his
attention has been drawn to a report
by a committee called the Council for
Civil Liberties, and what action the Government propose to take as regards this
document, which is not substantiated by
the publication of the evidence alleged
to have been taken.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have had
my attention drawn to the allegations
contained in the publication referred to,
and the Government propose to issue an
official reply. In the meantime, I would
respectfully suggest that no importance
should be attached to a document containing such misrepresentations. The
Government believe that this grossly
biassed publication emanates from a
similar source to other propagandists
whose sole ambition is to see the establishment of an All-Ireland Republic.
To this I need hardly say the loyalists
of Ulster will never agree. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Sir ROBERT LYNN: May I ask if
the right hon. Gentleman has taken into
consideration the fact that this Report
may encourage Sinn Fein gunmen to
repeat what occurred in 1921 and 1922?
The PRIME MINISTER: We have
not overlooked that aspect nor any other
consequences of this publication.

COUNTY
FERMANAGH QUARRY
WORKERS.
Mr. MIDGLEY (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Labour whether
the local employment exchange at Lisduff, Maguiresbridge, has supplied any
workers to a road contractor named P. J.
Clarke; whether he has inquired into
the wages and conditions of such men,
why their services were terminated at
short periods; whether he is satisfied
that all the necessary insurance conditions have been fulfilled by their employer; and, if not, whether he will
take steps to prevent any further labour
being provided by the employment
exchange.
Mr. ANDREWS: As my hon. Friend
knows, I have had very little time to
ascertain the facts, but I feel I will be
justified in saying that since the
beginning of April, the employment
exchange at Enniskillen has supplied
thirteen men to the employer named for
quarry work. The wage notified to the
exchange by the employer was 21s 4d per
week. My Department has no evidence
that the services of these men were dispensed with after short periods or that
insurance contributions in respect of
them were not duly paid.
Eight men who were recently submitted by the exchange for further
vacancies with this employer, and who
refused the employment, alleged that the
employer was not willing to pay the wage
of 21s 4d per week notified to the exchange, and inquiries into their allegation are at present being made.
Adjournment of the House (Summer).
Resolved: "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until 12 noon
on Tuesday, the 23rd of June, and that
after the report of Royal Assent to Bills
agreed to by both Houses, Mr. Speaker
do adjourn the House without Question
put, until Tuesday the 13th of October,
provided always that in the event of any
Bill or Bills being returned from the
Senate with Amendments, the House shall
meet on Wednesday, the 17th of June,
and shall transact its business as if it had
been duly adjourned to that date, and at
its rising shall adjourn until 12 noon on
Tuesday, the 23rd of June; and further,
provided that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation
with the Government, that the public
interest requires that the House shall
meet at any earlier time during the
Summer Adjournment, Mr. Speaker may
give notice that he is so satisfied, and
thereupon the House shall meet at the
time stated in such notice and shall
transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date."-(The Prime
Minister.)

the remaining stages of the Appropriation

Mr. BEATTIE: I think an opportunity is afforded me on this occasion of
going into points arising under this Bill
which I feel should be emphasised.
has been very widely and loudly expressed in the Six Counties that we are
living beyond our means, and that if we
do not put some check on the wasteful
expenditure that is taking place we may
find ourselves in the position of a ship.
whose waterline is far below the water
and gradually sinking to the bottom of
the sea. I would make every effort to
save that position from the point of view
of the unemployed, widows and orphans
and old-age pensioners. We had the
Budget statement by the Minister of
Commerce and a surplus was presented
that in our mind was a very handsome
figure. Certainly since 1924 we have not
had a figure commensurate with that
amount. The point arises what is the
best thing for the Government to do with
that amount? Is it a question of preserving the lives of the citizens of Ulster
and giving them the decency and comfort
that everyone agrees they are entitled to?
In my opinion that is the way the money
should be spent, but we find that we are
not spending the money in the Six
Counties. We are to hand over that
amount of money to Great Britain, and it
will be spent amongst the British workmen and population. If we were a rich
State and had that golden harvest each
year, perhaps my objections would not be
so strong on this occasion.
we are in an
May I say
I say that
impoverished state. We are absolutely
hanging to the poverty line. The working classes, especially the unemployed,
are really in a position that could not
be compared with that prevailing in any
area in Great Britain. They are living
here under conditions which are limited,
and they are restricted and prevented
from enjoying the step by step policy to

being handed over so that the people in

Mr. BEATTIE: I am sorry I transgressed to that extent. I was coming to
the Estimates, but, perhaps, my points.
in leading up were rather lengthy. The
money which I was referring to could
