The Parity Agreement, which brings in
£550,000, was conditional on the
Government honouring the step-by-step
policy in regard to benefits and conditions. The Northern Government has
not honoured that condition, and that in
my opinion, is the first violation that
has taken place regarding the Parity
Agreement. The second point is that the
qualifications are far harder to fulfil in
the Six Counties than in Great Britain.
I have no doubt about that statement,
Appropriation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
and I am going to give an illustration.
In our Estimates provision is made for
the public assistance grants. We have a
condition set out by the House as to
where this money can be applied. We
put down a regulated form, which was
compiled by the British Authorities,
that the scales of benefits were to be
paid in accordance with the household
means. That seems to be all right in
words, but in actual working out it is
all wrong. It is all very detrimental to
the interests of family life.
Last week I had the experience of
having a Scotsman and Irishman presenting their case to me. The Scotsman gave
me his views as to the conditions applying to him in Glasgow. He lived in the
home of his father and mother, two
sisters and a brother. His father and
brother were employed and one sister was
employed half-time. This man, who is
30 years of age, resided in that home.
When he went to the Assistance Committee they applied a regulation which
was suitable to the district and made a
grant to that man although his family
income exceeded the amount laid down
by 30s. a week. Let me give the case of
an Ulsterman whom I represented last
week. He is living with his father, two
sisters and a brother. His father was
recently employed and his brother was
employed. The difference between the
ages of the Scotsman and the Ulsterman
was three years the latter was 27. He
was told last week by the court at which
I was present that the family income
exceeded the amount laid down in
regulation by £1 and, therefore, he
would have to expect his father and
other members of his family to maintain him while he was unemployed. That
is laying down the law very definitely
in this area. It is certainly more elastic
in Glasgow.
When a boy becomes 25 or 30 years of
age surely it will be agreed that parental
control has passed away and that he
becomes a self-dependent person and has
no right to look to his parents to maintain him? I want to come to the point
that the conditions under the grants for
public assistance are applied more rigidly
in Northern Ireland than in Great
Britain. They are preserving the family
life in Great Britain, but we here, by a
rigid adherence to the conditions, are
breaking it up. That will never, I hope,
be accepted by this House. The Minister
may try to explain away the statements
I am making, but I make them with full
authority behind me, knowing the mode
of procedure.
I go a further step and ask the
Minister why he refuses to give the
grounds of the disallowances at those
courts after the courts have come to
their decision. That is getting away
from the step-by-step practice. Under
the Unemployment Insurance Act I can
appear at the court and present my case,
and at the end of the summing up they
give their decision. It is handed to me
at the end of the court, but a public
assistance court absolutely refuses to give
the decision which it has arrived at,
proving conclusively they have not the
courage to tell the applicant the reason
he is disallowed. Why do you not follow
step by step with Great Britain? The
instructions are that no decision must be
given to the applicant or his representative, but after they have gone money
must be spent in posting the decision on
to the applicant. That is an extravagant
method of administration. The applicant
has to wait a period of two days so that
they can spend 1d. on a stamp in posting the
the decision. I appeal to
Minister to direct that public assistance
courts shall give their decisions in the
same way as the unemployment insurance courts. That would save the people
of Northern Ireland a very heavy postage
charge.

Then I come to the question of education. Our educational services and
administration in Northern Ireland are
not getting a fair crack of the whip. We
set out in 1923 with the object of making
this area what I may call a New
Jerusalem as far as education is concerned, and we attained a certain amount
of success. We established a very high
standard of efficiency, but what do we
find in 1936. When prosperity is still
round the corner we are putting round
education anchors that are likely to
hinder or hamper the progress that we
have been making for the past number
of years.
I ask the Minister of Commerce, who is acting as Minister of
Finance, to go very slowly and to take
into consideration every element he
thinks necessary for the better carrying
on of our educational system before any
obstacle is put in the way of the
children receiving the full benefits of
the service. I make that appeal to the
right hon. Gentleman on the grounds
of, may I say, inside information.
I wish to refer next to blind pensions,
although I have sandwiched education in
between. The administration of old-age
and blind pensions has certainly been
tightened up. I cannot understand yet
why you hit the most helpless section of
the community so hard. The Blind Persons Act, in my opinion, is being very
harshly administered in so far as those
people who have a percentage of sight
are concerned. They may be able to see
enough to walk about the house, but
they cannot with safety cross the street.
Those persons have been denied blind
pensions. I think that indicates a
rigidity of administration which the
framers of that Act never intended, and
I make my annual appeal to the right
hon. Gentleman to give that matter
sympathetic consideration, and to relax.
that firmness he has applied so that it
will be administered as in Great Britain.
In regard to the old-age pensions at

The other point is on the administration of prisons. I think prison life in
Ulster is not just all it should be. You
can have all your reformers and have
them setting out on paper what should be
done to reform criminals, but is there any
such thing as a criminal? My experience
leads me to believe that the birth of a
man into the world and the environment into which he comes have a great
Ideal to do with his future in life.
may go the right way or he may go the
wrong way. It is an old saying that
there is a little bit of good in the worst
of us. I think that applies to our
prisoners. The life of prisoners in
Northern Ireland to-day-and when I say
prisoners I mean life prisoners and those
who are sentenced to three years or over.
I do not refer to short-term prisoners
sentenced to under three years does not
tend to give the reform which is necessary.
A man does not get that relaxation or
assistance which gives him a brighter
outlook in life. The stringent and
limited scope of the prison in which he
is domiciled tends, not to make him have
a bright outlook but to get into his mind
thoughts of evil, such as if he were once
If the Government would only take the
cue from me in this respect and build
the necessary prison we could secure these
reforms. I do not speak now of the old
hardened criminal type. We have young
men in prison in Ulster to-day who, in
my opinion, could be reformed and made
into good citizens. If you bring about
the same conditions in that prison as
exist, say, in some of the larger prisons
in England, you will get a very large
return of profit for the work you carry
out.
A penal settlement is necessary in
Northern Ireland, although there are only
thirty convicts. It would be necessary if
there were only one. I claim now, and
this is my last point on prisons, that
when a prisoner is sentenced to penal
servitude that sentence cannot be fulfilled under the present conditions of our
prisons in Northern Ireland. Penal
servitude carries with it an obligation on
the authorities to provide the necessary
conditions as implied in the sentence.
You cannot provide the necessary conditions, and, therefore, I might say you
are violating the conditions laid down by
the Courts when they sentence a prisoner
to over three years. I leave that matter
there in the hope that the future will hold
something better as far as the life of
prisoners in Northern Ireland is concerned.

Mr. O'NEILL: There is a matter in
connection with the Transport Board
services which I want to discuss to-day.
I noticed yesterday that they issued a
report in connection with their various
services and that some reductions have
been made in the fares. While I am not
much interested in regard to the fares, I
am considerably interested in relation to
the services. So far I think the services
which this Board is giving have not been
as good as they should be. Indeed I
think they will not be as good in the
future as they ought to be. When the
Bill which established this Road Transport Board was before the House I
mentioned the question of whether the
services would be likely to continue the
same as before, and was given to understand that in practically all instances they
would. I am speaking now in regard to
the question of bringing tourist parties to
the various towns, particularly on Sundays, though not altogther on Sundays.
but on Wednesdays and Saturdays as well.
I notice that in my own town of
Warrenpoint for the last two or three
weeks there have been practically no
buses. I believe this is altogther due to
the fact that these people have increased
the fares considerably and that they do
not organise these tourist parties at all.
Under the old system a bus owner who
had a service from various towns during
the week did not run that service on
Sundays but organised tour to the seaside. Unfortunately, there is no one to
organise such a tour now. It appears
that anyone who wishes can have a bus
provided he is prepared to undertake or
to guarantee a load. I do not expect
anyone would undertake that risk.
I suggest that the Board be asked to
organise these tours and appoint agents
in these towns. There are many towns
where this would be new additional traffic.
I think the Transport Board will seriously
retard traffic if they do not do something
in that respect. Another matter I wish
to mention is in connection with an
organised excursion that is about to take
place from, I think, one of the Government offices. I am not exactly certain

service to take them to Rostrevor. I

and that was all they could get. I am
not certain that is really correct, but if
it is the Transport Board must be condemned on that account.
I notice, too, in connection with the
tours which have been organised, that the

"Telegraph" have advertised a tour from
Belfast every Saturday to the Mourne
Mountains and various places. I understood that no one except the Transport
Board could undertake these services. It
would appear that Mr. Murphy, of Ballymena, had a case in which he was able to
establish the right to run these things, but
I understand an appeal has been lodged.
If the railway company have advertised
these would Mr. Murphy not have the

With regard to the reduction of fares,
I know that the reduction is really very

7s, which is really nothing. The fare

with the working-class people and I am
sure, like every other Member of this
House, I am appealed to with reference
grievances with regard to slight
shortage in stamps for unemployment
insurance. I have, on many occasions,
approached the officials, and I must say
they receive me very courteously. I do
not think there are any kinder-hearted
persons in this House than the Minister
of Labour and the Parliamentary Secretary. But, unfortunately, when we come
to press this matter they say the Act of
Parliament will not allow. I have been
wondering many a time could some change
not be made with reference to these very
hard cases. We find a woman with five
or six of a family whose husband was out
of work a short time before he died, so
that the poor woman and her family are
deprived of the pension. It is a very bad
case and it makes one feel very much that
the law is too hard and fast in these
cases. Then there is the other case of a
man who has unfortunately been out of
work for some time through no fault of
his own, and when he dies he has not
a sufficient number of stamps for the
widow to get the pension. I think it is
not impossible for the Government to take
into consideration some of these very hard
cases in which great distress must be felt.
I have, from time to time, gone to a
good deal of trouble and given officials a
good deal of trouble. Unfortunately the
law is against us. I would like to see
some amendment of that Act in order
that hard cases like these could be dealt
with in a sympathetic manner.

annual holidays.

as

and working conditions. The hotel

You know the subsequent history.
You know the reputation Belfast got
as a result of the industrial dispute. I must say that whilst I was
confined to the house ill I was responsible
for communicating the facts to leading
British newspapers, and there is scarcely
a part of Britain at the present time
where the conditions in regard to hotel
workers in Belfast are not known. I
do not want to create the impression in

are not, but seeing this has become a
question of some importance the national
newspapers, principally the "Manchester
Guardian," mentioned the fact that this

of Belfast represented the most degrading and inhuman conditions which were
apparent in all the large cities of Great
Britain. The "Manchester Guardian"
went on to express the hope that the

I want to tell this House something
else. You all know the discreditable
history which attached to that dispute.
You know that many workers went on
the street. Does any Member of this
House think that those workers went on
to the street as the result of diabolical

They were well aware from their personal experience of the sweating which

Northern Ireland, and which warranted

Those people suffered a great deal

I have a document here which would
simply amaze one in regard to conditions

hon. Members may be familiar with
some of the conditions prevailing in

staff, wash dining-room windows, also
hall inside and out, and call visitors
who require calling before 8 a.m.;
8 a.m. until 8-30, breakfast; 8-30 a.m.
until 12-30, attend dining-room doors,
meet all trains, both incoming and outgoing; 12-30 until 1 p.m., dinner;
1 p.m. until 3 p.m., on duty in the hall;
3 p.m. till 5 p.m., off duty, except when
any visitor may be leaving, in that case
work must commence at 4-30; 5 p.m.
until 1 a.m. (8hours) on duty in hall,
clean boots, shoes, etc. Total working
hours, 115; wages, 8s 6d per week."
That is for a man in a hotel at Portrush, which is famous for its natural
attractions, but not for any other kind
of attraction. I want to ask the House
to face up to this. Does that represent
the best that can be done? If it does
not represent the best how are you going
to get something better as a first step
in the right direction? I submit that if
it can be demonstrated beyond the
shadow of a doubt that it has been possible by negotiation to improve fundamentally the conditions in the catering
trade elsewhere it is not beyond the wit
of mankind in Belfast to do the same.
I was in contact with the representatives
of the Oxford Group movement during
the industrial dispute in Belfast-they
came to me, I did not go to them-in
regard to industrial problems. I found
them in many cases to be men who had
explored the economic and industrial
question in relation to the spiritual side
of life, and they informed me that in
some centres across the water the principle has already been put into practice
of fixing the conditions of employees in
hotels on the basis of a given wage per
week, cutting out the principle of
gratuities altogether.
Here in Belfast we have never faced
up to the possibility of this. In our own
country we can obtain a classic illustration of what can be done in regard to
hotels. I am going to submit that intellectually the people of Dublin are no
better than we are. The difference
between the two sections is that we are
a
more industrialised community than
the city of Dublin. If it can be demonstrated that in Dublin it was possible
to settle certain questions of wages and
conditions in hotels by negotiation, and
that that is working out well in practice,
why should we not face up to the
possibility of it here? We have a body of
employers in Northern Ireland who are not
prepared to do so unless a state of civil
war almost exists-which is something
nobody with an ounce of intelligence
wants. Nobody wants to plunge the
community into an upheaval, industrially
or otherwise. Therefore, seeing we are
faced with that position, and that we
have the disposition to avoid trouble, we
are compelled, in view of the adamant
attitude of the employers in the catering
industry, to come to Parliament and show
that all the fundamental reasons that
existed for applying Trade Boards to
other sweated industries apply to even a
greater extent to the catering industry in
Northern Ireland.
The Minister of Labour himself has
testified to the efficacy of Trade Boards
this afternoon. He has pointed out to
the House that Trade Boards are working well, and that the general administration of them in the industries to which
they are applied has worked out as a
good proposition for Northern Ireland.
I understand from him that approximately 55,000 or 60,000 workers in
Northern Ireland are covered by the

another Motion on the Paper, I do not
wish to take up the time of the House

appeal to the House to let us have a vote
on these Motions. Let us see what public
opinion is in regard to the advisability of
setting up some protective machinery for
these workers. I ask the House to look at
the history of Trade Boards. Had I the
time at my disposal I could go into the
history of the coming of the Trade
Boards, the conditions which preluded
them, the conditions which made them an
absolute inevitability in the economic life
of Great Britain and Ireland, firstly under
the Imperial authorities and then under
our own Government. And I want to
emphasise this point so that it will be
understood beyond the shadow of a doubt
that the conditions which existed in Great
Britain prior to the establishment of
Trade Boards are in existence in the
catering industry in Northern Ireland
to-day. I may be told by the Minister of
Labour or some Member of this House
that on one occasion in the history of
Great Britain a Labour representative, by
the name of Miss Margaret Bondfield,
expressed the opinion that this was not
a trade to which a Trade Board could be
applied. I want to state that that point
of view has been absolutely rejected by
the trade union Labour movement in
Great Britain. Miss Bondfield is not now
accepted as an authority on that question.
At Easter last I was present at a very
large centre in Great Britain at which
one thousand delegates attended and
amongst the questions debated was the
application of Trade Boards to a certain
industry. At that conference a demand
was put forward for the application of a
Trade Board to the catering industry,
and the sentiments expressed by the
speaker were received with applause by
the delegates present, who endorsed the
convictions of that particular speaker.
I refrained from indulging in any discussion at that time, because I wanted
next time I go to that conference to be
able to tell them that the bold pioneer
spirit of Northern Ireland had once
again come to the top and we were
pioneers in setting up a Trade Board for
the catering industry. If the Minister
will accept this Motion to-day it will
enable me to do so, and I hope the room
will ring on that occasion with the cheers
of the assembled delegates in appreciation of the efforts of the Minister of
Labour of Northern Ireland.
All the elements required by Great
Britain and envisaged by the statesmen
who set up the first Trade Board are
present in Northern Ireland. The hotel
industry of Northern Ireland is a
sweated industry. I have challenged
privately, and I now challenge publicly,
the representative of the hotel proprietors' association to meet me in conference in a public hall on a public platform or in the Press and to prove
beyond doubt that the hotel industry is
not a sweated industry. I will state the
case against them. In addition to being
a sweated industry the hotel industry is
a bad and insufficiently organised industry. Why? Because of the grave
unemployment problem with which we
are confronted and which enables hotel
proprietors like other bodies of employers
to get whatever kind of labour they want
almost at whatever time they like and
on whatever terms they like to dictate.
Because of the present abnormal unemployment problem they have been able
to fetter upon the industry conditions
which not only apply to the material
side of life but also to the spiritual side
of life. By the spiritual side of life I
mean giving expression to one's individuality. Why should the employer
deny the right to the worker that he
himself exercises? Why should the
Grand Central Hotel state to their em-

Just one word in conclusion on the
question of these hotels. The Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland, Viscount
Craigavon, attended a luncheon in the
Grand Central Hotel not so very long
ago. I got a cutting from the "Belfast
Telegraph" dealing with that luncheon,
and the luncheon was under the auspices
of the Ulster Tourist Development
Association. Prominently associated with
the Ulster Tourist Development Association are the hotels of Northern Ireland.
The Prime Minister made a speech on
that occasion. He was in happy vein,
and in that happy vein he used this
sentence:
"I do hope that the hotel proprietors of Ulster will never get so
swollen-headed that they will refuse to
offer to even the most distinguished
Oxford guests some of those Ulster
characteristics which bred the Ulster
race and which are still alive amongst
us, or lose the feeling that while we are
Ulster men we are still Irishmen."
Lord Craigavon expressed that sentiment and it was received with applause.
I re-echo that sentiment and I say in the
first place that ought to be applied in
regard to the treatment of the workers
under the hotel proprietors. If they
cannot deal justly and humanely with
the workers they cannot extend the
characteristic attributes of North of
Ireland people to the most distinguished
guest from Oxford. I appeal to the
Members of this House to try to develop
the same conscience in this matter-the
conscience that I have in regard to the
hotels of Belfast, that if I were invited
I would not enter the portals of one of
these places whose proprietors keep
grinding their workers down. Every
time I receive an invitation to a civic,
State, or private function carried out
under the jurisdiction of such hotels I
will send a polite intimation, as I have
already done, that I cannot associate
with people who are not prepared to deal
humanely with their workpeople. I ask
the Government to develop that conscience.
The Minister of Labour goes to the
Grand Central Hotel. Why does he not
try when in the Grand Central Hotelperhaps he does-I would like the Minister of Labour and the Minister of
Commerce to look upon it as a civic and
national duty every time they come in
contact with the people who own these
places to put up to them as professing
Christians and, good gracious, I do not
like to use that argument for it is the
most prostituted argument under heaven,
because all the poison gas extermination,
the starvation of mothers and fathers
and the degrading of wages and long
hours almost to chattel slavery-all
these things can be defended by people
who regard themselves as professing
Christians. In the most sacred sense I
Iwould ask the Cabinet Ministers and the
back benchers on both sides to take into
account the fact that these people have
been living for generations under intolerable conditions, that these conditions
bear no relationship to the economic
advance we have made and that they
ought to be changed as soon as possible.
One of the ways in which they can be
improved with success to the whole industry with attendant security is under
the guidance and administration of a
Trade Board. That is number one.

these people. I think the heroism and

In industry it is very easy to see
that it is extremely difficult for the man
with high ideals to put his ideals into
practice if he has other men competing
with him who are harsh in their opinions,
and who are not prepared to recognise.
his principles and ideals. In this industry,
just as in many others, it is a case of all
moving together or none moving at all.
The tendency is when one firm is competing with another, or, as in this case, one
hotel with another, for the standards of
labour to be pulled down to the level of
the very lowest, and that is the reason
why I think the facts that have been put
before us should receive the careful consideration of the Minister. I may say
that the tendency in industry for many
years has been to resist anything in the
nature of sweating, even when sweating
seemed to be inevitable. There were times
when we were told that industry, for instance, in the cotton mills of Lancashire,
could not be run without child labour.
There were times when we were told that
the mines could not be worked economically without the labour of women, and so
it is suggested to us to-day there are industries which could not exist save on
conditions which seem to us to be very
harsh.
In addition to these general remarks,
I would like to say that I think the
employers of labour in these industries
would find that the establishment of a
board such as this would not militate
against their interests to the same extent
that perhaps at the moment they imagine
it would. When satisfactory conditions of
labour were established in the cotton mills
and the mines neither the cotton mills nor
the mines were compelled to close down.
In fact, the results were sometimes surprising, and it is possible that if a higher
standard in regard to conditions of work
was made compulsory in these industries,
the owners would find that the conditions
did not really militate to any great extent against their success.
So far as the cinemas are concerned,
judging by their appearance, there would
not seem to be any great poverty, and so
far as the hotels are concerned, even
although there might be great difficulty in
fixing grades of pay, I think that possibly
the hours of work might be regulated by
a Trade Board, even though the Trade
Board were for the moment confined to
regulations of that sort. I may say I
am not very conversant with the facts

fair to judge a case, having heard only
one side. I rose simply to say I
sympathise wholeheartedly with the
whole Trade Board idea, and I would be
glad to see it extended to any industry
to which it was thought it could be
applied.

Trade Boards are also a recognised
feature of our economic system in Northern Ireland. I am told there are 55,000
people protected and shielded by these
Trade Boards in Northern Ireland, and
the extension of the Trade Board system
to these particular industries surely cannot work any harm. It has not worked
any harm in any other case. I do not
know whether the hon. Member for Mid
Antrim dissents or not. I know of no
injury of any serious kind being done by
a Trade Board to either employer or
employee. They do prevent sweating.
Surely every Member of this House should
set his face like steel against the system
of sweating. There was a time when
sweating was supposed to be recognised
as an essential part of industry. That
was when the principle of laisser-faire was
in full swing, and when sweating prevailed in mines and factories. Men at
that time justified it on the ground that
you must not interfere with the liberty
of the individual; you must not hamper
the freedom of contract.
We have got long beyond that stage.
Sweating is unfair, and if there is any
trade to-day in which sweating exists I am
sure the feeling of the community, as a
whole, would be that that trade
if it cannot exist without sweating
ought not to exist at all. On those
grounds I do
do think these Motions
ought to commend themselves to the

the Minister will be well advised, if I

be done to either side by the setting up of

form of an arbitrator between the
workers on the one hand, and the employers on the other. It would probably
tend to prevent such a thing as the strike
which recently existed in Belfast, and
which must have inflicted very serious
injury on large numbers of poor people.
If a strike of that kind can be averted
by the wise and judicious intervention
of the State in the form of a Trade Board,
surely it is to the good of the community
that the experiment should be tried.

Now, I would like to say, on behalf of
the Government, that we do not desire
that any worker should be unreasonably
remunerated, nor do we desire that any

are special difficulties, as I think hon.
Members will admit. There is the
question of many of the employees receiving food and also board. There is also
the question of tipping. I am not going
to say, nor do I feel it necessary for me
to say, whether tipping is a good or a
bad system. What I do say is, that it
has been frequently tried in the United
Kingdom and elsewhere to do away with
it, and it has not been found possible to
do so. The reason is that people themselves generally like to pay directly for
services which they receive, and, if a
person visits a hotel and receives attention from an employee of the hotel, he or
she, as the case may be, desires to give
something in return. That, I take it,
was why tipping was established, and
that is why tipping remains part of the
system in connection with hotel management.

cent. I would give the job to someone
who had no pension-some disabled ex-
Serviceman. The people outside this
House will tell you that the Government
are simply creating jobs for people who
had been wealthy at one time. It is not
fair that the State should be saddled with
the burden of these people who, in the
ordinary way, could not get jobs at all.
I cannot understand why the Prime
Minister of this country gets such a salary
for the services he renders. We are not
an overworked assembly. It is only once
in a while there is any overtime. I think
some steps should be taken to reduce the
Prime Minister's salary and emoluments
by 50 per cent. I am living in hopes that
the day will come when the Prime Minister will receive only half the salary he
receives at the present time. I am not
speaking about the Prime Minister
personally, because I give way to no one
in this country in my admiration for the
Prime Minister as a man. I am referring
now to whoever was responsible for fixing
the salary of the Prime Minister at the
beginning, and for giving him a castle.
for a residence.
The cost of keeping up that castle is
absolutely terrible. Even the Minister of
Commerce, who is listening very patiently,
does not know the full cost of the upkeep
of that castle. It should have been
abolished long ago, and I would almost
have agreed with the proposal to build a
smaller house for the Prime Minister, and
the castle could then have been utilised
for State purposes. But no. Almost
every item he requires, from a needle to
an anchor, is supplied to the Prime
Minister. The Prime Minister should
rent or purchase a house, like every other
Member of the Cabinet, out of his salary.
I regret to have to say that, but in fairness to the people I represent, who are in
starvation, I have no other alternative.
I also believe there is a great duplication of services. Here is a case in point.
For half-an-hour, while the Serjeant-at-
Arms is away, we have a gentleman taking
his place who is drawing £570 a year.
The position of Serjeant-at-Arms and his
deputy could easily be filled by disabled
ex-Servicemen. When you contrast their
salaries with those paid to the attendants
and the charwomen it is amazing how
cruel the Government are to the poor and
how kind they are to the rich. The whole
thing is wrong, and the Government will
have to take drastic action to put a stop
to this evil of giving cushy jobs to their
political friends. They are creating a
system that will bring about the ruination of the country. There is a time
coming when the Government will have
no jobs to give away. What are they
going to do then? There is not a constituency in Northern Ireland from which
some of the Government's political friends
have not been pitchforked into a job.

pleasure of travelling about 300 miles
and seeing millions and millions of trees
planted on the mountain sides. These will
be a great asset to Great Britain in the
next twenty years. What has Northern
Ireland done of any importance in regard
to afforestation? Woolworth's has a
bigger stock of Christmas trees on
Christmas Eve than are planted on the
hillsides of Northern Ireland. There is
plenty of barren ground that could grow
beautiful trees. I contend that the
Minister of Agriculture could employ
hundreds of people, if not thousands, on
afforestation work. It would bring tears
to a stone to see fertile fields that have
no cattle on them. Is there not something seriously wrong when we see so few
cattle and so little crops grown? Why
should the fertile land of any country be
in grazing only? The land was created to
feed the people. You have only to go
outside the tram lines and you see the
most beautiful country, but it is just like
a derelict ship on an angry ocean.
The
land is being sadly neglected by an
apathetic Minister of Agriculture.
thought that when that young man came

What are the facts? Northern Ireland
gets as much sun as some other countries
that produce tomatoes. No encouragement is given to farmers to grow
tomatoes. In an odd area there are some
people who grow tomatoes, but they have
never been encouraged in this work by an
apathetic Ministry of Agriculture.
Thousands and thousands of crates of
lettuce which means millions and
millions of heads of lettuce-are brought
into Northern Ireland. If research work
on a proper scale had been carried out
farmers here could produce these lettuce.
The growing of lettuce would give employment in a season to a thousand men, who
would be engaged in weeding and thinning them out. The Government, however, is allowing the Ulster people to be
fed on Danish lettuce. That is a matter
of vital importance. Where has research
work been done in regard to foreign eggs?
What is the best thing to do to combat
the importation of anything from any
other country? It is to carry out educational and research work so as to teach the
farmers to produce the things that are
imported. No research work has been
carried out in this respect.
I saw the yolks and the whites of

The Free State Government-the right
hon. Gentleman might not have read this
in the Press-are going to manufacture
linen in the near future. They are going
to grow flax in the three Ulster counties
that this loyal Government deserted, that
is, Cavan, Monaghan, and Donegal.
They are going to pay the farmers a
subsidy to enable them to grow flax and
make a profit. If the Free State Government, in their wisdom-and I take no
interest beyond what I see in the papers
in the Free State-have definitely decided
that it would be in the interests of the
country to give a subsidy for flax, do you
not think it would be advisable for this
Government to do the same thing for the
farmers of Northern Ireland?
This is the finest country in the world,
and our people are the finest people in
the world. There are thousands of acres
of land suitable for the growing of flax.
How does it come, then, that there is
practically no flax-growing of any importance in Northern Ireland? Our manufacture of linen goes back a very long
time. Is there any reason why a larger
amount of flax should not be produced in
Northern Ireland instead of being
imported from Russia? Why do you encourage the Bolshevists and all the rest
to grow flax? Is there any earthly reason
why the Minister of Agriculture should
not call a conference of the farmers of
Northern Ireland and say to them, "If
you are prepared to grow more flax we
will give you a subsidy that will give you
a profit; in other words, we will guarantee
the price." There is no earthly reason
why the Minister of Agriculture could not
do that.
Unless this Government take drastic
action in so far as agriculture is concerned it is going to be very serious for
this Province. If in the event of a war
between Great Britain and some other
nation which might take place at any
time-Russia will have the flax markets
of the world in the hollow of her hand.
The Belgians will be in the same position.
Where is Northern Ireland going to get
the flax from which to manufacture
linen? I read recently that the Germans
were, practically speaking, prepared to
purchase all the flax that Russia could
produce. What will be our position in
Northern Ireland, a country which
depends on linen as one of her staple
industries, if we cannot procure the flax
necessary for the production of Irish.
linen? It is going to be a serious matter
in view of the millions of yards of linen
that are utilised in the construction of
aeroplanes, and it is deplorable that the
Ministry of Agriculture is so apathetic in
regard to the production of flax.

I could go on pointing out how the
Minister of Agriculture has neglected the

but it is not my intention to do so. I
would say, however, that a greater effort.
should be made by the Minister of Agriculture. After all, you must remember

The Minister of Agriculture is a wonderful man for looking after pigs, and the

Why is he not as brilliant in looking

The result is that the confidence of the
people is sometimes badly shaken. As an

Unless the minutes of the Mental

of the poor patients in these mental homes

I think that the different processes

the scientific treatment of boiling and

Northern Ireland to-day is consuming

industry created in this country. To

Madame Tussaud's is not in it.
dummies there melt in the sunshine, but

Take the
the Minister of Agriculture.

The Minister of Agriculture has now

here about six dictators.

Socialistic scheme of handing over the

of Ulster manufacture. Every time a

When the Belfast Corporation decide.
to build a school they have first of all
terrible trouble with the Ministry of
Education to get them to say whether
they will allow them to purchase the site
or not. When the site is purchased we
send the plans to the Ministry of
Education and what the architects of the
Ministry are doing is more than I can
understand. I think the last school that
was erected was in Tennent Street and,
notwithstanding the fact that we have one
of the most competent school architects
to be found in any part of the Empire, a
man who knows exactly what is required
for a modern public elementary school,
when the plans of that school were sent
to the Ministry if one letter passed there
were a dozen before the plans were returned. In many cases the Corporation.
have had to wait at least three months
before they got the approval of the Ministry for the erection of some of these
schools.
The hon. Member for Dock has been
one of the pioneers in regard to free
school books for all children. That is a
matter which deserves the serious consideration of the Ministry. I think the
hon. Member would even agree to forego
the city of Belfast getting free books if
they were given to poor children in agricultural districts for a start. If the
agricultural labourers' children get free
books then, on behalf of the people we
represent, we will agree to suspend the
operation of the scheme in Belfast for a
year. That would start the ball rolling.
If we want to make the children attending these elementary schools competent to
take over the reins of office when we lay
them down we must have them properly
educated. The feeding of these children
and the provision of free books are two
important matters.
The Government could easily find the
money, not only for free books and free
milk, but also to do something in the
matter of transport. The Ministry of
Education apparently do not worry at all
about how the children get to school.
Some of the children in the thinly populated areas have to walk three and four
miles to school. They are up in the early
hours of the morning. I was going over
the Dungiven Mountain to Derry one
morning between six and seven o'clock
when, to my amazement, I saw children
walking along the road with their schoolbags. I found out from them that by
the time they reached the school it would
be about half-past eight or a quarter to
nine. Just picture those sons and

[Mr. Henderson]
daughters of agricultural labourers and
the predicament they would be in if it
began to rain before they reached the
school.
I have made many suggestions to the
various Ministers concerned as to how, if
they so desired, they could bring about a
revolution so far as the living conditions
of the people of this country are concerned. You have ample scope. Nature
has endowed the Ulster people with the
finest land in the world. I do not think
there is more fertile land to be found
anywhere. Nature has put on to this
earth Ulster men and women, the equal
of whom can hardly be found in any
place. You cannot beat an Ulster man
or an Ulster woman for hard work, craft,
or pioneer work. Let the Government
supply the "dough" to help these people
to carry on the work of making Ulster
more progressive than it is at the present
time. I feel that I am quite justified in
the stand I have taken to-night in trying
to force the Government to do something
for the people who sent me here. They
are not the idle rich. They are the
workers, who have slaved unceasingly for
years and many of whom are at present
unemployed. On their behalf I appeal
to the Government to get going and to
provide work for them. I hope that at
least some of the matters of which I have
spoken will receive serious consideration.
re-
I have pointed out to-night, or rather
this morning, that there is nothing you
can mention so far as the animal world
is concerned, for which a Bill has not
been introduced to alleviate suffering.
The Ministry of Home Affairs was
sponsible for seeing that COWS were
despatched as quickly and as humanely
as possible. I do not want humanity
despatched, but I do want the same consideration given to the alleviation of the
distress that exists amongst the working
people of this country. I want them to
get the same consideration when it comes
to a question of the food they eat. The
cattle of Northern Ireland are well fed
and well housed, and you have special
veterinary surgeons to see that everything is done to make them healthy. I
want the same thing applied to humanity.
I want the Government to give the same
consideration to the people who are in
poverty.
Now that the Minister of Home Affairs
is here may I point out that it is rather
surprising that, despite his assurance
that when it came to a question of houses
obtaining the subsidy nothing but Ulster
or British made material would be used,
millions and millions of Belgian bricks
are coming into this country every day in
the week. I hope the Minister of Home
Affairs will take that matter up. If there
is a subsidy given the proper thing to do
is to see that nothing but Ulster material
is used in those houses for which it is
given; and failing that, Empire material
should be used. Under no circumstances
should we allow foreign material to be
used in the construction of those houses.
The Minister of Home Affairs has listened
with great attention to me, and I hope
he will see that a special effort will be
made to bring about a reduction in the
rents of houses. We here, representing
the intelligent people, are trying to
induce the Government to do something
for the downtrodden in the area. I was
marching along the countryside and I
felt terribly depressed in spite of the lark
singing over such beautiful scenery.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Was it a lark
or a cuckoo ?
Mr. HENDERSON: I am an expert
about birds. What I wanted to point
out was that the fields were like a quagmire, and there was not a COW or a
bullock or a horse to be seen for miles.
I think you might give assistance to
bringing in some form of drainage. Then
again the Government forget that there
is in existence in Northern Ireland a
paper mill. If they would only purchase
£500 worth of paper or stationery in the
year from them it would give some
employment.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
now repeating a former part of his
speech.
Mr. HENDERSON: I want to point
out everything I want the Government
to do for the emancipation of the working people. You could create more work
by building better houses and giving a
better public health service. I suggest
now that you put these schemes into
operation and give Ulster people some of
the benefits. We are not getting the

COST OF ALL-NIGHT SITTING.
2. Major HALL-THOMPSON asked
the Minister of Finance the number of

keeping the Houses of Parliament open
from 6-30 p.m. until 4 a.m. on Wednesday.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked to
reply on behalf of my right hon. Friend.
It is a condition of their employment
that the staff attached to this House is
required to be in attendance for such
time as the House sits and no increased
remuneration is paid as the result of late
sittings. The extra cost of lighting and
heating arising out of an all-night sitting
is practically negligible.
With regard to the cost of printing prolonged speeches of hon. Members, I am
sure that the hon. and gallant Member
will agree that oratory cannot be
measured in mere terms of monetary
value.

latitude and longitude?

are a violation of the working conditions
of the tradesmen and others employed in
this House, and whether he will recommend the Cabinet to pay overtime rates
immediately to employees attached to this
building for time worked exceeding an
eight-hour day?

STAFF ACCOMMODATION AT
STORMONT.
HALL-THOMPSON
(by
Major
Private Notice) asked the acting Minister
of Finance: In view of the rumours current in the Press can the Minister inform the House as to the nature of the
action which the Government propose to
take to relieve the congestion in the staff
accommodation in this building consequent on the growth of the various Marketing Schemes.
Mr. BARBOUR: I am glad that the
hon, and gallant Member has tabled this
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
question, as it affords me an opportunity
to inform the House at the earliest possible moment of the Government's decision
in the matter.
As hon. Members are aware, the policy
of marketing schemes under Government
control has received a further impetus by
It was
legislation passed by this House.
estimated a year ago that the removal of
the Ministry of Education to a building
purchased in the city, which will be
available for that purpose in the autumn,
would set free sufficient accommodation
to enable the use of the passages and
basement at Stormont for staff purposes
to be discontinued. The situation, however, has since been altered by continued
legislative activity, chiefly directed towards further agricultural development.
It was found that that scheme would not
provide for the return to Parliament of
the rooms on the ground floor which have
been temporarily loaned to the Government, and for which I desire to express
the appreciation of the Government not
only to the Speakers and Members of
both Houses, but also to members of the
Press Gallery. Accordingly, fresh consideration has had to be given to the
problem, and the Government has been
carefully considering the most economical
and effective manner of making provision
for all anticipated needs of a permanent
character.
After full examination of the question.
the Government has decided that the
most satisfactory and by far the cheapest
course is to construct rooms on the roof
of Stormont buildings. Not only can
this be carried through at a reasonable
cost because the expense of ground rent
in the city will be avoided, and because
the heating, lighting and sanitary
arrangements can be adapted at a comparatively small expenditure, but also the
concentration of staff in the building
rather than its dispersal in various offices
elsewhere will mean a saving in overhead
costs and in ancillary services, such as
messenger staff, supervision and so forth.
Before making this decision the Government has, of course, consulted Sir
Arnold Thornley, the architect of the
building, in order to ensure that their
proposals were sound from a constructional point of view, and also that there
were no objections of an æsthetic character,
and I am glad to be able to state that he
has intimated that in his view the proposals will in no way mar the beauty of
the building, and he is investigating the
constructional details. I may add that
owing to the height of the surrounding
parapet the new construction will be completely hidden from sight.
In providing extra accommodation on
the roof for an additional staff of 200 at
an estimated cost of £24,000 the Cabinet
has thought it advisable to look ahead
so as to ensure that as far as can be foreseen no further additions will be required.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the
expense to the Government of administering the various marketing schemes is
recouped by means of levies made on the
interests concerned, and in calculating
such costs a rental value is placed on the
accommodation in which the staff is
housed; to that extent, therefore, the
Exchequer will be relieved of the annual
charge in respect of the cost of this proposed new construction as well as of the
other services rendered.
It is not anticipated that the precincts
of the House itself will in any way be
disturbed during the progress of the
reconstruction works.

being tabled in the House this afternoon.
I avail myself of the opportunity to remind hon. Members that, when the first

averaging approximately 4 per cent. out

The last part of that order is a mockery

I need not say anything at all about his

is sufficient proof of character. I need

Mulgrew's statement:
"I am 38 years of age, and was born
and reared in Belfast. When a boy I
joined the Ulster Volunteers and was
one of Lord Carson's bodyguard at
Craigavon prior to the war. All the
Ulster Volunteer Force at Craigavon
at the time were fully armed and instructed to resist by force any military
or police attempt to arrest our leaders
or raid Craigavon. At that time excitement was high, and some of the
generals and military in Dublin refused
orders to come North, so that we believed the Army was with us. Later,
the war broke out and I joined the
Army, saw active service at the
Dardanelles and other places.
I was
duly disbanded from the Army, and
joined Brown Square B Special Constabulary at the formation of the force.
In December, 1923, I was arrested in
my home while an active member of the
Special Constabulary and taken to
Dover Street barracks. From there I
was taken to the Central Police Station
at Chichester Street and kept locked in
a cell night and day for a week in the
coldest of weather. From Chichester
Street I was taken to Crumlin Road
jail, and kept there for a few weeks.
Then I was taken to Londonderry Jail
and interned there for several months.
During all that time I never got a trial
nor was I allowed a visit from any of
my friends except on one occasion my
sister was permitted to speak to me in
the presence of the warder through iron
bars. After some months I was discharged from Derry Jail and sent back
to Belfast. On return to Belfast I
reported for duty to my station commandant and was continued on as an
active member of the B Class Special
Constabulary until three months ago.
No charge was ever made against me
and no compensation or apology was
ever offered me for the punishment, indignity and degradation imposed on
me by the Minister of Home Affairs.
(Signed) James Mulgrew.

2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked
Minister of Home Affairs if any persons
have been brought to justice for the
stoning in Ballymacarrett on Sunday
night, the 7th instant, of trains conveying passengers, mainly women and
children, from Newcastle.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have caused
inquiry to be made into the matter referred to by the hon. and learned Member, and I am glad to say that the
account of the incident as reported in
the Press is greatly exaggerated.
The facts are that an excursion party
while on its outward journey to Newcastle, when passing through Ballymacarrett gave considerable provocation by
making use of disloyal and objectionable
expressions.
As a result special police precautions
were taken to prevent molestation of the
excursionists. No stone-throwing was
observed by the police, but it was subsequently ascertained that on their return,
while the train was passing through
Ballymacarrett in the evening, some
stones were thrown, two carriage windows
were cracked and broken, and two of the
excursionists received slight cuts from
broken glass.
The police have endeavoured to trace
the parties responsible for the stonethrowing and are continuing their inquiries, but so far no person has been
made amenable.

say that the stoning of this train is a

Oral Answers to Questions.
SUGGESTED 40-HOUR WEEK.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to
bring in a Bill establishing a 40-hour
week for those engaged in industrial
work; and whether he is aware that
several leading industries have already
adopted the 40-hour week.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The introduction of a 40-hour
week in Northern Ireland by separate
legislation on our part would expose our
industries to disastrous competition not
only by industries located in other parts
of the United Kingdom but also abroad.
In the circumstances the matter can
only be dealt with satisfactorily on a
basis common to the United Kingdom
as a whole, as the hon. Member must
know, and so far as foreign industries
are concerned by an effective International Convention.

FREE BOOKS FOR ELEMENTARY
SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he is prepared to
bring in a Bill to provide free books for
all children attending elementary schools.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): In view of

the Ministry is not prepared to adopt the

Mr. BEATTIE: Is the hon. Gentleman aware that the education of the

a
WAGES OF GOVERNMENT
CLEANERS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE: asked the Minister
of Finance if he is aware that the rates
of pay and conditions of service of
cleaners employed by the Northern Ireland Government at Stormont and in
the several Government premises in the
city compare most unfavourably with
those of cleaners in such comparable services as that of the Imperial Government
(in e.g., the Belfast Post Office) or that
of the Belfast Corporation in the City
Hall, in that they are wholly denied paid
annual leave and paid sick leave, which
are accorded in the services cited, and
are, moreover, paid for actual work
done at a very considerably lower hourly
rate; and whether he will afford the
officially recognised representatives of
these Government workers an early
opportunity for discussion with him of
the inequitable conditions under which
they serve.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Pollock) (who was received with
cheers): Male cleaners at Stormont and
Government offices in the city (who are
exclusively disabled ex-Servicemen) are
allowed paid leave in respect of bank
holidays and the King's Birthday, a total
of nine days per annum. Paid annual
leave as ordinarily understood is not
allowable except that up to a week's
leave with pay is permitted if the
cleaner's fellow workers make up
equivalent time, without extra pay, for
the absentee. They are not entitled to
paid sick leave. The remuneration is at
the rate of 1s per hour, and the men
work 48 hours per week.
I understand that in the Head Post
Office in Belfast the male cleaners work
a 48-hour week and are paid on a scale of
45s, rising by 2s to 49s per week. They
are allowed one day's leave with pay for
each month's continuous service, plus
bank holidays, and when sick are
allowed leave at two-thrids rate of pay
for a limited period.
With regard to cleaners in the City
Hall, I am informed that they work 441
hours per week for a wage of 50s, and
after 12 months' service are allowed six
days' leave per annum in addition to
six public holidays. Substitutes are not
engaged to replace absentees. No paid
sick leave is allowed.
If the men themselves so desire I am
prepared to hear a small delegation from
their number.
Perhaps I should add that cleaners in
the service of the Government of Northern Ireland work a continuous shift
daily, whilst in the other cases cited
there are split duties, that is to say, two
shifts, which is something of a handicap.
Finally I might say that the question
of paid sick leave for these men has
been receiving my sympathetic consideration.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the statement of the right hon. Gentleman I
think this question of cleaners and their
conditions will be best spoken to on the
adjournment of the House.
HOLIDAYS WITH PAY.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to
introduce a Bill making it compulsory on
all employers to grant their employees
a fortnight's holiday each year with pay.
Mr. ANDREWS: If an Act of this
nature were in force here when similar
Acts were not operative in other manufacturing countries it would place our
industries at an economic disadvantage.

Failing, therefore, international agreement on the subject this Government
does not propose to pass separate legislation.
COST OF FOOD IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to
appoint a Select Committee to inquire
into excessive cost of food in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. ANDREWS: No, sir, I have no
evidence pointing to the conclusion that
the price of food is any higher in Northern Ireland than in any other part of
the United Kingdom.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
reply has the right hon. Gentleman
seen the reply from the Government to
a resolution from Newry in to-day's
papers in which they admit that the fourpound loaf is sold at a penny more in
Northern Ireland than across the water?
Mr. ANDREWS: No; I have not seen
the article the hon. Gentleman refers to,
but I imagine that what it refers to is
only one item.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the cost of rents,
eggs and bacon has gone up in Northern
Ireland to a very considerable extent in
the last two years?
Mr. ANDREWS: And probably also
in Great Britain.
Mr. BEATTIE: Not to the same extent.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
reply, would the right hon. Gentleman
not be as generous to the widows of small
farmers in Northern Ireland as they are
across the Border in the Free State?
Mr. ANDREWS: Speaking from
memory, I think we are more generous,
and in many services at any rate I am
quite certain the Free State are behind
us.
Mr. HEALY: Is it not true that in
the Free State the widows of small
farmers are entitled to the pension, and
is it not also equally true that they are
not entitled in Northern Ireland?
Mr. GRANT: Will the hon. Member
not consult the Imperial representatives
for Fermanagh and Tyrone and bring
this matter before the Imperial Government?
Mr. HEALY: If the hon. Member
knew anything of the proceedings he
would understand the Imperial Parliament has nothing to do with the question
of old-age pensions here.
TRAINING OF THE UNEMPLOYED.
7. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to
introduce a scheme for the training of
the unemployed.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have already
taken steps to set up a committee to
advise me
on the extension of instructional courses for unemployed juveniles
under 18, and other aspects of training
are receiving my careful consideration.
WIDOWS' AND ORPHANS'
PENSIONS.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is prepared to
introduce legislation granting pensions to
all widows and orphans in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. ANDREWS: Pensions for
widows and orphans are on a uniform
basis throughout the United Kingdom,
and it is not practicable to introduce
legislation which would break up this
uniformity.

Mr. ROBB: This matter is receiving
the careful consideration of the Government.

Mr. NIXON: I think, perhaps, in
this very small Parliament we might be
told why this Consolidated Bill is to be
referred to a Select Committee and not
left to the House. The Select Committee will be a committee selected by
As a matter of fact I
accidentally found this afternoon from
the Chief Whipone man.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I may explain the procedure to the hon.
Member. Of course we have had
Consolidation Bills in the past. The
practice of Parliament has always been
to appoint a Joint Committee of both
Houses in order to discuss the question
as to whether these Bills have been
properly consolidated or not. The hon.
Member, of course, understands that no
discussion takes place at any stage with
reference to the Bills themselves. The
Joint Committee is appointed simply to
go into the question of whether the Bills
have been properly consolidated or not.
That is the Parliamentary procedure; it
has really nothing to do with the Government.
Mr. NIXON: Is it Mr. Speaker's
ruling that that is done in the Imperial
Parliament and, therefore, we should
follow it?
Mr. SPEAKER: So far as I am concerned I have to use my own judgment
as to the proper procedure in this Parliament. What the Imperial Parliament
do has nothing to do with us. We have
our own procedure here, but the Imperial
Parliament have the same procedure in
appointing a committee.
Question put, and agreed to.
Ordered, That a message be sent to the
Senate to acquaint them therewith and
desire their concurrence.

pensions paid to widows.

hon. Member for Woodvale quite understands the procedure in connection with
these particular Consolidated Bills. The
only point that the hon. Member can

Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the
enactments with respect to the Capital
Fund established under the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, and to extend the
maximum period for the repayment to
the Government Loans Fund of advances
made to the Claims Fund.”—(Governor's recommendation signified.-Mr.
Barbour.)
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In moving this Resolution, which is preparatory to the introduction of an Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Bill, I propose to avoid details
and to deal only with general principles.
The Bill itself will be a very short one,
consisting of only two Clauses.
The first portion of the Resolution,
which relates to a new use of the Capital
Fund, arises from the fact that under
the new Reinsurance Agreement between
this Government and the Imperial
Government, which received the sanction
of this House earlier in the year, there
is no longer any necessity for the Capital
Fund to accumulate the income from its
investments. Hon. Members may
recollect that this fund in the main is
composed of the Northern Ireland share
of Irish Funds which were held for
particular purposes, such as agricultural
development and so forth. Instead of
leaving these services charged to the
funds it was decided by legislation in the
year 1923 that all such expenditure
should be placed on the annual Votes, the
apportioned moneys transferred to a
Capital Fund and the income of that
fund paid to the Exchequer. Subsequently, however, when the Ministry of
Finance was faced with the difficulty of
finding money to liquidate the old
borrowings of the Unemployment Fund
rl
1987 Financial Provisions
Census Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Barbour]
legislation was passed with the object of
accumulating the Capital Fund and its
accruing income until it was sufficient to
cancel the old debt.
Under the new Reinsurance Agreement, however, the old Unemployment
Insurance debt is to be liquidated by the
Government of Northern Ireland over a
period of sixty years at the rate of
£40,000 per annum, but only a small
proportion of this sum will be an ultimate burden on the Northern Ireland
Exchequer as the Agreement provides
that this yearly allocation shall rank for
contribution from the British Exchequer
in the same way as other excess expenditure in Northern Ireland on Unemployment Insurance.
For the foregoing reasons the Bill
which will follow this Resolution will
provide for reversion to the old method
of paying the income from the fund into
the Exchequer and will also make provision for drawing on part of the
invested moneys of the Capital Fund in
certain eventualities. I do not propose
to go into this last point in detail at the
moment as the purposes will be set out
more fully in the Bill.
With regard to the second portion of
the Resolution, this relates to the loan
made from the Government Loans Fund
to the Intoxicating Liquor Claims Fund
mainly in the year 1924. As the result
of intoxicating liquor legislation in 1923
abolishing spirit grocers' licences the
compensation to the holders of these
licences was to be met by means of a levy
of the
on the remaining members
licensed trade, the Government in the
meantime advancing the money which
was to be repaid by means of an annuity.
The amount necessary to pay
annuity is collected by a compensation
levy collected along with the ordinary
annual licence duty.
the
Under the Act of 1923 no definite
period was laid down for the repayment
of these moneys, but in the amending
Act of 1925 a period of forty-five years
from the date of the passing of the 1923
Act was provided. It is now proposed
to increase this period to sixty years,
that is to say, to allow the loan to run
for another forty-seven years instead of
thirty-two vears. This concession has
been sought by the licensed trade
because of the fact that despite the
abolition of the spirit grocers the
expected increase in the trade of the
remaining licencees has not taken place,
owing to the diminution in the consumption of alcoholic beverages. The
consequence is that the payment both of
the ordinary Licence Duty and of the
Compensation Levy is throwing an
unduly heavy burden on many licensed
premises. The extension of the loan will
afford some relief, and as there is no
question of any loss to the Exchequer
I am sure that it will have the approval
of the House. I would ask hon. Members to reserve any questions on points
of detail until the Bill is actually circulated. I beg to move.

Mr. POLLOCK: It had been my
hope, for financial and other reasons, to
avoid taking another census of population
until 1941, in which year we could have
come into line with the usual decennial
census in Great Britain and, indeed, in
other parts of the British Empire. The
last census in Great Britain was in 1931,
and in the Irish Free State in April of
this year.
Circumstances have arisen,
however, which suggest that it is at least
desirable to take a modified census of the
people in Northern Ireland at an early
date. It is more than ten years since
the last census was taken, and the estimates of population made from time to
Census Bill-
Second Reading
13 OCTOBER 1936
time for Northern Ireland as a whole
may now be regarded as of doubtful
value. The importance of this matter
will be fully appreciated when it is
remembered that Belfast, which contains
roughly one-third of the population of
Northern Ireland, has under consideration the possibility of an extension of its
boundaries. Apart altogether from
such questions of boundary changes, the
absence of reliable figures of population
renders it difficult to secure satisfactory
vital statistics, material which it is
essential to obtain for the formation of
sound policies in the matter of public
health alone.
The House will also readily realise
that following the economic collapse
which commenced in 1929, emigration to
countries outside Europe has virtually
ceased, and, indeed, at the present time
there is a small net inflow from those
countries. The extent to which this
cessation of emigration has been offset by
movements from Northern Ireland to
Great Britain may be material but has
not been recorded. Moreover, there is
some reason to believe that in recent
years there has been a tendency for
people to move from the Irish Free State
into Northern Ireland. A census taken
now will at least show the effects of these
movements. The present time is suitable for taking such a record since there
is some reason to think that emigration
to other parts of the British Empire at
least may be resumed at no distant date.
since
Again the House will realise that in
the matter of housing the Government
have spent nearly £3,000,000,
1926 in providing subsidies for the
building of houses. The redistribution
of population in Northern Ireland must,
therefore, be considerable, a redistribution toward which the development of
road transport in recent years has greatly
contributed.
A further point of some substance
which I desire to bring before the notice
of the House is that since 1926 the
number of births occurring in Northern
Ireland from year to year has been
steadily decreasing. In 1935, for
example, as compared with 1926 the reduction amounted to 12 per cent. This
trend has steadily continued in spite of
some very remarkable increases in the
marriage rate in recent years. It has a
very real bearing on educational
questions. The various points which I
have brought to your attention do not
exhaust the case for a census of population, but the House has my assurance
that in the opinion of the Government
the case to-day is sufficiently strong to
warrant the expenditure which will be
incurred.
Coming now to the provisions of the
Measure itself, it is perhaps sufficient
to say that the Bill is framed upon lines
similar to those adopted in the Census
Act (Northern Ireland), 1925. From
this general statement there are two
major exceptions, firstly with regard to
the date of the census, and secondly with
regard to the range of questions to be
asked. Broadly, the Bill provides that
a census of population shall be taken by
the Registrar-General under the supervision of the Ministry of Finance, that
for this purpose the officers and men of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary shall act
as enumerators, and that the Registrar-
General shall prepare reports and census
returns and lay such reports before both
Houses of Parliament at as early a date
as may be found practicable following
the census enumeration.
I should like to take this opportunity
to acknowledge the fact that the
operation of census taking involves an
inquiry into some of the intimate affairs
of each household in Northern Ireland,
an inquiry which some people have described as somewhat inquisitorial, but
which is absolutely necessary. Recognising this fact the House will appreciate
the need for the various safeguards
which appear in the Measure for the
purpose of securing that any information
obtained for the purposes of the census
will be treated as confidential.
In my
opinion this matter is of the utmost importance in order to remove any barrier
to the provision of information which
is as accurate as the circumstances will
allow.
With these more general remarks I
should like to couple a particular appeal
for care and accuracy in the census
taking. I do so, since in compiling the
results of the 1926 census it was discovered, for example, that the number
of people recorded as aged 50 was nearly
Census Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
contwice the number recorded as aged 51.
Moreover, so far as infants were
cerned it was evident that many of those
at the youngest ages had been omitted
from the census returns, either because
individuality had not been recognised by
the head of the family or possibly for
reasons of a more embarrassing nature,
for example, that the births had not been
registered within the period prescribed
for this purpose. Accuracy of record is
essential as a basis for well ordered progress.
Returning now to the special features
of the Bill, the first of these is to be
found in Section 1, in which the census
day is given as Sunday, 28th February,
1937. From 1851 onwards the census of
population has been taken at the end of
March or the beginning of April, and in
1926 it was as late as the 18th April.
The time of year was chosen primarily
as one at which the movements of people
from their own homes on holiday, etc.,
would be at a minimum, and in this
feature I suggest that the 28th February
will not depart from the established
principle, and may indeed be preferred
as holiday movement even though it may
only be for week-ends now begins earlier
in the year than formerly. For the sake
date
of the enumerators, however, a
early in April normally provides them
with more daylight and better weather
conditions for their rather arduous task.
This task, from the earliest stages of
the preliminary review of enumeration
areas to the final settlement of queries
may extend over a period of from two
to three months. To choose, therefore,
the 18th April or thereabouts in 1937
would involve the enumerators being still
occupied in census work at a time when
many of the activities of the Province
will be directed towards the celebrations
which will naturally accompany the Cornation of His Majesty King Edward
VIII. It is for this reason that the
earlier date has been finally determined
on.
The only outstanding matter to which
I need draw the attention of the House,
a matter not least in importance, is the
scope and nature of the questions to be
addressed to each householder. The
questions to be asked are set out in the
Second Schedule of the Bill, and in conjunction with that Schedule the provisions of Section 5 (2) should not be
overlooked. The questions which were
asked in 1926 relating to orphanhood and
dependency, education, occupation and
industry, National Health Insurance,
afflictions, and nationality, have been
omitted from the Schedule of the Bill
now under consideration. The reduction
in the scope of the inquiry is thus very
material.

former question has been inserted in

thing objectionable in the Bill. While

Another point which the Minister

the meeting held in the Ulster Hall

if the right hon. Gentleman has reason

regarding children at public elementary

Ireland where the birth rate is well up

It has been stated that the span of

will confirm that. Indeed, I think it will

extended. Then there is another important thing on which the census will
give us information. On the very
high authority of the Prime Minister,
the highest authority we have in Northern Ireland, this is a Protestant Parliament for a Protestant people. We will
be able to see the number of Protestants
of all denominations in Northern Ireland
when the census is completed. I hope
we will more than hold our own, but we
must wait and see.
Regarding the people employed in the
offices correlating the returns, a very
important question arises. A great many
competent clerks in Northern Ireland are
unemployed and I hope they will get
this work to do. You have enough men
of your own to do this work and to do it
well. But before you go outside to look
for anyone be sure you
exhaust the
supply at home, and if you do you will
not have any occasion to bring in hands
from across the water. You will get any
amount of Ulster people competent to do
the work, and there are no people who
have suffered more from unemployment-
I think the Minister of Labour will agree
with me than the people here. There
are clerks, and some of them in high
positions in the various businesses, and
those businesses failed and they found
themselves out of work. For that reason,
as well as for others, I do not think the
Bill will be opposed. At all events I am
not going to oppose it.

FINANCE (COMPANIES STAMP
DUTY).
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the law
relating to relief from capital stamp
duty and transfer stamp duty in the case
of reconstructions or amalgamations of
companies, and to grant relief from
transfer stamp duty in the case of the
transfer of property as between associated
companies."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The purpose of this
financial resolution is to authorise certain
concessions with regard to capital stamp
duty and transfer stamp duty which will
bring the statutory position here into
line with that in Great Britain.
Section 55 of the British Finance Act,
1927, granted relief from companies
capital duty in certain cases of reconstruction and amalgamation of public
companies. The Section was re-enacted
in Northern Ireland by Section 4 of the
Finance Act (Northern Ireland), 1928.
The British Act was subsequently
widened by the Finance Acts of 1928
and 1930, and it is now proposed to
extend these amendments to Northern
Ireland. The effect of these amendments
is of a somewhat technical character, and
hon. Members will do well to await the
circulation of the Bill before raising
any points.
At present I am simply concerned to
obtain the Committee's approval to the
general principle contained in the financial resolution, of extending to Northern
Ireland these concessions which already
operate in Great Britain. Hon. Members will readily appreciate the necessity.
for ensuring that a company registered
in Northern Ireland is not prejudiced
by that fact as compared with a company registered in Great Britain.
The last part of the resolution refers
to the proposal to extend to Northern
Ireland the provisions of Section 42 of
the British Finance Act, 1930, which
provides for relief from transfer stamp
duty in the case of the transfer
of property between
panies. I beg to move.
