Mr. BARBOUR: Shortly before the
last International Tourist Trophy Motor
Car Race the Government was approached
by the Race Committee with the request
that it should again make up the deficiency in the funds publicly subscribed.
to pay the expenses and prize money of
the race or raised by the promoters under
the powers conferred by the Motor
Vehicles (International Race) Act passed
by this House last May. Having regard
to the necessity of a satisfactory Prize
Fund being available for the competitors
and the absence of any other source, the
Government made a grant not exceeding
£1,280 on the terms set out on the face
of the Estimate. At the same time it
was emphasised that this grant was not
to be treated as a precedent for future
years. Of this amount £110 was refunded as not all the prizes were won
and the net amount now remains to be
voted. I do not anticipate that any
further refund will be forthcoming
under the condition attaching to the
grant.
The requirement of £426 under subhead J is due to a somewhat unusual
Land Purchase Annuity case. Hon.
Members are aware that ordinarily the
Land Purchase Annuity takes precedence
over all other charges on the land. In
this case however, when the Ministry
came to sell the holding for arrears of
annuity, the statutes did not give the
annuity this protection against a rentcharge created out of the lands prior
to their sale under the Land Purchase
Acts.
In the circumstances the Ministry had
no alternative to agreeing with the owner
of the rentcharge that the holding
should be sold free from annuity and
that the proceeds of sale should be
applied firstly in paying off the arrears
of the rentcharge, and secondly in redeeming the land purchase annuity. The
amount thus received did little more than
meet arrears, and the sum now sought
is required to supplement the balance.
in order to enable the annuity to be
cancelled.
Turning now to subhead K, a scheme
was negotiated by the Ministry some
years ago for repairing the embankments
protecting certain reclaimed lands on
Lough Foyle, in respect of one portion
of which a substantial land purchase
annuity was payable to the Ministry.
The occupiers of the land concerned.
agreed to pay that portion of the expenditure which was not covered by
grants from the Irish Society, the
L.M.S. Railway Company, and an unemployment relief grant. One owner,
however, of a piece of ground, stated to
be derelict, refused to participate, and
as his share could not fairly be placed
on the other owners, the Ministry has
decided to pay the small amount involved.
Apart from the importance of the work
itself in checking inroads of the sea and
providing for a proper scheme of future.
maintenance, this scheme, which was
carried through by the railway company as agents for all interested parties,
was instrumental in giving much-needed
employment in one of our hardest-hit
areas.

the linen trade from

in the home market.

The Government in the matter of

Mr. POLLOCK: As my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Barbour) announced
changes in taxation in his Budget statement, this Bill deals only with the miscellaneous points referred to by him at
the conclusion of his speech. It is, therefore, only necessary for me to refer very
briefly to the various Clauses of the Bill.
Clause 1 makes it mandatory upon
hawkers using motor vehicles to pay
hawkers' licence duty of £2. As hon.
Members will appreciate, the Hawkers'
Act of 1888, which provides for the payment of licence duty by hawkers, contains no reference to the motor car.
Many hawkers now use the motor car in
plying their trade, and most of them
do in fact, so far as is known, take out
a hawker's licence. Legally, however,
doubt has arisen as to whether it is
mandatory for them to do so, and the
present Clause will place this matter
beyond all doubt.
Clause 2 corrects a small mistake which
was made in the Revaluation (Consequential Provisions) Act. In that Act
publicans' licence duties were made to
conform to the new valuations, and in
the case of refreshment house licences
the operative date was made 1st April,
1937. It was thought that the licences
had already been issued by the Customs
and Excise Department (who act as the
Ministry's agents) for the current year
on the old valuations, but it was later
found that this was not the case.
Accordingly steps were taken to ensure
that this type of licence holder had not
in the current year to pay more consequent on the mistake in the date, and
statutory effect is now given to this by
the present Clause.
Clause 3, which relates to refund of
portion of the liquor licence duties when
premises are vacated, is a reinstatement
of a Clause in the Finance Act, 1917.
Through a mistake by the Statute Law
Revision Committee in Great Britain the
Clause in the 1917 Act was repealed by
the British Statute Law Revision Act,
1927, and this repeal had effect not only
in Great Britain but in Northern Ireland. The British Revenue' Authorities
only discovered this error last year and
reinstated the Clause in their Finance
Act, 1935.
Clause 4 is designed to prevent evasion
of death duties by deposits being made
in two names in Joint Stock Banks-a
method of evasion very common in
Ireland. It may be mentioned that a
provision of a similar scope is already
included in the Treasury Regulations
governing Trustee Savings Banks in the
United Kingdom.
Clause 5 is taken from the British
Finance Act of the present year. It
removes the exemption from estate duty
given by the Finance Act, 1894, to certain classes of property situate abroad,
but in removing this general exemption.
it makes certain specific exceptions.
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
Clause 6 has been adopted from the
British Finance Act of the present year.
It was introduced in that Act at a very
late stage in the British House of Commons consequent on representations made
by the hon. and gallant Member who
represents County Antrim in that House,
Sir Hugh O'Neill, who had first raised it
in correspondence with my right hon.
Friend. The effect of the Clause is to
relieve from double taxation in the two
areas, viz., Northern Ireland and Great
Britain, property in which a surviving
spouse
has a
life interest when the
locality of the property has changed between the two deaths. To take an
example: If landed property in Northern Ireland were sold on the death of
a husband, the wife having a life interest.
in that property, and the
invested
money
in British Stocks, the locality of the
property would have changed, and on
the second death, death duties would
have to be paid a second time. This
obviously was contrary to the general
intention of the Government of Ireland
Act, and the present Clause, together
with the corresponding Clause in the
Finance Act, 1936, corrects this for the
future.
Clause 7 gives exemption from death.
duties to property left to the National
Trust. In Great Britain such exemption
is in force, but as the National Trust
has only within the last year begun to
operate in Northern Ireland, no necessity has previously arisen to grant similar
exemption here.
Clause 8 has been inserted at the suggestion of the India Office and continues
exemption from death duties in the case
of certain Indian pensions whose locality.
under the Government of India Act is
now being altered from India to London.
Clause 9 is designed to assist the
Valuation Department in obtaining continuous statistics of the values of property
changing hands on being leased. Prior
to the Budget the proposals embodied in
this Clause were discussed in outline
with the Incorporated Law Society, and
since then correspondence has taken
place. The Clause has been drafted to
give effect to the Society's views so far
as it has been possible to do so without
defeating the purpose for which it is
designed.
Clause 10 brings into force as regards
transferred revenues a change which was
made as regards reserved revenue by the
British Finance Act of last year: it
makes the ordinary summary jurisdiction.
procedure apply to every type of revenue
prosecution and not merely to some.

Mr. NIXON: I think perhaps the
Minister of Finance might be able to enlighten me and the country as well on
a very important matter. I did not give
notice of this because it is not necessary
to do so. It is a thing the Minister will
know all about. I understand that for
a very long time there has been
vacancy for a county court judge.
there is one thing the Government have
a right to be proud of-and we are all
proud of it-that is the higher judiciary
in Northern Ireland, but a great number
of us do not think that it is good policy
to keep a county court judgeship vacant
for a long time and to appoint a K.C.,
no matter how eminent, to act as temporary county court judge. A man who is acting temporarily is always wondering if
what he does will please his superiors.
He is always afraid to do some thing
that might be calculated to prevent him
from getting the permanent appointment when it does come.
I think it is about time this practice
was stopped and that when there is a
vacancy for a county court judge or
any other position in the higher judiciary
the appointment should be made at once.
The public would then be in a position
to have that confidence which I am proud
to say we have in the higher judiciary.
But who could have confidence in a mau
who is only acting temporarily and who
knows that if he does not please his
political bosses he will hardly be made
permanent? This is going on too long.
Only the other day a temporary resident magistrate was appointed. When
the Act abolishing justices of the peace
was passed we were told that the
administration of the law was going to be
in the hands of resident magistrates who
would be in permanent positions and who
could not be removed without a Resolution from this House. The way they are
getting round this is to appoint temporary resident magistrates.
men
It is not long since I was in court
when a temporary resident magistrate
was hearing a case against a man who
was not popular with the Government.
This magistrate was not content to decide
the case, but he also gave a lecture.
He thought if he did not do the job
properly he would not be permanently
appointed. He did it properly and was
made a permanent resident magistrate.
It is a slur on the administration of
justice for the Government to keep these
in
temporary positions. The
appointments should be made right
away. Another thing, resident magistrates are transferred here and there to
try cases by order of the Ministry of
Home Affairs. I submit that resident
magistrates after appointment should be
under the Lord Chief Justice's Department. We have all the greatest confidence in the Lord Chief Justice and
all the other judges and county court.
judges, but the Government are shaking
our confidence in the administration of
justice by keeping these temporary
county court judges and resident magistrates to decide such cases as they think
fit.

Oral Answers to Questions.
WORKING HOURS OF
AGRICULTURAL SCHOOL PUPILS.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
hours which the pupils in Cookstown
Agricultural School have to work each
day; whether they were ever employed
pulling weeds on Sunday; what their
hours of leisure are and whether there is
any restriction on using the grounds
attached to the school for walking during
leisure hours; and whether he can state
the number of pupils who failed to complete their full course of training during
the past two years.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The working
day of pupils at the Ulster Dairy School
varies according to the nature of the
course of study. The maximum number
of hours worked, including practical and
study hours, varies from 8 to 93 per day.
In no case do the hours of leisure fall
below 3 per day and meals occupy 21
hours per day. On Saturday afternoons
and Sundays essential work only is performed by the pupils in the poultry and
dairying divisions, no pupil being called
on to work for more than 4 hours during
that period.
Pupils have never been required to pull
weeds on Sundays.
Pupils are allowed to walk during
leisure hours in any part of the school
grounds which are available for recreation purposes. Generally the arrangements at the Ulster Dairy School
correspond to those prevailing in other
educational establishments.
During the two years ended September,
1936, 9 pupils out of a total of 152 who
received instruction during that period
left the school for various reasons, including illness, during the course of terms.

not

15 OCTOBER 1936
AN AGRICULTURAL WAGES
BOARD.
4. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is prepared to
give sympathetic consideration to the
establishment of an Agriculutral Wages
Board similar to that operating in Great
Britain.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: An Agritural Wages Board is in operation in
England, but not in Scotland, where in
certain respects conditions are more akin
to those in Northern Ireland than in
England. I am just as anxious as the
hon. Member to assist in bringing about
as big an improvement in the economic
status of the agricultural labourer as the
industry can afford. It is common knowledge that the wages of agricultural
labourers in the North of Ireland are
rising. I am watching the position carefully and sympathetically, but I do not
think, in the interests of the agricultural
labourer, that the opportune moment has
come for the creation of Agricultural
Wages Boards.
THE SHEEP DIPPING
REGULATIONS.
6. Mr. ROWLEY ELLIOTT asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
prepared to amend the Sheep Dipping
regulations as at present applied to
County Tyrone so that the sheep owners
in that county will be protected against
unnecessary interference; and whether he
will have them placed in the same position
as their neighbouring farmers in County
Fermanagh.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Ministry's
Sheep Dipping Orders give local authorities very full powers to make regulations
which they consider are suited to the local
circumstances.
County Fermanagh has availed itself
of these powers and has made regulations
which require flocks of less than 100 to be
dipped in the public baths provided by
the Council under the supervision of the
local sheep dipping inspector, and at such
times as are advertised. This, in fact,
practically covers all sheep in County Fermanagh. The local authority has provided the necessary baths, and owners of
flocks of less than 100 sheep are advised
of the time and place at which the
dipping will be done. This relieves the
great majority of sheep owners in the
county of the requirement to give the
police notice of their intention to dip.
Only those farmers who own flocks of
100 or more sheep are required to notify
the police.
In County Tyrone, the local authority
has made a regulation requiring flocks.
of 40 sheep or under to be dipped in the
public baths. The time at which the
dipping has to be carried out is not, however, stipulated, with the result that all
sheep owners in the county must notify
the police of their intention to dip. This
notification is required so that the local
authority may supervise the dipping if
necessary and expedient.
ELECTRICITY BOARD ADVISORY
COMMITTEE.
7. Mr NIXON asked the Minister of

of the gentleman appointed by the Minister to act on the Advisory Committee to
the Electricity Supply Board; the date
on which the Advisory Committee was
set up, the number of meetings held by
the Committee, and the matters referred
to the Committee for consideration.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Advisory Committee
on electricity was set up in November,
1931, and I propose with the concurrence
of the hon. Member to circulate with
the Official Report a list of the present
members, each of whom is appointed by
me, though the majority are nominated
in the first instance by local bodies.
The Committee has met on four
occasions, when they have reviewed the
general progress of electricity development in the area under the jurisdiction
of the Electricity Board, and have considered certain projected extensions of
the Board's development area.

ex-
Sir DAWSON BATES: Section 16 of
the Road and Railway Transport Act of
1935 does not distinguish between
carriers who use horse-drawn vehicles
and those who use motor vehicles.
Prior to the passing of the Act carriers
were not licensed.
Under that enactment the Ministry of
Home Affairs is obliged to grant a local
carrier's licence to every person who was
carrying on the business of a local carrier
in Belfast on the 31st day of May, 1934,
and who continued to carry on that
business until after the 31st day of July,
1935.
no
One hundred and seventy-five local
carriers' licences have been issued for the
County Borough of Belfast and
licence has been granted to any person
who did not satisfy the Ministry that
he was fully entitled to hold a licence.
As a licence cannot legally be granted
to any person who was not engaged in
carrying on the business of a local
carrier in Belfast before and during the
period mentioned, no increase has or can
take place in the number of carriers.
The only circumstances in which additional persons could be licensed would
be where the Ministry was of opinion

was insufficient to meet the requirements
of the public.
the

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Restoration of Salary Scales to Teachers.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move:
"That in the opinion of this House
the action of the Government in refusing to restore the 1920 salary scales
which were fixed by agreement with the
British Government is to be condemned,
and that this House refuses to sanction
the proposal to stabilise salaries at a
point approximately 10 per cent. below
the 1920 scales, and demands the
immediate restoration of the 1931
Economy Cut, and further, in connection with the lump sum paid on retirement, demands full recognition of the
past services of teachers."
was
The salary scales for Irish primary
teachers were formulated in November,
1920, and were the result of agreement
between representatives of the British
Treasury, the Commissioners of National
Education and the Irish National
Teachers' Organisation. This agreement
confirmed by the Civil Service
Arbitration Board. These salaries were
fixed for normal times and were not to
vary with the cost of living. Though the
scales were agreed to in November, 1920,
teachers did not reach their full placing
in the scales until 1st April, 1922. On
the 1st January, 1926, the Government
of Northern Ireland decided to enforce a
cut of 7 per cent. in primary teachers'
salaries and 10 per cent. in capitation
grants and certain other payments. I
submit that the Northern Government,
as the successors of the British Government in this area, were bound by the
Teachers' Salaries
Teachers' Salaries
15 OCTOBER 1936
agreement of 1920, and their action in
thus arbitrarily reducing salaries constituted a violation of that agreement.
The action of the Government in inflicting this first cut in salaries came as a
great surprise, but this was nothing to
the shock received when the Prime Minister, on the occasion of the opening of
Parliament, 1931, announced that they
were to suffer a further reduction in
emoluments, and teachers in all parts of
the area have given full expression to
their feelings regarding this second violation of the 1920 Agreement. Whilst they
resent the action of the Government in
making this further cut, they desire
also to make an emphatic protest against
the manner in which it was done.
Without calling the teachers into consultation
and without the slightest warning the
Government simply stated that the reduction was to take place.
was
Contrast this treatment with that meted
out to the English teachers. Their
salary scales, fixed by the Burnham Committee about twelve years ago, were
stabilised for a period of five years, and
when this expired the Burnham Committee was called together to formulate
new scales, and when the respective panels
representing the education authorities.
and the teachers failed to reach an agreement regarding the new scales, all parties
agreed to have the matter referred to
arbitration, and Lord Burnham
appointed arbitrator. By his award the
teachers' salaries were fixed at a little
over 95 per cent. of the original scales,
and it was decided that the new scales
should be operative for six years ending
31st March, 1931. Thus in 1925 the
English teachers lost scarcely 5 per cent.
whilst our teachers lost 7 per cent. in
salary and 10 per cent. in other emoluments. The cuts have been restored to
all English teachers. This procedure
shows that the teachers in England are
at least treated with a greater appearance
of fairness than teachers in Northern
Ireland.
There was a rather sinister connection
between the cuts made in elementary
teachers' salaries in 1926 and the developments in educational expenditure which
followed immediately after these cuts.
A statement in the Ministry of Education
Report of 1923/24 was that the Ministry
proposed to finance the developments envisaged by the Act of 1923, not by
increasing the Parliamentary Votes for
educational services but rather by
economies made on these services. I contend that there was a definite connection
between the cut of 1926 and the grant
made by the Ministry of Education in
respect of provided schools. Those in the
P.E. schools seemed to have been singled
out from all other branches of the teaching profession and other public servants.
In 1926, when the first cut of 7 per cent.
was made, no other teachers were affected.
The Irish National Teachers' Organisation demanded the following scales of
salaries on behalf of their members:-
Assistant teachers-£250, rising by six
annual increments of £15 to £340, and
thereafter by eight annual increments of
£20 to a maximum of £500. Principal
teachers To receive on promotion to
principalship two annual increments in
the above scale, and to proceed to a
maximum of £600. Junior assistant
mistresses £150, by annual increments
of £5 to £200. The scales were to be
made operative as from April 1st, 1919.
The following scale was agreed to as a.
normal scale:-The normal scale for
trained men teachers shall commence at
£170, and rise by 17 annual increments
(16 of £12 and one of £8) to a maximum
of £370. The normal scale for trained
women teachers shall commence at £155
and rise by 15 annual increments (14 of
£10 and one of £5) to a maximum salary
of £300 per annum. The increments
shall be granted annually, provided no
adverse report is received from the
inspector.
This scale was agreed upon after the
Central Executive Committee of the Irish
National Teachers' Organisation decided
unanimously on the 19th June, 1920, that
the time had now come when additional
temporary bonuses could no longer meet
the claims of the Irish National Teachers,
and that only a just and satisfactory
permanent scale could be accepted by the
teachers of Ireland, and as a result formal
application was made to the Civil Service
Arbitration Board to fix a permanent
scale of salaries. The Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury
declined to allow the matter to be referred
for arbitration, but offered better war
bonuses, which the teachers declined to
accept. After protracted negotiation the
Arbitration Board decided against the
Treasury Contention and referred the

agreement between the parties. As a result,
at a meeting between a sub-committee
of the Commissioners of National Education and the representative of the Irish
Treasury, when no teachers' representatives were present, the following
official minute was adopted :-
"The question whether the new scale
should be a scale based on normal cost
of living with a sliding scale of war
bonuses was considered, and it was
agreed that the new scale should be a

and should not be subject to variation,
according as the future cost of living

In subsequent negotiations when, in
addition to the representatives of the
Commissioners and the Irish Treasury,
the Irish National Teachers' Organisation representatives were present, the
teachers agreed to accept a lower scale
than the Treasury representative was prepared to concede had the sliding scale
been adopted, and an agreement was
arrived at on this distinct understanding.
This agreement seems to be ignored completely by those who refer to reductions
in the war bonuses suffered by other
public officers, and I am unaware of any
other public salaried servants who have
had their agreements violated. With
regard to the reduction in the cost-ofliving bonuses, suffered by those affected,
while we deplore the hardships thus
inflicted we must, in justice to teachers,
emphasise that this is merely the carrying out of the contract to which these
public officials subscribed.
Legislation in Northern Ireland is
presumed to proceed step by step with
that across the Channel, and when salaries
were reduced in Great Britain by 5
per cent, exclusive of pension premiums,
full advantage was taken to inflict a
minimum reduction of 7 per cent. in
salary scales and a 10 per cent.
reduction in other emoluments on
the teachers of Northern Ireland,
but the Government of Northern Ireland
refused to give equality of treatment in
the matter of superannuation, although
the Irish teachers had always a contributory pension scheme. It is true an offer
to improve pension conditions on prohibitive premiums was made in 1925, but
subject to terms that make the offer
oppressive to young teachers, and to such
unfair devaluation conditions as rendered
it valueless to teachers of long service who
had existed for the greater part of their
lives on salaries so justly described as a
disgrace to the Empire. The many
educational advantages resulting from the
passing of the Education Act, Northern
Ireland, 1923, justly entitle this Measure
to be called the "Children's Charter";
but while this is so the policy of financing expanding charges due to education
reform at the expense of the elementary
teachers renders this Act a penal instrument which in numerous cases gravely
affects the status and emoluments of those
who, despite the most adverse conditions,
had made a success of Irish education
in the past. Even their critics refer with
pride to the many successes of the pupils
turned out under most unfavourable circumstances.
Teachers fear that they alone are being
made the victims of an economy campaign due to the increasing cost of our
social services, because any hardships
inflicted on them will not lead to a dislocation of the trade or industry of the
country. While they might, like other
dissatisfied employees, adopt a ca' canny
policy, no teacher worthy of the name
would employ such tactics when the
interests of the youth of the Province
are at stake, and we fear that full
advantage may again be taken of this
attitude of the teachers.
Some criticisms have been directed
against teachers because a small number
have been able to indulge in the luxury
of a motor car, or to take advantage of
the cheap Continental holidays now available; but, I would ask, are these
advantages to be denied to teachers alone.
when professional men, shopkeepers,
farmers, and all others employed in commercial or industrial pursuits also avail
themselves of these amenities of modern
life? Must those entrusted with the
moral training, character formation, and
education of the young be in a class
subordinate to all others? While teachers
are assured of a certain permanency of
employment, I must emphasise the fact
that they are not in a position to reap
the advantages which accrue to those
who in prosperous periods reaped to the
full the just rewards appertaining to industry, grit, enterprise, and initiative.
In addition to this handicap must the

teachers alone among existing officials be
liable to a reduction in what was unanimously agreed to be permanent scales of
salaries wholly independent of periods of
boom or depression?
I wish to put the facts properly before
this House and let them judge for themselves whether the case for the reduction
in teachers' salaries is a just case, or
whether it is the reverse. This sudden
change of policy on the part of the Government is certainly a very remarkable
thing. I have here in my hand a
"News-Letter" report of a speech delivered
by the Minister of Finance,
the official Unionist Headquarters, on
the 11th December, 1930. With reference
to the financial position of Ulster and
to the demands for economy, the right
hon. Gentleman, dealing with education,
made use of these words:
at
"They might, of course, expect some
relief by reducing the cost of education,
as
some people suggested, but they
would remember that almost threefourths of the total cost of education
represented the salaries of their school
teachers, which amounted to not far
from £1,500,000. Although that
single item was no less than three times
the size of the balance available for
Government administration, he failed
to notice any suggestion, either in
Parliament or outside, that the salaries
of these teachers should in any way
be interfered with."
Mr. POLLOCK: What is the date
of that speech?
Mr. BEATTIE: The 11th of December, 1930, just three months previous to
your taking the 7 per cent. cut from the
teachers. A little later in his speech he
also made use of the following expression:-
"I am perfectly satisfied that if we
saved by reducing the total of our
local expenditure, we would not be free
to use the money for the purpose of
reducing taxation. On the other hand,
I am practically certain that the
savings thus made, or at any rate a
large proportion of them, would be
claimed for the purpose of the Imperial contribution."
The right hon. Gentleman is neither
a prophet nor the son of a prophet, but
he did prophesy rightly on that occasion
because this year we sent away £400,000
out of Northern Ireland.
In view of that statement from such
an authority as the right hon. Gentleman, to whom I have referred, this
sudden change in the attitude this volte
face on the part of the Government is
an extraordinary thing, but I think no
one expected or anticipated that those
reductions, in so far as the members of
the elementary branch of the teaching
profession were concerned, would be
permanent.
This House will agree with me when
I state that up to 1920 the salaries of
elementary school teachers in the whole
of Ireland were a disgrace to education
and to the fair fame of this country.
Those salaries had been fixed in 1900 on
a very small and meagre scale. After
seventeen years of persistent agitation
on the part of the Irish National
Teachers' executive they were increased
in the case of some teachers by £7 a
year, and in the case of other teachers—
the most favoured teachers-by £10 a
year. The House will be astonished if
they reflect that on the 1st July, 1916a date memorable in the history of Ulster
-a bonus on teachers' salaries was introduced amounting to 3s a week in the
case of all teachers whose salaries were
less than £3 a week. From that statement it is perfectly evident that in 1916
and during the war years, and at a time
when even unskilled artisans in our shipyards were earning between £8 and £10
a week, we were paying the majority of
our elementary school teachers a mere
pittance of £2 a week and in some cases
£3 a week or under. Is it any wonder
that at the end of the war the teachers
began to be clamant, began to demand
that justice should be done to their legitimate claims?
Accordingly, in 1920 they entered into
negotiations with the Civil Service Arbitration Board, who submitted the matter
to the British Treasury and the Commissioners of National Education. And
during all those negotiations, if one takes
the trouble to read into details, he will
find that what the teachers demanded was
not an additional salary plus a sliding
bonus but a permanent salary, and that
they were quite willing to forego all
chances and possibility of obtaining a
bonus.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
It is perfectly evident from an official
minute and from the agreement which
ultimately became an official award, that
the whole basis, the whole gist of that
agreement was that the teachers were to
receive a permanent salary not subject
to any fluctuations whatsoever. And, by
an extraordinary coincidence, in November of that year it also happened that
the cost of living, according to the Board
of Trade returns, had reached its apex
figure and was then, on November 1st,
176 per cent. greater than in the basic
year, 1914.
So that the teachers, not
through any wisdom or any foresight
on their part, benefited by the fact that
from the very moment that this agreement was signed and had the force of a
binding obligation, the cost of living
began to come down. But the teachers
took their chances; it might very well
have happened the other way, and no
one could have foretold at that time that
the cost of living was just about to suffer
a decline. I mention this for the purpose
of refuting the argument which has been
used by the Government that the salary
was not permanent, that it was not fixed,
but that it was liable to suffer fluctuations just as the bonus in the case of
the civil servants, but I think the facts
which I have already put before the
House demonstrate very clearly and very
forcibly that such is not the case.
This agreement, as I understand, came
into effectual operation, that is in so far
as the benefits under it were fully
reached, on the 1st of April, 1922. But
some four years later the Government
appointed a Departmental Committee to
inquire into teachers' salaries, and the
majority who fashioned the majority
report of that Departmental Committee
decided, or proposed, that the teachers'
salaries should be reduced by 7 per cent.,
and in some cases by 10 per cent. I am
not going to refer at any length to that
decision but in my opinion it constituted
a distinctly gross and flagrant breach of
contract with the teachers. It might have
been argued that this Government were
not bound by the actions of the Imperial
Government, but I submit that the
Ministry of Education here are the lineal
of the Commissioners of
National Education in Ireland, and that
the Ministry of Finance in Northern Ireland represents and is in direct descent
from the British Treasury. Therefore I
successors
say that the Government in Northern
Ireland should have, and were bound to
have, honoured the agreement of 1920,
which may be known as the teachers'
charter.
But that is not the end of the Government's injustice. The teachers believed
in 1926 that no longer would they be
subjected to any further reductions. They
thought the Government would not dare
again to propose any further violations
of their treaty. But suddenly in a
moment, in March of the year 1931, the
Prime Minister announced that the
teachers were going to be subjected to a
further reduction of 7 per cent. I
characterise as most unfair the manner in
which this second violation was brought
about. The Prime Minister, early in
April, 1931, although he had never consulted the teachers, proclaimed at a public
meeting at Mossley that he was glad that
the teachers had loyally submitted to
these reductions. I do not understand
the mentality of the noble Lord.
may have been simply uttering a holiday
sentiment, for the day was Easter Monday, or he may have been stimulated by
the bracing atmosphere of Mossley. The
facts were different indeed. At that time
the teachers' congresses were assembling
and making most indignant protests
against the treatment to which they had
submitted. I submit they should have
been consulted, and I will submit further
that if they had been consulted they
would have gone a long way towards
assisting the Government and towards
making a voluntary sacrifice in a way
which the Prime Minister and the Government could not have anticipated.

That is a sort of historical review of
the scale arrived at in November of 1920.
It has been challenged on the ground of
its permanency. But I challenge any
Member of the Government, by documentary evidence both before and at the
time, to deny that the intention of the
Treasury and of the teachers and of the
Arbitration Board was to fix a permanent
scale for normal times. Now, are we not
in normal times at the moment? I am
open to correction. Just at that period
when the Treasury presented that second
scale to the teachers, which was agreed
upon, the organisation's application was
there on the Table starting at £250. The
British Treasury at that time were prepared to give £200, plus a very sub-

stantial war bonus on the sliding scale
basis. And as the right hon. Gentleman
is aware, because there is no one in this
House has a fresher memory on this
question than he has, the teachers
absolutely refused to have anything to
do with anything that was not of a permanent nature. They hung out and they
finally got a scale of salaries fixed permanently for the Irish national teachers.
That was not done just on the spur of
the moment. The history of the fight for
the establishment of that scale dates back
90 years, and the life of the school teacher
during that period is no credit to any
country.
After all these 90 years
struggle they were able to get a fixture
which they accepted for all time, and
they accepted a lower scale on that distinct understanding. Of course we see
where it is now. The Resolution says
the scale has now been fixed by the
Government at 10 per cent. below, which
means that after all these years of hard
fighting and suffering and spending of the
organisation's money they accomplished
their ends. Now we have got a native
Government, composed of our own fellow
citizens, because I think every Member
of this House is really a Northerner.
We get them coming along and giving
sympathy to this claim prepared in 1920.
There was not a Northern Member of the
British Parliament who was not wholeheartedly with the claim of the Irish
National Teachers. The Irish National
Teachers' Organisation tried to court the
favour of the English Conservative Party
and the Liberal Party, but they could
find no friends in these parties to come
to their assistance, but by the co-operation of the Northern M.P.'s with the
British Labour Party we got our case
tabled before the proper authority. The
outcome was shown in the 1920 Agreement, and I claim that we are entitled
to it.
The reason I speak from this angle is
this. The Irish National Teachers'
Organisation claim this agreement to be
their agreement. No other organisation
existed for the primary teachers of
Northern Ireland for that period. We
still claim we represent 90 per cent. of the
Irish national teachers, and we still claim
that the agreement entered into in 1920
should be adhered to by the powers that
be, both in this State and in the Free
State, and we are determined to go on
claiming what we call a just right, that
is, the re-establishment of the agreement
as fixed by the British Treasury with the
Irish National Teachers' Organisation.
Then I find again that new scale of salary
as set out really amounts to a 10 per cent.
reduction. Under the agreed scale £170
was the starting rate. Under the reduced scale, as set out by the Government,
it is £155 for men against this £170.
The new scale for women is starting £140
against £155 as set out in the 1920
Agreement, and the maximum for men is
£335 and for women £270. I quote
these just for this purpose. As I have
said, the agreed scale was far below the
demand of the Irish National Teachers'
Organisation. It was far below the concession the Treasury was prepared to give.
Their scale was higher, but on a moveable basis. We accepted that scale in
good faith. Now we are put down to a
point 10 per cent. below that point.
I find from the "Daily Herald,"
which I have an extract from, that the
clerical worker in the British Civil
Service is now rated at £335, the same as
the Northern Ireland Government is
rating the teacher. I am going to say
quite openly to the Government, that the
educational report will give the highest
standard of efficiency to the teaching profession operating in any part of the
world. When we realise that of upwards
5,000 teachers there are only about 15
less than efficient, I think there is no
profession can show such a high standard
of efficiency as the Northern
teachers. That is proven by documentary
evidence, not set out by me, but by the
Ministry of Education. And when we
got that salary scale from the British
Treasury we were about 16 per cent. less
than efficient. Now we have got a high
standard of efficiency, and because we
have reached that high standard of
efficiency we are cut down 10 per cent.
below that salary scale.

It is not my intention to push the

per cent. could have been granted on the

was going to British armaments, I say

and I hope the Ministry of Finance will

in this part of the world. I know, and

are forced-
Mr. POLLOCK: To surrender.
Mr. BEATTIE: We have not surrendered, and I, as an Ulsterman, say,
"No surrender!" I want him to
honour the agreement of 1920. I want
him to reflect on the undue interference

I want him to bring in in the Supplementary Estimates £62,000 for the full

The next point I come to is the lump
sum on retirement. I do not want to
waste the time of the House, but these
things have to be dealt with, and the
only way by which they can be dealt
with properly is by bringing them before
those who matter. The lump sum was
introduced in 1925, but there was a prohibitive figure put down and the teachers
could not accept it. The lump sum has
now been introduced in Northern Ireland
in a way that the older teachers resent,
as serving teachers up to 1st July, 1936,
are not taken into consideration. Those
who have built up education to the high
standard of efficiency to which I referred
are going to be ignored in regard to this
lump sum. Let me try briefly to state
the English conditions in regard to the
lump sum. I do this for the guidance

This Bill, the Education (Ireland) Bill,
was introduced into the Imperial Parliament by Mr. Ian Macpherson, Chief
Secretary for Ireland. This Measure
proposed to give a lump sum to all Irish
teachers as the English teachers had
secured a lump sum the previous year.
The action of the British Government in
bringing in this Bill indicated their intention of giving Irish teachers equality
of treatment with the English teachers.
That proved beyond the shadow of a

1919 had in mind a lump sum to all
Irish teachers. I want to inform the right
hon. Gentleman now-I speak subject

paid a pension premium. They paid it

Mr. POLLOCK: Yes.
Mr. BEATTIE: The English teachers.
have not always paid a pension premium.
They were free from pension premiums,

that every teacher serving on that particular date if he retired six months

In Northern Ireland the right hon.

Therefore, in the first year of the lump
sum the right hon. Gentleman will have
£13,000 income, and working it out on

The second year he will have been paid
£26,000, and will be paying out £2,000,
working on that basis right up to a period
of 30 years.
That income received from
the one per cent. of the teachers' salaries
will meet the requirements of the lump
sum for 30 years; in other words, the
Government will not be contributing one
penny to the lump sum until 30 years
have expired.

Those are the two cardinal points,

the mover of the Motion has said on
this subject. I do so without any compulsion whatever. We sometimes hear
a cheap sneer made inside this House

are compelled to do so by our trade
unions. We are under no compulsion

throughout the period of the war, while

country were able to improve the conditions of their workers owing to a
shortened market caused by a national
scarcity, the teachers were lagging far

they were able to secure even a slight
improvement, equivalent to what would.
have been granted to the lowest section
of unskilled worker, and it took them

The Member for South Derry (Mrs.
Parker) has quoted statements from a
report showing there was an honourable
obligation entered into which the
teachers were led to regard as a settlement that would be lasting. I think
the teachers have a splendid case from

badly treated in years gone by, and
right up to the post-war period, and

I am very glad to be able to associate

the teachers throughout Northern
Ireland.

But the seven per cent. cut imposed
in 1931 is on an entirely different footing. That cut was brought in with the
object of effecting economy, just as the
cuts were made in the salaries of civil
servants, Members of Parliament, and
others. I do not press that the whole
of that seven per cent. should be
restored to the teachers now, but what
I would press on the Government is
that they should not say: "We are
restoring three-and-a-half per cent. of
that seven per cent. cut, but the other
three-and-a-half per cent. you are never
going to see." I can understand the
Minister of Finance saying: "I can
only afford to give three-and-a-half per
cent. back this year." I would ask
him not to adopt this-I do not like
to use such a term, but it is a highhanded way of getting a reduction in
the salaries of the teachers.
You make a reduction on the ground
of economy, and everyone accepts it with
more or less grace, and then, although
other people who suffered the reduction
are coming back more or less to the
position they were in before the storm
in 1931, you say to the teachers, "No.
You will have to have a permanent threeand-a-half per cent. cut." There must
be a reason for that, and that reason
must be that the Government consider
that teachers' salaries were too high
before the cut. Personally I think they
are completely wrong. I am aware, as
everyone in this House is aware, that
there is a large number of people in the
. country who think that school teachers'
salaries are too high, but there is also
a very large number of people in this
country who think that every other man
has a soft job, and the less they know
about that job the more absurdly they
think the other man is paid.
I think a good many people who object
to school teachers' salaries are not really
aware of the kind of position the teacher
holds. They are not aware of the long
and fairly arduous preparation he has to
undergo in order to be able to take that
job. When the Minister of Finance rises
to reply-and may I here say how glad
I am to see him in his place again-I
hope he will not express the opinion that
the salaries of teachers in the past have
been too high, and that they ought to
be permanently lowered by three-and-ahalf per cent.

the British Government in 1920 made

THE EDUCATION LEVY.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state what
is the total estimated amount to be
raised in the financial year 1936-37 by

raised is to be applied.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The total estimated amount to
be raised by local authorities in the

ALBERTBRIDGE
ROUNDABOUT.
10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
a memorial from the residents and shopkeepers in the Albertbridge Road and
Madrid Street area demanding the
abolition of the roundabout system for
motor traffic in this district, and requesting the restoration of the former straightforward method of traffic control;
whether he is aware that the new system
is dangerous to life and very bad for the
business traders of this part of the city;
and whether he is prepared to set up a
committee, composed of traders and
residents and others interested, to try
and find a solution of the present grave
injustice foisted upon this district.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received a copy of a memorial relating to
the matter to which the hon. Member's
question refers.
As I reminded the hon. Member on a
previous occasion, the roundabout system of traffic control which is in
operation at the junction of Albertbridge
Road and Madrid Street was introduced
experimentally in order to reduce traffic
congestion on the adjacent portion of the
Albertbridge Road, at the instance of
the Police Committee of the Belfast Corporation, in whose jurisdiction the
control of traffic in such cases lies.
It is still in the experimental stage,
and I understand that at present it is
receiving careful consideration from the
appropriate Committee of the Corporation, with whom I propose to take
the matter up further, and to bring
before them the representations which
the hon. Member has made.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that before this experimental stage comes to an end business
will be wiped out altogether in that area,
and is he aware that very serious
accidents have occurred? In view of this
position of affairs will he try to force
the Police Committee to have the matter
settled to the satisfaction of all concerned.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I certainly
will do all I can in consultation with the
police and the Police Committee to try
to improve matters.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thank you.

THE VACCINATION LAW.
16. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
prepared to amend the legislation governing vaccination so as to recognise the
just claims of conscientious objectors for
exemption.
Sir DAWSON BATES. I am not prepared to believe that it would be in the
interests of the public generally to admit.
the claims of conscientious objectors to
exemption from the Vaccination Acts.
Vaccination is, so far as is known at
present, the only real protection against
small-pox, and I would point out that
in Ireland where the Vaccination Acts
have been enforced there have been only
a few cases, and these imported; while.
in England where exemption is allowed,
cases have been numerous.
SLUM CLEARANCE.
17. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether the Government contemplate early legislation having
for its object the development of a
housing policy based upon complete slum
clearance throughout Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government considers it desirable that time
should be given to see the effect of the
large number of houses erected under the
Housing Acts (Northern Ireland) before
undertaking any further housing legislation. Although the houses built under
the Acts referred to may not have been
directly provided for slum dwellers it is
to be expected that indirectly they have
to some extent relieved the situation by
making available for slum dwellers
houses vacated by people who have
moved into the newer and better houses.
The Government, however, will watch
the situation carefully with a view to
deciding whether any further action is
necessary.
In the rural districts, operations under
the Labourers Acts, which were for some
time suspended, have now been resumed,
and the Rural District Councils have in
the course of preparation schemes
which it is hoped will substantially meet
the demands for cheap dwellings in those
areas.
The Government is prepared to assist
and encourage local authorities in any
way within its powers in connection with
this matter.
Mr. SPEAKER: Mr. Midgley.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that some of the houses
erected during the past two or three
years are slums?

for Shankill did not hear me call the

line with the civilising

It

1; and granting relief from Transfer

Teachers' Superannuation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: This is also a short
Measure consisting of three Clauses.
Clause 1 relates to the undertaking given
in my right hon. Friend's Budget speech,
that the pensions of teachers who retired
from the year 1931, when the economy
cuts were imposed, will be adjusted as
from 1st July last, so as to give them in
their pensions the benefit of the new
scales of salary which took effect from
that date. It would obviously be unfair
that teachers who retired during that
period should have their pensions permanently reduced. As teachers' pensions
are calculated on the average of the salary
of the three years preceding the date of
their retirement, it follows that the
economy cuts would continue to affect the
pensions of teachers who retire during the
next three years, and the Clause makes
the necessary provision to counter this
effect.
Most salaries of teachers are fixed by
statutory rules, but in one or two cases,
such as the teachers at the training
colleges, they are merely fixed by direction of the Ministry of Finance, hence
the provision in sub-clause (2) (b) of this
Clause.
It may be asked why these amendments
have not been embodied in superannuation schemes instead of an Act of Parliament; the reason why statutory enactment is thought necessary is that the
calculation of pensions on a hypothetical
salary is against the general principles of
superannuation, and it has, therefore,
been thought desirable to obtain definite
Parliamentary sanction for the proposal.
Clause 2 relates to the grant of lump
sum superannuation benefit to teachers.
on retirement, as announced in the
Budget speech. The payment of this
benefit is being provided for in a number
of amending superannuation schemes,
which have been laid before the House,
and the only reason why it is necessary
to refer to this matter in the present Bill
is to obtain Parliamentary authority to
the principle of funding the teachers'
additional contributions towards this
benefit for a period of at least seven years.
The hon. Member for Pottinger, in the
debate on teachers' salaries last week,
gave certain figures, designed to show
that the Exchequer would not be involved
in any burden from this lump sum for 30
years. If the teachers' contributions
were not funded this would be 80, but the
effect of this method of finance would be
to use up the teachers' contributions long
before the full burden of the new benefit
had emerged, and the next generation
would have found itself faced with more
than its fair share of the additional
burden to the Teachers' Pension Fund of
£40,000 a year. When it is borne in
mind that in the year 1966 the burden on
the Exchequer, without the new addition,
will have grown to £240,000 from the
present figure of £98,000, it can be understood why the Government thinks that
the easy course should not be adopted.
To assist in spreading the burden more
evenly from the outset, the Bill pronoses
that the teachers' contributions for a
period of not less than seven years shall
be added to the capital of the fund and
invested, leaving the growing burden of
the benefit on the Exchequer for at least
that period. How far this funding pro-

[Mr. Pollock]
cess should continue after that period will
depend on the actuarial advice that may
be tendered in the meantime.
Finally, I should like to say that the

teachers' superannuation benefits should

Despite the increased cost, my right hon.

us to make it retrospective.
Clause 3 really involves what is somewhat in the nature of a drafting Amendment of a Clause in the Superannuation
Act of 1925. Section 3 of the Act of

teacher was making no contribution
towards a pension fund. It will be remembered that the Government as a

ultimately become a civil servant.
present substituted Clause puts this

few former teachers who became civil
servants before any teachers' pension
scheme existed in their case at all, and
who otherwise would be deprived, in toto,
of any benefit in respect of that earlier
service. I beg to move.

I should

The service of these teachers was not

Perhaps the House is not aware that all

At the moment we have upwards of 5,000

sufficient to meet the lump sum requirements for all serving teachers; that is provided the Minister of Finance will give
to the teaching profession some of the

now.
Making a rough calcuation on the

amounts to £1,700,000. That amount

1926 and 1931.

There is another thing I want to say,

This is not the complicated, actuarial

at a public elementary school. If I
receive an income of £13,000 per annum,

a balance at my command to set aside for
the purpose of meeting any deficiency that
the fund may incur.
You have that every year. At the end

£226,000, and you will have had an

accumulated interest on the amount of
money at your command should cover a

We are handing on to posterity part of

We are not paying all the cost of the
Great War. Generations yet unborn will

struggle. We have no right to assume

is going to happen 40 years from now.
I believe that the Government are openminded enough to give the serious consideration to this point that it is entitled
to receive, because a discontented body
of teachers would be ruinous from many

you will not get that from a discontented

of the country to the highest educational

country.

As to the tourist traffic, I have always
in mind a man who was the pioneer of
the tourist traffic in Ulster. His name
was Henry McNeill of Larne, and
Knockemdown was his soubriquet. His
name was a household word in this
country and in England and Scotland.
That man by means of rail and buses and
hotel simply brought these people over
here from Scotland and England, and
they or their successors are coming today. We hope they will always come.
Indeed, that traffic has grown in recent
years, and we have men like Gaston,
Pentland, Stewart, and O'Neill, and
others, who have followed in the wake
of Henry McNeill and have contributed
to the development of the tourist traffic
in our midst. And so far as Mr.
Murphy of the Antrim Hotel is concerned, that man started in to do the
same thing, and I believe with great
success. But what happened? This
Board applied to take his buses from
him, and actually to stop his tourist
traffic. They failed in that and they
appealed and failed again. And now I
am told they are pursuing this man even
to the House of Lords. What are we to
think of it? That man is doing the best
he can for the tourist traffic. I cannot
understand the mentality of a Board of
that kind. It has no face on it. Even
the Prime Minister has given his blessing to the tourist traffic. The Tourist

pounds and yet this is allowed to happen.
It is hard to understand.
I suppose if "Knockemdown" came

accepted, that if this uneconomic competition continued they would be forced
to close down. It was generally agreed

of the Province.
It was to meet this serious state of
affairs that the Transport Board was set
up, and, accordingly, when the Board
is criticised as if it were simply an
alternative to the old system-when
complaint is made that in some isolated
case it is charging a somewhat higher

to whether the old fare was utterly
uneconomic or not-then it can only be
that the main issue has been entirely
lost sight of or was never appreciated.
And now I come to the existing
system. Hon. Members of this House
are, I know, with few exceptions, perfectly familiar with its provisions, but
in view of the charges that have been
made I feel it is my duty to outline its
essential features. The position, put
consent.
as shortly as possible, is this: -With

save for hire by the Board, or some
person to whom the Board has issued a
This affords the machinery

acquire the various undertakings as and
when they are in a position to operate

therefore, illustrate the working of this

What happens is, that in the first
instance the Board issues consents to every
undertaking operating lorries in Northern
Ireland. Persons operating under these
consents carry on exactly as before; they
are in no way under control of the Board,
and they charge what they please, and the
profits or losses that accrue to them are
their own affair. Then, when the Board
is in a position to take over one of these
concerns, it serves notice
a
them
upon
that it will take over as from a certain

Board, must, of course, pay compensation
for the undertakings it acquires. It is
ridiculous for the hon. and gallant Member to suggest that the Board confiscates
them; it buys them in accordance with
the machinery I will mention later.
If a purchase price is agreed upon.
between the Board and the undertaking,
then, of course, the matter is settled at
once, but if there is any difficulty about
the price to be paid, then the arbitration
procedure provided by the Act comes into
operation. This procedure ensures that
there can be no undue delay in settlement,
if the owner of the undertaking wishes
the matter to be settled without delay.
One month after offering to the Board a
price for their acceptance, the owner of
the undertaking may, if his offer is
not accepted, notify the Arbitration
Tribunal that agreement as to price
cannot be reached, and the Tribunal
then proceeds to hear both parties
and to fix the price to be paid.
And I may say that in the three
cases that the Tribunal have had submitted to them, their award was issued
within five days of the close of the proceedings. Therefore, the hon. and
gallant Member cannot say that delay in
assessing compensation is due to any fault
of the Act or its administration.
After all, the Board have nothing to
gain but much to lose if they delay
settlement of claims, for under the provisions of the Act they are obliged to pay
5 per cent. interest between the date of
taking over and the payment of the price
fixed or agreed. Hon. Members will
realise that if the Board want money it
can get it very readily at a very much
lower price than 5 per cent. I would add
that, as a matter of actual fact, it is the
practice of the Board, though they are
not obliged to do so, to pay undertakers
substantial sums on account where they
have received reasonably satisfactory
figures, but where some delay in final
agreement seems likely. Hon. Members
will, I am confident, therefore, agree that
complaints about delay in the settlement
of claims are, on the face of them, absurd,
and can only emanate from persons who
are unfamiliar with the arbitration provisions of the Act, which are an essential
feature of the whole system for the protection of the operators.
As to complaints concerning the basis
or amount of compensation that, after all,
is a matter for the Tribunal. I would
point out that if there were any fault
here it can only arise either from incorrect interpretation of law, or incorrect
assessment of facts and figures. With
regard to the possibility of incorrect law
-and I think the point the hon. and
gallant Member has raised is a mixture
of law and fact-if it is a question of
law and the Tribunal give what the
applicant thinks is an unfair interpretation, it is open to him to go to the
Supreme Court on appeal.
With regard to the assessment of facts
and figures, this must, necessarily be a
matter of opinion; but how could a fairer
Tribunal be arrived at than one composed of Mr. Justice Megaw, who, I
think, is known to all of us; an eminent
and successful businessman in the person
of Mr. Morrison, and an eminent
chartered accountant? How anybody
could conceive a fairer Tribunal I do not
know. That Tribunal sits and hears
evidence from both sides. It hears the
Board's point of view, and it hears.
experts on behalf of the applicant.
Figures are produced showing the earning powers of the business, and a decision
is arrived at. In some cases the Board's
figures at which they are prepared to
purchase are raised and in others reduced. The hon. and gallant Member
rather suggested there was some corruption between the Board and the
Tribunal, and I think that on reflection he will admit that no fairer Tribunal
could be set up than the one I have
described. I do not wish to enter into
any discussion as to the basis on which
those decisions are arrived at. It would be
most improper to do so, because to a

Passing now to the question of
passenger fares and freight charges, in
the first place, I would remind hon.
Members that the Board is not in the
ordinary sense a profit-making concern.
It pays the rates of interest fixed by statute
on its stock and any profits it makes
over and above what is necessary to
secure the payment of such interest must
be returned to the public in the way of
cheaper fares or improved services.
There is, therefore, no incentive to the
Board to profiteer as was suggested by
the hon, and gallant Member.
Apart, however, from this general
consideration, the Act makes ample provision for the protection of the public.
It provides, in effect, that any person.
who feels aggrieved by any fare or rate
charged by the Board, or by any defect
in its services, may complain to the
Ministry of Home Affairs; it then becomes the duty of the Ministry to
investigate the complaint, and if it finds
that it is one of substance to endeavour
to obtain satisfactory remedy from the
Board. If it fails to secure this, then it
is its duty to submit the matter to an
Appeal Tribunal-the Transport Appeal
Tribunal-provided under the Act,
which is empowered to make such order
or issue such instructions to the Board
as may seem to it proper.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Since the establishment of the Transport Board the number of such complaints has by no means increased, in
fact I am prepared to say that there has
been a very definite diminution in them.
In such cases as we have received I
think I may say we have invariably been
able to satisfy the complainants, either
by arranging with the Board to remedy
the matter complained of (and I may say
that the Board have always shown themselves most anxious to remedy anything
in the nature of a reasonable complaint),
or by putting such facts and figures
before the complainants as to satisfy
them that they had no reasonable
grounds for their criticism.
The hon. and gallant Member suggested that there had been what he
described as a wholesale rise in fares.
What are the facts as to fares and rates?
The facts are that there has been nothing
approaching a general rise in these
charges since the Board assumed control.
In some particular cases fares have gone
down, and in a few individual cases (very
few, as a matter of fact), where the old
fare was utterly uneconomic, they have
gone up. But the general level has not
altered. As regards freight charges, the
same remarks apply. Here it is quite
possible; indeed, it is suspected that in
certain instances operators were giving
specially low rates, either out of motives
of personal friendship or for some other
reason, to particular individuals, and
these individuals would now doubtless
feel much annoyed at being asked to pay
on the same basis as their neighbours.
But they cannot expect the Board to do
this sort of thing, and it would indeed
be most improper and quite illegal if
they did.
I cannot, of course, reply to the particular cases to which the hon. and gallant
Member has referred, as I have not had
notice of them, but if I tell the House
the actual facts concerning the only
concrete cases put forward by the
Chambers of Commerce, I think hon.
Members will be able to form an opinion
as to the reserve with which they should
accept vague allegations of a general
character, and even particular allegations.
In the case of the Derry Chamber, two
instances were put forward. The first
was with regard to the charge for the
carriage of batteries, which is a very
small item of traffic. Admittedly, in the
first instance, by a mistake an increased
charge was made, but as soon as the
charge was challenged and inquiries were
made it was reduced, and the matter
has been put right, without any difficulties being made about it. The second
charge was that a County Antrim farmer
had to pay 2s 3d per head for the
carriage of sheep from Parkmore to
Belfast, whereas it was alleged that previously the price had been 1/- per head.
On investigation, it turned out that the
price charged in this particular case was
not 2s 3d but 1s 9d. No evidence has
yet been produced by the complainant,
and the Board have been unable to find
any evidence that the old charge was 1/-;
even if it were so, it was a cut rate
which was entirely ridiculous for sending
a lorry a distance of over 50 miles.
In the case of Armagh, the chairman
of the Armagh Chamber of Commerce
stated at a public meeting that the fare
from Keady to Armagh had been raised
from 10d to 1s 6d. The fact was that
the charge from Keady to Armagh for
several years before the Board took over
was 1s 1d single and 1s 7d return, while
the Board's charge is 10d single and
ls 4d return, so that for both single and
return fares the Board's charges are not
higher but substantially lower than those
in force before they took over.
I only
mention that to show you how unfair it
is for people to make statements without
really investigating the facts.

When it is remembered that many of

vehicles were in such conditions as to call

I think, no mean accomplishment on the
Board's part to have been able to avoid
something in the nature of an all-round
increase in rates and fares.

The Transport Board have had to face

The Board is giving the public of Northern Ireland an excellent service in good
and reliable vehicles run on a proper
economic basis, so that the tendency will
be for the services to improve even
further, and for fares and rates to
come down eventually, throughout the
Province, to the lowest possible level
that good and economical administration
can secure.
I should like to say a word about the

as a lot, the best and most courteous on

I come now to the case of Alderman

got my position in the Corporation as

been elected his supporters chaired him,
a thing they always do.

and we want people in that area compensated.
It was not with any pleasure that I
rose to deal with this matter. If there
had been any sympathy expressed by the
right hon. Gentleman in his reply to the
question on Thursday last I certainly
would not have brought this matter
before the House. Not only did I bring
the Inspector-General, the Minister of
Home Affairs and the City Commissioner
to visit this area, but I brought the
Chief Whip, who is its representative in
the British Parliament. As we expected
he expressed his sympathy with the people
in that district and said that so far
as he was concerned he would take all
possible action.
Now, after eighteen months, we are
told on the floor of this House that the
legal advisers of the Minister of Home
Affairs state that the police were perfectly justified in their action—justified
in wrecking houses and in terrorising
respectable women and children-and
there is no expression of regret from the
Department concerned. We will be told.
in this House, I suppose, later on by the
same Department that it was the people
of Grove Street who attacked the Orange
demonstration on the 12th of July, because there is just as much face in the
one argument as there is in the other.
I do hope that before very long we will
have a public withdrawal of these statements by the right hon. Gentleman.
It being Seven of the Clock, Mr.
Speaker adjourned the House,
without Question put, pursuant
to the Standing Order.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Oral Answer to Question.
HOUSING CONDITIONS IN
CASTLEWELLAN.
Mr. HEALY (for Mr. Campbell) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether,
owing to the very bad housing conditions.
in Castlewellan, about 30 labourers'
cottages were promised some time ago;
whether the local councils are anxious
that the work should be undertaken but
cannot move without the sanction of the
Ministry; whether the Ministry is holding up this work; whether there have
been recent outbreaks of scarlatina in
overcrowded tenements there; whether a
family of eleven occupies two rooms in
one such tenement; whether several such
tenements have been long condemned as
unfit for human habitation; and whether
the Ministry will take early steps to bring
this impasse to an end.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Downpatrick
Rural District Council advertised in
February last that they proposed to make
a scheme under the Labourers Acts, and
were prepared to receive applications for
cottages. The scheme requires the
approval of the Ministry, but much preliminary work has to be done in negotiating for sites, preparing maps, etc., before
it can be submitted to the Ministry.
The submission of the scheme has been
retarded to some degree by unavoidable
delay in obtaining plans for the cottages,
but these are now available, and the
Council are in a position to proceed with
the preparation of the scheme for the
Ministry's approval.
I am aware, from the reports of my
Ministry's inspectors, that there is a
number of unsanitary houses in Castlewellan, but have no information as to
the number of persons living in such
houses.
Only three cases of scarlatina have been
reported from Castlewellan during the
last three months.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Employment of Women and Young
Persons Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): This is a very
short and concise Bill, and I propose to
show the changes in comparison with
previous legislation and how those
changes are made for the benefit of the
workers concerned. The main provisions
which regulate the employment of women
and young persons are contained in the
Factory and Workshop Act of 1901. The
employment of women and young persons
is limited to the day and must fall within
fixed periods, as from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.,
from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., and in some
industries from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Previous
to the Great War, the employment of
such persons on the shift system was, in
general, prohibited by the Factory Acts.
Before the war, in fact, employers felt
no great need for shift employment. If
excessive pressure arose the plant and
machinery were usually overhauled at the
end of the working day, so that overtime
generally met the requirements of the
situation.
During the war new conditions were
required to meet a new situation. It
became necessary to use existing premises
and plants to their utmost capacity, and
under certain public emergency provisions of the Factory and Workshop Act,
1901, the employment of women and
young persons on the shift system became
widespread. The Armistice effected an
immediate change. The need for
munitions had disappeared; on the other
hand, manufacturers who had been
diverted from their normal output during
2165 Women & Young Persons Bill- 21 OCTOBER 1936

Second Reading
the war years found themselves overwhelmed with orders for commodities required for purposes of reconstruction,
and employers pressed the British Home
Office, which then administered the factory
legislation throughout the United Kingdom, for authority to continue to employ
women and young persons on the shift
system.
The Home Office, with the concurrence
of the Ministry of Labour, considered
that it would be justified in allowing,
during a limited period, the employment
of women and young persons on a twoshift system where it was considered
necessary. Although this system has not
been much used in Northern Ireland, it
is felt that it could be of advantage if
there was a sudden demand for increased
output or where there was a break-down
of the plant in use. This system obviates
the necessity for working unduly long
hours and, undoubtedly, will give
additional employment through engaging
other workers. The existing law requires that before a shift system can be
introduced in a factory a joint application by the employer and the majority
of workpeople must be made, and an
order then issued by the Ministry of
Labour. Once an Order is made it continues in force indefinitely, provided
abuses do not arise in the factory.
In 1934 the Secretary for the Home
Department in Great Britain appointed.
a committee to enquire further into the
working of the system, and to advise
whether or not this system should be continued on a permanent basis. The committee, which was a most representative
one, including all sections of political
thought, unanimously recommended that
the hitherto temporary provisions should
be made permanent, with certain modifications designed to secure greater
simplification of procedure and improved
safeguards against abuses. A Bill, based
on the recommendations of this committee, has been passed through the
Imperial Parliament, and we desire that
there should be uniformity of legislation.
throughout the United Kingdom. Hence
the reason for introducing this Bill in
this House.
One of the changes it proposes in the
existing law is to abolish the joint application by the employer and the workers.
It has been found that in practice the
procedure of a joint application was open
to criticism, inasmuch as the worker
might feel it incumbent upon him to vote
for a system to which he was opposed.
The new method is much simpler. An
application from the employer is followed
by consultation of the workers in the form
of a secret ballot, as provided for in
Clause 1, sub-clause (2). This is a more
satisfactory method of ascertaining the
views of the workpeople concerned.
The consent of the majority of the
workers is still an indispensable condition
for the granting of an authorisation to
use the two-shift system except in the
case of a new factory, where, obviously,
there would be no workers to consult,
and where every person accepting employment knew under what conditions he was
being employed. I would also like to
direct the attention of the House to the
fact that provision is made for a modification of the eight hours' daily limit by
providing for an increase up to ten hours
if the factory is working on the five days
a week system.
In granting an application under this
Bill, certain conditions of welfare may
be imposed in the matter of proper
accommodation for clothing, suitable
facilities for meals and transport and
reasonable opportunities afforded young
persons attending continuation classes.
Every precaution is taken to make the
conditions acceptable to those engaged in
the industry concerned, and should any
abuse arise Clause 2 provides for revocation. If a substantial period elapses
during which the system has not been
operated a new authorisation is necessary
before the system can again function.
I have touched on the principal
changes which the Bill makes. While
this Bill helps employers to secure a
greater output with, perhaps, a lower
cost of production, it makes for a shorter
working day, for a reduction of overtime,
and for a wider distribution of employment. It enables many branches of industry to meet changing conditions of
trade, facilitates new developments, and
meets the difficulty of seasonal rushes.
It is more elastic than overtime and less
fatiguing. For all these reasons I have
pleasure in moving the Second Reading.
Question proposed. "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

I quite agree that shorter hours would
be desirable on an international basis,
but it is absolute nonsense for hon. Members, if I may say so, to suggest that here
in Northern Ireland we can work shorter
hours in our industries than are being
worked across the Channel or in foreign
countries. Hon. Members must know
that that would be ruinous to our industries here. How, for example, could our
shipyard compete with shipyards across
the Channel if a 40-hour week was the
maximum here while 47 or 48 hours were
being worked there? We would be completely out of it when estimating for
work, and the result would be that our
shipyard would be idle and unemployment
would become more rife than it is at the
present time.

Mrs. PARKER: I do not understand

Mr. HEALY: The hon. Member for

Mrs. PARKER: If he is logical.
Mr. HEALY: It would be wrong, and

Mr. HEALY: I know the country as

people who are unemployed. They are

require much defence by the Members of

-many of them ex-soldiers should be

unfortunate position for them. People
in the country districts deal with pedlars
more out of sympathy with them than by
reason of the fact that they bring stuff
which is cheaper than that sold by local

a great amount of their produce is
