What it is desired to secure by this
Amendment is this. In the ordinary
case of an appeal against a valuation a
certain number of other houses or dwellings will be referred to which are said to
be comparable, and which, therefore, are
used for the purpose of suggesting that
the value should be fixed with reference
to them. It seems to me eminently
desirable that if all this information
obtainable under Clause 9, or at least
facilitated by Clause 9, is made available
to the commissioner it should also be made
available for the appellants in the case
of an appeal. I certainly recognise the
difficulty that would arise if the appellants
were to be given a roving commission to
investigate all these particulars to be
accumulated from all parts of the city.
My suggestion would be this. I think
certain particulars are to be used on the
hearing of the appeal, and it is only
fair that the commissioner who is using
these particulars should state that he
intended to refer to a certain number
of houses in fixing the valuation. On the
other hand the appellant, who is appealing against a valuation if he intends to
use certain comparable units of valuation, should also furnish particulars of

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read the Third
time".-(Mr. Pollock.)
Mr. BEATTIE: The right hon.
Gentleman seems to be pushing this
matter very fast, and I should like to
know his real reason for doing so. The.
Bill went through the Committee Stage
to-day without the Minister giving any
consideration to the representations made
to him, and now he wants finally to close
the door by securing the Third Reading.
This is a Measure which will be very
detrimental to the interests of education.
It is a very contentious Measure and is
not going to meet the requirements of
the teaching profession. The Minister
seems to take the teaching profession so
lightly at the moment that he is prepared to risk the whole education of the
youth of Northern Ireland because of a
paltry concession. He is taking a great
responsibility on himself in pushing this
through without consultation with any
of the representatives of those affected.
We know the results of the failure
of the Government to apply themselves
in a proper way to the settling of dis
putes. They have on two occasions made
reductions without consultation, and now
they want to make a binding arrange
ment under Act of Parliament prohibiting the past services of teachers to be
recognised. I do not like wars. I do not
like the word " war," but the Minister
is going to have an educational war in
Ulster in view of the position in which
he is now placing the serving teacher.
From the point of view of the education
of our youth I do not think it is fair for
the Government to push the Measure
through its Third Reading to-day. I
desired to have time for further consultation to see if any further suggestions
could be made by the teaching profession
which would enable the Minister of
Finance to recognise the just rights of
the teachers of Northern Ireland, but he
has now closed the door to that opportunity.
I oppose this Measure being passed. I
do not do so from the point of view of
an official, but from that of justice, from
that of giving the Northern Ireland
teachers the same conditions of service
as were granted to the English and
Scottish teachers, and because of the
lump sum which has been denied them
since 1919, and which was promised by
the British Government. Now the
teachers are being asked to carry on their
services as they have done in the past
despite all the insults cast on them during
the progress of this Bill. As a Member
of this House, and outside my official
capacity, I will not stand for that. I
can assure the right hon. Gentleman
I will help to lead an army of attack
on the Government for the manner in
which they have dealt with the teachers
in this respect. There is no justification
for the Minister doing this thing. I could
understand it if there was financial stringency or a matter of that kind, but there
is no financial stringency in regard to
granting the lump sum for past services.
That being so, I intend to divide the
House on the Third Reading. This is
not a fair Measure, and is not calculated

THE ROYAL ULSTER
CONSTABULARY CUT.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
it is the intention of the Government to
restore the 2 per cent. cut in the
salaries of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I presume
the hon. Member refers to the deductions made from the pay of members
of the Force as a contribution towards
their pension charges. The pension deduction at present in operation (5 per
cent.) is equivalent to that which obtains
in every police force in Great Britain,
and is regarded as equitable. It represents in fact only a small proportion of
the actual value of pension rights and it
is not proposed to make any further
reduction.
BY-PASS ROAD TO BANGOR.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state the progress that has been
made in regard to the suggested bypass road to Bangor, and when this work
will be started, so as to give employment to some of the large number of
unemployed in Belfast.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will probably appreciate that
a work of the complexity and magnitude
of the proposed by-pass road cannot be
commenced until extensive preliminary
work has been completed.
Conversations have already taken
place with representatives of the Harbour Board and of the railway companies whose railway lines will have to
be crossed and portions of whose
property will have to be acquired.
For the past three months an expert
engineer has been engaged in examining
the proposed route and in surveying it
with a view to ascertaining the most
suitable manner in which effect can be
given to the proposal, and I hope to
receive the engineer's report at an early
date.
I can assure the House that no time
will be lost in putting the scheme into
operation.
ACCIDENTS AT THE DEVIL'S
ELBOW.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that a number of fatal accidents
have occurred on the Bangor Road at
the Devil's Elbow, and what steps are
being taken to have this very dangerous.
corner widened.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
fully alive to the nece sity for improving
the Belfast-Bangor Road at the place
known as the Devil's Elbow, and the
Down County Council, the highway
authority responsible for the maintenance
of the road, has also fully appreciated
the need for effecting improvements and
some time ago prepared a scheme for
making the road safe at this point.
That scheme was submitted and was
approved by my Ministry who will make
grants to the County Council towards.
the expenditure involved. The negoti
ations by the County Council for the
acquisition of the lands needed and the
impossibility of carrying out the necessary works during the summer while the
traffic on the road is very heavy, have
delayed the commencement of the works.
It is, however, expected that it will
be possible to commence the work by the
beginning of the new year at the latest.

Finance Bill. It is not so much a

minor matter. It was provided that
those who had joint deposits most necessarily require a certificate from the
proper Ministry that everything in

important part of the Measure. Whether
the amount is to be £100, £400 or £500
is not a matter for contention. The
estate duty on an estate over £100 and
up to £500 is £1. There is no duty
chargeable on any estate under £100.
The present state of the law regarding
bank deposits in joint names is that
the survivor of a joint deposit of this
amount is in law bound to disclose it
and bring it into assessment. It may be
that the circumstances may show that it
is not liable to estate duty, but legally
it is property passing on death. The
difficulty is to ensure that it is returned.

ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): The basis of this Clause
appears to have been lost sight of by the
House, and I think it would be easier for
hon. Members on both sides to understand the arguments put forward if the
basis of the Clause was explained again.
There is a way in which money can be
lodged in banks which has led to a great
deal of trouble in the past. People can
lodge money on a joint deposit receipt,
which is a system almost entirely peculiar
to Ireland. Money lodged in this way
can be drawn by either of two joint
holders or the survivor. While the two
parties are alive the one who holds the
deposit receipt is in complete control of
the money.
You cannot draw the money
without the document, and therefore,
although the name of the second person
is on the deposit receipt, the only person
who can deal with the money is the one
who holds the document. During his
life, therefore, he is in complete control
of the cash. Upon his death the other
joint holder can walk into the bank,
without any notice to the Exchequer, and
without passing any estate account, and
can draw out that money. The bank is
bound, as our law stands at present, to
pay the money without giving notice to
anybody.
The result is that very large sums of
money are lost to the State, because
people have taken this way of disposing
of their property without making a will.
If a person makes a will his executors
have got to go into the Probate Office and
prove the will, and they cannot prove
the will unless they have passed the
appropriate estate duty with the Revenue.
They have to make a declaration that all
money that has passed under the will is
disclosed in that document, but under the
system by which these deposit receipts
have been operated, a person can leave
any sum of money he likes upon joint
deposit receipt, payable to either or the
survivor, and the very day his death
occurs the survivor can walk into the
bank and draw the money. This gives
rise to very fruitful litigation.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is there any limit to
the money that can be lodged in that
way?
None
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
at all. I was in a case not very long ago
where this very thing was done in an
estate of some thirty or forty thousand
pounds. The money was drawn out of
the bank the day after the person's death
without passing any estate duty and
without the Revenue being a bit the wiser.
Judges in the High Court have, over and
over again, commented upon this practice
and said it was time it was stopped. The
only effect of this Clause is this; it puts
people who pass their money to their successors by means of this particular transaction on the same footing as people who
pass money to their successors by will,
and I do not think any Member on either
side of the House will consider that a
hardship.
So far as the limit of £100 is concerned,
I understand it was put in the Clause for
this reason, that on estates up to £100
there is very little, if any, duty payable.
Mr. POLLOCK: There is no duty
payable.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Therefore, this particular form of fraud does
not operate until you get over £100, but
after that there is no limit, and millions
can stand on joint deposit receipt in the
banks and can be passed out by the
banks. The bank would have to pay out
the money on the day of the death of the

under our Loans Guarantee Acts.

companies, and what steps have been

Now, it was very easy for his Department to answer it, but they did not do

Mr. Pollock: I would refer the hon.
Member to Part II. of the Parliamentary Return for the year ended
31st March last, which sets out in

It will be noted from that return that
the largest proportion of these issues

1931-that is to say, they are temporary payments made in cases where
the Ministry is satisfied that the sums

I consider that it would not be in the
public interest or in the interest of the
companies concerned to publish their
names.-(Official Report, 20th October,
1936, vol. 18, col. 2095).
In some
cases it might not be in the
public interest and in some it might. It

the directors I happen to know. Take

The ATTORNEY - GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): This is a Bill which comes
up every year and is getting more and
more attenuated. In the present
Measure there are only four Acts which
require to be continued. The first is the
Glebe Loan Act, 1870, and the second
the Courts (Emergency Powers) Act,
1914. This latter Act is one which was
passed during the war by way of a moratorium in respect of certain decrees of the
courts which were granted and which
were to be held up from time to time and
could not be executed without an application to the court. The Government has
been looking into the matter, and it is
hoped that perhaps next year it will be
able to abandon this Act, because the
returns show there are very few of these
judgments outstanding. Then there is

Mr. MIDGLEY: I wish to raise a
matter of which I gave notice two days
ago, arising out of a reply given to me by
the Minister of Home Affairs. For the
purpose of refreshing the memory of
every person present I wish to refer to the
question I asked on Tuesday, and also
the Minister's reply. The question was
as follows:
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the amount of
money deducted weekly for rations from
members of the staff, made and female,
including nursing staff, farm staff,
tradesmen, and domestic staff in
Purdysburn Mental Hospital; whether
rations, uniform, laundry and light
are supplied at cost price, and if
accounts of income from staff payments
are available for inspection by the staff
or their trade union representatives;
whether he can state the amount of
profits accruing from these deductions.
from the staff and for what purposes
are the profits utilised; whether he can
state the reason why resident nursing
staffs should be charged rent when they
are compelled to occupy rooms for the
necessary management of the hospital
and safety of the patients; and whether
the Minister is aware of intense dissatisfaction amongst the staff at the failure
of the committee of management to
meet the representatives of the staff;
whether he can state the number of
resignations, especially from the nursing staff, during the last six months,
and what action he is prepared to take
to deal with this important matter.
I want the House to take notice of the
Minister's reply to that very comprehensive, and I might say all-embracing,
question in regard to the administration
of this hospital. Here is the Minister's
reply:
I am afraid I have no information
at my disposal which would enable me
to reply to the various points raised by
the hon. Member in his question.
The hon. Member will, I am sure,
realise that, while certain definite
duties are placed upon me by statute,
these do not include, and I think very
properly so, what I might term the
internal administration of mental
hospitals. The resident medical superintendent, acting under the committee
of management, is responsible for the
matters mentioned by the hon. Member, and I am assured that, if any
member of the staff feels that he has
a grievance, the resident medical superintendent will be only too glad to
receive him and to discuss it.-(Official
Report, 20th October, 1936, vol. 18,
col. 2105.)
I should like Members of the House to
observe from that reply that the Minister stated in the first place that he could
not give me replies to the various points
in the question because he had not the
information. He had two days' notice of
my intention to ask this question, and I
think that any information he was not in
possession of at the time he should be in
possession of at the end of two days.
Secondly, I suggest that the Minister
cannot absolve himself by saying that his

Time and time again, in the Belfast Corporation and in this House, when

This is a very important point indeed.
On various occasions, when members of
the local authority in Belfast, including

local authority in regard to the internal

been told that the committee of management is a statutory committee, more
under the control of the Government than
the local authority, and that we are not

have it both ways. You cannot say
to
us, in our capacity as municipal representatives, that it is a statutory committee and that we are not entitled to
information, and then when we come up
and address ourselves as State representatives and make a request for information, tell us that the committee has not
got it, because the committee is entrusted
only with the administration of the
hospital. You have to face up to the

answering all questions in regard to any

I want to ask the Minister is that

Is that money,
which accumulates as a result of deductions for rations expended in providing
the necessary food for the staff in the
hospital, or is it not a fact that substantial savings have accrued to the
hospital in consequence of those reductions? If substantial amounts have
accrued what is being done with the
money? Furthermore, I want to consider the point mentioned in the question
-why are deductions made in certain

these people must, in the interests of the

be made with regard to rent? I am told
that as much as £50 per week has been
made by the hospital in respect of the

figures I have got seem to suggest that
there is a great deal of foundation for
this statement. For example, I have
got a calculated week's dietary made out
in regard to the feeding of the staff. The

There is another question which I have
raised time and again. There have been
complaints made in regard to the quality
of the food served to the staff in the
hospital. It is alleged-I say so advisedly
-that on one occasion the standard of the

but the only consideration they got on

from the medical superintendent that if

not take up duty in so many minutes
steps would be taken to vacate their posts.
I am advised that proof of these allegations can be found in the abnormal
number of resignations, especially from
the nursing staff, that have taken place
during the last six months. Hon. Members will realise that was one of the points
in my question-to ask the Minister was
he cognisant of the abnormal number of
was he in a
resignations, and if so,
position to advance any explanation. I

ought at least to take sufficient cognisance
of the position to have an inquiry con-

ducted as to what is producing the conditions that entail so many resignations.
We have been told already by the

men individually and discuss
any
grievances. I want to say that that is

in a public institution like the Purdysburn Mental Hospital. In every branch
of local government, in civilised portions
of the globe like Belfast-I do not know

Secretary not realise that is very often

The position is that there is a striking
manifestation of unanimity on the part
of the employees, especially in the
nursing staff, in favour of the recognition
of the bona fide trade union representatives, so that the latter who are familiar
with every aspect of the question, shall
be able to go before the officials or committee of management and there represent the staff and put their point of
view. It has been impossible so far to
achieve that. I want to impress on the
Parliamentary Secretary and the Members of this House that it is not good
enough to maintain a position in the
year 1936 which is in violent contradiction to the principles and practice of
every department of local government.
There is another point I should like
to stress. During all the years that these
people have had these deductions made,
no accounts have been proffered for
their examination. No accounts are
available. They feel that as deductions

are being made in respect of food and
if an account is kept of that, the
accounts ought to be available for their
bona fide representatives. I do not
want it to be assumed that this is a
petty trifling grievance in regard to loss
of diginity on the part of some trade
union official. That is not the point.
The big point is that in the hospital at
the present time there is such a seething
mass of discontent that it is quite possible if it is not allayed in better fashion
than hitherto the results will be more
serious, and, as regards the inmates,
that would be a most deplorable condition of things.
In view of all the points I have
mentioned dealing with the quality of
food, the amounts deducted in respect
of food, the allegation that there is a
substantial surplus and that it is not
known to what that surplus is devoted,
I maintain that the principle of collective bargaining should be adopted.
We can get no headway in regard to
this hospital. There seems to be a
dictatorship of the most autocratic
character prevailing in the hospital. I
am not saying that it is due to
perversity on the part of the medical superintendent. I do not know
the medical officer personally. Any
dealings I have had with him on the
telephone have been of the kindliest
description, and good opinions have been
expressed to me about his administration.
But I do know that I have attempted to
get public information in the Belfast Corporation, and I have found an attitude
of unbridled autocracy on the part of
public representatives and those behind
the scenes.
The hospital staff are waiting anxiously the outcome of this discussion in order to see whether the
grievances they labour under are going to
be dealt with between their bona fide
representatives and the managing committee, or if they are going to be consigned to a condition of insecurity and
uncharitableness during the next twelve
months, as they have been during the past
six months. I make an earnest appeal
to the Parliamentary Secretary to consider the advisability of having this
question thoroughly investigated.

I would like, first of all, to let the
House know something of the facts relating to the fixing of the salaries for these
employees. In 1920 a new scheme of payment of remuneration was adopted. Up
to that time there had been a system of a
salary, plus allowances in kind for rent,
rations, and so on. In the old days-and
I am taking now the case of one of the
ordinary attendants-the salary was £35
and all allowances, and those allowances
were computed to be value for about £38.
In June, 1920, a new arrangement was
made, and a salary was fixed and all these
allowances were done away with. The
salary now paid to a person who used to
get £35 and allowances is £140 8s. At
the time that salary was fixed it was
agreed between the members of the committee and the then staff of the Mental
Hospital that deductions would be made
in respect of rent, rations, and certain
other things, and that the staff would pay
for those; otherwise how could the pension
rights of the employees be assessed. The
only deduction that is made now is for
uniform, but not in respect of the first
year, when it is provided.
The Member for Dock complained of
difficulty in ascertaining the facts and
figures relating to this matter, but as a
matter of fact they are published in a
report every year and are made available
to the general public, and they must be
available to the members of the Belfast
Corporation and all people interested.
Before I go on to develop my point,
may I express the opinion of the Ministry
and all people interested in hospital work,
that the Mental Hospital at Purdysburn,
!

whether regarded as a mental institution

The hon. Member asked the Minister
whether he could state the amount of
money deducted weekly for rations from
members of the staff, male and female.
The amount is 2s 1d per head per day.
The hon. Member rather suggests that
that is outrageous. What do they get
for it? Breakfast in the morning begins
with porridge and new milk, followed by
bacon and eggs, tea, and three or four
kinds of bread and marmalade, all for 7d.
They need not take it unless they like,
and if they do not take it there is no 7d
deducted. Is there anybody who is not
at Purdysburn who would not pay 7d for
a breakfast like that? Then for lunch
there is soup, meat, pudding, potatoes,
and three kinds of vegetables for 10d.
Tea costs 5d, and supper 3d. But the
point is that they need not take it, and
if they do not take it there is no charge
made. Rations and uniform are charged
at cost price; there is no profit. There is
a charge of 4s 8d per person per week in
respect of residence, fuel, light, and
laundry. The cost of those things to the
institution, ascertained actuarily, is
12s 5d, but all the employees are charged
is 4s 8d. I am sure the hon. Member
does not want any change made in that
direction.
I ask the Member for Dock to accept
from me the statement that in 1929 the
then employees, with the full approval of
others, accepted this as a fit and proper
thing to do. I tell the hon. Member
that there are no profits. He quoted
from a dietary which purported to show
that there is an actual expenditure of
£80, but there is a charge amounting to
something like £133. I wonder whether
in those figures the hon. Member has
made any allowance for capital charges?
There has to be a cook and attendants,
and they are not provided for in that
dietary.

Prime Minister regrets the unfortunate
accident as much as any person in the
world. I do not wish the Prime Minister to take anything that I say as an
attack on the Government, because it is
not so intended. In the figures given
by the Minister of Home Affairs the
other day he said, I think, that 18 persons had been killed and 40 had been
injured in motor-racing accidents in Northern Ireland during the past ten years.
I watched the Tourist Trophy Race
on three occasions and I felt I do not
wish to hurt anybody-that something
of the nature which occurred on the last
occasion would occur sooner or later.
With cars travelling at, say, 100 miles
per hour, and people lined on both sides
of the road, the stewards cannot do anything to keep the people back, because
if they ventured to do so they would be
running a risk themselves. We all know
what happened, and I know that it is
greatly deplored by everybody. The toll,
in my opinion, is too heavy. I admit at
once that the race helps the hotels.
There is no disputing that fact. In my
opinion, the race gives young people a
craze for speed, and both before and
after the event you will see them speeding along the roads at a terrific rate. If
there is an accident they are hauled
before the Court. I am not going to
labour the point further, but will now
ask the Prime Minister to make a statement. I am sure he will make his statement in accordance with what he believes
to be in the best interests of the people
of Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am
afraid I will not be able to give the hon.
Member for Woodvale a very complete
answer to-day. It has to be borne in
mind that the Tourist Trophy race is
organised by the R.A.C., and it has also
to be borne in mind that local authorities are involved. The Government have
not as yet been approached by anybody
with regard to the coming year. If at a
later period the hon. Member will
address another question to me on the
subject I will be only too glad to give
him the views of my Colleagues and my
self in regard to the prospects for 1937.
I cannot say more to-day because the
matter has not come under review by the
Government, no request for another race
having so far been received. I do not
know what attitude the R.A.C. or the
manufacturers will take.

POMEROY WATER SUPPLY.
1. Mr. STEWART asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that the inhabitants of the eastern
portion of the town of Pomeroy have not
an adequate supply of water for domestic
and that, as a result of this
purposes,
state of affairs, those engaged in the
milk industry are unable to comply with
the regulations of the Milk Board.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I indicated in
my reply to a similar question put by
the hon. Member in June, 1935, the
question of the water supply in the town.
of Pomeroy has for some considerable
time been receiving the attention of my
Ministry.
During the summer and autumn of
1935 the technical aspects of the matter
were carefully examined by the Rural
District Council's engineer and my
Ministry's inspector, and serious difficulties connected with the supply of water
from available springs were revealed by
that examination.
It was found necessary, for this and
other reasons, to recast completely the
original scheme.
I understand that the revised scheme
on the preparation of which the engineer
has since been engaged is now practically
complete and will be available for
examination by my Ministry's inspector
almost immediately.
Major MCCORMICK Arising out of
that reply, will the Minister state if it
is not a regulation of his Department
that water in Pomeroy or in any other
district is not to be added to milk?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not
quite understand the hon. Member's
question. All I can say is that the
Ministry of Home Affairs is not like
Moses. It cannot make water if there
is no water.
BELISHA TRAFFIC SIGNALS.
2. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
in favour of the system of Belisha signals for traffic points, and whether he
will see that proper signals and places
for crossing by pedestrians are fixed for
city centres, especially in Belfast.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am in
favour of any contrivances which are
of assistance in ensuring the safety of
pedestrians and other road users.
I understand that as an experimental
measure, the Belfast Corporation proposes installing pedestrian crossings at
the Union Infirmary on the Lisburn
Road and opposite the Ravenhill Road
School.
The crossings will be marked as elsewhere in Northern Ireland by steel
studs inserted in the roadway; a Belisha
beacon will be erected at each end of
each crossing and guard rails will be provided on each footpath to ensure that
pedestrians will cross at the proper
places.

At another point a pedestrian crossing
similarly marked by steel studs is being
provided as an experiment, but instead
of having a beacon to indicate its

by pressing a button.

R.U.C. CADETSHIPS.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if appointments for cadetships
are in the first place offered to members
of the Roval Ulster Constabulary and
what examination, experience and age.
is required in the case of outside applications.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It has for
some time been my policy to fill cadet
vacancies from amongst serving members
of the force whose educational and other
qualifications are considered suitable.
No difficulty has been experienced in
obtaining suitable applicants by this

outside the force.

the Mountpottinger area the police

TO COMBAT TUBERCULOSIS.
6. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state what steps he proposes to take
to combat the increase of tuberculosis
throughout Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Local authorities have already ample powers enabling
them to combat tuberculosis by the
provision of medical attention and treatment in sanatoria or at dispensaries or
in the patients' own homes, and in fact
these powers are exercised by all the
appropriate local authorities in Northern
Ireland.
I wish, however, to point out that the
suggestion in the question that tuberculosis is increasing is not borne out by
the Registrar-General's returns which
show that for the last 30 years, the war
years excepted, the death rate from this
disease has fallen steadily. In the last
ten years the rate has fallen from 1.67
per thousand of the population (1925)
to 1.05 per thousand (1935).
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of
that answer might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman is he aware that there is
not sufficient sanatorium accommodation
for all the patients suffering from tuberculosis, and is he prepared to get the
Ministry of Home Affairs to give a grant
of, say, 50 per cent. to the county
councils for this purpose?
SO
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am certain
if the local authorities who are
ably represented by the hon. Member
will put up a scheme the Ministry will
give it favourable consideration.
Mr. HENDERSON: Has the Department not turned down the scheme of
the Belfast Corporation which was intended to combat this scourge, and in
the event of the Corporation securing a

Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I further
ask the right hon. Gentleman is he prepared to give his permission to the
Antrim County Council to carry out

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure the
hon. Member behind me will not ask

Member opposite, I feel justified in

taken by the Home Office in turning

Sir DAWSON BATES: Surely the

Mr. HENDERSON: May I ask if the

CANCER RESEARCH WORK.
7. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that cancer is on the increase in
many districts of Northern Ireland, and
whether the Government are prepared to
give a grant for research work to combat this disease.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Although
according to the figures given in the
Registrar-General's reports the number
of deaths from cancer would appear to
be increasing it should not be assumed.
that this means that the disease is now
more prevalent than formerly. It is
possible that the apparent increase is to
a great extent due to more accurate
diagnosis.
As a committee appointed for the purpose has been conducting research work
in connection with cancer in Great
Britain since 1923, I think the suggestion contained in the latter part of
the hon. Member's question would only
involve unnecessary overlapping.

COST OF INSTALLING
ELECTRICITY.
16. Mr. MINFORD asked the Minister of Commerce whether he is aware of
the keen disappointment existing in
rural areas on account of the price demanded for installation of electricity for
power and light, and the five year
guarantee demaded by the Electricity
Board of Northern Ireland, and whether
he will consider making arrangements
whereby the cost of installation would be
spread over a period of years so as to
enable residents in those areas to get
electric light and power at an economic
price.
Mr. BARBOUR: The question of
providing facilities for the extension of
supplies of electricity in rural areas to
farms or groups of farms has recently
been engaging the attention of the
Electricity Board and of my Ministry.
As the hon. Member will be aware,
the Electricity Board as a self-supporting, albeit non-profit earning body, must
have regard to ordinary commercial considerations in the conduct of its business.
It follows that before sanctioning extensions in rural areas some assurance
must be forthcoming that there will be
an adequate return in revenue to cover
the necessary payments of interest and
sinking fund on the capital expenditure
involved. Accordingly, it has been the
practice of the Board, before sanctioning
expenditure on extensions, not only, I
may mention in passing, in rural areas,
but also generally throughout its area
of supply, to look for a gross return on
the capital cost calculated to cover their
outgoings in connection with the proposed extension.
I should also like to draw the hon.
Member's attention to the considerable
sum involved in connecting up an
isolated dwelling-house with a hightension line. I am advised that in giving

(No. 2) Bill.
Considered in Committee.

CLAUSE 1 (Amendment of enactments
relating to the Capital Fund) ordered to

repayment to the Government Loans
Fund of Claims Fund advances).
Question proposed: "That the Clause.
stand part of the Bill."
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would respectfully ask the Minister to give the Committee a little more information on this
Clause. On the Second Reading of the
Bill the Minister described this as a concession to those engaged in the licensed
trade, and I would like him to say what
services they rendered which entitle them
to receive such a concession. I presume
the levy has been lowered each year,
which would mean that less money would
come into the Exchequer. The extension
of fifteen years will make it a longer
period before the Exchequer receive a
final settlement. I would like the Minister to say is he charging interest and
at what rate, and will the Exchequer
suffer anything in the long run?
Mr. POLLOCK : The reason that
impelled the Government to agree to the
extending of the period for recoupment
of the levy in connection with the extinction of the spirit groceries was that conditions have entirely changed. Business
has been very much depressed during the
past years. The object is to make the
burden less heavy on those people who
were paying this levy. This extension
of 15 years is a slight advantage to them.
In the end they have to pay the cost of
compensation. I cannot give any further
explanation than that. These people are
engaged in legitimate business which has
been very bad. That is evident from the
returns I have made from time to time to
this House in regard to the reduction in
the consumption of alcoholic liquors.
Therefore, there is no use in pressing them
too
hard and, perhaps, causing embarrassment. It is better to get the
money comfortably than under difficulties.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Is there any
interest?
Mr. POLLOCK: The rate of interest
is 4 per cent.

Employment of Women and Young
Persons Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Employment of women
and young persons on a system of shifts).
(1) The Ministry of Labour (hereinafter referred to as "the Ministry")
may, upon the application of the
occupier of any factory or workshop,
authorise in the factory or workshop,
or in any department thereof, the employment of women and young persons
of the age of sixteen years and upwards on a system of shifts whereby
each shift may be employed between
such times as may be specified in the
authorisation being times during the
period between the hours of six in the
morning and ten in the evening on any
weekday except Saturday, and between
the hours of six in the morning and
two in the afternoon on any Saturday.
so however that, subject as hereinafter
*
provided, the system of shifts shall be
such that the hours for each shift shall
not exceed an average of eight hours
per day:
Provided that, where the work or
process for which the system of shifts
is authorised is not carried on on more
than five days in each week, the system
may be such that the hours exceed the
said average per day but so that the
hours are not more than ten in any day
and in the aggregate do not exceed
either forty-eight hours in any week or
eighty-eight hours in any two consecutive weeks.
(2) The Ministry shall, by special
order made under section one hundred
and twenty-six of the Factory and
Workshop Act, 1901 (hereinafter referred to as "the principal Act"),
make provision as to the manner in
which workpeople concerned are to be
consulted and for the ascertainment of
their opinions by secret ballot before
any application is granted under this
section, and, subject as hereinafter
provided, no such application shall
be granted unless the Ministry is
satisfied that the requirements of the
special order have been complied with
and that the majority of the workpeople concerned consent to the granting of the application:
Provided that, where the Ministry
is satisfied that the application relates
to a factory or workshop which is about
to be, or has recently been, newly
established and that the system of shifts
is intended to be permanently adopted
therein for the employment
women and young persons of the age of
sixteen years and upwards, the application may be granted without any such
consultation, ballot or consent as
aforesaid.

You require a long range of time in order to
work the two-shift system. For instance, if
we were to agree to a two-shift system
beginning at 8 o'clock and to stop at 8
o'clock, it would simply mean that the
hours of work 'on the morning shift
would be 33 hours and the afternoon
shift 27 hours, or the average of the
two shifts would only be 30 hours.
That would obviously defeat the whole
intention of the scheme and for one of
two reasons. Either the workers would
suffer a great loss of wages beyond what
they should be expected to suffer, or else
the employers would have to shoulder
the burden of paying for 30 hours, on
the average, wages for 48 hours.

Mr. ANDREWS: The effect of that
would be that unless the workers received the pay for extra hours they would

the system from an economic point of

position that the only way of dealing
with a special emergency would be overtime, and the whole trade union movement are opposed to overtime. One of
the reasons for introducing this Billwhich is the counterpart of the British
Measure passed not years ago, but only
a few months ago-is to prevent the
necessity in cases of emergency of overtime having to be adopted, and remember that, when overtime is adopted, very

being consulted at all. But in the case
of the two-shift arrangement the workers
must be consulted by means of a secret
ballot.
The hon. Member for North Armagh
said there was no break in the period.
There is a break of half-an-hour between
6 o'clock and 2 o'clock and another halfhour break between 2 o'clock and 10

the interests of the workers are being
safeguarded in every direction. Some
hon. Members have suggested that this
is going back to the old days when the
workers were asked to start at 6 o'clock
and when they had to work until 6 o'clock.
There is no comparison between the two
systems. This is a case when in special
circumstances, with their own consent,
they start at 6 o'clock and stop at 2
o'clock, with a half-hour break-a very
different thing altogether. So that it is
really a gross exaggeration of the position

would approve of
resurrecting. And, further, I would like

Mr. BYRNE: I beg to move "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
I propose to state briefly why I ask
this House to give this Hairdressers' Bill
a favourable Second Reading without
dealing with the aspects of it, which
could be more fittingly dealt with by the
Members of the House who
are the
esteemed representatives of the medical
profession here. I wish to say that
in the First Schedule (Part I) of
the Bill the words "First members of
the Association" should be "First members of the Board." The points in
favour of the Bill are: It is the duty of
Parliament to safeguard public health
when public health is affected by the
skilful or unskilful, clean or unclean,
methods by which one of our most extensive public services hairdressing-is
carried on. The more extensive the
public service is the more necessary is
legislation for safeguarding and promoting public interest in that connection. The entire public of Ulster without distinction of age or sex require.
attendance by hairdressers for purposes
of cleanliness, comfort, or better personal
appearance. Hairdressing, therefore, is
one of the most essential and extensive
public services of to-day. It is being
carried out by the use of electrical
appliances in permanent waving-which
all women are requiring-and articles
of toilet such as razors, combs, brushes,
towels, covering gowns, or cloths for
haircutting, etc.
This service is affecting public health,
for good or ill, to the extent as is indicated, by eliminating or disseminating
infectious diseases according to the
standards of the proficiency-in using
electrical appliances-and cleanliness
Iwith which it is carried out. For these
reasons public health interests demand
that this public service must be carried
on in a thoroughly skilful and clean
manner by the operation of law for that
purpose as is proposed by this Bill.
The objects of the Bill are similar to
those of the present maternity, nursing,
and dentists' Registration Acts, also
those of the existing laws which have
operated under the direct or indirect
supervision of the Ministry of Home
Affairs in safeguarding public health as
affected by the work of the public service
concerned. That cannot be compared
with the benefit to the entire public
which would be derived by the operation
of this Bill, which would provide the
means for the instruction of hairdressers
in hygiene and a highly skilful use of
electrical appliances to prevent accidents.
or injurious effects from permanent
waving. This would mean benefical
results to the general public.
For these reasons I think the House
will approve of the objects of the Bill.
Members may feel justified in approving
of the Bill on account of the important
considerations that the responsible public
health authorities throughout their constituencies have approved of the principle of it, and this approval includes
that of the Municipal Authorities
Association of Northern Ireland. To
achieve the ends to be made by the
united efforts of the employing and
employed sections of the hairdressing
trade of Ulster, the Measure by Clause 1
proposes the organisation of the Hairdressers' Association of Northern Ireland," which would be constituted of
two sections one of the employers and
the other of the employed hairdressers.
They would elect by means of the P.R.
system and on a 50-50 basis; their
respective representatives to be appointed by the Ministry of Home
Affairs as the Board of the Association,
which-with the co-operation of the
representatives of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, Ministry of Education, public
health authorities, and medical profession-would deal with matters required to work the proposed Act and
make such regulations as are necessary
for that purpose.
No proposed regulation can operate
without the approval of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, and the Ministry is
empowered to have the Board make a
regulation to assure the impartial,
efficient, and beneficial operation of the
Act to all persons affected by its working. In view of the considerations mentioned, particularly that of public
health, I earnestly and honestly appeal

before the right hon. Gentleman the facts

the loyalists of Ulster are being conscripted. In any case I hope the Parliamentary Secretary who was a trade
unionist will listen. I question whether
he takes part in the trade union movement now, but if he does he will know
that the trade unionists of Belfast are
protesting against the exploitation of the
skilled workers of Northern Ireland. At
the present time the unemployed are
signing at the labour exchange, and a
representative of one of the shipyards at
Barrow-in-Furness came over here and
asked for a number of men, when there
was no earthly reason for that man to
go out of England at all as in many industrial districts there skilled artisans
are signing. What happened? Belfast
workers who have been out of work for
five or six years are being sent to Barrow,
and here are the conditions under which
they are sent. They are brought down
to the labour exchange and they are
told: "You have an offer now to go to
Barrow, but if you can put up a reasonable case it will be quite all right."
Immediately any man refuses to go what
happens? His unemployment benefit is
stopped immediately.
During the past three weeks at least
a dozen men's money has been stopped,
and then they had no alternative but to
go to Barrow. I believe on Saturday
night the scenes that took place at the
Barrow boat equalled some of the scenes
during the Great War. The women of
Northern Ireland were seeing their
husbands off who were conscripted for
Labour in England. They were crying
about their going away without leaving
a farthing behind them and without a

28 OCTOBER 1936
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 28th October, 1936.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Business of the House.
Resolved, "That notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Order No. 1
(Sittings of the House) business be not
interrupted at half-past Six o'clock this
day." (Mr. Pollock.)
Unemployment Assistance (Determinaof Need and Assessment of Needs)
Regulations.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I beg to move
"That the Regulations made by the
Ministry of Labour on the 15th day of
September, 1936, under sub-section (2)
of Section 46 of the Unemployment Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, prescribing
the manner in which the need of an
applicant for unemployment assistance
shall be determined and his needs
assessed, be hereby approved.
""
Before I turn to an explanation of the
Regulations for which I now ask the
approval of the House, I think it is
desirable that I should give a brief summary of the events which have led up to
the making of these Regulations and the
present position. I also hope to be able
to remove some misunderstandings which
undoubtedly exist. The Regulations
before the House to-day are called "The
Unemployment Assistance (Determination of Need and Assessment of Needs)
Regulations, " and I wish to answer at
the outset the question often asked why
a needs test should be required for unemployment assistance, when none is required for unemployment insurance.
The titles of the two schemes supply
the clue to the answer. The Unemployment Insurance Scheme, like the National
Health Insurance Scheme and the Contributory Pensions Scheme, is based on
the principle of insurance. The aggregate contributions of employers and employed, together with the Exchequer
contribution, form one common insurance
fund. The weekly payments made from
the fund to unemployed contributors are
as large in amount as the pool of the
contributions admits, consistently with
maintaining the solvency of the fund.
The payments have no relation to the
individual's need, and are given to him
apart from any resources he may have,
provided he satisfies the statutory insurance conditions.
The Unemployment Assistance Scheme,
on the other hand, is not on a contributory basis, and unemployment allowances
are not paid from the Unemployment
Insurance Fund. The scheme has been
expressly established to assist those ablebodied unemployed within the industrial field who are outside the scope of
unemployment insurance, as well as those
who, though included in insurance, have
either not yet qualified for insurance
benefit or have exhausted their rights.
The allowances granted are not related
to contributions made by the applicant.
They are related to the fact that the
applicant has no work or only such parttime work as does not enable him to earn
sufficient for his needs, as explained in
the Act, and that he is in need of an
allowance.
To explain how this assistance scheme
came into existence we have to go back
to the early days of the Unemployment
Insurance Scheme of 1920, and take
account of the experience that has been
gained in working the Act of 1920 and
the subsequent Acts during the intervening years. When the industrial
depression fell upon the world in 1921
it became obvious that, if benefits under
the insurance scheme were to be limited
by the amount of money available in the
form of insurance contributions, there
would be a large number of workers for
whom no provision would be made during
prolonged unemployment, apart from the
poor-law. In the absence, therefore, of
a separate scheme to deal with those
workers who had exhausted their statutory right to benefit, it became necessary
in various Unemployment Insurance
Acts since 1922 to ease the conditions
for the receipt of benefit. As a result,
payments were made out of the Insurance
Fund, under several names, such as uncovenanted benefit, extended benefit, and
transitional payments, which had
relation at all to the income derived from
the insurance contributions.
no
Unemployment Assistance 2332
Unemployment Assistance HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
In this way there was thrown upon the
fund a burden much greater than could
be met by the contributions paid into
the fund. To meet this excess outlay it
was necessary to resort to borrowing. The
result was that in 1931 the debt on the
Insurance Fund in Great Britain had
grown to £115,000,000, and the debt on
our fund to over 21 millions, apart from
our suspense debt which, at that time,
stood at £2,800,000. It was obviously
most undesirable that this borrowing
should continue indefinitely. Further
borrowing, therefore, was stopped by
legislation, which provided that the payments that I have just mentioned should
be made in future from voted Exchequer
moneys, instead of from the Insurance
Fund.
was
Meantime, the whole working of the
Unemployment Insurance Scheme
exhaustively investigated by the Royal
Commission, which had been asked by
the Government to recommend what the
future scope of the insurance scheme
should be, and how it could best be made
solvent and self-supporting. The Commission had also been asked to recommend
what arrangements should be made outside the insurance scheme for those unemployed persons who are capable of and
available for work, and who are not
entitled to insurance benefit. The Commission reported towards the end of 1932.
After very full consideration had been
given to its recommendations new legislation was introduced, which became the
Act of 1934, and which is the basis of
our present Unemployment Insurance
Scheme and also of our Unemployment
Assistance Scheme.
That Act laid down that the cost of
insurance benefit shall alone be chargeable against the Insurance Fund. I
think we will all agree that that is right
and proper. It established a separate
Fund-the Unemployment Assistance
Fund to meet the cost of giving assistance to those able-bodied unemployed
who do not qualify for insurance benefit,
or have drawn all to which they are
entitled. Arrangements were also made
in our Act of 1934, as well as in the
Great Britain Act, for the gradual funding of the accumulated debts of the
Insurance Funds. The effect of the
legislation of 1934 has been to place the
Insurance Schemes on sound financial
foundations. As a result the rates of
benefit, which had to be reduced in 1931
to meet the precarious financial position
of the Funds, have been restored to their
former level. They have even been
brought above that standard in certain
respects, such as the extension of the
benefit period in many instances and the
increase in rates of benefit to dependent
children. It has been possible also to
enlarge the scope of the Insurance
Scheme, and more recently to reduce the
contribution rates.
The Unemployment Assistance Scheme,
established by the 1934 Act, provides, as
I have mentioned, for those able-bodied
persons who either are not able to qualify
for insurance benefit or who have
exhausted their right to benefit. Part 2
of the Act creates the Unemployment
Assistance Fund sustained entirely from
public moneys, and not by the contributions of those entitled to participate in
its benefits, as in the case of the Insurance
Fund. It is administered by the Unemployment Assistance Board, and allowances are paid, like the transitional payments which preceded them, subject to a
test of the applicants' needs. I should
say at this stage that I consider we have
indeed been fortunate in obtaining persons to serve on the Board who are most
sympathetic and whose one desire is to do
the right thing at the right time.
There has been much ill-founded
criticism of this needs test-sometimes
called the "means test." It should be
remembered that the test does not in any
way affect the majority of the applicants
for assistance, and it is quite unfruitful
to criticise it in a general way. A harsh
application of the test could not, in my
opinion, be justified. But, on the other
hand, a reasonable and sympathetic
application of a condition of the kind is
absolutely necessary in fairness to the
members of the public, who, as taxpayers,
and, to a small extent, as ratepayers, are
providing the money out of which this
unemployment assistance is given.
A means test is no new thing. It has
always been applied in connection with
income tax, super tax, and death duties,
not, of course, for the purpose of seeing
how much shall be given, but in order to
arrive at how much shall be taken away.
It has also always been associated, without criticism so far as I know, with the
payment of Non-Contributory Old Age
2333 Unemployment Assistance

28 OCTOBER 1936
Unemployment Assistance
Pensions. Obviously, if public money
was paid out without any test of the kind
all would be entitled to it-those who
need it and those who do not, and this
would be both absurd and unjust. I
wonder how those who loudly denounce
the test propose that this obvious difficulty could be got over. Perhaps, we
will hear to-day. Let me give you an
example:-two women, let us assume,
are working in a mill and they both
become unemployed. After receiving all
the insurance benefit to which they are
entitled on their contributions, they
apply for unemployment assistance.
The one is married, and her husband
earns, say, about £2 a week, or more.
The other is single and has no resources
at all. Is it suggested that each should
be treated the same at the public
expense?
For my part, I do not believe that
members of the same family, close relations, living in the same house, eating at
the same table, are not prepared to help
each other, always provided that the help
it is proposed they should give is reasonable, having regard to their personal
requirements and circumstances. It will
be for me to show later that the Regulations which it is my duty to ask the
House to consider and approve to-day
are reasonable and just.
Hon. Members are aware that since
the 7th January, 1935, when the Unemployment Assistance Board began to
administer the Unemployment Assistance Scheme, unemployment allowances
have been assessed, both here and in
Great Britain, either on the basis of
regulations approved by this House
which were made on the 31st December,
1934, or on the old transitional payments basis of the area in which the
applicant resides. The Board applies
whichever basis gives the applicant the
more favourable rate.
was
This dual system of assessment
sanctioned by Parliament, because it
was found that those provisions of the
existing Regulations which deal in
particular with rent are not sufficiently
flexible to meet the case of persons living
in relatively low-rented houses. It was
considered, too, that there were strong
grounds for easing considerably, having
regard to personal requirements, the
position with regard to the treatment of
earnings coming into the household from
adult members of the family.
To afford an adequate opportunity for
investigating the whole situation, therefore, Parliament, both here and at Westminster, authorised, as a temporary
measure, the restoration of the old
transitional payments basis in all cases
where it would prove more favourable
than the Regulations basis.
a
During the intervening period, the
position has been exhaustively reviewed
throughout the Kingdom, and, as
result, it is proposed to bring into operation as from the 16th November, 1936,
new Regulations which will be uniform
here and in Great Britain. It is
intended to adjust the old system to the
new gradually over a period of eighteen
months.
The Regulations, which I am asking
the House to approve to-day, have been
submitted to me by the Northern Ireland
Unemployment Assistance Board in
terms similar to those of the Regulations
submitted by the Great Britain Board
and approved by the United Kingdom
Parliament. This is in conformity with
the principle adopted by the Board when
it assumed responsibilty for administering the scheme. It is in accordance too,
as hon. Members know, with the policy
and practice of our Government in connection with our social services. It complies also with the principle underlying
the revised Reinsurance Agreement
which this House has approved and
sanctioned and which extends to the cost
of unemployment assistance in Northern
Ireland the same financial cover that
applies to the Exchequer costs under the
General and the Agricultural Unemployment Insurance Schemes.
I am sure hon. Members recognise the
great value to our unemployed, and the
community generally, of the old Reinsurance Agreement and of the new one,
both of which have enabled us to maintain a uniform provision throughout the
United Kingdom for our unemployed.
The Regulations that I am asking the
House to approve have been available for
hon. Members to study for some time,
together with the explanatory memorandum by the Unemployment Assistance
Board which has been circulated as a
White Paper. It does not seem
necessary for me,
therefore, to go
Unemployment Assistance 2336
Unemployment Assistance HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
through the Regulations in great detail.
I wish, however, to explain the main
alterations which they will bring into
effect, if this House gives them its
approval, on the sixteenth of next
month. The alterations fall into three
groups, and I would like to emphasise
that every change, as compared with the
existing Regulations, will be in favour of
the recipient.
First of all, many of the scale rates of
allowances have been improved, and, as
the existing rates and the proposed rates
are summarised in the Board's Memorandum, I will not occupy the time of the
House by going through them. I need
only point out that, in addition to the
increases in rates of allowances which the
new Regulations will provide, there will
no longer be any reduction in the aggregate scale allowance of households of more
than five members. Applicants, moreover, who are householders with dependants, and without an available margin
of resources, will in general receive not less
than the rates of unemployment benefit.
The only exceptions to this will be
possibly in the case of an applicant having a relatively small rent to pay, or
living in a rural area, or subject to the
considerations mentioned in paragraph 1
(2) (a) of Regulation IV. I would ask
hon. Members to note that I have
stressed the phrase "available margin of
resources," as, under the Regulations,
there will be certain earnings and other
sources of income which will not be taken
into account to reduce the amount of
the unemployment assistance allowance
granted.
The second group of changes relates to
the payment of rent. Sub-paragraph
(2) of paragraph 1 of the First Schedule
to the Regulations deals with the power
to vary allowances to meet the varying
situations which arise in the matter of
rent. While these provisions, like the
corresponding provisions of the existing
Regulations, are framed broadly on the
assumption that a household will spend
a quarter of its allowance on rent (which
includes rates), the new provisions have
been made much more elastic than those
in the existing Regulations. They give
a wide discretion to the Board's officers,
in consultation with the Advisory Committees, to increase the allowance where
the rent actually paid by the household
is more than a quarter of the scale rate,
and, on the other hand, to waive reduc
tions in appropriate cases where the rent
paid is less than a quarter. I think it will
be agreed that this flexible arrangement is
well suited to meet the variations in rent,
which, naturally, arise as between one
locality and another, even for households
of the same size.
I now come to the third group of
changes under the Regulations. They
deal with the method of calculating how
much of the resources of the members of
an applicant's household may be taken
into account in assessing what allowance
an applicant should receive from public
funds. Briefly, the changes increase the
amount of the earnings of members of
households that are to be treated as
available for their own personal requirements, and not for the maintenance of
the common household, and the alterations reduce the circle of members of a
household who are to be regarded as contributing substantially to its support.
Our Parliament has already laid down
in the Act of 1934 that certain items of
income and certain capital savings are
not to be taken into account as a ground
for reducing an applicant's allowance
from public funds. Part 1 of the
Second Schedule to the Regulations
reproduces the provisions of the Act in
this respect.
The first 5s a week of any sick pay
from a friendly society, the first 7s 6d a
week of any benefit under the National
Health Insurance Act, and the whole of
any maternity benefit under that Act
(exclusive of any increase of such benefit
by way of additional benefits, and of any
second maternity benefit), the first £1 a
week of any wounds or disability pension,
and one half of any weekly payment of
workmen's compensation, are to be dis
regarded in reckoning an applicant's
Of course, that is all to the
benefit of the applicant.
resources.
Again, no savings up to £25 are to be
taken into account at all, and savings
over that figure up to a total of £300 are
to be reckoned as yielding a weekly
income of one shilling-only for each
complete £25. In effect, therefore, even if
an applicant for assistance has just under
£50 laid by, his allowance from public
funds will not be diminished on that
account.
Unemployment Assistance
Unemployment Assistance

28 OCTOBER 1936
Any savings in excess of £300 belonging to an applicant, Parliament has
already laid down, must be treated in
ordinary circumstances as directly available for the applicant's current needs
before he calls upon the public to
support him. But the new Regulations
provide that it is only savings in excess
of £400 that are to be regarded as
directly available for current needs,
when the savings belong to some member
of a household other than the applicant,
his wife, husband, father or mother. In
their case, too, as regards the amount
under £400, instead of one shilling a
week for each complete £25, merely the
actual income produced by the capital is
to be taken into account. That, I think,
is a very generous provision.
I now come to the way in which the
new Regulations deal with allowances
out of earnings for the personal requirements of the earning member of the
household. This matter is dealt with in
paragraph 1 of Part 2 of the Second
Schedule. The principal change affects
married sons and daughters living in
their parents' household or married
brothers and sisters of the applicant
living in the same household who have
dependants of their own for whose
on
support they are directly responsible.
Under the existing Regulations the
allowance made to the married son is,
apart from the allowance at the scale
rates for the maintenance of himself and
his own dependants, calculated
exactly the same basis as the allowance
to the unmarried son. Paragraph 1 (4)
of Part 2 of the Second Schedule of the
new Regulations provides that in future
in such a case the allowance for personal
requirements shall be an amount calculated on the basis applicable to unmarried
sons and daughters, brothers and sisters,
together with such further sum as is
reasonable in all the circumstances. In
effect, under this new provision, the
earnings of such a person will not be
regarded as available for the support of
the applicant to any greater extent than
if the wage-earner were a boarder paying
a reasonable weekly sum for the keep of
himself and his wife or children.
In the case of other wage earners in
the household also the new Regulations
are more advantageous to them in the
treatment of earnings. May I give an
example, leaving out for the sake of
clearness the intermediate steps in the
calculations.
Let us assume the case of a household
consisting of the applicant who is a
father, his wife, and an adult son and
daughter, both unmarried. The son and
daughter are employed and earn between.
them 50s a week. Under the present
Regulations the father in normal circumstances would qualify for an unemployment allowance of only 7s a week.
Under the new Regulations, 43s of the
50s earned will be regarded as needed
for the personal requirements of the son
and daughter, and the father in normal
circumstances will qualify for an allowance of 17s a week, notwithstanding that
there is coming into the house an additional 50s.
Over and above the number of ways
in which the Regulations have been
modified in favour of applicants, an overriding discretion is given to the Board
and the Appeal Tribunals to increase the
allowance to a wage-earner for personal
requirements in special circumstances.
A case for the exercise of this discretion
would be that, for example, of an
elderly applicant with a long industrial
record, but with
poor prospects of
employment for the future. If hitherto
he has not qualified for an allowance
because sons living with him are earning
good wages, the Board under the new
Regulations can regard a larger proportion of the sons' earnings as required for
their personal needs and not available
for the support of the household. By
this means in proper cases the Board will
be able to grant some allowance to the
father and thus ease his continuous and
complete dependence on his sons' earnings. That, I am sure the hon. Members will admit, is another very
substantial improvement.
Again, paragraphs 2 and 3 of Regulation IV, relating to cases in which
special circumstances or needs of an
exceptional character exist, reproduce
those provisions of the existing Regulations which have enabled the Board in
many cases to give exceptional allowances, for example, towards the cost of
special diet in cases of illness or towards
the cost of replacing, in appropriate.
cases, household equipment.
There are two other points in the
Regulations which I will mention.

Unemployment Assistance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
Paragraph 1 (2) (a) of Regulation IV
repeats the provision of the existing
Regulations whereby the amount at
which the needs of an applicant may be
assessed is limited to the sum which
would ordinarily be available for the
support of the household out of the earnings of the applicant and of any other
member of the household whose needs are
taken into account, if these persons were
employed at their ordinary work. The
Regulation now makes it clear, however,
that this rule is not to apply where
special circumstances or exceptional
needs exist.
Secondly, paragraph 1 (2) (b) of
Regulation IV provides for such adjustments as may seem reasonable in the
allowance of a person residing in a rural
locality, having due regard to circumstances connected with the general
character of that locality, and
and any
recommendations made by the Advisory
Committee for the area.
If hon. Members will please turn to
paragraph 37 of the Board's Memorandum, they will see that the Board estimates that the new Regulations will
result in increased allowances for
between 7,000 and 8,000 persons.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Query.
Mr. ANDREWS: I think we have to
take the Board as a good authority on
the matter. Whether the hon. Member
is or not remains to be seen. That is,
more than one-third of the present number of applicants will benefit by the
application of the new Rules-and these
increases will take effect as quickly as the
current allowances can be reassessed.
On the other hand, in a minority of cases
adjustments in a downward direction
will be necessary in consequence of the
anomalies created by the present dual
system of assessment. These changes,
however, will in general be made by
instalments and in close consultation
with the Local Advisory Committees,
and the process will be spread over the
period of eighteen months prescribed in
Article IV (3) of the Regulations. All
those whose allowances may require
adjustment in this way will have the
opportunity, should they so desire, of
having their cases reviewed by the appeal
tribunals.
The additional cost of applying the
new Regulations will, the Board estimates, amount to about £22,000 a year
on such assumptions as it is practicable
to make, and will rise to possibly
£29,000 a year after the Second
Appointed Day. These figures, however, depend entirely on the course of
employment, the classes of applicants for
assistance, the trend of their circumstances, and the discretionary considerations to be taken into account by the
Local Advisory Committees and by the
Board-all of which are factors which are
inevitably conjectural.
I have referred several times to the
part which it is hoped local advisory
committees will take in the administration of the Regulations. These committees have been set up under the powers
of the 1934 Act, which directs the Unemployment Assistance Board to establish
advisory committees for the purpose of
securing the advice and assistance of
persons having local knowledge and experience in matters affecting the general
administration of the Unemployment
Assistance Scheme. The Board has
appointed, therefore, an advisory committee for each of its nine administrative
areas in Northern Ireland, and under
the new Regulations the committees will
be asked to advise on the treatment of
rent, the adjustment of allowances to
conditions in rural areas, and the gradual
assimilation of assessments to the new
provisions.
There is one other matter that I must
mention before I conclude. Hon. Members will observe that it has now been
decided, both here and in Great Britain,
that the beginning of next financial year,
namely, the 1st April next, shall be the
date of the Second Appointed Day.
From that date the responsibility for all
persons within the scope of the Unemployment Assistance Scheme will be taken
from the shoulders of local authorities
and placed on the Unemployment
Assistance Board.
I know there is a feeling in some
quarters that, because it was not possible.
to bring the scheme into complete effect
on the date originally proposed, our local
authorities have been left to continue to
carry a financial liability in respect of
the able-bodied unemployed for a longer
period than was intended. I wish to
emphasise that this is not so. The local

Unemployment Assistance
authorities have been generously treated,
and will continue to be fully compensated
until the Second Appointed Day, for the
liability which they have continued to

able-bodied, and of which they would
have been relieved if the date of the

actually been at some financial advantage by reason of the postponement.
I ought to point out too, in view of
the complaint that has been made by
some, about the burden which recent
legislation has placed on local rates, that
so far as the support of the able-bodied
unemployed is concerned the Unemployment Assistance Scheme relieves our
local authorities of a very substantial
part of an obligation which, for many

of local rates as distinct from central
taxation.
I am obviously not in a position to
forecast with great precision the course
of unemployment over a future financial
year, nor can I, at this stage, indicate
the precise amount of the local authority
contribution to the assistance scheme in
the future. Nevertheless, I can give the
House a picture of the new financial
arrangements which will operate when the
new scheme is in full operation, if I take
what would have been the experience
during last financial year as the probable
basis of cost in a future year.
The total cost of the unemployment
assistance service during twelve months
would, it is estimated, amount to approximately £1,400,000, including administration. Of this sum over £1,312,000—
about 94 per cent.-would be provided
by the Exchequer, and only £88,000about 6 per cent.-by the local authorities in the form of a contribution to the
Unemployment Assistance Fund. The
consideration for this contribution is the
fact that they will be relieved by the new
scheme of the liability for meeting the
cost of assisting the able-bodied unemployed. When the full public cost of relieving our unemployed is considered;
that is, the combined expenditure on the
insurance scheme and the assistance
scheme out of central and local taxation,
the Exchequer, we find, would contribute
£2,700,000 a year and the local authorities £88,000, or only just over 3 per cent.
of the total cost.
I hope I have not gone too much into
detail in explaining the provisions of
these new Regulations. I feel, however,
that it is most important that they should
be fully understood. They will constitute the basis on which assistance will
be given to all unemployed and needy
able-bodied persons between the ages of
16 and 65 who are at present within the
scheme. From the beginning of next
financial year the scope of the scheme will
be widened still further. It will then
include all such unemployed persons
within the field of insurable employment
in agriculture, industry and commerce,
who are either unqualified for unemployment benefit, or have received all the
benefit to which their contributions entitle them. Altogether the scheme will
comprise some 370,000 of our people.
I think it will be admitted that I have
not spoken to-day in a political or party
sense. I have felt that I have been dealing with a great human problem, and I
am confident that the more carefully
these Regulations are examined the more
evident it will be that they are reasonable and fair, and the more impressed
hon. Members will be with the great
advance they mean towards assisting our
fellow-citizens in need. I beg to move.

These Regulations bristle with injustices,

not
give to the working-class people
normal comfort, normal means of subsistence, and they are harsh towards
large numbers of the poor people who
seldom get good food for any length of
time or even good clothing. I would like
to submit, in connection with these
Regulations, some reflections that they
awaken in one's mind. There are certain
rights which are indisputable. They may
not be acceptable here, nevertheless they
are rights, and it is my duty to state
them. I do submit to this House that
every man in Northern Ireland has a
right to what is necessary to support himself and his wife and children in comfort.
Mr. ANDREWS: Hear, hear.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I submit, further,
that he has a right to earn his living by
is toil; that he has a right to maintain
himself by that toil and also maintain
those who are dependent upon him. He
has the right to obtain by work the
necessary means of subsistence. I was
reading quite recently the words of a
colonel of the Parliamentary Army during the Civil War, in the time of Charles
I. Colonel Rainboro used words, which
I have no doubt he put in the quaint
English that was used at that time. He
said:
Really I think that the poorest he
that is in England hath a life to live
as the richest he.
Has "the poorest he" this right in
Northern Ireland to-day with all these
Regulations? Is it recognised that if a
man cannot get work he ought not to
lose his right to subsistence and support
in such a state as befits a human being?
There is a duty cast upon society in some
way or other to provide the ways and
means to enable him to procure the
necessaries of life. If society, as now
organised, cannot achieve this, society
should be reorganised on a basis that
would secure to the unemployed either
work or just maintenance. Three
thousand years ago it was said in Holy Writ
that the first-born of the poor should be
fed and the poor should rest in confidence.
We have not obtained that day even yet
when 3,000 years have gone by. I do
admit that if a man will not work when
work is available for him he ought to pay
for idleness. He then is at fault. If
the work is there and he will not work
the fault is his, and he is wrong and ought
to pay the penalty for that. But if a
man is willing honestly to work and cannot get work then society is at fault.
and the penalty for that fault should not
rest on his shoulders.
After all the exhaustless granary of
this old earth of ours is rich enough to
minister to the wants of all, and if
organised society deny to a man work,
then the penalty, I say again, should not
be visited upon him. That man should
not on that account be driven to hunger
and a reduced standard of living. Why
should he be penalised for no fault and
no misdoing of his? The time, I believe,
will come when it will be universally
recognised that in that case the upkeep
of that man is and ought to be a State
charge. There is no justification for
putting upon a man of that type, an

My reading of this is not perfect, but it
is not my fault. It is due to the bad
