I want to say that the new Regulations
have created despair in the minds of the
unemployed, who cannot see any brightness in the distance or any possibility of
being absorbed into employment.
The
old regulations of 1934 were put into
operation by the National Government,
but owing to public indignation against
them the Government withdrew them and
set up temporary regulations. The scale
was withdrawn and local authorities were
allowed to apply themselves to a higher
standard than was set out under the old
regulations. I want to point out at the
beginning that Northern Ireland never
attained to the high standard of allowances meted out to the unemployed in
Great Britain. In some areas in Britain
the allowance was 26s per week for a man
and wife.
We in Northern Ireland never had any
higher figure than 24s, and, therefore, I
want to justify my statement on a
previous occasion that we are not following a step-by-step policy. That statement has been proved by the debate on
the new Regulations in the British House
of Commons. Mr. Brown has condemned
some local authorities for their extravagance in that direction, but nevertheless
it has been admitted by those in authority
in England that 26s was the joint rate
applicable to a man and wife. Therefore, Englishmen, Scotsmen and Welshmen had 2s more than the men in
Northern Ireland. There is opposition
to this new Regulation from the whole
organised labour movement. That is not
the political movement as a unit, but the
whole organised labour movement to
which these Regulations will at some time
apply. What do they say?
When the Regulations were issued in
London the trade unions called a conference of representatives of all workingclass people.
They stated that the
Regulations of the Unemployment Assistance Board, which were issued towards
the end of 1934, were destroyed by a
spontaneous outburst of indignation.
There was indignation and disapproval
from almost every quarter because of
their shameful inadequacy. In the view
of labour-and I refer now to the new
Regulations there is an advance for a
portion of the unemployed over the hated
Regulations of 1934, which were contemptuously rejected by the nation. The
new Regulations give some concessions
and certain scale rates have been
increased. The rent rule has been made
more flexible and the rule regarding contributions by members of an applicant's
household has been modified.
On the other hand, the scale is still
too low for the physical well-being of
numbers of workless people, especially
those who have been out of work for the
longest period. They will ultimately
receive less than they are receiving under
the stand-still arrangement. That is a
very important part of these new Regulations, and one that this House should
concentrate upon.
Those who have been
out of employment for the longest period
are going to receive less than they were
receiving under the stand-still arrangements. That is the purport of the conditions which apply under the new
Regulations. Another point is this, at
least one in four of the present applicants
on the means test will suffer a reduction
in benefit. That one in four applies to
industrial areas.

We have only what we might call two
industrial areas in Northern Ireland,
which means that a bigger proportion will
suffer a reduction in Northern Ireland
than in Great Britain. I know I will be
challenged by the statement that we cannot deviate from the step-by-step policy.
I say you have already deviated from it.
The percentage of reductions is to be
higher in Northern Ireland than in Great
Britain, and, therefore, the Regulations
framed for Great Britain cannot apply
here, without doing serious injury to
large numbers of unemployed in the rural
areas. The effect of the new Regulations
on the purchasing power of the unemployed population will be negligible, and
it follows, therefore, that they cannot
bring substantial relief to the homes of
the workers. That is to say, any increase
that is given will not move the home
market. The increase is so small that the
home market will be at the same point
as under the old stand still Regulations.
The object of putting more money into
the hands of the people is really to move
the market, to increase consumption. If
there is bigger consumption there will be
improvements in other directions. This
Regulation is not going to give any help.
in that direction, because it is too small.

This paragraph provides that where

Unemployment Assistance

families into lodgings. It always seems
to me the most elementary feeling in
man is the obligation upon the parents
to clothe and feed their children, and
then, if these children were in need
subsequently, to house them and look
after them as far as is in their power.
I have always thought that the most
elementary feelings of humanity demand.
that the child which has been brought
into the world and has been clothed, fed
and educated must bear feelings of
gratitude and human decency towards
the parent who has treated and taught
and looked after it in this way. It

to be congratulated upon or admired
or praised, because it is just the
elementary feeling of humanity that the
family should hold together. I think
it is only a proper and decent feeling
that would resent support from outside
where it is possible in any way to give
the support oneself.
The hon. Member for Central stated
that the means test-I think I am
correct in saying this-was a negation
of Christianity. When I heard him saying that I could not help thinking that
I always understood that Christ's teaching was to help others, and he never
taught that fathers and sons should refuse to help each other and to throw
their obligations on the outside world or
the State. A great deal has been said
and I know a great deal more will be

The only other matter to which I wish

on a Committee that sits in this House,
whose Members have a good knowledge
of this subject, and into whose hands the
destinies of the wild birds in Northern
Ireland have been placed. Up to the
present they have safeguarded
interests of the birds. I have listened
to a lot of talk in this House about
unemployment, but if this Clause was
passed you would take away the livelihood of many people. I need only refer
to the fable of the frog and the boy.
The frog said, "What is play to you is
death to me." It was going to be play
to a certain class, but it was going to be
death to the wives and families of the
poor shooters who lived by this means.

you aware that the birds we are trying
to protect do not breed in Northern

Vaughan's Charity (Administration)
Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. POLLOCK: This Bill, which
comes from the Senate, is really for the
purpose of implementing a decision of
the Chancery Court in respect of an
ancient Trust. I should mention that
this Trust was formed nearly two hundred
years ago; to be correct, in 1753, by a
called
philanthropic gentleman
Mr.
George Vaughan who created a Trust and
endowment covering a large portion of
his estate, if not all of it, including a
substantial eighteenth century building,
and leaving endowments which are to be
found in the Third Schedule to the Court
scheme embodied in the Bill. They were
obviously intended for the benefit of the
persons who were living on these large
estates. The greater of these investments
are the proceeds of the sales, under the
Land Purchase Act of 1925, of the lands
in County Fermanagh which were the
property of the Governors of the School.
The original will of George Vaughan
contained a number of private bequests
and these were so intermingled with the
charitable bequests, including not only
the setting up of the Charter School but
also the building of a church, that it
required an Act of the Irish Parliament
of the year 1775 to clear up the position
and also to incorporate the governors of
2403 Vaughan's Charity Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Pollock]
the school. It is historically interesting
as showing the continuity of Parliamentary institutions in Ireland that it now
comes to this House to amend an Act
of Parliament passed by the Old Irish
Parliament in College Green. It is, in
fact, mainly because of the existence of
that Act of Parliament that it is impossible for the Northern Irish Courts of
their own powers to amend the conditions
of the original trusts.
Those trusts were, apart from the
erection of a church and the enclosure of
a churchyard, to build a school capable
of lodging three hundred boys and two
hundred girls who should be brought up
-I use the actual words of the original
will-in the several branches of the
linen manufacture, such as knitting,
spinning and sewing for the girls,
husbandry, flax-dressing and weaving in
which each boy is to be instructed,"
preference to be always given to the
children on the Vaughan Estate. The
court scheme, bearing in mind changed
conditions in modern times, has kept
as closely as is feasible to the original
intentions of the founder.
The scheme is divided into two parts,
firstly, educational trusts involving
grants to the managers of the public
elementary schools on the Vaughan
Estate for the purpose of providing free
books or meals for children attending
the schools. There are also to be technical scholarships for girls who have
attended these schools, while opportunity
for the future education of the boys from
these particular schools is provided under
the agricultural trust portion of the new
scheme.
The agricultural trusts obviously are
close to the intentions of the founder,
involving the utilisation of the buildings
and the immediately adjoining farm as a
centre where young farmers will be
trained in the objects which are set out
in Clause 22 of the scheduled scheme,
Scholarships to the school will be given
by County Committees of Agriculture,
and in order to preserve the rights of
the immediate locality the County Committee for Fermanagh is given a certain
preference in their nominations, including nomination of persons resident on
the Vaughan Estate. These students
will be intern students, but there is a
special provision in
in respect
respect of the
Vaughan Estate for scholarships for six
extern students, who will be entitled to
special allowances out of the Trust funds.
Any surplus lands not required for the
purposes of the Institute will be sold and
the proceeds added to the Trust funds.
There are also certain initial payments
to be made from the funds in hand, which
are in the nature of winding up the old
Trust. These are set out in Clause 7
of the scheme, and I should perhaps
mention in particular the payment of
£750 to the select vestry of the parish
in which the building is placed. The
grounds for this payment and for the
grant of a site for a rectory referred to
in Clause 3 of the scheme are that the
original Trust had certain provisions
dealing with religious education, including money provision for a chaplain for
the school, who for many years actually
resided on portion of the premises which
was therefore used as the rectory for the
parish. The parish is now deprived of
any control in the building, and alternative money provision-not of a
tinuing character-has been made.
con-
The governing body is set out in paragraph 17 of the scheme, and it is designed
to preserve the educational and agricultural aspect of the original Trusts. These
trustees will be responsible for the proper
utilisation of the income received by them
from the investments which will be held
by the Ministry of Finance in its capacity
as Commissioners of Charitable Donations
and Bequests, and will be the governing
body for the new Agricultural Institute.
The trustees will have the full responsibility of any trustees of a charitable
or educational endowment. One of their
first tasks will be to set the Institute in
proper order for the reception of pupils.
This will involve substantial capital outlay, which could not be incurred without
seriously crippling the endowments. I am
happy to say that the Carnegie trustees
have undertaken, if this scheme is
approved by Parliament, to contribute a
substantial sum of money towards capital
outlay, and will also make a contribution
towards the running expenses of the
school during the initial period. I am
sure that every Member of the House
will appreciate the substantial help that
this will give in starting the Institute
on a sound footing.
The covering Bill merely sets out the
approval of Parliament to the scheme as

CLAUSE 1 (Employment of women
and young persons on a system of shifts).
(1) The Ministry of Labour (hereinafter referred to as "the Ministry'')
may, upon the application of the

authorise in the factory or workshop,

Provided that, where the work or
process for which the system of shifts
is authorised is not carried on on more
than five days in each week, the system
may be such that the hours exceed the
said average per day but so that the
hours are not more than ten in any day
and in the aggregate do not exceed
either forty-eight hours in any week or
eight-eight hours in any two consecutive weeks.

and twenty-six of the Factory and

any application is granted under this

satisfied that the requirements of the
special order have been complied with.
and that the majority of the workpeople concerned consent to the granting of the application:

Adair's Divorce Bill.
The following Report was made from
the Joint Committee on Divorce Bills:
"That they had considered Adair's
Divorce Bill and that the averments in
the Preamble had been proved to their
satisfaction, and that they had gone
through the Bill, and directed the same
to be reported without Amendment to
the House."
Resolved: "That the promoters of
Adair's Divorce Bill which has been
introduced into this House in the present
Session of Parliament shall have leave
to introduce the same in the next
Session of Parliament, provided that
notice of their intention to do so be
lodged in the Library not later than
three o'clock on Tuesday, March the 2nd,
and that all fees due thereon, up to that
period, be paid.
"That the Bill shall be deposited in the
Library not later than three o'clock on
or before the third day on which the
House shall sit after the next meeting
of Parliament, with a declaration
annexed thereto, signed by the agent,
stating that the Bill is the same in every
respect as the Bill at the last stage of
the proceedings thereon in this House in
the present Session.
"That the proceedings on the Bill shall
be pro forma only in regard to the stage
through which the same has passed in
the present Session; and that no
fees be charged in regard to this stage."
-(Chairman of Ways and Means).

THE EDUCATION LEVY.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
amounts to be raised by the educational
levy on the new valuation of each of the
Six Counties, together with the County
Borough, for a full year.
Mr. POLLOCK: I shall not be in a
position to frame reliable estimates by
county areas of the yield of an education
levy of 1/- in the £ based on the new
valuations until Budget time, for as
the hon. Member may be aware, the
education levy is based on the net yield
of the rates of the previous year after
allowing deductions for vacant ratings,
rates written off as irrecoverable, etc.;
and the current year is the first year on
which the rates have been struck on the
new valuations. The yield of the levy
for the Province as a whole based on
the new valuations should, however, be
approximately £230,000.
THE BANN FERRY SERVICE.
5. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
since the stoppage of the ferry service
over the River Bann at Newferry, midway between Toomebridge and Portglenone, there is no possible means of
getting to the opposite side of the river;
whether a ferry service was run at Newferry for generations past until about
four years ago by the Kelly family;
whether the absence of this ferry service
breaks the connection of a main road
direct from Ballymena to Magherafelt
and causes much hardship to the residents of both County Derry and County
Antrim, especially on fair or market
days; whether petitions of residents of
both counties have been sent to their
respective authorities appealing for the
renewal of this ferry service, or for the
erection of a suitable bridge; whether
the matter has been discussed by these
public boards; whether the Government
will take up this matter on behalf of
these residents and ratepayers, mostly of
the farming class, who are much affected
by the absence of a bridge or other means
to cross the river at this place.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I understand that
a ferry was formerly provided at Newferry by means of a row boat but that
in the year 1935 Mr. David Staunton,
the proprietor of the boat, decided to
discontinue the ferry service because the
revenue which he received from it was
not nearly enough to pay the wages of
the working man who operated the boat.
Deputations representing the inhabitants of the areas which the ferry served
brought the matter before the Ballymena
and Magherafelt Rural District Councils
suggesting that a bridge should be provided.
These Councils then submitted the
matter to the Antrim and Londonderry
County Councils, but when the latter
bodies examined the position with the
assistance of their technical staff it
appeared that the volume of traffic which
had used the ferry was small and that
a suitable bridge could not be built at a
lower cost than £21,000.
was
The matter was exhaustively discussed
by the County Councils but it
eventually decided that the amount of
traffic to be facilitated was much too
small to justify such a heavy outlay.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
In the meantime Mr. Staunton appears
to have agreed to continue to operate
the ferry if adequately subsidised, but
while one of the Rural District Councils
was evidently prepared to contribute
something or share the cost of providing
a ferry the other Rural District Council
was not prepared to contribute anything.
as
In view to the very limited amount
of traffic involved it seems clear that the
expenditure of such a large sum
£21,000 for the construction of a bridge
would not be justified and the question
of what other provision should be made
is really a matter for the two Rural
District Councils who are familiar with
the needs of their respective areas.
In the circumstances it does not seem
that I could usefully interfere in the
matter.
LABOURERS ACT SCHEMES.
6. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is the intention
of the Ministry to sanction schemes
formulated and submitted under the
Labourers Act where provision is only
made for allocating one-quarter of a
statute acre to each house, and why it is
necessary to reduce the amount of ground
by half that allocated to houses built
under the former Labourers Acts.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The reply to
the first part of the question is in the
affirmative. It is, however, not correct
to say that this means reducing by half
the amount of ground allotted to houses
under former Labourers Acts.
Under the Acts the local authority may
allot ground to each cottage not exceeding one acre, the exact quantity within
that limit being left to the discretion of
the local authority, in many previous
schemes only one-quarter of an acre of
land was allotted.
It is to be presumed that the local
authority knows the needs of its own
district in a matter of this kind, and I see
no reason for interfering with whatever
decision they may come to in regard to it.
HOUSING IN DERRY CITY.
7. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of houses in the city of Derry
condemned by the medical superintendent
officer of health as being beyond repair, or
otherwise unfit for human habitation;
whether he has seen the last report of the
medical superintendent that there has
been no material progress towards
remedying the deplorable position in
respect of housing in the city, and what
steps, if any, it is proposed to take to
provide suitable dwellings at economic
rents.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number
of houses condemned by the medical
superintendent officer of health of Londonderry County Borough as being beyond
repair since the 31st March, 1936, is 28.
Some of these have been reconstructed.
There were none in the preceding 12
months.
I have seen the annual report of the
medical superintendent officer, in which
he makes the statement referred to in
the question. The remedy lies with the
local authority, which is empowered,
under the Housing Acts, to take steps for
the demolition of houses unfit for habitation and to build any houses needed to
re-house the occupants of these houses.
No representation on the matter has been
received from the Londonderry Corporation, but if any application is made I
shall be prepared to facilitate it in every
way possible.
TRANSPORT BOARD AND THE
CARRIERS.
8. Major McCORMICK asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he can state
if it is a fact that a man named
Weatherup, an official of the Transport
Board, has been going round various
carriers and notifying them that they will
not be allowed to attend certain markets
and convey cattle therefrom, and has
threatened them that if they do so he will
take the plates off their vehicles; and, if
this is a fact, what steps he proposes to
take to put a stop to this intimidation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am informed
that it is not a fact that any official of
the Transport Board has been acting as
is suggested. Every owner of a goods
vehicle is aware that the Board has no
jurisdiction as regards the plates attached
to vehicles, and the alleged threat would,
therefore, have been perfectly futile.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
29 OCTOBER 1936
The information that appears to have
been supplied to the hon. Member is
typical of the misrepresentations that are
being made generally in connection with
the Board's operations, and I, therefore,
propose to deal with the facts in this
matter at some length.
The Transport Board in acquiring the
hauliers is proceeding, as it must in
practice do, by districts. Two main
difficulties have confronted it in this procedure. One is where hauliers who do
not live in the area about to be taken
over, and who have not previously done
any business in that area, come into it
when the Board has acquired the regular
carriers operating there for the purpose
of competing with the Board.
Where instances of this kind come to
light it is the practice of the Board to
warn such carriers that they must stop
this practice or else steps will be taken to
acquire their undertaking.
The propriety of this course cannot, I think, be
doubted.
The other difficulty arises out of rather
different circumstances, and here the
Board is going out of its way to be
scrupulously fair. The circumstances
here are that a carrier who is not resident
in an area that is about to be taken over
has been doing work in that area. Where
cases of this kind come to the Board's
notice it approaches him and inquires if
he is likely to be hurt by its acquisition
of the transport in the area. If he
satisfies it that he is likely to be hurt the
Board offers to acquire his undertaking,
although it is not ready to acquire the
other vehicles in the area in which he is
residing.
I would give one actual case as an
example. A man resides at Edenderry,
but his principal work is in the Ballynahinch area, although he resides outside
it. He is also engaged in carrying bricks
to Ballywalter. The Board has not taken
over the Edenderry area and, therefore,
has not acquired this man's lorries. It
has, however, taken over the Ballywalter
area, and it is, therefore, in competition
with him there. He has complained to
them that their rates in Ballywalter were
undercutting him (which I would remark
is rather a commentary on the suggestion
that the Board's rates are unduly high).
When he made this complaint the Board
realised that its operations in the Ballywalter area were affecting a substantial
part of his business, and accordingly it
is taking him over, although he is residing in an area with which the Board is
not prepared to deal at the moment.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the reply,
supposing the Board, having acquired an
area neglects to provide transport for
that area, do they also object to any
other persons providing that transport?
Major McCORMICK: Arising out of
the Minister's statement, will he accept
from me information as to two persons
who have been intimidated in this way?
Mr. SPEAKER: I cannot allow the
hon. and gallant Member to give the
right hon. Gentleman any information in
a supplementary question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the hon.
and gallant Member furnishes me with
any particulars I will inquire into them.
Major McCORMICK: Thank you, I
will.
WARRENPOINT URBAN COUNCIL
AND THE FAIR WAGES

observing building trade rates and

Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand

Council recently passed a resolution to the
effect that a fair wages clause should be
included in all contracts entered into by
them, but that through a misapprehension
such a provision was not inserted in the
contract for street flagging to which the
hon. Member refers.

Close Seasons Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
I am informed that the contract, which

unions in the Warrenpoint district.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I would like to ask

argument against the Bill is that you

all the wealth of the world and the

nature of the age. I do not think the

Mr. YOUNG: There is a point of view
in connection with this Bill which has
not been put forward by either side of
the House. The matter has been looked
at from the point of view that the Bill
is only for the benefit of the employers

many occasions on which the Bill might
be to the advantage of the
ployees. I do not believe there is any
class in the community that is more
humanitarian and thinks more about
their fellow workers than the working
classes of Northern Ireland. I am going
to instance a case in which the workers
would probably volunteer to work on a
two-shift system for the benefit of their
fellow employees.
Take the case of a big manufactory
employing, roughly, 1,000 hands, 500 of
them in the finishing department and 500
in the preparing department. A motor
or shaft breaks down in the preparing
department, and puts half of it out of
commission. That means that automatically for the next two or three weeks
some 250 of the preparers are out of
work. Because the preparing department
is off about 250 hands in the finishing
department have also to go out. I believe
that on an occasion like that the preparers
would be the very first to volunteer for
a two-shift system whereby one half of
them would work on a morning shift and
one half on the afternoon shift. The
result would be that the finishing department would be entirely supplied, and as
a consequence of the two-shift system 500
preparers would make the sacrifice of
starting at six o'clock in the morning
week about, which would mean that 250
workers in the finishing department would
also be employed instead of being unemployed.
It appears that it has been legal to
do this in the past, although I, and I am
sure many other employers, did not know
that such a thing was legally possible.
However, this Bill makes it clear that a
two-shift system can be worked in a case
of emergency of the kind I have referred
to, and it would be in the interests of
the workers themselves. I believe there
is So much humanity and kindness
amongst the working classes of Northern
Ireland that they would make that little
sacrifice for a week or two in order to
keep their fellow workers in employment.

another. But there are other reasons
why, in my opinion, a system of this
kind should be possible. One is an
exceptional demand. Sometimes firms,
especially those engaged in what is more
or less seasonal work, get a demand, and
unless there is some latitude given to
them either in this way or by overtime,
to which we are all opposed, that exceptional demand could not be taken
advantage of here, and the work would.
be done by employers and workpeople
across the Channel, who would be more
favourably situated to do it. It seems
to me as clear as a pikestaff, to use an
old saying.
Again, a change in the demand for
commodities produced can make unemployment, because some commodities
produced require more effort by one
Civil Service Salary Scales

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. Andrews]
branch or department than other commodities produced would necessitate, and
in that way very often one department
will get behind another department. If
that happens and there is no way out of
the difficulty, it means that people are
unemployed. This Measure will create
additional employment, a thing that we
all desire. We all desire that new industries should be brought to Northern
Ireland. Hon. Members on both sides
of the House have frequently expressed
that desire, a desire that is shared by
our whole community, and, if employers
are to be placed in a less favourable
position than employers in Great Britain,
it certainly would not be an incentive
for them to come and spend their capital
in establishing industries in this part of
the world. Therefore, now that the Bill
is in this shape, I feel that the workers'
interests are securely safeguarded, and
there will be no fear that they will be
asked to do what is unreasonable or unfair, or that they themselves will consent to do what is unreasonable
unfair.
or
Hon. Members-and this is my last
point-have frequently compared this
two-shift system with the old long-hours'
system that was in operation a generation.
ago when work started at 6 or 6-30 o'clock
and went on till 5-30 or 6 o'clock in the
evening. This system is nothing of the
kind. If there is an early start there is
an early stop. This system really means
that instead of more hours being worked
than the normal hours, which is the effect
of overtime, fewer hours will be worked
than the normal hours, so I do not think
any hardship is created. Even if there
is an early start, we must recognise that
the end of the day's work is 2 o'clock,
a very different thing to what it was in
the days gone by.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PRICES OF FEEDING STUFFS.
1. Mr. FRYAR asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if anything can be done to secure to producers
of milk, beef and pork, adequate compensation for the increased prices they
have to pay for feeding stuffs, and to try
to prevent the middlemen, who have less
trouble with the article than anyone else,
from receiving the greater share of the
profit.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I am replying
for my right hon. Friend, who is unable
to be present here, as he is representing
this House in another place.
As everyone connected with the agricultural industry must realise periodical
fluctuations occur in the price of feeding
stuffs and other farm requisites. The
level of feeding stuff prices to-day is on
about the same basis as in the autumn of
1934. In the interval prices fell by
percentages varying up to about 40 per
cent. to a low level in the summer of
1935 and have since risen again. I am
sending the hon. Member a table showing
the monthly fluctuations in prices that
have taken place since the autumn of
1934. So far
So far as pork is concerned,
farmers are protected against a rise in
prices of feeding stuffs by the operation
of the pig price formula, which makes
proportionate allowance for changes in
value of feeding stuffs. In the case of
milk, prices are fixed by the Joint Milk
Council, having regard to all the factors.
in the situation, including the costs of
milk production, and a review of milk
prices in the light of the rise in feeding
stuff prices recently took place. As
regards the production of beef cattle,
farmers receive a Government subsidy
of 5s per cwt.
In reply to the latter portion of the
hon. Member's question, the operations
of the Marketing Schemes have, of
course, greatly improved the position of
the producer, and the margin allowed to
the distributor or middleman is now in
many cases determined by independent
bodies, such as the Pig Industry Council
and the Joint Milk Council.
Major McCORMICK: Arising out of the
reply given by the Parliamentary Secretary, might I ask would he consider fixing
a price which would satisfy both the
producer and the consumer, and make
that the standard price.
Mr. GORDON: It would be difficult
to fix a price that would satisfy every
person.
CIVIL SERVICE SALARIES.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Finance whether he is now in a position
to make an announcement in regard to
the stabilisation of Civil Servants' salaries
in Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: My right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance
asked me to reply to this question in
his absence on official duties in London.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
12 NOVEMBER 1936
After discussions with representatives
of the staff regarding the stabilisation of
Civil Service salaries, I am glad to be
able to announce that the position now
is such as will enable the Ministry of
Finance to notify Departments of the
decisions arrived at in the course of a
few days.
I may add that the question of the
Technical Staff and the leave to be
granted to cleaners employed in Government offices is being sympathetically
dealt with at the same time.
Major MCCORMICK: Arising out of
the reply given by the noble Lord, might
I ask him if the attendants in this House
and the messengers come under that
category.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes.
Major McCORMICK: Thank you.
VACANCIES IN JUDICIAL POSTS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if
there is a vacancy for the position
of County Court Judge or Resident
Magistrate; whether temporary men
are appointed to act in these positions; the length of time the position.
of County Court Judgeship is vacant;
also the length of time it is proposed to
keep the position vacant; the object of
keeping these positions vacant; whether
it is in the public interest that important
legal actions and Crown prosecutions
should be decided by men who hold their
temporary positions at the pleasure of
the Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: No vacancy
exists for the position. of Resident
Magistrate.
The vacancy for the position of County
Court Judge dates from the 31st January,
1935. I am not prepared to make any
statement at the moment in regard to a
permanent appointment, but meanwhile
I am quite satisfied that the pubic interest
has been in no way prejudiced as a result
of the present arrangement.
I may add that I resent most strongly
the suggestion contained in the latter
part of the hon. Member's question which
casts an unwarrantable and completely
unjustifiable reflection upon the impartiality, and indeed upon the integrity,
of the acting County Court Judge.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the Prime
Minister's reply, is it not a fact that
there is a temporary Resident Magistrate
acting at the present time, and, furthermore, is a reflection not cast on the
Government and not on the persons
appointed temporarily by the Government?
The PRIME MINISTER: I have no
objection to any reflections being cast
upon the Government, but I strongly
resent the implied stigma which is cast
by the hon. Member upon the acting
County Court Judge. I am sure, if he
will consult his finer feelings, he will
realise that a sting of that sort in a
question in this House is improper.
Mr. NIXON: The reflection is on the
Government, and intended to be on the
Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: That is all
right.
Mr. NIXON : The Government do
manipulate these cases in order to have
temporary men trying them.

PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as
follows:-
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of his Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further, I
am commanded to invite this honourable
House to attend in the Senate in order to
hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
report that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, when the following Proclamation proroguing this present.
Session of Parliament was read by the
Speaker of the Senate: -
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the Present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance
of certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon, prorogue and dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
twenty-fourth day of November, one
thousand nine hundred and thirty-six:
Now I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the Most
Noble Order of the Garter, Knight of
the Most Illustrious Order of Saint
Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland,
by this Proclamation do publish and
declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the
said Parliament be, as from the reading
of this Proclamation in the Parliament
of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the twenty-fourth day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and thirty-six.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to
be that the said Parliament shall on
the said twenty-fourth day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and thirtysix, assemble and be holden at Stormont
for the despatch of divers urgent and
important affairs. and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
GIVEN this twelfth day of November,
one thousand nine hundred and
thirty-six.
(Signed by his own hand)
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Third Session (opened
